Introduction

The Long Way Around

There is a gap between the businesses in business books and the businesses actual people run. This book lives in that gap.

The first business book I ever bought, I bought to impress a man named Henk.

Henk was my first mentor, though neither of us would have used that word. He was a retired machine-parts wholesaler who drank his coffee black, smelled faintly of cigars even though I never once saw him smoke, and had the unsettling habit of being right about things he had no business being right about. I was nineteen and building websites for local shops. He was the uncle of a client, and he had taken an interest in me the way some retired men take an interest in a stray cat: gruffly, and against his own stated principles.

The book was a famous founder memoir. You have probably read it, or at least nodded at it in an airport. I brought it to Henk's kitchen table because I wanted him to see that I was serious, that I was studying, that I was the kind of nineteen-year-old who reads.

Henk picked it up, read the back cover, flipped to a page in the middle, read for maybe ninety seconds, and put it down.

"This man remembers wrong," he said.

I asked what he meant. Was the guy lying?

"No, no." Henk waved his hand like he was clearing smoke. "Worse. He is telling the truth about the decisions and lying about the weather. Every choice in this book, he makes it in a clean room, with all the information laid out on the table. I promise you he made half of them at two in the morning because a customer was screaming and the bank was closed." He tapped the cover. "Read it if you want. But when you have your own company, do not compare your Tuesday to his book. His Tuesday looked like your Tuesday. He just doesn't remember."

I did read the book. It was good. And Henk was right anyway, which took me about fifteen years and three companies to fully appreciate.

This book you are holding is my attempt to write the one Henk would not have put down: a field guide to the actual phases of building a business, written by someone who has done it badly, then done it less badly, and taken notes both times.

Hindsight Is a Liar with Good Manners

Here is the problem with most business books, and I say this as someone who owns shelves of them and loves many: they are written backwards.

The author starts at the ending. The company sold, or went public, or became a household name. Then they walk back through the years and arrange the events into a line that points at the ending. The pivot becomes "we saw the market shifting." The desperate hire becomes "we knew we needed world-class talent." The product that only exists because a big customer threatened to leave becomes "customer obsession."

None of this is lying, exactly. It is what memory does. Memory is a helpful colleague who tidies your desk while you are at lunch and throws away everything that looks like a mistake. By the time you sit down to write the book, the mess is gone. What remains is a story where each chapter causes the next one, where the founder's beliefs were vindicated, where the strategy was a strategy and not a series of dodges.

And then a real person, in a real business, reads that book on a bad night. Their biggest customer just left. Their cofounder is acting strange. The tax bill arrived and it is not the number they wrote in the spreadsheet. And the book says: we always believed in our vision, and we executed relentlessly.

The reader concludes, reasonably, that something is wrong with them. Everyone else apparently builds companies the way the books describe: forward, on purpose, in order. Only they are doing it like this, sideways, in the rain, making it up.

I want to say this as plainly as I can, because it might be the most useful sentence in this book: everyone is doing it sideways, in the rain, making it up. The books are cleaned-up transcripts. The businesses were live radio.

There is a second, sneakier form of the lie, which is the lie of sequence. Business books love numbered steps. Step one, find your why. Step two, validate your market. Step three, build your MVP. Steps imply that the world holds still while you complete them, and that step four politely waits for step three to finish. In my experience, step nine shows up during step two, uninvited, holding an invoice.

So this book has phases instead of steps, and the difference matters enough that it gets its own section.

Why Phases, Not Steps

A step is something you complete. A phase is something you enter.

When you build a business, you never finish deciding who the company is. You never finish figuring out the money. You never finish hiring, or selling, or leading. What happens instead is that different questions take the foreground at different times. In the beginning, the identity question is loud and the scaling question is a distant rumor. Five years in, it may be the reverse. But the identity question never actually goes away. It just gets quieter, waits for a merger or a scandal or a growth spurt, and then walks back into the room like it never left.

That is what a phase is: a period when one set of questions is loudest. The sixteen chapters of this book are sixteen sets of questions, arranged in the order they usually get loud for the first time. Identity before mission. Mission before vision. The founding team before the hiring machine. The money chapter early, because the money questions arrive early and never leave.

But, and I need you to hear this part, the order is a courtesy, not a law. Businesses do not respect it. You will be neck-deep in the sales phase while your identity quietly rots. You will hit the scaling questions before you have honestly answered the mission ones, and the scaling will go badly in ways that trace directly back to the skipped chapter. The phases loop, overlap, and interrupt each other.

Nobody builds a business in order. You build it in the order the fires start, and then you tell people it was a plan.

Let me make that concrete. At the routing company, we wrote our values in year one, on a Friday afternoon, mostly to fill a slide. Then we spent year four in a mess that looked like a sales problem: deals stalling, discounts creeping, two good account managers gone in a single quarter. We tried sales fixes. New pipeline stages, a new commission plan, a workshop with a consultant who said "buyer persona" forty times before lunch. Nothing moved. The actual problem lived three chapters earlier: we had never honestly decided what kind of company we were, so every salesperson improvised a different answer, and customers could smell the improvisation. The fire was in the sales phase. The fuel was in the identity phase. That pattern, fire in one chapter and fuel in another, repeats so often in this book that you could call it the plot.

So why arrange the book as a sequence at all? Because a map drawn in the order of a typical trip is still useful even when your trip is not typical. When your business is on fire, it helps enormously to know which kind of fire it is, and that other people have had this exact fire, and that there is a chapter about it. The sequence gives you a spine. Life will provide the interruptions.

One more thing about phases. Because they are entered rather than completed, you can be in several at once, and you usually are. A founder at year three is typically living in four or five chapters of this book simultaneously. That is the job, not a sign of chaos. The trick is knowing which one deserves your best hours this month, and the map at the end of this introduction is meant to help you make that call with your eyes open.

Who I Am, and Why You Should Stay Skeptical

You should know whose voice this is, and you should know it early, so you can calibrate your skepticism.

My name is Wouter Simons. I started my first business at nineteen, building websites for local shops: a butcher, two hair salons, a shop that sold garden furniture and, inexplicably, aquariums. I charged too little, delivered too slowly, and learned more about business from the butcher's complaints than from anything I studied. He paid me 350 euros and made me earn every cent twice.

At twenty-two, my friend Sam and I started a recipe app. We were going to change how people cook. We had a logo before we had a user, a growth model before we had a recipe, and eighteen months later we had neither users nor money nor, for a few tense weeks, a friendship. The app died. The friendship recovered. You will hear more about the recipe app in this book than about anything that went well, because failure keeps better records.

Then came the company I spent most of my adult life on: a logistics software business I will call the routing company. We helped delivery fleets plan their routes. It was unglamorous, difficult, and wonderful. I grew it slowly, hired people better than me, broke most of the things described in the later chapters of this book, repaired some of them, and eventually sold it. The selling has its own chapter, because nobody warned me about the part that comes after the wire transfer, and I intend to warn you.

These days I run a company called Lionsville. That is the first and last time it will be named in this book, and I will not tell you what it does, because the moment I do, this becomes a book about my company instead of a book about yours.

Now, the skepticism. I am one founder, from one small corner of Europe, who built one kind of company well and two kinds badly. Where my experience runs thin, I have leaned on people who filled the gaps: friends who built agencies and bakeries and venture-backed software companies, who let me interrogate them over long dinners and longer walks. But every author of a book like this is generalizing from a sample size you could count on your hands. When something in these pages contradicts what you are seeing with your own eyes in your own business, trust your eyes. The book is a map. You are standing on the terrain.

Who This Book Is For

This book is for people building something with other people, where the something has to pay for itself.

That is a deliberately wide door. Through it fit the two engineers in a rented office, the woman turning her consulting sideline into a firm, the brother-in-law with one bakery and an itch, the founder at forty employees wondering why everything feels harder than it did at twelve. It fits people who want to raise venture capital and people who would rather eat glass. It fits first-timers and, I hope, second-timers, who will read some chapters nodding and some chapters wincing.

It is not really for people seeking a side hustle they can automate from a beach, and it is not for executives at large companies looking for innovation frameworks, although both are welcome to eavesdrop. The assumptions throughout are small-to-medium, founder-led, and paid for by customers rather than by slideware. If your company has a legal department, some chapters will feel quaint. If your company is you and a laptop and a nervous feeling, you are exactly who I pictured.

A word about the range of businesses inside. The stories here come from software companies, a design agency, a chain of bakeries, a machine-parts wholesaler, and a few one-off characters you will meet along the way. That mix is deliberate. The startup world has convinced itself that its problems are special, and the bakery world has convinced itself that books like this are not about bakeries. Both are wrong. A cofounder dispute works the same whether the asset is code or ovens. Cash runs out at the same speed in both, which is to say: faster than the spreadsheet promised. I have tried to write every chapter so that the software founder and the ninth-bakery owner can both see themselves in it, because from where I sit, they are in the same business. The business of keeping a promise to customers without running out of money or friends.

You do not need an MBA to read it. I do not have one. I looked into it once, decided the tuition would fund about fourteen months of the routing company's server bills, and chose the servers. I have tried to write so that the only prerequisite is that you care whether the thing survives.

How to Read This Book

There are two correct ways to read this book, and I designed it for both.

The first way is front to back. The chapters are arranged in the order the phases usually get loud, so reading in sequence gives you the whole arc: from the identity questions nobody thinks they need to answer, through money and people and market, into the machinery of a growing company, and out the far end to selling it and, possibly, starting again. If you have not started yet, or you have just started, read it this way. Consider it a long walk with someone who has been up the road and is willing to describe the potholes with unusual honesty.

The second way is to raid it. If your business exists and something is bleeding, do not read in order. Go directly to the chapter you are bleeding in. Cofounder trouble, chapter five. Cash sweating, chapter six. Nobody buying, chapter nine. Twenty-five employees and a creeping sense that nobody tells you anything anymore, chapter eleven. Each chapter stands on its own legs, restates what it needs from elsewhere, and ends with a summary blunt enough to be useful at midnight. Raiding is what field guides are for.

Whichever way you read, I make one request: do the exercises. Every chapter has one or two blocks marked "Try this," and they are small on purpose, things you can do today with a pen and an honest hour. A business book you only read is entertainment. I have written plenty of entertainment into this one, but the exercises are where it earns its price.

Try this

Before you read another page, take a pen and write down, in one sentence each: the phase your business is loudest in right now, and the phase you have been avoiding. Not the one you are worst at, the one you avoid. Fold the paper, put it inside the back cover, and check it when you finish the book. Mine, for the record, said "sales" and "sales." It was lying about the first one.

Field note

If you are currently in a genuine crisis, the emergency chapters, the ones raided most often in my experience, are six (money), five (founding team), and twelve (yourself). Go. The rest of us will be here when you get back.

A Note About the Stories

This book is full of stories, and you deserve to know what kind of true they are.

They are true the way bar stories are true. Every story in this book happened, in the sense that its bones are real: real founders, real invoices, real 2 a.m. phone calls. But I have changed names, merged people, moved events between companies and years, and rounded the dialogue to what was meant rather than what was said. Henk is real and also three people. Marta, whom you will meet in the next chapter, ran a design agency the way I describe, except she is also two other people and one of her disasters belonged to someone else entirely. The details are rearranged to protect the guilty, and the guilty, in most of these stories, is me.

I did this for two reasons. The first is decency: my friends told me things over their second drink that they would not want traceable over anyone's first. The second is usefulness. A composite story can be more honest than a factual one, because it keeps the pattern and discards the coincidence. What you need from a story about a cofounder blowup is the shape of the thing, so you recognize it coming down your own hallway.

So: the stories are made up, and they are not. This is the only chapter that will carry this disclaimer. From here on, I will just tell them straight, and you can trust them the way you trust a friend across a small table: not on the details, but on the point.

The Map: A Walking Tour of Sixteen Phases

Here is the whole road at a glance. Sixteen phases, four bends, one loop at the end that a surprising number of us take. We will walk it briefly now, a sentence or two per stop, so you know where everything lives. Think of this as reading the trail markers, not taking the hike.

Part I: Who You Are Before What You Sell

1. Designing an identity. Before the product, before the pitch, there is the question of who this company is: the values you actually hold, as opposed to the ones that look good on a poster. Most founders skip this and pay for it later with interest.

2. Deciding on mission. The job your company does in the world, written sharply enough that you can use it to say no. A good mission is less a banner and more a bouncer.

3. Articulating vision. A postcard from the future: where all this is headed if it works. We will untangle vision from mission from strategy exactly once, in one table, and never make you sit through it again.

4. Building the product or service strategy. What you sell, to whom, and why they care, starting from their problem rather than your cleverness. Includes the painful art of not building things.

Part II: People and Money

5. Getting the founding team together. Cofounders, equity, and the prenup conversation almost nobody has while they still like each other. The recipe app makes its first full appearance here, as a cautionary exhibit.

6. Managing money. Cash versus profit, runway math, and how to read a P&L without crying. If you only ever raid one chapter, most people raid this one.

7. Evolving the business plan. The plan as a living document with assumptions and kill criteria, not a 40-page PDF that dies the day you print it.

Part III: Going to Market

8. Building the brand. Brand as reputation, not logo: what people say about you when you leave the room, and how to influence it without becoming insufferable.

9. Sales approach. Founder-led selling, discovery that actually discovers, and pipelines sized for your business rather than for a software demo. Also: how to lose a deal without losing your dignity.

10. Hiring people. First hires, interviews that predict instead of charm, onboarding, and the hardest paragraph in the book: letting someone go kindly.

Part IV: Building the Machine

11. Building the skeleton and nervous system. Structure and information flow as you grow: roles, meetings, documentation, and metrics that carry signal instead of decoration. For everyone who has ever said "nobody tells me anything anymore."

12. Evolving your own management and leadership skills. The uncomfortable phase where the biggest bottleneck in the company shaves your face every morning. Delegation, feedback, and getting help before you need it.

13. The entrepreneurial operating system. Operating rhythms and frameworks, EOS and its cousins: when they save a company, and when they curdle into theater with better paperwork.

14. Scaling up. When to scale, what breaks first (spoiler: people, process, cash, and you, roughly in that order), and how to grow without sanding off the soul.

Part V: Endings and Beginnings

15. Selling the business. Why founders sell, what valuation feels like from inside, surviving diligence, and the emotional cliff on the far side of the wire transfer. I have been off that cliff. I brought photographs.

16. Doing it again. What transfers to a second company and what dangerously does not, the ego trap of the sequel, and why, despite everything in the preceding fifteen chapters, you will probably do it again anyway.

One Last Thing Before We Start

Years after that kitchen-table conversation, I told Henk I might write a book someday. He was older by then, slower on the stairs, still faintly cigar-scented, still never smoking. He thought about it for a while, the way he thought about everything, as if the question had to clear customs first.

"Fine," he said. "But write the weather."

That is what I have tried to do. The chapters ahead contain frameworks, tables, exercises, and opinions I will defend at any dinner table in Europe. But underneath all of it, the promise of this book is smaller and, I think, worth more: I will tell you what each phase feels like from inside, while it is raining, before anyone knows the ending. What you do out there on the road is yours.

Take the long way. It is the only way there is.

Chapter 1

Designing an Identity

Your company already has values. They are whatever you did last Tuesday, when doing the right thing cost you something.

The poster had been hanging in Marta's agency for two years before anyone actually read it.

It hung by the coffee machine, in a tasteful grey frame, and it said, in a tasteful grey font: Passion. Excellence. Innovation. Integrity. Forty people walked past it every day, most of them designers. Designers, mind you. People who will stop a print run over a comma that sits half a millimetre too low. Nobody looked at the poster, because nobody looks at posters like that. They are the visual equivalent of the safety card in an airplane seat pocket.

Then a junior designer, three days into the job and still in the phase where new people ask dangerous questions, raised her hand at the Friday all-hands. Two client teams had just spent twenty minutes politely fighting about whether to tell a client his beloved new packaging design was failing every test they ran. One team wanted to tell him straight. The other wanted to soften it, stage it, maybe let the test results do the talking in a month or two. The junior pointed at the poster and asked, with the innocence of someone who has not yet learned what not to ask: "Which of those four words applies here? Integrity says tell him today. Passion, I guess, says protect the relationship. Which one wins?"

Silence. Then laughter, the good kind. Then Marta, who tells this story against herself and insists I keep this part in, said: "Honestly, I don't know. I don't even remember writing those."

She had not written them. That was the thing. After the meeting she asked her office manager where the poster came from, and the office manager checked, and found that the previous tenant had left it behind. An insurance intermediary. The words on the wall of one of the most respected design agencies in the region were the corporate values of an insurance broker who had moved out two years earlier, and in two years, in a building full of professionals trained to notice everything, not one person had noticed. Including the founder.

It gets worse, and this is the part that matters. The same month, Marta lost a pitch she should have won. The work was strong, the chemistry was good, the budget fit. She called the client afterwards, as you should always do with a lost pitch, and asked what tipped it. The client was kind and specific, which is the most useful combination and the rarest. "Your work was the best," he said. "But we could describe the other agency in one sentence, and after three meetings we still couldn't describe you. We knew what you make. We never worked out who you are."

And the same month, a senior designer who had been there since year two handed in her notice. Her resignation letter contained a sentence Marta can still recite: "I no longer know what we are trying to be, other than busy."

Marta called me on a Tuesday evening, which is when the honest calls happen. "Fifteen years," she said. "Forty people. Good clients, good margins, awards on the shelf. And I have just discovered that my company has no personality. It has revenue and no character. I have built a very profitable ghost."

This chapter is about the question underneath that phone call: who your company is. What it does, where it is going and how it looks all get their own chapters. Who it is comes first, and it comes first on purpose, because this is the phase almost everyone skips, and the interest on the skipped phase compounds for years before the bill arrives, usually addressed to a different department.

The Question Nobody Asks on Purpose

Nobody starts a company to answer the question "who are we?" You start a company because you saw a gap, or you were fed up with your boss, or a customer offered you money and you said yes before thinking. The doing comes first. The doing should come first. If you spend your first six months on identity workshops instead of customers, you have a customer problem wearing a philosophy costume.

But here is what I have watched happen, in my own companies and in every founder story I have collected over long dinners: while you are busy doing, the identity forms anyway. Every company has one. It forms the way an accent forms, from a thousand small sounds repeated until they stick. You answered an angry customer at 23:00 or you didn't. You quietly redid the sloppy work or you shipped it. You paid the supplier on time even in the bad month or you sat on the invoice. Each one felt like an isolated decision. Together, they were the company introducing itself.

So the real question of this chapter is whether you designed that identity or inherited it from your own unexamined habits, the way Marta inherited a poster from an insurance broker.

Let me define the word before we go further, because "identity" gets used to sell a lot of expensive workshops. When I say identity, I mean the character of the company. The values it actually holds, the temperament it shows under pressure, the things it would never do even for money, and the things it always does even when they cost money. Identity is who the company is when nobody senior is in the room and a weird situation walks in the door.

Three of identity's neighbours have their own chapters, and I intend to stay out of their gardens, so let me draw the fences now.

Your mission is the job your company does in the world, and writing one sharp enough to say no with is the whole business of chapter 2. Your vision is the postcard from the future, which gets chapter 3. Your brand is your logo, your name, your website, all the ways the identity shows up in public, and it lives in chapter 8. Identity sits underneath all three: the character they grow from. Mixing them up is how founders end up hiring a branding agency to fix a character problem, which works about as well as buying a new suit to fix a marriage.

The relationship between them is the oldest metaphor in the book, and I am going to use it anyway because it is old for a reason. Identity is the trunk. Mission, vision and brand are branches. They grow out of the identity, they are fed by it, and when the trunk is hollow, you can tell from the branches long before the tree falls over. Marta's lost pitch looked like a brand problem, a chapter 8 problem. Her senior designer's resignation looked like a retention problem. Both were branches showing symptoms of a trunk nobody had grown on purpose. It fed on whatever lay around, which turned out to be an insurance broker's poster and Marta's improvised taste.

One more thing about why this is chapter one and not chapter nine. You can survive for a surprisingly long time without a deliberate identity. Years. Marta did fifteen. What you cannot do is scale without one, and I mean scale in the humblest sense: any growth past the point where you personally are in every room. Up to about ten people, the founder is the identity, walking around, correcting course in real time. Past that, the company starts making decisions in rooms you are not in, and it makes them by asking "what do we do here?" If the only honest answer is "whatever the founder would do," you have built a company that runs on guessing. And customers, as Marta's lost pitch showed, can smell guessing through three layers of good design.

Four Words in a Grey Frame

Let us talk about the poster, because your company either has one or will be offered one soon.

Here is how companies make poster values, and I describe the process with the confidence of a man who has committed the crime himself. The company reaches a size, usually somewhere between fifteen and forty people, where the founder feels a vague draft, a sense that the place needs "more culture." Someone books a day. Sometimes a facilitator, at rates that would make a plumber blush. Flipcharts appear. Everyone shouts words they associate with the company at its best, and the words go on the flipchart, and by mid-afternoon the flipchart holds forty perfectly nice words, and then the wordsmithing begins. Wordsmithing is the process by which forty specific words become four generic ones. "The way Tom stayed until midnight rebuilding the order that got corrupted" becomes Dedication. "The time we refunded the client because we knew the work wasn't our best even though he was happy" becomes Excellence. All the blood drains out, somebody laminates the corpses, and the laminate goes up by the coffee machine.

At the routing company we did exactly this, in year one, on a Friday afternoon, mostly to fill a slide for a customer presentation. I mentioned it in the introduction and I will now make the confession complete: our four words were Reliability. Innovation. Teamwork. Customer focus. I did not have to look them up just now. I had to look them up in year three, when a job candidate asked me what they meant in practice, and I heard myself improvising, and the candidate heard it too. He took the other offer.

The problem with poster values is that they are unfalsifiable. True enough, sure; nobody at Marta's agency was against integrity. But the words fail four cheap tests, and I want to give you the tests before I give you the table, because the tests are the part you can use tomorrow morning.

The competitor test. Could your nearest competitor hang the exact same words without anyone blinking? Then you have written a category description. "Fresh ingredients" on a bakery wall says nothing. Every bakery claims fresh. "We bake twice a day and give the evening surplus away at closing, which is why we sometimes run out and will not apologize for it" is an identity. A competitor would have to actually argue with it.

The dissent test. Could a reasonable, competent person disagree with the value? Nobody has ever stood up in a meeting and argued for dishonesty, sloppiness or hating the customer. If no sane person would oppose it, adopting it cost you nothing and tells nobody anything. Real values are contestable. "We show clients unfinished work" is a value precisely because plenty of excellent agencies believe you should never do that.

The invoice test. When did this value last cost you something? Money, a deal, a convenience, a comfortable silence. Values show themselves under load, like bridges. If a stated value has never carried weight, you do not know whether you hold it, any more than you know a rope holds you because it looks thick.

The recitation test. Ask three people, separately, what the company's values are. You want the actual operating rules, whatever hangs on the wall. If you get three different answers, the wall is decoration. If you get roughly the same answer and it fails to match the wall, congratulations, you have real values, and you published the wrong ones. That last case is more common than you would think, and it is good news in disguise.

Here is the whole contrast in one table. I suggest reading the right-hand column twice, because the right-hand column is the rest of this chapter in miniature.

Real values versus decorative values: how to tell which kind you own
Decorative valuesReal values
Where they come fromAn offsite, a facilitator, a menu of respectable virtuesExcavated from decisions the company already made under pressure
How they soundSingle abstract nouns: Passion, Excellence, IntegritySentences with a trade-off inside, slightly risky to say out loud
The competitor testAny rival could hang the same poster, and most doAt least one rival would genuinely object to at least one of them
What they costNothing, ever, by designMoney, deals, comfort, and the occasional customer, on a regular schedule
How people learn themAn onboarding slide, forgotten by FridayStories veterans tell new people at lunch, unprompted
When someone violates oneNothing happens, especially if the numbers are goodSomething happens, especially if the numbers are good
Where they show upThe careers page and the pitch deckIn actual decisions, in rooms the founder is not in
Shelf lifeRewritten with every rebrand or new HR leadSurvive rebrands, office moves, pivots, and at least one crisis

Notice the row about violations, because it is the one founders flinch at. The moment a top performer breaks a stated value and nothing happens, every person in the company updates the real rulebook, the one they keep in their heads, the one the poster never sees. The update reads: that value is decorative, and results are the actual value. You will never see the update happen. You will see its consequences, a year or two later, in some room you are not in, and you will wonder where the culture went. It went where you sent it, the day you looked away.

Values Are Archaeology

Now the constructive part, and it begins with a demotion. You do not get to invent your values. You are not that free. By the time you care enough about this question to read a chapter on it, your company has a history, and the history has already voted.

The work is archaeology. You dig through the decisions the company has actually made, especially the expensive and uncomfortable ones, and you look for the pattern that keeps showing up when nobody was trying to be consistent. The pattern is the value. Your only authorial choices are whether to name it, whether to keep it, and whether to say it out loud.

Let me show you the dig at the routing company, because we did it properly exactly once, in year five, after the poster embarrassment with the job candidate. I sat down with my two most senior people and a bottle of decent wine, and we listed every hard decision we could remember, the ones with a bad taste to them, where doing one right thing meant doing another right thing less. Board-slide strategy stayed off the list. We got to about twenty before the wine ran out, and then we looked for repeats.

Three patterns fell out of that list so clearly it was almost embarrassing, like finding your own face in a police lineup.

First: we told customers bad news early, always, even when there was a decent chance the problem would fix itself and they would never have known. Twice this had cost us real money, once a renewal. We kept doing it anyway, without ever having agreed to. When we asked ourselves why, the answer came from the product itself: our customers ran delivery fleets, and the one thing a fleet planner cannot absorb is a surprise. Somewhere along the way we had absorbed our customers' deepest need into our own reflexes. We named the value that night: no surprises, in either direction. We warned about problems early and we also refused to spring last-minute miracles that operations couldn't absorb.

Second: we had turned down, repeatedly, features and projects that were more exciting than the boring reliability work, even when customers waved money. We had told a huge prospect no about a flashy real-time map because it would have destabilized the planning engine for everyone else. At the time each refusal felt like a one-off judgment call. Stacked in a row, they were a conviction: boring is a feature. Our customers did not want to be excited by their routing software. They wanted to forget it existed.

Third, and this one we almost missed because it seemed too small: we answered the phone. An actual human, during business hours, usually within three rings, at a time when our whole industry was migrating to ticket portals. It had never been a policy. It was just that I had answered the phone in year one, and the first employees copied me, and the next ones copied them. It cost us real money in support staffing, and we had defended that cost in three separate budget rounds without ever once articulating why. That is what a real value looks like in the wild: a cost you keep re-approving without needing to discuss it.

Notice what made the list. Nothing about passion. Nothing about excellence. Our actual values turned out to be a temperament, mildly obsessive, allergic to drama, more proud of uptime than of cleverness. When we finally wrote them down, a new employee read them and said, "So the company is basically a Dutch dad." I have never received a better compliment, and I have received exactly one review in a trade magazine that used the word "visionary," which my team printed out and hung in the toilet.

So how do you run the dig on your own company? Five trenches, in rough order of usefulness.

Where to dig

One: the hard-decision list. As above. Ten to twenty decisions that hurt, from the whole life of the company. What tipped each one? Ignore what you said at the time. Look at what you did.

Two: praise and punishment. Whom have you celebrated, promoted, quietly given the good projects? Whom have you eased out, and for what? People metabolize this data in a week and remember it for years. Whatever the celebrated people have in common, that is a value, whether or not it is a value you would admit to at a dinner party.

Three: what you tolerate. The uncomfortable trench. The rude genius you keep because the work is brilliant, the chronic lateness nobody mentions, the client who mistreats your staff and keeps getting his calls returned because of the size of his invoices. Tolerated behaviour is endorsed behaviour, at one remove. Every company's real values include a few it would rather not own, and you cannot fix the inventory until you have counted it honestly.

Four: money under pressure. Where does the money go in a bad quarter, when every euro has three jobs? What survived your last cost cut without discussion? At the routing company, phone support survived every cut. That was the value announcing itself in the only language that cannot lie, which is the accounting.

Five: the lunch curriculum. What do veterans warn new people about in the first week, in the quiet advice over lunch that never makes the onboarding deck? "Never let him find out from someone else." "Don't show her anything half-finished." "Here we always call the customer back the same day, even with nothing to report." The lunch curriculum is the real values document, maintained collectively, updated instantly, never once out of date. If you can get an honest transcript of it, you can skip half this chapter.

Try this

The decision autopsy, one honest hour, one pen. Write down the last five genuinely hard decisions your company made, the ones with a bad taste. For each, one line: what did we actually do, and what did it cost? Ignore what you said at the time and what you wrote in the deck. Now look for the repeat, the thing you keep choosing when choosing hurts. Write the pattern as one plain sentence beginning with "Apparently we believe..." That sentence is a value. You may be pleased to meet it. You may not. Both results are worth the hour, and the second is worth more.

A Real Value Has a Price Tag

Everything in this chapter balances on one idea, so let me set it down carefully: a value is only real if it costs you something, at least sometimes, and preferably at the worst possible moment.

I mean that as a definition, cold as arithmetic. A value is a rule for choosing between two things you want. If a stated value never collides with anything else you want, it never chooses anything, and a rule that never chooses is a mood. "We value quality" costs nothing until the deadline arrives and the work is not right, and you must pick. The picking is the value. Everything before the picking was marketing, aimed mostly at yourself.

Watch how this plays out across very different businesses, because the mechanism holds even when the stakes smell different.

The baker who says quality is everything proves it at 17:30, when the last batch came out pale and dense and technically sellable. Real value: the batch goes to the chickens and the case sits half empty and tomorrow a customer grumbles. Decoration: the batch goes in the case, because it is one batch, because margins are tight, because nobody will notice. Somebody notices. Somebody always notices, and the somebody who notices most is the baker's own staff, who now know exactly how much everything-is-everything costs before it bends: one batch.

The agency that says honesty proves it on the phone call where the campaign is underperforming and the client has not looked at the numbers yet. The software company that says customer first proves it when fixing the old customers' pain and building the shiny thing for new prospects need the same two engineers in the same quarter. The consultancy that says sustainability proves it when the biggest RFP of the year arrives from a company whose business model the consultancy privately finds indefensible, and the RFP is worth two salaries.

In every case the structure is identical. The value sits there, cost-free and gleaming, for months. Then one afternoon it presents an invoice, and what you pay, or refuse to pay, is the actual identity of your company being written, one line item at a time. Nobody will see most of these moments. Identity is mostly built off-camera.

A value that has never cost you anything is decor, waiting for its first invoice.

Because the invoice test is the load-bearing test, here is a table of common stated values with their price tags attached. Hold it up as a mirror. Find your own claimed values in the left column, then ask, with a pen in your hand, when you last paid the middle column.

The invoice test: what common values cost when they are real, and how they look when they are not
Stated valueWhat it costs when it is realWhat it looks like as decoration
Craftsmanship / qualityMissed deadlines, redone work at your expense, thrown-away batches, saying "not yet" to a paying customerThe word "premium" in the brochure and a quiet shrug at 17:30 on deadline day
Honesty / transparencyAwkward calls made early, mistakes admitted before discovery, margins explained when a customer asks"Open communication" on the wall, bad news released only when it can no longer be contained
Customer firstRefunds without a fight, engineers pulled off the roadmap to fix an old promise, phone answered by humansA satisfaction survey after every ticket and a support queue nobody staffs on Fridays
SustainabilityTurned-down revenue, pricier suppliers, uncomfortable answers to "why are you more expensive?"A green leaf in the logo and one paragraph in the annual review
SpeedShipping things that are 85 percent polished and taking the criticism, paying for the occasional public stumble"We move fast" in the careers ad, four approval layers in the workflow
People firstKeeping the workload promise in the busy season, losing a client who abuses your staffFruit in the office and a burnout rate nobody graphs

Two honest caveats before we move on, because I can hear a reasonable reader objecting.

First: no, you cannot pay every invoice every time. A company that upholds every value at any cost in all conditions is a company run by a saint, briefly, until the money runs out. There will be a Tuesday where the rent collides with the principle and the rent wins. That makes you a business, and businesses have rent. What separates a company with real values from one with decorative values is what happens after the miss: the real-values company notices it, names it out loud, and treats it as debt to repay rather than as the new normal. The decorative company never even feels the bump.

Second: the invoice test cuts both ways, and this is the freeing part. If you dig through your history and find that a value you love saying has never once cost you anything, you have two honest options. Retire it from the poster, with thanks for its service to the pitch deck. Or start deliberately paying for it, this quarter, with a specific decision, and see whether you can afford the habit. Both are respectable. The only disreputable option is the one everyone defaults to, which is leaving it on the wall, unfunded, where it teaches your whole company that the wall is where words go to mean nothing.

Watch out

People use values as weapons, and the weapon usually points down the org chart. When "not a culture fit" becomes the unexamined verdict for anyone who disagrees with the founder, or when someone invokes "positivity" to shut down the person naming a real problem, the values have become a uniform. A decent stress test: your values should constrain the most powerful person in the company more often than they constrain the most junior one. If in the last year your values only ever came out against people below you, and never once stopped you personally from doing something you wanted to do, be suspicious of what you have built. How values do and do not belong in hiring decisions is chapter 10's business, and it will pick this thread up properly.

You Are the Company, and That Has an Expiry Date

Here is a sentence that took me most of a decade to be able to say without flinching: in the beginning, you are the company's identity, and that is fine, and if it stays that way, it will quietly strangle everything you built.

The early overlap is total and it is supposed to be. A three-person company does not need written values. It has you, in the room, all day. Every decision passes through your hands or within earshot of them. The company's temperament is your temperament with a VAT number. This is efficient. It is also, and founders hate this framing, a form of technical debt. You are borrowing coherence from your own presence, and like all borrowing it is cheap right up until the bill arrives.

The moment arrives on a schedule you can almost set your watch by. Somewhere between ten and twenty people, the company starts having experiences you are not part of. A customer call you never hear about. A quality judgment made at 18:00 when you are at your kid's football match. A new employee learning "how we do things" from someone who has been there eight months and is improvising. The company begins to develop an identity in your absence, assembled from guesses about you. And guesses drift. A photocopy of a photocopy is how identity transmits when nobody wrote it down, and photocopies degrade.

Three specific rots set in when founder identity and company identity are never separated, and I have personally cultivated all three, so I describe them from the inside.

The bus problem, without the bus

Everyone knows the morbid version: what if the founder gets hit by a bus? But the real version is smaller and happens daily: you are in another meeting. The company needs to know what it believes at 14:00 on a Wednesday in a room you are not in. If its only method is "guess what Wouter would do," then your company's decision quality degrades with distance from your desk, like wifi. You can watch this on the faces of your best people: the slight hesitation, the "let me check with him first" that adds two days to everything. That hesitation, multiplied across every decision in a growing company, is one of the most expensive things you will never see on a P&L.

The quirk calcification problem

When the founder is the identity, the company cannot tell your convictions from your habits, so it preserves both with equal reverence. At the routing company, we had no meetings before ten. People joined the company believing this reflected some deep philosophy about maker time and deep work. The truth is that I drove my kids to school. That was it. That was the whole philosophy. But nobody asked, and I never said, and by year six "no meetings before ten" had hardened into folklore, complete with justifications I had never made, and when a new operations lead tried to schedule an 09:00 standup for a team that wanted one, a veteran informed her it was against our culture. My school run had become doctrine. It is funny until you count how many of your company's "values" are exactly this: fossilized founder logistics, defended by people who were never told the difference.

Do the sorting while it is cheap. Take the things everyone believes the company believes, and sort them into three boxes: convictions, the things you would defend with money and discomfort, which belong in the identity. Preferences, the things you like but would trade, which belong in a policy, clearly labelled as changeable. And habits, the things that are just true because they have always been true, which belong wherever the evidence says, once someone finally checks. The sorting takes an afternoon. Not doing it takes years, because unsorted, everything defaults into the conviction box, and then every operational change feels like sacrilege to somebody.

The mirror problem

The third rot is the deepest. When founder and company share one identity, the company cannot grow past the founder's self-image, because any change to the company reads, to the founder, as a criticism of the founder. Watch a founder who thinks of himself as a scrappy underdog try to lead a company that has become the market leader. Watch a founder who identifies as "the creative one" respond when the company needs to become excellent at boring delivery. The company strains toward what it needs to become, and the founder, without ever saying so, hauls it back toward what he needs to keep being. Half the strategy fights inside founder-led companies are one person's identity crisis with a company attached.

Story

Two weeks after the poster discovery, Marta ran an experiment she now recommends with the fervor of the converted. She gathered her twelve most senior people and asked one question: "Describe this agency to me. One rule: you may not use my name."

Silence. The bad kind.

Forty seconds in, a designer who had been there nine years said, "We're the agency that does whatever Marta would do." A pause, and then, because the room was already ruined, he finished the thought: "And lately, we guess."

Marta says the word "guess" hit like a diagnosis. All the symptoms suddenly had one cause. The pitch feedback, the client who couldn't say who they were after three meetings: the client had been listening to five people guessing. The senior designer's resignation letter, "I no longer know what we are trying to be": she had lost confidence in her guesses. The endless small escalations to Marta's desk: people upgrading their guesses to certainties the only way available. Marta had assumed her constant involvement was the identity working. It was the identity failing, loudly, in the form of a queue outside her office.

"The worst part," she told me later, "is that I liked the queue. The queue felt like being needed. I had built a company that could not describe itself without me, and some honest part of me had built it that way on purpose."

The picture below is the whole section in one drawing. Nobody is asking you to leap from the left side to the right side by Friday. The founder's circle never fully leaves, and it shouldn't: your convictions are the roots of the tree we drew earlier. The work is the middle picture, the deliberate, melancholy work of letting the company become a character that overlaps with you without being you. Melancholy because it is a small goodbye, and I will not pretend otherwise. It is also the only version with a future, including, if you ever reach chapter 15, a future in which the company can be worth something to anyone who is not you.

Writing It Down Without Embalming It

At some point the archaeology is done, the founder sorting is done, and you have to write the thing down, because an identity that lives only in your head has the bus problem, and an identity that lives only in the lunch curriculum drifts one retelling at a time. This is where most companies snatch defeat from the jaws of victory, because writing values well is a specific small craft, and the defaults of corporate writing are all wrong for it. So, five rules, learned by breaking each one.

Rule one: three to five, never more. Seven values is zero values. Nobody can hold seven rules in their head at the moment of decision, and the moment of decision is the only moment that counts. If you emerged from the archaeology with nine patterns, good, you are a rich civilization, but rank them by which ones you have actually paid the most for, and publish the podium. The rest live on as stories.

Rule two: full sentences, never single nouns. Single abstract nouns are how values die. "Integrity" is a tombstone. The sentence is what forces the meaning to show up. "The client hears bad news from us first, the same day we learn it" cannot be misunderstood, cannot be reinterpreted by a clever person under deadline pressure, and can be checked. Was it the same day? No? Then we broke the value, and we know it, and knowing it is the entire point of writing things down.

Rule three: the trade must be visible. Every real value chooses between two goods, so write the choice into the sentence, or at least keep it standing next to the sentence. "We choose thorough over fast" tells an employee what to do at 17:00 on a deadline day. "Quality" tells them nothing except that the poster committee met. A useful format when drafting, even if you polish it away later: we choose X over Y, even when someone waving money offers us Y.

Rule four: the opposite must be a strategy. This is the dissent test from earlier, worn as a drafting tool. Before a value goes on the list, ask: could a reasonable, successful company choose the opposite on purpose? "We show clients unfinished work" passes, because plenty of superb agencies would rather be seen dead than show a half-baked concept, and they thrive that way. "We do great work" fails, because no company on earth pursues mediocre work on purpose. If the opposite is not a strategy, the value is not a choice, and if it is not a choice it will never help anyone make one.

Rule five: every value gets a story, permanently attached. A story, with a date and a cost in it. The deal we walked away from, the batch we threw out, the call we made before we had to. Stories are how humans store values, which is why the lunch curriculum outperforms every laminated poster ever printed. When you publish your values, publish them with their scar tissue. A value without a scar is a rumour.

From poster word to working sentence: the same territory, rewritten so it can be used
The poster saysA working version saysThe trade it admits
Excellence"We would rather miss a deadline than ship work we won't put our name on, and we tell the client which, early."Speed and short-term comfort, sacrificed to standard
Integrity"The client hears bad news from us first, the same day we learn it."Comfort and short-term polish, sacrificed to trust
Customer focus"A human answers our phone within three rings, office hours, no menu."Efficiency and margin, sacrificed to reachability
Innovation"Every project ships with one idea the client did not ask for, at our cost."Billable hours, sacrificed to surprise and pride
Respect"We say the hard thing in the room, not in the corridor afterwards."Harmony in the meeting, sacrificed to honesty
Reliability"Boring is a feature. We choose the dull, proven path unless the customer explicitly buys the risk."Glamour and headlines, sacrificed to sleep

A note on that table: do not copy from it. I mean that literally, and not as false modesty. The sentences in the middle column are right for the companies they came from and would be wrong, even harmful, for a company with a different history. A trauma surgeon should not adopt "we would rather miss a deadline." A budget airline should not promise an idea nobody asked for. The table teaches a grammar; the vocabulary has to be yours. Your sentences must come out of your own dig, or they are just a newer, wordier poster, and you will have spent all this effort upgrading from an insurance broker's values to mine, which is barely an upgrade at all.

Try this

Take your current values, whatever exists, poster or folklore, and rewrite each one tonight as a trade: "We choose ___ over ___, even when it costs us ___." Maximum five. Then run a one-week tally, and this part is the actual exercise: keep the list where you work, and every time a real decision touches one of the values, mark it. Honoured, a tick. Violated, a cross. Never touched, nothing. After a week, read the marks. Values with ticks and crosses are alive, keep them. Values with nothing at all are either decorative or your week was quiet, so run a second week before you sentence them. And wear the crosses without shame. Crosses mean the value is real enough to have enemies.

How Marta Rebuilt It

Back to Marta, because I left her on the phone calling her company a profitable ghost, and because what she did next is the best worked example I know of everything this chapter has claimed so far.

Her first instinct, she admits, was to hire a branding agency. There is a comedy in that, a design agency hiring a design agency, but the deeper mistake would have been the category error we flagged at the start: she was reaching for a chapter 8 solution to a chapter 1 problem. New words, new look, same hollow trunk. She caught herself, partly because a rebrand had burned her badly once before, years earlier, in a disaster chapter 8 will tell in full, and partly because of a question her financial controller asked in passing: "Before we pay someone to tell people who we are, do we know?"

So instead of an offsite with a facilitator, she ran the dig. Two Friday afternoons, four weeks apart, the whole company invited, attendance voluntary, wine after. The instruction for the first Friday came from the archaeology playbook, sharpened: history only, no wishes. Tell a story about a decision this agency made that was expensive and that you were proud of, or a decision that was profitable and that made you ashamed. Both kinds went on the wall. Thirty-one stories by the end of the afternoon, some of them awkward, two of them about Marta personally, told while she was in the room, which she says was the price of admission and the proof the exercise was real.

Between the two Fridays, three people clustered the stories, looking for the repeats. The repeats were unmistakable, the way they always are once someone finally looks.

The proud-expensive stories kept featuring unfinished work shown early: half-built concepts put in front of clients at the sketch stage, at the risk of looking unpolished, because course-correcting at the sketch is cheap and course-correcting at the launch is a catastrophe. The agency had been brilliant at this for a decade without ever saying so. Half the client relationships that had lasted longest had a story in their first year about a messy sketch on a table and a client saying, relieved, "oh good, I can still change things."

The ashamed-profitable stories clustered just as hard, and most of them were about free pitching: the industry ritual where agencies do weeks of real creative work, unpaid, to win an account. Every free pitch had felt like a forced move at the time. Stacked on a wall, they read as a pattern of self-disrespect that everyone had privately hated and publicly accepted. Two of the agency's worst client relationships, the ones that ground people down, had both entered through a free pitch, which nobody had noticed until the stories sat next to each other on a wall.

And a third pattern that nobody expected: an enormous number of the proud stories featured a junior. Juniors given real work early, juniors' odd ideas making it into final campaigns, seniors spending unbilled hours teaching. It had never been a policy. It was just the kind of place Marta had built without noticing, the way you furnish a house one impulse at a time and then one day a guest says "this is so you," and you look around, surprised.

The second Friday, they wrote. Three sentences, argued over word by word, each with a story from the wall stapled to it.

We show work before it is ready.

We do not design for free.

Every project teaches somebody.

Hold those against the five rules. Three of them, well under the cap. Full sentences, zero abstract nouns. The trade is visible in each: polish sacrificed to honesty, revenue opportunities sacrificed to self-respect, short-term efficiency sacrificed to the pipeline of people. Every one has an opposite that is a legitimate strategy, and Marta can name specific admirable competitors who live by each opposite. And every one came with scar tissue attached, thirty-one stories deep.

Story

The expensive part came three weeks later, which is how you know the values were real: they presented an invoice within the month.

A national supermarket chain, the kind of account that reshapes an agency's year, invited Marta's agency to pitch. Free, naturally, against four competitors. The old agency would have said yes before the email finished loading. Now there was a sentence on the wall, three weeks old, with the paint barely dry.

Marta gathered the senior team. Her financial controller, the same one whose question had started all this, went pale doing the arithmetic and, to his eternal honour, said, "It's a terrible year to mean it. But if we don't mean it now, we never meant it." They wrote back declining the free pitch and offering, instead, a paid two-week discovery sprint at a fair rate, deliverables theirs to keep either way. The supermarket said no. The account went to a competitor. The number the agency walked away from had six digits in it, and Marta printed the decline email and pinned it to the story wall, where it remains.

Here is the ending, though. The senior designer, the one whose resignation letter said "I no longer know what we are trying to be, other than busy," was working out her notice period through all of this. The Monday after the supermarket decision went around the studio, she asked for ten minutes, sat down across from Marta, and withdrew her resignation. "You finally answered my letter," she said. And eight months later, a different retailer came to them directly, no pitch, paid discovery from day one. Their brief cited, as the reason for calling, "we heard you're the agency that says no to free work." The identity had walked out the door and started selling. Which is all a brand is, and chapter 8 will have much more to say about how to help that along on purpose.

I want to be careful with the varnish here, because the introduction promised you none. The transition cost Marta real money for real quarters. Two prospects walked when the no-free-pitching line held. One employee disliked the new explicitness, called it "corporate," and left, and he was good, and it stung. Deliberate identity is a decision about which invoices you will keep paying, made once, in daylight, instead of fifty times in the dark. The money she stopped burning on unpaid pitch weeks covered the walked prospects within the year, but she did not know that in advance, and neither will you.

Drift, and How to Notice It Before the Symptoms Do

An identity starts eroding the day you write it down. I wish I could offer you a version of this chapter where the work stays done. There isn't one, and the erosion mechanism is worth understanding because it is so gentle that no alarm you own will catch it.

Identity goes one reasonable exception at a time, never in a single dramatic decision. The biggest client asks for something that bends a value, and he is the biggest client, so you bend, just this once, and you are probably right to. The busy season arrives and the phone-in-three-rings rule slips to five, then to a callback, and every step had a good reason. Exceptions are like rounding errors: individually defensible, collectively a different number. The company that ends up with a hollow trunk almost never did anything wrong that you could point to in the moment. It just said "just this once" at a compounding interest rate.

You cannot prevent exceptions, and you should not want to. Rigidity is its own disease. What you can do is keep the books. Three habits, cheap enough that you will actually keep them.

Count the exceptions out loud. When the company bends a value, say so, in public, at the time: "We are making an exception to the three-rings rule for the season, and here is why, and it ends in March." Named exceptions stay exceptions. Unnamed exceptions become precedents, and precedents become the new identity, unratified. The sentence costs you twenty seconds and a small amount of pride, which is the entire maintenance budget of a company identity, and almost nobody pays it.

Run the annual invoice audit. Once a year, take your three to five sentences and ask for each one: when did this last cost us something? Get specific, with dates. A value with no invoice in twelve months has stopped operating, whatever the wall says, and you must either revive it with a deliberate decision or retire it honestly. This audit takes one hour, which is a suspicious bargain for what it does, and it pairs naturally with whatever annual rhythm you build later. Chapter 13 will give the rhythm a proper home.

Listen for the leading indicators. Drift announces itself in language before it shows up in numbers. Veterans saying "we used to be the kind of place that..." Explanations of the company getting longer, because coherent things are quick to describe and incoherent things take paragraphs. New employees asking "but what do we actually believe about X?" and getting different answers on different floors. And the classic: the fire that looks like it belongs to a later chapter. When sales conversations start feeling weirdly effortful, when good people leave citing vagueness, when the brand refresh somehow doesn't take, remember the pattern from the introduction. The fire is over there, but check whether the fuel is here, in the trunk, three chapters back from where the smoke is.

Field note

Strategy should change often, identity rarely. A useful rule of thumb: strategies are revised in years, identities in decades. If you find yourself rewriting your values every year or two, you had strategies in formal wear all along, and you can relax, rename them, and manage them as strategies, which is cheaper. Genuine identity change does happen, after a near-death experience, a generational handover, a true pivot, but it should feel like an amputation performed on purpose, announced honestly, and mourned a little. If it feels easy, either it wasn't real before or it isn't real now.

What All This Buys You

I have asked you to spend an entire chapter, and several honest hours with a pen, on something that produces no product, signs no customer and shows up on no balance sheet. It is fair to ask what you get. Let me give you the returns as concretely as I can, and then let an old man in a kitchen have the last word, as he tends to.

You get speed. This is the one nobody expects, because identity work smells slow. But watch what happens in a company where the values are real, written and scarred: decisions that used to escalate, stop escalating. The project lead at 18:00 does not need to find you, because "we show work before it is ready" already answers her question. Multiply that by every fork in every road in a growing company and you have bought back something scarce and unphotographable: everyone's best judgment, operating at full speed, in parallel, without you. Delegation without a shared identity is dice-rolling with extra steps. Delegation with one is just called working, and there is a whole chapter, 12, about the founder side of learning to let it happen.

You get coherence customers can feel. Marta's lost pitch was lost to a company that could be described in one sentence. Coherence reads as trustworthiness, because it is: a company that is the same in every room will probably also be the same after the contract is signed. Incoherence reads as risk, even when every individual interaction was pleasant. Customers rarely articulate this. They just pick the other agency and say something vague about fit.

You get cheaper coordination. Every organization pays a tax to keep its people rowing in compatible directions: meetings, approvals, check-ins, escalations. A shared identity is the cheapest coordination technology ever invented. It is a set of decisions made once, in advance, for everyone. The alternative is making the same value judgment over and over, per person, per incident, forever, which is roughly how Marta acquired a queue outside her office and mistook it for love.

You get ballast for the bad day. Every company gets its crisis: the lost anchor client, the public mistake, the year the market turns. In the crisis, everything becomes negotiable at once, and companies without a settled identity negotiate away things they needed, at panic prices. The settled identity is the list of what is not for sale today. It shortens the panic, because the hardest question in a crisis is "who are we allowed to be while we do this," and you answered it back when you could think.

And you get a magnet, working quietly. The right people start finding you, the way the second retailer found Marta, and the wrong people start filtering themselves out, which is worth even more. How to use that magnet properly when you hire is chapter 10's territory, and the words you wrap around it for the outside world belong to chapter 8. The trunk just has to be worth growing branches from.

Story

In year five of the routing company, after the wine-and-archaeology evening, I drove to Henk's house with our three freshly written value sentences in my bag. I was proud of them. I wanted him to be proud of them, which at thirty-one was apparently still the engine I ran on.

He would not take the paper. He physically waved it away, the smoke-clearing gesture, and said, "Don't tell me your values. Tell me your last five decisions that hurt, and I will tell you your values."

So I told him. The delayed release that cost us the deal. The flashy real-time map we refused to build. The support hire we made in a quarter when we could not afford it. The customer we let out of a contract early because the fit had gone bad. The bug we disclosed before the customer would ever have found it.

Henk drank his coffee and was quiet for a while, the way he was quiet, like the question had to clear customs. Then he said: "You keep paying money to make sure nobody is ever surprised. That is the whole company. The rest is fonts."

It was on our paper, near enough, and I said so, with some triumph. Henk shrugged, entirely unimpressed, and delivered the sentence I have carried around ever since and am now handing to you, because it is the shortest correct summary of this chapter that exists: "Good. Then you wrote down the truth. Most men write down the wish."

That is the standard, in the end: whether they are the truth. Inspiring is optional. The grey frame is optional. Write down the truth about who your company is, with its scars attached and its invoices on file, and everything that follows in this book has something to grow from. The next branch on the tree is the mission, the job your company does in the world and the noes it lets you say, and that is where we go now.

The Short Version

  • Your company already has an identity. The only question is whether you designed it or inherited it from your own unexamined habits.
  • Identity is the trunk. Mission (ch 2), vision (ch 3) and brand (ch 8) are branches. When a branch looks sick, check the trunk first.
  • If a competitor could hang your values poster without blinking, you own a category description.
  • A value that has never cost you money, comfort or a customer is decor. The invoice is what makes it a value.
  • Values are archaeology. Dig through your hard decisions, your promotions, your tolerated behaviour and your budget under pressure. The repeats are the values.
  • Write three to five of them as full sentences with the trade-off visible, each with a scar story attached. If the opposite could not be a reasonable strategy, it is not a value.
  • Separate founder conviction from founder habit before the company fossilizes your school run into doctrine.
  • Be the parent of your company's identity rather than its twin: raise a character that answers questions in rooms you are not in.
  • Identity erodes one reasonable exception at a time. Name exceptions out loud, and audit once a year: when did each value last cost us something?
  • The payoff is speed, coherence, cheap coordination and ballast in a crisis. Written down honestly, identity is the truth. Written down hopefully, it is just a wish in a grey frame.

Chapter 2

Deciding on Mission

Your mission is the sentence that decides what your company does on an ordinary Tuesday, and, more importantly, what it refuses to do. The sentence on the wall rarely qualifies.

The vinyl letters cost me 340 euros, plus another 60 for the man who applied them to the wall without bubbles.

This was early in the routing company, the year we moved out of the room above the bicycle repair shop and into a real office, the kind with a meeting room and a reception area and a large white wall that seemed to demand something. We were six people and one plastic plant. I had just come back from a weekend workshop about company culture with a notebook full of diagrams and a head full of fonts, and I had decided that what the wall demanded was our mission statement. I wrote it myself, over two evenings, feeling very much like a CEO. It said: Empowering the future of logistics through innovative technology.

Henk visited that Friday. He was in the neighborhood the way retired men are always in the neighborhood, meaning he had driven forty minutes on purpose. I gave him the tour, which took four minutes, and made him a coffee, which he inspected with suspicion because we had bought one of those machines with buttons.

He ended up in front of the wall. He read it the way he read everything, slowly, as if the words had to clear customs first. The office went quiet around him, the way offices do when somebody's mentor is thinking in public.

"Who is this for?" he asked.

"Customers," I said. "And the team. And candidates, when we interview. It sets the tone."

"Hm." He took a sip and grimaced, at the coffee or the sentence, hard to say. "Which customer woke up this morning wanting the future of logistics empowered?"

I started to explain that it was aspirational, that it captured our ambition, that the workshop had a framework. He let me finish, which was worse than interrupting.

"Let me ask it a different way," he said. "What do people pay you to make go away?"

I opened my mouth to answer and found, to my genuine surprise, that the fancy sentence on the wall was no help at all. So I answered like a human instead. I told him about the dispatcher at our biggest client, a man named Ruud who arrived at ten to six every morning to a wall of orders, forty vans, three hundred stops, two drivers calling in sick, and a supermarket that fined you per minute if you missed the delivery window. I told him about the puzzle Ruud solved by hand for two hours every morning, and how the puzzle followed him home, and how his wife had opinions about that. I told him that when our software worked, Ruud drank his first coffee sitting down.

"The morning," I said finally. "We make the worst part of the morning go away."

Henk nodded, slowly, and pointed his coffee at the wall. "Then why does it not say that?"

I said something about how a mission needed to inspire. He repeated the word inspire the way other people say the word mold.

"That sentence up there is a banner," he said. "Banners hang above the door and look nice on photographs. What you need is a bouncer. A bouncer stands in the door and decides who gets in. Next year a big customer will ask you to build something that is not your job, and the money will be good, and that banner will smile and wave it through. A bouncer checks it against the list and says no." He drained the coffee, grimaced again, and handed me the cup. "Buy a bouncer."

The letters stayed on the wall for six more years, partly because removing vinyl costs almost as much as applying it, and partly because I came to value them as a monument to the difference between the sentence you frame and the sentence you use. The one we actually used, we wrote about a month after Henk's visit, on paper, without a workshop, and it was about Ruud's morning.

This chapter is about that second kind of sentence.

The Job, Not the Poster

Here is the definition this whole chapter rests on, so let me put it up front where you can argue with it: your mission is the job your company does in the world.

Every word in that definition is carrying weight. Job means it is work, performed daily, for someone specific, who notices whether it got done. Your company means it belongs to the business, not to your personal sense of purpose, though the two should be on speaking terms. And in the world means outside your own walls: you measure the job in your customer's life, never on your roadmap. A mission written from the inside describes what you make. A mission written from the outside describes what changes for the person paying you. Only the second kind is any use.

In the last chapter we worked out who your company is, its values and its character, and if you skipped that chapter because values sounded soft, I will only say that a mission without an identity underneath it is a job application with no one attached. Identity is who you are. Mission is the work that someone with that identity shows up to do. A person of good character still needs an occupation, and so does a company.

Field note

If, while reading this chapter, you feel an itch to describe the destination, the world as it looks in ten years when the job is done at scale, you are itching for vision, and chapter 3 is entirely about it, including the one table in this book that untangles mission, vision and strategy for good. Park the postcard. This chapter is about the job.

The most useful mental move I know for finding the job is one you have already seen Henk perform: stop asking what you sell and start asking what you get hired for. Customers hire companies to do jobs, and they fire them, without warning and without an exit interview, the day the job stops getting done. The product is just the shape the job takes this year.

Take the butcher from the introduction, the man behind my first real invoice. He could not have cared less about websites, and he told me so, twice. What he cared about was the supermarket at the edge of town, which had opened a fancy meat counter, so that for the first time in thirty years people who wanted good meat were walking past his shop without a thought. He paid me 350 euros to stop becoming invisible. The website was just the tool I happened to use. If I had done the job with a newspaper ad and a better sign, he would have been exactly as satisfied. I have carried that lesson through three companies: the customer defines the job, and the job is almost never the thing on your price list.

I relearned it the expensive way at twenty-two, with the recipe app. Sam and I had a mission from day one, and I can still recite it, which tells you exactly where our effort went: to make the world fall in love with cooking again. It was a lovely sentence. It had one defect, which is that nobody had hired us to do it. The world, on closer inspection, was still perfectly fond of cooking. The world was tired on Wednesdays and wanted dinner to involve fewer decisions, and there were companies quietly doing that job, and we were busy with the love affair instead. We had written a mission about our own feelings and mistaken it for a job.
