Eighteen months later, when the app died, the mission was the only part of the company still in perfect condition: unused, gleaming, like a fire extinguisher recovered from a flooded house.

Why write the job down at all? Founders sometimes push back here, and it is a fair challenge. You know what your company does. You are there every day. The sentence lives in your head, so why laminate it?

Three reasons, in ascending order of expense.

First, speed. A written mission turns a certain category of debate into a lookup. Should we attend this trade fair, build this feature, chase this segment? Companies without a usable mission hold that debate fresh every time, from first principles, with whoever happens to be in the room. Companies with one check the sentence and move on. Over a year, that difference adds up to weeks.

Second, consistency. If the mission lives only in your head, then every employee is improvising their own version of it, in sales calls, in support tickets, in what they choose to work on when nobody assigns them anything. Six people improvising six missions is survivable. Twenty is not, and by the time you notice, the inconsistency has soaked into your customer base like water into a wall.

Third, and most expensive: without a written job, your company's actual mission becomes whatever the loudest customer wants this quarter. This happens gradually and feels like responsiveness. It is how a route-planning company wakes up owning a half-built customs module, a story I will tell you properly later in this chapter, because I lived it and the scar still itches when it rains.

A Banner Is for Admiring, a Bouncer Is for Deciding

Henk's distinction deserves a proper unpacking, because it is the sharpest test I know for whether a mission is real.

A banner mission exists to be seen. It goes on the wall, the website, the second slide of the pitch deck. Its author wrote it to impress people outside the company: investors, candidates, visiting mentors with strong opinions about coffee. Banner missions compete on how they sound, which is why they all sound the same. Empowering. Transforming. Unlocking. Reimagining. You can swap banner missions between companies in entirely different industries and no one will notice for weeks. I know this because a friend of mine once did it as a prank between two firms he advised, and the record was five weeks, and the person who finally noticed was an intern.

A bouncer mission exists to be used. It stands in the doorway of the company and checks every opportunity, every feature request, every partnership and pet project against the list. Its job is to keep the room the kind of room it is supposed to be; whether it looks good doing that concerns nobody. And like an actual bouncer, it holds no grudge and builds no wall. It lets in everyone the room is for, warmly. It is simply specific about what the room is for, and it works the door every single night, not just when the photographer is there.

How do you tell which kind you have? Two questions, and I encourage you to answer them out loud, alone, where no one can watch your face.

One: when did your mission last change a decision? I mean change it: kill something, redirect something, send someone back to their desk. Appearing in the slide where you announced the decision counts for nothing. If you cannot recall a moment when someone in your company said "we are not doing this, because of the mission" about something they otherwise wanted to do, then the sentence has never worked a shift.

Two: has your mission ever cost you money? This is the harder question and the better one. A working mission refuses things, and some of the things it refuses come with revenue attached. If every opportunity you have ever liked has also, conveniently, fit the mission, then you own a mirror, and mirrors approve of whatever stands in front of them.

Judge a mission by what it has refused. The day it turns away money you wanted is the day the sentence starts earning its keep.

I want to be fair to banners for a moment, because there is a seductive argument for them, and you will hear it from smart people. The argument goes: the mission is a marketing asset, it should be aspirational, it should make hearts beat faster, and the operational stuff can live in strategy documents. I half agree. Your company can absolutely have stirring language for the world; that is brand territory, and chapter 8 will treat it with respect. The mistake is letting the stirring sentence be the only sentence, because then, at the moment of decision, when the whale client is on the phone and the number has six zeroes, your company will reach for its mission and find only a poem. Poems are lovely. Poems do not say no to whales.

To make the door-work concrete, here is what a bouncer mission handles in an ordinary month at a small company. A customer asks for a feature that would serve only them. A partner proposes a co-branded something. A conference invites you to speak to an audience that contains none of your customers. A developer wants to rebuild the invoicing in this year's framework. A competitor's announcement makes everyone nervous for a week. None of these is a crisis, and that is precisely the point: each one is a small tax on your attention, and the mission's daily job is to pay those taxes fast, so that the slow, expensive thinking stays reserved for the few decisions that genuinely have no precedent.

The economics here are worth spelling out, because "say no" sounds like discipline for its own sake, and it is discipline with a balance sheet. A small company's scarcest resource is the attention of its best people; money runs out slower. Every yes rents that attention out. When your mission pre-decides the nos, you are protecting the only compounding asset you have: consecutive months of your best people working on the same job. Companies that say yes to everything die of fragmentation rather than of any single yes, spread across a dozen half-jobs, master of none, and the autopsy usually blames the market.

So the standard for everything that follows is a single question: can it work the door? The rest of this chapter is a practical manual for writing a sentence that can: where to dig for it, what altitude to fly it at, how to word it, how to smell-test it, and how to use it on the day the whale calls.

What Do People Pay You to Make Go Away?

Of all the questions that mentors, investors, consultants and one memorably blunt tax inspector have asked me across three companies, Henk's is the one I have reused the most. It looks simple. It is doing four jobs at once.

First, it forces the customer's point of view. You can answer "what do we sell" from your desk. To answer "what do people pay us to make go away" you have to stand, at least in your imagination, in the customer's kitchen or warehouse or inbox at the moment the pain shows up.

Second, it forces pain over pleasure. This sounds cynical and is merely accurate. People occasionally pay for delight, but they pay reliably, repeatedly, and at better margins to be rid of things: risk, waste, dread, chaos, embarrassment, Monday mornings of a particular shape. If your business genuinely sells joy, and some do, the question still works with one word changed: what do people pay you to make sure never happens? The village bakery is selling pleasure right up until the Sunday you arrive at your in-laws with supermarket cake, and then you understand what it was really selling all along.

A wedding photographer I know ran this exercise expecting to fail it, on the reasonable grounds that nobody hires a wedding photographer to make something go away. Then she interviewed her last five couples, and every one of them, in different words, named the same fear: that the day would blur, that in ten years they would remember the stress and not the faces. She now describes her job as making sure the day cannot be lost. She stopped competing with cheaper shooters more or less overnight, and she books a full year out. The question works on joy businesses. It just finds the fear standing behind the joy, holding its coat.

Third, it produces verbs. Answers to Henk's question arrive in words like stop, fix, prevent, take over, get back. These are load-bearing words, and later in this chapter, when we write the actual sentence, you will be glad to have a pile of them instead of a pile of adjectives.

Fourth, and most usefully, it is falsifiable. Nobody can check "we empower logistics." Anyone can check "we make the dispatcher's two-hour morning puzzle go away": walk into the dispatch office at seven and look at Ruud. Either he is drinking his coffee sitting down or he is not.

Henk mined that question out of forty years behind a counter, no seminar involved, and the story of how deserves telling properly.

Story

Somewhere in the early years of his machine-parts business, Henk told me, a farmer came in fifteen minutes before closing, filthy to the elbows, and asked for a bearing. Henk had the bearing. He also, being Henk, asked what it was for, and the farmer explained that his harvester had seized that afternoon, mid-field, with rain forecast for the day after tomorrow and roughly a year's income standing in the field.

"He wanted the harvest to keep moving," Henk said. "No man alive wants a bearing. The bearing was just the shape the problem took that day."

Most shopkeepers would have filed that under nice customer anecdotes. Henk rebuilt his company around it. He started opening at half past six, because machines break in the morning and every hour of downtime had a price he could calculate better than his customers could. He studied which twenty parts most often stopped an entire production line or harvest, and kept those twenty in triple stock, even when his accountant complained about the working capital. He hired a delivery driver with instructions that would horrify a logistics consultant: the van goes wherever the most expensive silence is. And behind the counter, where customers could not see it, he hung a hand-lettered sign for his own staff: Nobody wants parts.

He never wrote a mission statement in his life; he considered the phrase itself vaguely American. But every person who ever worked for him could recite the job in one breath: we get machines running again before the downtime costs real money. And here is the part I want you to notice, because it pays for this whole chapter: that sentence let him raise his prices. Nobody comparison-shops for a bearing while a year's harvest stands in the rain. His competitors sold parts and competed on price. Henk sold the end of expensive silences and competed on nothing at all.

Your business has an equivalent sentence, whether or not you have found it yet, and the raw material for it is lying around in three places.

The first is your last five closed sales, the ones with invoices, never the pipeline. For each, reconstruct the moment the customer decided, and ask what was happening in their life or business right then. People buy at moments, and the moment is almost always a pain spiking, not a feature launching. The second is your complaints. When a customer is angry, they drop the polite vocabulary and tell you what job they actually hired you for, in the words they really use. Support tickets are mission research that your customers write for free. The third is the repair conversation: ask a long-standing customer, over coffee and away from any renewal date, "what would you have to go back to doing yourself if we disappeared tomorrow?" The answer to that question is your mission, unpolished.

To make this concrete across the range of businesses I promised you in the introduction, here is what the question does to five companies that think they sell products.

What they sell versus what they are paid to make go away
The businessWhat they think they sellWhat people pay them to make go awayA mission with teeth
Wholesale bakery supplying cafésBread and pastryThe 6 a.m. dread that the delivery is short, late or stale on the one morning the café is fullEvery café we supply opens with a full counter and no surprises, every morning, including the bad ones.
Design agency for mid-size firmsBranding and design workLooking smaller and cheaper than they actually are when a serious prospect checks them outWe make good firms look as good as they are, everywhere a customer might check.
Route-planning softwareOptimization softwareThe dispatcher's two-hour morning puzzle and the fines when it goes wrongWe give dispatchers their morning back and their delivery windows their reputation.
Bookkeeping firm for owner-run shopsBookkeeping and filingsThe fear that lives inside every brown envelope from the tax officeOur clients open letters from the tax office without their pulse changing.
IT services firm for 20-to-200-person companiesManaged IT and support contractsThe morning everything is down, nobody knows why, and the person who set it up left two years agoOur clients never have an IT problem that is also a mystery.

Notice what the right-hand column has in common. Each sentence names a person or a place, contains something checkable, and quietly draws a boundary. The bookkeeping mission says nothing about growth consulting, so when a client asks the firm to help write a business plan, the sentence has an opinion. That is the shape you are digging for.

Try this

Today, with a pen: write down your last five sales, one line each. For each one, write what was going wrong in the customer's world in the week they said yes, in their words if you can remember them, not yours. No word that belongs on a poster is allowed; if you catch yourself writing "efficiency," stop and write what the inefficiency felt like at street level instead. Then finish this sentence once, covering as many of the five as you honestly can: "People pay us to make ___ go away for ___." That sentence is the ore, and the rest of this chapter is the smelting.

Finding the Right Altitude

Once founders accept that the mission is a job, they tend to make one of two altitude errors, and I have personally made both, in opposite decades.

Missions fail high and they fail low. Too high, and you are in the clouds with every other company on earth, unable to refuse anything because everything arguably makes the world better. Too low, and you have written this quarter's to-do list in a serif font, and the mission expires the day you ship. The useful altitude is the narrow band in between, and it is worth drawing.

Too High: The Cloud Layer

Cloud missions are the ones about bettering, empowering and transforming. They have two structural defects. The first is that they are indistinguishable: run the swap test, replace your company's name with your nearest competitor's, and if the sentence still works, it was never about you. The second defect is fatal for our purposes: a cloud mission cannot refuse anything. Should the routing company build warehouse software? Well, would it empower the future of logistics? Obviously. Should it open a café? Logistics people drink coffee; empowerment all around. A sentence that permits everything decides nothing, and a bouncer who lets everyone in is just a doorman with opinions.

Cloud missions usually come from a decent impulse gone soft: the founder wants the work to matter, and so reaches for the biggest available words. But mattering lives somewhere other than word size. Henk's business mattered enormously, to farmers standing in wet fields, and his sentence had no word in it longer than two syllables.

Too Low: The Task Layer

The opposite failure is writing your mission at the level of what you currently make. "Build the best route-planning software" was, for about a year, the routing company's real working sentence, after the vinyl letters and before Henk finished his renovation of my thinking. It felt refreshingly concrete after the empowerment era. It was also wrong, in a way that took me a while to see: it welded the mission to a product, and products are tools, and tools change. If a customer had found a way to fix Ruud's morning with three magnets and a whiteboard, our software would have deserved to die, and a mission that said "software" would have insisted we keep building it anyway.

The tell for a too-low mission is that it contains your deliverable: the word software, or bread, or campaigns, or audits. What you sell, to whom, at what price, is the work of your product strategy, and chapter 4 will spend its full length there. The mission sits one level up, where the deliverable could change without the sentence flinching.

The Working Altitude

The band in the middle has a simple boundary condition on each side, and together they make a rule you can apply in ten seconds. A mission should outlive your current product, but not your customer's problem.

Outlive the product: if you would have to rewrite the sentence after a major pivot in how you do the job, it is flying too low. Not outlive the problem: if the sentence would still make sense in a world where nobody had the problem anymore, it is flying too high, because it never attached to a real job in the first place. "We give dispatchers their morning back" dies on the glorious day dispatching becomes effortless for everyone, and that is correct. Missions are allowed to be completable. In fact the faint possibility of completion is a good sign, the way a real destination distinguishes a journey from a stroll.

To see the bands in action, take the design agency from table 2.1 and slide its sentence up and down the scale. In the clouds: "we unleash the power of creativity," which is true of every agency, every art school and several kindergartens. In the task layer: "we deliver brand identities, websites and campaign assets," which is a price list wearing a tie, and dies the day clients want something not on it. At the working altitude: "we make good firms look as good as they are, everywhere a customer might check." The middle sentence survives a pivot from print to web to whatever arrives next, because "everywhere a customer might check" moves with the times all by itself. And it can refuse. When a firm that is not good asks the agency to make it look good anyway, the sentence has a quiet opinion about that too, and agencies that overrule that opinion spend the following years discovering that a mission also exists to protect you from certain customers.

Writing the Sentence

Now the actual writing, and let me start with where not to do it: an offsite. I know, because I have run that offsite. Twelve people, a facilitator, a hotel with a name like a perfume, flipcharts sprouting adjectives by mid-morning. The problem is structural, not personal. Wordsmithing in a group optimizes for the sentence nobody objects to, and the sentence nobody objects to is the sentence that refuses nothing, which is the one thing your mission exists to do. Ten smart people will produce a sentence with ten clauses, each clause a small monument to one person's fear of being left out.

Write the draft alone, or with your cofounders, from the raw material of the last exercise: the go-away sentence, the customers' own words, the pile of concrete verbs. Then, and this matters, test it with the group instead of writing it with the group. Testing is something groups are excellent at. Give your people the draft and ask them to attack it with real decisions from the last quarter, and you will get honest, useful violence. Ask them to help write it and you will get a committee poem.

Warning

If your draft mission needs the word "and" more than once, you have two or three missions in a raincoat, each clause added to keep someone from feeling excluded. Cut until it hurts one person in the room. If it hurts nobody, it includes everything, and a mission that includes everything excludes nothing, which is the whole failure this chapter exists to prevent.

As for the sentence itself, it has three load-bearing parts: a verb, a customer, and a boundary. Everything else is decoration.

The Verb Does the Work

Mission verbs come in two families. There are working verbs, the kind you could mime: take away, get back, keep open, stop, fix, put, deliver, answer. And there are lobby verbs, the kind that only exist on walls: empower, enable, unlock, elevate, transform, inspire, leverage. The test between them is brutal and takes one second: could a customer catch you failing to do it? A café owner can catch the bakery failing to fill her counter by six. Nobody has ever caught anyone failing to empower.

Lobby words and what to use instead
Word on the wallWhat it tells anyoneWhat to write instead
EmpowerNothing. Universally applicable, universally unfalsifiable.Name the specific thing the customer can now do, or stop doing.
InnovativeThat you would like to be seen as clever.Delete it. If the method matters, name the method.
SolutionsThat a committee was involved.The actual noun: routes, payroll, bread, roofs.
World-classAn ambition about rankings, not customers.The standard the customer would notice: "before six," "first call," "zero surprises."
PassionateThat you felt the sentence was too short.Nothing. Passion is demonstrated, never declared.
Seamless / frictionlessThat you have never watched a customer use the product.The specific seam you remove: "no re-typing," "one invoice," "one phone call."
Leverage synergiesPlease see a doctor.Start over from the go-away sentence.

Name the Customer

The second load-bearing part is a person, and I mean a person, someone with a face and a shift that starts at a fixed hour. "The logistics industry" cannot hire you, get angry with you, or drink coffee sitting down. Ruud can. When your mission names someone specific enough to picture, three good things happen. New employees know whose face to imagine when they make small decisions, which is most of what culture is on a working day. Salespeople know instantly whether the prospect on the phone is our kind of customer, which shortens both the good calls and the bad ones. And you gain a quiet second filter: opportunities that serve someone other than your named person have to argue their way in, instead of drifting in unexamined.

Founders resist naming the customer because it feels like shrinking the market, and I want to push on that directly, because the fear is real and the logic is backwards. A named customer shrinks your message, and only your message, down to something that penetrates one group deeply, and depth is what small companies have instead of reach. The routing company's mission named dispatchers. We happily sold to fleet owners, finance directors and one memorable flower auction, but every one of those deals began with a dispatcher whose morning we had fixed telling someone about it. The named person is your beachhead and your compass, and when in doubt, the company points at them. Everyone else remains welcome to buy.

The flower auction, since you are wondering, arrived through a dispatcher too. She had fixed her mornings with our software at a previous employer, changed jobs, and called us in her second week, because carnations wilt on the same unforgiving clock everywhere. That is what a named customer does for a small company: they carry you into rooms your marketing budget has never heard of. People change jobs and make phone calls. Markets stay put.

The Boundary Clause

The third part is optional in the wording and mandatory in the meaning: the sentence should imply an edge, a place where your company visibly stops. Sometimes the edge is baked into the naming. "We get machines running again" quietly excludes selling new machines, and Henk turned away exactly that trade for decades, to the bafflement of manufacturers who courted him. Sometimes you need the edge said aloud, and the cleanest way I know is a second sentence beginning with the words "we do not." We give dispatchers their morning back. We do not run warehouses. Two sentences, eleven words, and the second one, as you are about to see, turned out to be worth more than the first.

One last craft note before the smell test. Keep the whole thing sayable in one breath, by one person, standing in a doorway. That rule comes from operations, not poetry: a mission nobody can recite from memory never makes it into a meeting, and a mission that stays out of meetings reverts to being a banner, no matter how good the verbs are. When we finally had ours, I tested it by asking people at random, in the corridor, without warning. The day the newest support engineer answered without blinking, and then added "which is why I told that prospect this morning we were the wrong choice for them," I knew the sentence had cleared probation. The wrong-choice prospect, incidentally, sent us two right-choice referrals within the year. Bouncers, it turns out, get a reputation.

The Mission Smell Test

Before you put a mission on the door, it should pass inspection itself. Over the years, first for my own companies and then for friends who kept asking, I have collected the recurring smells: the little tells that a mission is decorative, committee-built, or quietly dead. None of them is proof on its own. Three or more and you should open a window.

Run this test twice a year, calendar it, and run it on the real mission, meaning the sentence people actually say, which after a few years is not always the one in the onboarding deck.

The mission smell test
The smellWhat it usually meansThe fix
It would work equally well in your competitor's lobbyIt describes the industry, not your job in itAdd the person and the pain. Rewrite until the swap test fails.
It contains "solutions," "empower," "innovative" or "world-class"Written to impress outsiders, not to decide anythingReplace every lobby word with a word a customer has actually said to you.
It cannot be said in one breathA committee wrote it, and everyone's clause survivedCut clauses until exactly one person in the room objects. Keep cutting past the "and"s.
Nobody below the founders can recite itIt lives in slides, not in heads, and therefore in no decisionsShorten it, then use it out loud in real meetings until repetition does the memorizing.
It has never cost you moneyIt is a mirror, not a filter: everything you wanted has conveniently fitFind the next real opportunity it should refuse, and refuse it, on the record.
It names your product or deliverableFlying too low; the mission will expire with the current toolClimb one altitude band: from what you make to what it makes go away.
Every new opportunity somehow fits itFlying too high; the sentence permits everything and decides nothingDescend one band: add the named customer and the checkable standard.
It needed a launch campaign to introduce internallyIt describes a company you wish you were, and your people know itRewrite it to describe the job you already do on your best ordinary day, then grow the truth, not the sentence.
You feel a small urge to apologize when saying it to a customerEven you do not believe it, and belief leaksSay the go-away sentence to the customer instead, watch them nod, and promote that sentence.

Two of these smells deserve a paragraph of their own, because they are the ones founders argue with.

The launch-campaign smell first. If your mission requires a rollout, posters, a town hall and a mug, that is the sentence telling you it is news to your own company, and a mission that is news is a wish. The strongest missions I have encountered were, at the moment of writing, almost boring to the people inside: a crisp description of what the best people already did on the best days. The writing left the company exactly as it was, and made the existing job defensible, teachable, and refusable-against. If there is a gap between the company you are and the company in the sentence, close it from the company side. Growth toward a true sentence works. A sentence stretched over an untrue company just flaps.

Second, the apology smell, which sounds soft and is the most reliable of the lot. Say your mission, out loud, to a real customer, in a real conversation, and watch yourself. If some part of you winces, hedges, or hurries past it, your body has already run a smell test your slides cannot fool. I have watched founders discover in one sentence, mid-meeting, that they did not believe their own mission, and it is always the same tell: they say it in a different voice, the way people read terms and conditions. The fix is a truer sentence, every time. Elocution has never cured it.

Practically, running the test takes half an hour and goes better with a witness. Read each smell aloud, in order, and have someone who is not you, ideally your most literal-minded colleague, raise a hand at every smell they can attach a real example to. Do not defend anything. Just count hands. Zero or one, touch up the wording and carry on. Two, schedule a rewrite before the next busy season buries the intention. Three or more, declare the mission dead, and take heart: a dead mission diagnosed is one honest afternoon away from resurrection, while a dead mission defended can embalm a company for years.

Saying No Like You Mean It

Everything so far has been the training. This section is the fight. A mission earns its keep on perhaps five or six occasions a year, the moments when something attractive and wrong arrives at the door, and I want to walk you through the anatomy of those moments, because they never feel the way the textbook implies. The textbook implies a clean choice, mission on one side, temptation on the other. In real life the temptation arrives dressed as good news, carried by someone you like, and the mission's voice is the quietest one in the room.

Let me show you, at my own expense, both versions: the yes I should not have said, and the no that saved us.

Story

The yes came first, in the years before the mission had teeth. A mid-size client asked us to build a customs paperwork module. It was adjacent, sort of: their vans crossed a border, paperwork slowed the vans, we were the van people. The deal was worth about 80,000 euros and I said yes inside a week, feeling flexible and customer-obsessed. That module took fourteen months to build instead of four, because customs rules turned out to be a career and not a feature, and it consumed, at various points, my two best engineers, one of whom told me years later it was the closest he came to quitting. It sold to exactly one other customer. When we finally wrote it off, I calculated the real cost, salaries, delay to the core product, and one competitor catching up in a market we had led. The 80,000 euro yes cost roughly half a million, and that arithmetic, every yes has a denominator, is the cheapest expensive lesson in this book.

The no came three years later, and it was much bigger. Our largest client, a retail chain, asked us to build their warehouse management. Courted us, really: dinner, a tour of the distribution center, a projected contract that would have grown our revenue by about forty percent in one signature. I wanted it. My sales lead wanted it so much he had already sketched the org chart. We spent two weeks in a low-grade civil war, and the spreadsheet, I must be honest, sat firmly on the side of yes.

What tipped it was the second sentence. We give dispatchers their morning back. We do not run warehouses. Our quietest engineer, of all people, read it out loud in the third meeting and then said, "So which sentence are we deleting?" The room went silent in a way I still remember, because he had put the real decision into plain words: shall we delete the sentence. Framed that way, nobody wanted to delete it.

We said no. We said it with a referral to a warehouse software firm we trusted, we built a clean integration to them at our own cost, and I flew to the client personally so the no arrived with a face on it. The client stayed eleven more years. The warehouse firm sent us every routing lead they ever met. And the forty percent revenue we declined arrived anyway, about two years later than the spreadsheet promised, from dispatchers, doing the job the sentence said we did.

I want to pull four practical lessons out of that story, because they generalize.

First, the no needs a form of words that makes the real trade visible. "Which sentence are we deleting" did in six words what two weeks of spreadsheets could not: it converted an abstract mission question into a concrete act everyone could feel the weight of. Steal it. When an opportunity conflicts with the mission, ask the room which sentence gets deleted, and watch the conversation change temperature.

Second, a good no has aftercare. A bare no burns the relationship and teaches your team that the mission is expensive. A no with a referral, an integration, an introduction or a face on it strengthens the relationship, because it proves you know exactly what you are and are not, which is precisely the quality the client hired you for in the first place. In eleven subsequent years, that client never once tested our boundary again. Bouncers, as I said, get a reputation.

Expect the no to have a domestic cost as well as a commercial one, and budget for it. My sales lead barely spoke to me for a month after the warehouse decision, and he had a point: the company had just declined the easiest forty percent he would ever find, and nobody had adjusted his targets to match the principle. We repaired that late, and I would tell you to repair it early. If the mission makes a decision that costs a specific person their bonus, their pet project or their easiest quarter, then the mission, meaning you, owes that person a visible repair. Otherwise you teach your best people that the sentence on the wall eats their lunch, and they will quietly stop bringing you opportunities altogether, which is a worse disease than the scope creep you were defending against.

Third, most nos carry an expiry date, and pretending otherwise makes them harder to say. The honest categories are three: no, because it is not our job and never will be; not yet, because it might become our job and we will look again on a named date; and no for us, but here is who you should call. Sorting an opportunity into a category is easier, emotionally and politically, than issuing a verdict on it.

Fourth, and this is the discipline that separates companies that say no once from companies that can keep saying it: write the nos down. Memory, as we established in the introduction, is a helpful colleague who throws away your mistakes, and it is just as cheerful about throwing away your refusals. Six months after a hard no, when the mood has shifted and someone new is in the room, the opportunity will come back, and without a record you will re-litigate it from zero, minus the people who remember why. The fix costs one page. I call it the no ledger, and at the routing company it lived in the same folder as the mission itself.

The no ledger, one row per refusal
FieldWhat goes thereThe warehouse example
The opportunityOne honest line, including who brought it and why it was attractiveBuild warehouse management for our largest client, at their request
The money attachedThe number that made it tempting, written down so nobody inflates it laterRoughly +40% revenue over two years
What the mission saidQuote the exact words that decided it"We do not run warehouses"
The decision and its categoryNo forever, not yet, or no-but-referralNo, with referral and integration to a partner
What the no cost usHonestly, including feelings; this line keeps the ledger credibleThe revenue, one furious quarter from sales, two dinners' worth of goodwill to rebuild
Review date, if anyWhen, if ever, this gets a fresh hearingNone; permanent unless the mission itself changes

The ledger has a second, sneakier benefit. Read back over a year of it and you have an X-ray of your mission's health. Lots of rows means the sentence is working. Empty pages mean either your market is unusually polite or, far more likely, everything has been getting in, and it is time to reread the smell test with the lights on.

Try this

The retroactive bouncer, twenty minutes, pen and one sheet. List the last five significant yeses your company said: deals, features, hires into new areas, partnerships. Hold each one against your draft mission and mark it in or out, honestly. If all five pass, do not celebrate. A mission that blesses everything you already wanted is a mirror, so tighten the sentence until at least one past yes would have been a no, and then sit for a moment with what that yes has actually cost you since. That discomfort is the feeling of a mission growing teeth.

Missions for Businesses That Do Not Want to Change the World

I need to spend a section pushing back on an inflation, because it quietly excludes most of the people this book is for.

Somewhere in the last few decades, companies that intend to reorganize civilization annexed the mission statement, and the vocabulary inflated to match. Missions now come with planets in them. And the practical consequence, which I have watched over many kitchen tables, is that the owner of a nine-person installation firm, or a village bakery, or a bookkeeping practice, concludes that missions are not for them, because they have no intention of disrupting anything. They intend to fit boilers properly, which apparently no longer qualifies as a purpose.

Let me say this at full volume: the size of a mission has nothing to do with the size of the words. A mission is a job, and jobs are dignified at every scale. "Nobody in this village starts a Sunday with bad bread" is a complete, working, load-bearing mission. It names a customer, it is checkable by seven a.m., and it can say no: no to the supermarket wholesale deal that would gut quality, no to the second location two towns over that would break the word village, no to the food-service contract that pays well and turns craft into logistics. I know the baker behind that sentence, more or less; you will formally meet Jonas, my brother-in-law, in chapter 4, and how one bakery became nine without deleting its sentence is his story to carry there.

The same goes for the trades and the practices. "No family in our postcode spends a second night without heating" is a mission; the emergency van, the stocked parts, and the premium price all fall out of it logically, the same way Henk's half-past-six opening hours fell out of his. "Our clients open letters from the tax office without their pulse changing" is a mission, and it tells the bookkeeping firm exactly which clients to resign: the ones who create the letters faster than anyone can prevent them.

Notice something else about these small missions: none of them needs publishing. There is a persistent confusion between the mission and the slogan, and it dissolves the moment you remember who each is for. The slogan is for customers, and belongs to your brand, which gets its own treatment in chapter 8. The mission is for the people inside, a decision instrument, and it is allowed to be as unglamorous as a good tool usually is. Henk's mission hung behind the counter, facing the staff. The customers never read it. They felt it, every time the van showed up before the silence got expensive, and feeling it is the only publication a mission needs.

If your ambition is genuinely planetary, wonderful; write the checkable version anyway and let the planet be implied. And if your ambition is a full counter in one village, write that, in exactly those words, and put this book down for a moment if anyone tries to make you feel small about it. They are confusing altitude with worth. Some of the best-run companies I have ever seen fit their entire mission inside a breath and their entire market inside a postcode, and they say no with a fluency the planet-reorganizers could learn from.

When the Mission Changes

Everything I have said so far argues for holding the line, so let me now argue honestly for the other side, because missions do change, and pretending otherwise turns a working tool into a relic.

The question is how a mission should change, and the answer has three words in it: rarely, deliberately, and out loud. The failure mode is drift, which is change without a decision: one accommodating yes at a time, each defensible, none announced, until the company wakes up doing a different job than the one on the wall and cannot name the day it started. Drift is how the customs module happened to us. Nobody ever decided the routing company was in the customs business. We just never quite decided it was not.

A deliberate change is the opposite animal. It happens in the open, it has a date, and it comes with the same courtesies as any serious change of occupation: you tell the people it affects, in person where it matters, and you update the ledger, because some old nos may deserve a fresh hearing under the new sentence. If changing your mission does not feel slightly ceremonial, slightly expensive, and slightly sad, you are probably drifting with paperwork and calling it a change.

How do you know when a deliberate change is actually due? Three signals, in rising order of seriousness. The mildest: your no ledger shows the same "not yet" coming back season after season, each time with better evidence, until refusing it starts to require ignoring your own customers. The middle signal: the honest version of the go-away exercise, rerun with fresh sales, produces a different sentence than the one on file, meaning the company has already moved and the words are lagging. And the loudest: the customer's problem itself is dissolving or migrating, technology or regulation or habit slowly closing the job down. That last one is the existential case, and it is exactly where Henk, of all people, earned his opinion.

Story

In the nineties, cheap imported parts arrived in Henk's trade like weather. Catalogues first, then fax orders, then the early internet, and suddenly the bearing he stocked at a proud margin could be ordered from abroad for a third of the price by anyone with patience. Two of the three wholesalers in his region responded by cutting prices and doubling catalogue thickness. Both were gone within a decade.

Henk sat with it for a while, in his customs-clearance way, and then did something that looked like nothing. He reread his own counter sign, the one that said nobody wants parts, and concluded that nothing about his job had changed. Farmers still paid to make expensive silences go away. The imports were only a change in tools, and cheaper tools, he reasoned, were arguably good news for a man whose actual product was speed. So he kept his prices, stopped competing on the catalogue entirely, and put the money into the two things the fax machines could not do: stock within an hour's drive of every customer, and a phone that a human answered at half past six. He even started ordering from the cheap importers himself, cheerfully, for anything that could wait.

"The others thought the mission was selling parts at a margin," he told me, decades later, in the kitchen. "So when the margin died, they died with it. My job was silence." He tapped the table twice, his version of italics. "The job stays. The tools change. And you do not repaint the sign just because you bought a new van."

That last line is the whole doctrine, and it gives you the test to run before any rewrite: is it the job that changed, or only the tools? Tool changes, however dramatic they feel from inside, new technology, new product, new channel, do not touch the mission, and rewriting it for them is a way of playing with the sign instead of driving the van. Job changes are rarer and deeper: the person changed, or the pain changed, or the pain is going away on its own. Those deserve the ceremony. Everything else deserves a calm rereading of the sentence you already have, which, if you wrote it at the right altitude, was built to survive exactly this.

Where the Mission Lives

Last thing, briefly, because a mission that has passed every test in this chapter can still die of loneliness. A sentence only stays sharp if it gets used, and using it means giving it standing appointments in the ordinary machinery of the company. Habits, four of them, no framework required. They carried most of the weight for us.

In hiring, the mission opened every first interview, one breath, no slides, followed by a question: "what would you want to know about that?" What a candidate asks about your mission tells you more than anything they claim about their passion for it. In sales, it worked as the qualifying gate: prospects whose problem was not our job got a fast, friendly no with a referral, which cost us nothing and built us a strange, durable reputation for honesty that eventually became a sales asset in itself. In the weekly planning meeting, it sat at the top of the page, less as inspiration than as jurisdiction, the answer to "why is this on our list at all." And twice a year it stood inspection: the smell test, the ledger review, and one honest hour on whether the job had moved.

If your company is still just you, or you and one other person, you do not get to skip this section on the grounds of having no meetings. The solo version matters more, if anything, because the loudest source of drift in a very small company is the founder's own enthusiasm, at eleven at night, admiring an adjacent idea in the glow of a laptop. The whale client comes later. My rule from the website years, adopted far too late to help the website years, was to copy the go-away sentence onto the first page of every new notebook, and to reread it before quoting any new job. That one habit turned down more bad work than any bouncer I ever hired, and it charged nothing.

You will notice none of that requires the wall. If the machinery for turning a mission into quarterly goals, metrics and meeting rhythms is what you are hungry for, that is chapter 13's territory, and it will still be there when you arrive. The mission has to be true and used before it is worth cascading; cascade a poem and you get a very organized poem.

As for our vinyl letters: they finally came down years later, when we repainted the office, and I stood there with a heat gun expecting to feel something. Nothing. Nobody so much as mentioned it for a month, and the day someone did, a new hire asking what used to be on the wall, three people answered by reciting the real mission instead, the one that was never printed anywhere. That is where a mission lives, in the end: in the doorway, working. The wall was only ever decoration.

The job, then, is decided. What remains, before we get anywhere near products and customers, is the question the job quietly raises: if we keep doing this well, for years, where does it all end up? That postcard from the future is vision, and writing one that is not a hallucination is the next chapter's work.

The Short Version

  • Your mission is the job your company does in the world, written in the customer's terms.
  • Start with Henk's question: what do people pay you to make go away? Dig the answer out of your last five sales and your angriest support tickets.
  • A mission is a bouncer, not a banner. If it has never changed a decision, and never cost you money, it is decoration.
  • Fly at the working altitude: the sentence should outlive your current product, but not your customer's problem.
  • Build it from a working verb, a named customer, and a boundary. One breath, sayable in a doorway. "We do not" is a legitimate second sentence, and often the more valuable one.
  • Draft alone or with cofounders; let the group attack it with real decisions, never write it by committee.
  • Run the smell test twice a year. Three smells or more, open a window and rewrite.
  • Sort every no into a category: never, not yet with a date, or no-but-here-is-who-to-call. Deliver big nos with a face on them.
  • Keep a no ledger. An empty ledger means the door is letting everything in.
  • Change the mission rarely, deliberately, and out loud. The job stays, the tools change, and you do not repaint the sign because you bought a new van.

Chapter 3

Articulating Vision

A vision is a postcard from the future, and this chapter is about writing one that people want to visit.

Priya keeps a whiteboard in her office that nobody is allowed to erase.

The whiteboard is small, one of those sixty-by-ninety ones you buy at an office supply store when you do not yet trust yourself with a wall-sized one. It hangs crooked next to her desk, and across the top, in red marker and capital letters, it says DO NOT ERASE, followed by a date. Below that, in her ordinary handwriting, sits a single paragraph. When I visited her office a few years ago, the paragraph had been there long enough that the marker had gone from black to a tired grey, and someone had traced over the fading letters with a fresh pen, the way you retouch a fresco.

You should know who Priya is, because she will keep turning up in this book. She was one of the first product people at the routing company, back when our idea of an office plant was a cactus somebody had abandoned, and she was better at her job than the company deserved. Then she did the thing your best people eventually do: she left to start her own company. Hers is a B2B software business that helps mid-size manufacturers catch quality problems on the factory floor while they are still small, instead of discovering them months later in a spreadsheet, at which point they have become recalls, lawsuits, or very long meetings.

The paragraph on the whiteboard says, roughly, this. I am quoting from memory and she would correct three words, but the shape is right:

"It is a Tuesday in March, six years from now. At 7:40 in the morning, a production manager walks onto a factory floor in Eindhoven. A machine on line three started drifting out of tolerance at 6:15. By 6:25, the one technician who could fix it knew about it, saw what the machine saw, and fixed it before the first batch was scrapped. Nobody filled in a form. Nobody will reconstruct the problem in October from a spreadsheet. In every factory like this one, from Porto to Gdańsk, quality is something the floor sees in minutes, not something the office discovers in months. We built the thing that made that normal."

Here is how that paragraph came to exist. In her second year, Priya did what second-year founders with a bit of money do: she hired help. A strategy consultancy ran a two-day offsite in a hotel near Utrecht, with breakout groups and flip charts and a facilitator who said "alignment" the way other people breathe. At the end of it, the consultancy delivered, among other laminated artifacts, a vision statement. It read: "To become the leading European platform for smart manufacturing quality solutions."

Priya told me she read that sentence out loud to her team, watched eleven intelligent people nod the way you nod at a stranger's holiday photos, and felt something in her chest that she later identified as shame. The sentence was accurate, defensible, and nothing. It could have hung in the lobby of any of her competitors without a single word changed. It described no morning, no factory, no person, no changed world. It described a ranking. Nobody starts a company to hold a ranking.

She came back to the office alone on the Saturday after the offsite, still angry, mostly at herself, because she had paid real money for the sentence. She stood at the little whiteboard and asked herself the only question that ended up mattering: if this works, completely works, what does an ordinary Tuesday look like for the person we built it for? Then she wrote the paragraph, dated it, wrote DO NOT ERASE above it, and went home.

The laminated card went into a drawer, where it remains, presumably still leading Europe.

The whiteboard, meanwhile, got a job. Engineers started walking over to it mid-argument, reading it, and settling feature debates without her in the room, because "does this get us closer to 6:25?" turns out to be a question two engineers can answer alone. New hires read it on their first morning, and Priya says she can tell within a minute, from their faces, whether the hire was right. When a big customer asked her to build a general-purpose reporting module, a good, sensible, revenue-bearing request, she looked at the whiteboard and said no, and the whiteboard took half the pain out of it. And on the genuinely bad days, of which her company has had several worth their own chapter, the paragraph did the one thing a spreadsheet cannot do: it reminded everyone what all the suffering was supposed to purchase.

That paragraph is a vision. The laminated sentence was lobby art.

This chapter is about writing yours: what a vision is, how it differs from the mission you wrote in the last chapter and the strategy you will build in the next one, how far into the future it should look, what the good ones are made of, and how to keep one alive for years without it curdling into wallpaper. By the end you should have a postcard from your own company's future, in your own handwriting, worth writing DO NOT ERASE above.

A Postcard, Not a Prophecy

Let me give you the definition I will use for the rest of the book, and then spend a chapter earning it.

A vision is a postcard from the future. It is a short, concrete, sensory description of the world as it looks if your company succeeds, written as if you are already standing there, addressed to the people who have to do the walking.

Every word of that definition is load-bearing, so let me take the postcard apart the way you would an actual one from a friend.

A postcard is written from a place. Nobody writes "we intend to be among the leading visitors of the Italian coast." They write "the water is so clear you can see your feet, and the man at the bakery knows our order now." The writer stands in the scene, sand still on their shoes. That is the tense of a vision: it is six years from now, and here is what is true. The moment you write from inside the future instead of pointing at it from the present, the future starts demanding decisions about what is actually there, and that demand is most of the value.

A postcard is specific. It mentions the bakery, the water, the feet. Priya's paragraph has a time of day in it, twice. It has Eindhoven in it. It has a technician in it. Specificity is what separates a vision from a horoscope, and I will be rude about horoscopes later in this chapter, because most published vision statements are exactly that: sentences engineered to be true of anyone and falsifiable by no one.

A postcard is short. One card, one side, room for a stamp. A vision that needs a slide deck is a plan wearing a costume. A paragraph is the right size. A single sentence can work if it is muscular enough, but in my experience one sentence buys brevity by selling detail, and detail is what your people will use.

A postcard is addressed to someone. This is the part founders forget. The postcard goes to the people who have to walk to the place on the card: your team, your future team, and on the bad nights, you. The market, the press, and the pitch deck can read adaptations later. Write the vision knowing exactly who will read it and when, and the when is usually a moment of doubt.

And a postcard says, implicitly, wish you were here. It describes somewhere worth the journey. This is the emotional job of a vision, and it is a real job, not decoration. Humans sustain effort for people and places, never for abstractions. People stay late, twice, for the technician at 6:25, for the queue outside the second shop, for the dispatcher who gets home for dinner. "Leading European platform" has never kept anyone past six. If the place on your postcard is not somewhere your own people would want to live, no amount of wordsmithing will fix it, because the problem is the destination, not the description.

The postcard has edges, and the edges matter as much as the picture. You are choosing a future, out of all the futures you could aim at, and committing the company's walking in that direction; whether you chose right stays an open question until the grading ceremony at the end of this chapter, and prophecy never enters into it. The roads belong to strategy, as we are about to see; the postcard stays silent about them. And nothing on the card gets assigned to anyone. The moment your vision contains the word "Q3," something has gone wrong that this chapter will try to prevent.

One more reassurance before the machinery. You may be reading this as the owner of a bakery, an agency, a plumbing firm, a two-person consultancy, and thinking: postcards from the future are for the software people, I just want a second shop. I promise this chapter is for you, arguably more than for the software people, who at least get vision talk forced on them by investors. "It is five years from now. There is a queue outside both shops on Saturday morning, half the town knows our bread by name, and three kids who started as weekend help are running counters of their own" is a complete, working vision, and it will do for a bakery exactly what Priya's whiteboard does for her factory software: settle arguments, sort job applicants, and make the fourth year of hard mornings mean something.

The same goes for the agency, the consultancy, the installation firm, any business where the temptation is to say "our vision is to do good work and grow a bit." I understand the modesty, and the modesty is the problem. "Good work" is a standard, not a destination, and it gives your best people nothing to aim their ambition at, so they will eventually aim it somewhere else, usually at a competitor or a company of their own. An agency postcard might read: "It is three years from now. Clients come to us for the one thing we are named for, before they know our prices. We have said no to two kinds of work all year, publicly, and both noes brought us better clients than the yeses would have. Nobody here works for a client they are embarrassed to name at a birthday party." That is modest in size and immodest in clarity, which is the correct ratio.

Vision, Mission, Strategy: Once, and Never Again

Now the untangling I promised in the introduction. These three words cause more confusion per syllable than anything else in business vocabulary, partly because consultancies benefit from the confusion and partly because ordinary usage genuinely overlaps. We are going to pin them down here, in one table, and then this book will never re-explain them. Later chapters will use the words and trust you to have been here.

The fastest way in is through a question each one answers.

Your mission answers: what job do we do in the world, every day, for whom? You write it in the present tense because it is already true, on your very first day, at your very smallest. The previous chapter was about writing one sharp enough to say no with, and I will not repeat its mechanics here; if you skipped chapter 2, that is where mission lives.

Your vision answers: if we keep doing that job well, what does the world look like in the end? You write it in the future tense, or better, in Priya tense: the future described as present. The mission is the walking; the vision is the place.

Your strategy answers: given where we stand, what is in the way, and what we are choosing not to do, how do we get from here to there? It is conditional, argumentative, and mortal. It changes when the facts change, and the facts change often. Chapter 4 builds your first one for product and service, and chapter 7 deals with keeping plans alive, so here I only need strategy as a contrast color.

Vision, mission, strategy: the one table. Bookmark it, because this book will not explain these words again.
MissionVisionStrategy
Question it answersWhat job do we do in the world, and for whom?What does the world look like if we succeed?How do we get from here to there, given what is in the way?
TensePresent. True on day one.Future, written as if you are standing in it.Conditional. "Given X, we will do Y, not Z."
HorizonTimeless, until the job itself changes.Three to ten years.One to three years, revised when facts change.
How often it changesRarely. Changing it means changing the company.Rarely. You rewrite it when you arrive, or the world moves.Often. A strategy that never changes is a strategy nobody is checking.
Sounds likeA promise. "We do X for Y so that Z."A postcard. "It is 2031, and here is what is true."A bet. "We win by A, which means saying no to B."
Test of a good oneYou can use it to say no, today, to a real request.People can picture it, want it, and would notice if you arrived.It excludes real options a sane competitor might pick.
Fails by becomingA slogan too vague to refuse anything.A horoscope, or a trophy shelf for the founder.A to-do list, or a budget with adjectives.
Who reaches for it mostEveryone, in daily decisions.Everyone, on dark days; recruits, on their first one.Leadership, quarterly, with the door closed.

A worked example makes the rows breathe. Take Priya's company. Mission: we help mid-size manufacturers see and fix quality problems on the floor within minutes. Present tense, true when she had one customer. Vision: the whiteboard paragraph, the Tuesday, the 6:25. Strategy, at the time I visited: win the Dutch and German mid-market first, integrate with the three machine vendors that cover most floors, stay out of enterprise deals we cannot service, charge per line rather than per seat. Notice how mortal that third sentence is. Two of those four commitments have since changed, and rightly. The whiteboard has not.

Or take the bakery, because the software people have had enough attention. Mission: we bake bread good enough that the town plans its Saturday around it. Vision: the queue outside two shops, the weekend kids running counters. Strategy: second shop on the north side rather than the market square, because the rent there buys three years of patience; hire a second baker before a second seller; no franchising, ever, or at least no franchising this decade. Same species of thinking as Priya's, different flour.

The three form a chain, and the chain has a direction. Identity, from chapter 1, tells you who is walking. Mission tells you what the walker does. Vision tells you where the walking leads. Strategy picks the road. When the chain is intact, decisions at the bottom can be traced to beliefs at the top, and a new employee can learn the whole of it in an afternoon. When a link is missing, you get the classic failure smells: a company with vision and no mission is a dreamer that cannot describe its own workday; a company with mission and no vision does honest work that accumulates into nothing in particular; a company with strategy and neither of the others is a mercenary, briefly effective and permanently for sale.

Two confusions are worth clearing while we are here, because they generate most of the bad documents I get asked to read.

First, the direction of dependence. Strategy serves vision, never the reverse. If your vision has become "whatever our current strategy achieves if it works," what you own is a forecast with lighting. The tell: every strategy pivot triggers a vision rewrite. Real visions survive pivots; they are the reason pivots have a direction.

Second, the boundary with goals. A big goal makes a poor vision, and a stack of goals adds up to a taller stack of goals. "One hundred million euros in revenue by 2030" is a milestone someone might set on the road to a vision, but it describes nothing about the world except your bank account, and your bank account inspires exactly one person, sometimes. How visions decompose into annual and quarterly goals is chapter 13's business, and I will not poach it here. For now, hold the distinction the simple way: a goal is what you check off, a vision is what you check against.

How Far Away Is the Horizon?

The first practical question everyone asks, usually within a minute of agreeing to write a vision, is: how far out? Three years? Five? Ten? Twenty-five, like the corporate sustainability reports? The honest answer: "the future" comes in several distances, each distance is good for a different thing, and most vision documents fail by treating them as interchangeable.

Henk, who you met in the introduction and who never wrote a vision statement in his life while possessing one of the clearest visions I have ever encountered, put it in his usual way when I once tried to impress him with a ten-year plan for the routing company. He listened, sipped his coffee, and said: "You are describing next year's weather in ten-year words. From the dyke you can see the sea. You cannot see the waves." I asked him, a little wounded, what he could see at ten years when he ran the wholesale business. "Direction," he said. "Every workshop in the region orders from us before they check anyone else. That was the whole thing. I could not have told you the turnover, the building, the number of vans. I could tell you the direction with my eyes closed, and I steered twenty years of Tuesdays by it." Then he pointed out that my ten-year plan had a headcount table in it, and asked whether I also knew what I would be having for lunch on the fourth of March in nine years. It took me an embarrassing number of years to unpack the dyke line, so let me save you the time.

Stand where you are and look forward. There are three usable distances, and a fourth that fools people.

Now is where your feet are. It is made of facts: your customers, your cash, your capabilities, your reputation, this morning's inbox. You write every vision standing here, whatever its dateline says, and pretending otherwise produces fantasy. The now is chapter 6's and chapter 7's raw material.

Three years is the distance of the photograph. Close enough that you can describe it in checkable detail: roughly how many people, which kind of customer, what a Tuesday looks like, what you are known for. Far enough that it outgrows this year's plan. Three years is where Priya's paragraph mostly lives, whatever its nominal date says, and it is the distance I recommend for the postcard itself. You can see individual waves at three years. You can be wrong at three years, which is a feature: a vision you cannot fail to reach was never pulling you.

Ten years is the distance of the direction. At ten years, detail is dishonest. You do not know your headcount in ten years, and anyone who writes it down is decorating. What you can know at ten years is a heading: the change in the world you are walking toward, the kind of company you refuse to become on the way. "Quality is something the floor sees in minutes, everywhere" is a ten-year heading. It is a compass bearing, not an address, and it should survive the failure of any particular three-year photograph.

Beyond ten years is the fog of someday. Statements set there are unfalsifiable by construction, which is exactly why a certain kind of founder loves them: nobody living will be held to account. A vision that only works at the twenty-five-year distance is an alibi.

So a complete vision, in practice, has two moving parts: a ten-year heading in one sentence, and a three-year postcard in one paragraph, written in the direction of the heading. Priya's whiteboard happens to contain both, which is why it works: the Tuesday morning is the photograph, and "from Porto to Gdańsk, quality is something the floor sees in minutes" is the bearing. When the three years pass, and they will pass faster than any spreadsheet suggests, you write a new postcard from further up the same road. The heading stays. The photographs succeed each other like stages of a long walk.

What each distance is for, and what it is made of.
DistanceWhat it isMade ofBelongs toHonest level of confidence
NowWhere your feet areFacts: customers, cash, capabilities, reputationMoney and planning, chapters 6 and 7High, if you are honest, which is harder than it sounds
1 yearThe planCommitments, budgets, hires, launchesThe living plan, chapter 7; goal rhythms, chapter 13Medium. You will be wrong in the details and roughly right in the shape.
3 yearsThe postcardA checkable picture: who you serve, what a Tuesday looks like, what you are known forThis chapterLow on specifics, and that is fine. It is a choice, not a forecast.
10 yearsThe directionOne sentence: the change in the world, the bearingThis chapterNone, honestly. It is a commitment, so confidence is the wrong axis.
BeyondThe fog of somedayAdjectives, mostlyNobody. Leave it alone.Unfalsifiable, which is the problem
Field note

If your business is a bakery, an agency, a workshop, anything without a venture capitalist in the room, you may feel the ten-year heading is theater. Skip it if you must, but keep the three-year postcard. In twenty years of watching small companies, the single best predictor I know for surviving year four's grind is whether anyone can describe year six out loud without checking notes.

What a Good Postcard Is Made Of

Suppose you accept the assignment: one paragraph, three years out, written from inside. What separates a paragraph that becomes a whiteboard from a paragraph that becomes a drawer? Having now read more company visions than any person should, including several dozen I was paid to be polite about, I can report that the good ones share five properties, and the bad ones fail the same five ways with remarkable discipline.

It contains a person who is not you

The strongest visions have a character in them, and the character is a customer, a user, a person on the receiving end of the work. The production manager at 7:40. The dispatcher home for dinner. The Saturday queue. When the only actor in your vision is the company itself, "we will be, we will have, we will dominate," you have written a trophy inscription, not a postcard. The world of your vision should be recognizably better for someone with a name-shaped hole in the sentence, because that person is what your team is actually working for, whatever the pitch deck says.

It could be observed

A good vision is made of things a camera could film or a visitor could notice. Times of day. Queues. Rooms. Numbers of shops. Sentences customers say. No camera can film "trusted partner." One phone call can check "the three biggest machine vendors ship with our integration in the box." The test I use: could a sceptical journalist visit your company in three years and verify, or falsify, most of the paragraph in an afternoon? If no one could ever witness anything in the vision, no one will ever work toward it, because no one can tell progress from drift.

It would frighten the current company a little

A postcard from somewhere you have already arrived is a review. The paragraph needs at least one sentence that your current operation cannot deliver, one that makes the honest reader swallow: every factory from Porto to Gdańsk, when today you have eleven customers and nine of them are within cycling distance of Eindhoven. The gap is the engine. A vision with no gap generates no pull, and a vision that is all gap, colonies on Mars for a company that has not shipped, generates no belief. You are tuning a distance: far enough to pull, near enough to believe.

It excludes futures you could plausibly have

This is the least understood property and the most valuable. A vision is a choice among available futures, and a choice that rejects nothing chooses nothing. Priya's paragraph excludes several companies she could have built: the enterprise-only vendor, the general analytics platform, the consultancy with software on the side. All were available. All had money in them. The paragraph closes those doors, which is exactly what allowed her team to settle arguments at the whiteboard without her. When you read your draft, ask: what attractive company does this sentence forbid us from becoming? If the answer is none, you have written weather, not a destination.

Your own people would want to live there

Finally, the wish-you-were-here property. Read the paragraph and ask whether the people who work for you, the real ones, with their actual mortgages and their actual reasons for joining, would find the described world worth their next three years. Forget whether it impresses strangers; ask whether it moves insiders. A vision that excites the founder and bores the team is a vanity plate. This is also the property that keeps visions humane: somewhere in that future Tuesday, implicitly, your own people are doing work they are proud of, and if you cannot see them in the picture, they will notice their absence long before you do.

Because the failures are so uniform, you can diagnose most weak visions by phrase. Here is the field guide I wish someone had handed me at the routing company, in the years when our vision was a revenue number with a halo.

The postcard test: phrases that mean the vision is not finished yet, and what to do instead.
When the draft saysWhat is actually wrongAsk insteadWhat the fix sounds like
"The leading provider of…"It describes a ranking, not a world. A ranking is about you; nobody else can want it for you.If we were leading, what would be true for a customer on an ordinary Tuesday?"A dispatcher in Liège plans 200 stops in ten minutes and the last driver is home for dinner."
"World-class", "best-in-class", "cutting-edge"Adjectives standing where evidence should be. Class is awarded by others, later.What would a visitor see that would make them use those words unprompted?"Competitors demo against us by name, and we win the ones we designed to win."
"Empowering X to unlock Y"Verbs with no scene attached. No camera can film it, so no one can check it.Empowered to do what, visible how, by when in the morning?"By 6:25, the one technician who can fix it knows, and fixes it before the first batch is scrapped."
"€100 million by 2030"A milestone impersonating a destination. Describes your bank account, not the world.If we hit the number, what changed for the people we serve? Write that instead; keep the number in chapter 13's machinery."Half the mid-size factories in the Netherlands catch defects the same morning they start."
"To be our customers' trusted partner"True of every company that has not yet been caught. Excludes nothing.What do customers do, observably, because they trust us?"Customers put us in their own audits, and give our reports to their regulators unedited."
A 400-word paragraph with three sub-clauses per sentenceA plan smuggled into the postcard's envelope. Nobody will hold it in their head, so nobody will use it in an argument.What would survive being read aloud at a funeral pace in under sixty seconds?One paragraph. One side of the postcard. Room for the stamp.

You will notice every fix in that table adds a person, a scene, or a time of day, and deletes an adjective. That is the whole craft. You improve a vision by trading abstraction for furniture, and by almost nothing else.

Writing Yours

Now the pen part. I am going to walk you through the process I use with founders, which is also, unromantically, the process Priya reverse-engineered on her angry Saturday. It takes about two hours the first time, most of which you will spend deleting. You do not need an offsite, a facilitator, or a hotel near Utrecht. You need a door that closes and your own handwriting, because handwriting slows you down to the speed of meaning, and typing lets you produce "leading European platform" without consulting your brain.

Step one: pick the day, not the achievement

Start with a calendar rather than an achievement. Pick an ordinary day roughly three years out, a Tuesday, deliberately skipping launch days and award ceremonies, and write the date at the top of the page. The discipline of ordinariness matters: anyone can imagine their triumphant day, the funding announcement, the ribbon on the second shop. Triumphant days are rare by definition and tell you nothing about what the company is like. The vision question is what an unremarkable day looks like when the work has succeeded, because unremarkable days are what a company is made of. If the ordinary Tuesday is good, the company is good.

Step two: choose whose morning you are watching

Pick one person on the receiving end of your work, as concrete as you can make them: the production manager, the dispatcher, the woman third in the Saturday queue. "Our customers" is a fog bank, and fog has no morning. If you did the mission work in chapter 2 you already know who this is, because it is the person whose problem you exist to make go away. Now watch their morning, three years from now, in the world where you succeeded, and write what happens to them. What time is it? What do they no longer do? What happens in minutes that used to take months? What do they say about you to a colleague, in their own words, when you are not in the room? That last one is dangerous and useful; it is also the seed of chapter 8, where reputation gets a whole chapter to itself.

Step three: widen the lens twice

A single morning is a scene, not yet a world. Widen twice. First to the company: on that same Tuesday, what is true about you? Roughly how many people, in what kind of rooms, doing what kind of work, known for what? Resist precision theater; "about thirty of us" is honest, "34 FTE" is astrology with a spreadsheet. Then widen to the field you play in: what has changed out there because you exist? This is where the ten-year heading first shows its face, the Porto-to-Gdańsk sentence, the change that would remain worth pursuing even if this particular photograph turns out wrong. Write one sentence at that widest setting, no more. One is a bearing. Three is a manifesto, and manifestos are where headings go to gather adjectives.

Here is the widening done for the bakery, so you can see the mechanics rather than take them on faith. Scene: it is a Saturday, three years out, and the woman third in the queue has driven from the next town, because her sister served our bread at a birthday and she has been coming since. First widening, the company: two shops, a night baker in each, and the Saturday shift is run entirely by the two weekend kids who started three years ago, now trained, now trusted, now paid like it. The owner has left both counters to them; she is at the market negotiating for spelt, on the first free Saturday morning of her adult life. Second widening, the field: in this town, "we will just get bread there" has become a default sentence, the way it used to be a decision. One bearing: bread good enough to plan a Saturday around, in more towns, without ever becoming a factory. Notice what ended up on the page: a driver from the next town, a free Saturday, a spelt negotiation. Furniture, all of it, and every stick of it checkable.

Step four: delete until it fits on the card

You now have a page or two. The vision is the paragraph hiding inside it. Delete every adjective that a competitor could also claim. Delete every sentence about being rather than doing. Delete the parts that are secretly this year's plan, and put them where plans live, in chapter 7's machinery. Delete the number that is secretly a goal, and give it to chapter 13. What survives should be five to eight sentences with a person, a time of day, a company you can glimpse, and one bearing. Read it against the five properties from the previous section, especially the fourth: name, out loud, the attractive company this paragraph forbids you from becoming. If you cannot, sharpen until you can.

Step five: read it aloud to the wrong person
