This feels backwards to a founder who needs revenue, and the founders who need revenue most can least afford to skip it, because the scarcest resource in your company is your weeks. Every week spent courting a deal that was never real is a week taken from a deal that was, or from finding one.

Founders avoid the hard qualifying questions because the questions might kill the deal. Sit with that logic for a second: if a question can kill the deal, the deal was already dead, and the question is just the coroner. Asking "is there actually money for this?" in week two costs you nothing but an illusion. Discovering the same answer in month five costs you the months. The worst case of asking early is losing a deal you were always going to lose, minus the suspense. And a paradox works in your favor: buyers trust sellers who are visibly willing to walk away. The founder who asks blunt questions reads as someone with other options and a real business, which, usefully, is also what the questions are helping you build. Desperation is the only thing I know of that customers can smell through a video call.

The hardest skill is the pause

The mechanics of asking are simple. The discipline is in what you do after asking, which is nothing. Ask, then stop. The silence after a hard question feels, to a nervous founder, like a smoke alarm, and the instinct is to smother it: suggest possible answers, soften the question, answer it yourself. Every time you do this you buy comfort with information. The customer was three seconds away from telling you the true thing, the thing after the official answer, and you paid them to stop. Count to five in your head if you must. The best answers in every discovery call I have ever run arrived in second four.

Story

Priya's second meeting with the gearbox people was a fifty-minute demo to nine attendees, three more than last time, which she took as momentum. It was free entertainment. She walked them through every module. Heads nodded. Someone asked about single sign-on. Afterwards she could not answer a single new question about their situation: not what the document chaos cost them, not who owned the budget, not why this year instead of last year. Two weeks of silence followed, and the deal was quietly dying of politeness.

What she did next she still calls the hardest sales advice she ever took: she asked for one more meeting and went in with no laptop. No demo, no slides, a notebook and a pen. She told the head of quality, "I realised I've shown you a lot and understood very little. Can I ask you to walk me through what actually happens when a supplier document is wrong?" He talked for forty minutes. He drew their process on the whiteboard, all fourteen factories of it, and somewhere in the middle of the drawing he stopped, tapped the marker on one box, and said, "This is where we failed the Küpper audit." A customer audit, eight months earlier. It had cost them a contract worth more than Priya's entire company. Nobody had mentioned it in either previous meeting, because nobody mentions the wound while the vendor is performing.

The deal changed shape in that minute. Saving hundreds of hours was the polite version, the parking garage version. The real purchase was never again standing in front of a customer's auditor with a missing certificate. Priya's proposal, when it finally went in, opened with audit risk and mentioned saved hours on page three. The head of quality forwarded it to his board sponsor within an hour, because she had finally written a document he could get in trouble for ignoring.

That is the whole argument for discovery, told as one meeting. The demo meeting produced enthusiasm. The notebook meeting produced the deal. Enthusiasm is what people give you instead of information. Information is what closes.

Try this

In your next sales conversation, whatever you sell, forbid yourself statements for the first fifteen minutes. Only questions. Bring a pen, and write down, verbatim, the exact words the customer uses to describe their problem, not your translation. Then use their words, and only their words, in every email, proposal, and conversation that follows. When a proposal says "eliminate certificate chaos before the next customer audit" instead of "streamline document workflows," the customer recognizes their own voice, and people do not argue with their own voice.

A Pipeline That Tells You the Truth

Once you have more than a handful of conversations running, you need a pipeline. I want to be precise about that word, because software vendors have decorated it beyond recognition. A pipeline is a list of your open deals, each tagged with how far along it honestly is, what happens next, and when. That is all. It can live in a CRM, a spreadsheet, or, below ten deals, on a whiteboard. The tool is a detail. The truth is the point.

A pipeline answers three questions memory cannot. Where is each deal really, as opposed to where I feel it is? What is the next concrete step for each one, and whose move is it? And is there enough in here, at honest odds, to pay for the next few months, or do I need to find more conversations this week rather than polish the ones I have? That third question saves companies. Deals take time, which makes the pipeline a weather forecast for your cashflow two or three months out, and the runway mathematics of chapter six is exactly why you cannot afford to discover a drought the month it arrives.

The failure mode is universal, and I say that as someone who has audited his own pipelines and winced. Left alone, a pipeline becomes a list of people who were nice to you. The friendly conversation from February still sits at "proposal stage" in July, not because anything moved but because deleting it feels like defeat. You start defining stages by what you did, "demo given," "proposal sent," instead of by what the customer did, so the pipeline records your activity while saying nothing about your prospects' intentions. Then one evening you multiply the hopeful numbers by the invented percentages, get a figure that feels like a salary, and relax, which is the most expensive feeling in sales.

A pipeline is a list of people with a problem, a budget, and a date. Everyone else in it was just being nice to you.

The cure is exit criteria. Define each stage by evidence, something the customer did or said that you could prove to a skeptical stranger, and let no deal advance without its evidence, however warm the last call felt. Here is a set that fits founder-led selling in a consultative or small-enterprise motion. Rename freely, but keep the spine: every stage earned by customer action, never by yours.

Pipeline stages with exit criteria: a deal moves forward only on evidence
StageWhat it meansEvidence required to leave this stageThe honest question to ask yourself
1. LeadSomeone who fits your customer profile and might care.They replied and agreed to a real conversation with a date on it.Do they fit, or do I just have their email address?
2. ConversationYou have talked. A problem may exist.They described a real problem in their own words, and agreed a concrete next step with a date.Can I quote their problem back verbatim? If not, what did we talk about?
3. QualifiedA real opportunity: misery, money, mandate, moment all confirmed.You know what doing nothing costs them, where the budget lives, who signs, and why now. Ideally you have met more than one stakeholder.If I described this deal to a skeptic, which of the four would they laugh at?
4. ProposalThey have seen the price and scope, and are still talking to you.They responded to the proposal with engagement: questions, objections, a negotiation, a meeting about it. Silence parks the deal right here.Whose move is it right now, and is there a date attached?
5. ClosingA verbal yes exists. Paperwork, procurement, security, legal.Signature. Then, and I say this from scar tissue, the first invoice actually paid.What could still kill this, and have I met that person?
Won / Lost / No decisionThe three exits. Log every one with a reason.Won: money arrived. Lost: they chose someone else. No decision: they chose the status quo, the most common exit and worth its own label.What did this deal teach me that the next one can use?

Two warnings about numbers, because pipelines invite arithmetic and early-stage arithmetic lies. First, with eight deals in play, conversion percentages are astrology. Two wins out of eight is two wins; calling it a twenty-five percent win rate dresses luck up as statistics. Percentages start whispering truth somewhere past thirty or forty closed outcomes; before that, read the stories, not the stats. Second, weight nothing by feel. A qualified deal is in or it is out. The moment you record a deal as "80% likely," you have invented a number whose only function is to make Sunday evening feel better.

What should the funnel look like between stages? Leaky. Honestly, healthily leaky, and mostly near the top, where leaking is cheap. Here is the funnel nobody prints on the sales software marketing page.

Read that diagram the way a plumber reads a wall. A big leak after conversations is healthy: it means you disqualify politely and early, and spend your hours on real deals. A big leak after proposals is expensive: a proposal takes a day to write, and if half of them vanish into silence, the fault usually sits two stages back, where misery, money, mandate, or moment went unverified and you proposed to a documentary watcher. And the leak labelled "doing nothing" deserves respect, because in most founder pipelines the status quo beats every named competitor combined. You will lose more often to a shrug than to a rival, which is why "what happens if you do nothing?" appeared in the discovery table and will keep appearing in this book.

A pipeline only tells the truth if you visit it, so give it a standing appointment. Mine was Friday afternoon, thirty minutes, coffee, and the same three questions for every deal: what did the customer do since last week, what is the next step and its date, and do I still believe this one, truly, or am I keeping it for company? Deals with three consecutive Fridays of "no customer movement" got either the honest email or the honest exit. The ritual matters more than the tooling, and it has a second function: it forces the go-find-more decision. A rough rule of thumb wants three times your revenue target sitting in qualified pipeline, because roughly two thirds of even honest deals will leak. Hold the rule loosely at founder scale, your numbers are too small for the ratio to be science, but hold the question tightly: if everything in this list closed at believable rates, would it be enough? If the answer is no, the most important sales work this week is starting conversations you do not have yet. That work vanishes first when the calendar gets loud, because it has no meeting invite and nobody is waiting for it. Friday is when you catch it escaping.

I mentioned in the introduction the year the routing company's sales stalled and we tried to fix it with pipeline stages and commission plans, when the rot lived three chapters back, in who we were. I will not retell it, but the one lesson that belongs here: a pipeline is a measuring instrument, not a motor. When sales are sick, the pipeline shows you where the deals die, and that is real value, but the cure is almost never "more stages." The cure lives wherever the deals are dying, and sometimes that is nowhere near the sales chapter at all.

The Pricing Conversation

To be clear about lanes: what your product should cost, how to package it, whether you charge per seat or per loaf or per project, all of that is strategy, and chapter four settled it, or at least made you face it. This section is about something smaller and somehow harder: the moment in a live conversation when a human being asks "so what does this cost?" and you have to answer with your voice.

I have watched confident, competent founders fall apart in that moment in ways they never would in a product discussion. The number comes out wrapped in apology: "so, the price, and obviously we're flexible on this, and it really depends, but roughly, and again this is negotiable, it would be somewhere around..." By the time the number lands, the founder has told the buyer four times to ignore it. Buyers listen. Every softening word is an invitation to negotiate, and worse, a signal that you doubt the price yourself. If you doubt it, why on earth would they believe it?

The mechanics of doing it well are almost insultingly simple. Say the number in a full sentence with context on either side, then stop talking. "For your fourteen factories, the platform is 38,000 euros a year, and that includes onboarding and the audit module. Most customers see it pay for itself within the first audit cycle." Then silence. The same five-count from the discovery section, redeployed. The pause after a price feels geological. Let it. The buyer is doing arithmetic, comparing, deciding what to ask next, and every word you add while they think is a word spent negotiating against yourself. The first person to speak after a price usually concedes something. Know, at minimum, that the game has started.

Practice this out loud. I mean it. Stand in your kitchen and say your biggest price into the empty room until it sounds like a fact instead of a confession. Founders practice demos for hours and never once rehearse the twelve seconds where the money happens. The number will feel enormous to you, because you know what the product cost to build and you privately suspect you would never pay it yourself. Both feelings are irrelevant. The customer is buying the shrinkage of a problem, and if discovery did its job, you know what that problem costs them, and your price is standing next to that figure looking modest.

Story

Early in the routing company's life, a mid-sized parcel carrier, our biggest prospect by far at the time, reached the pricing moment with me. The operations director looked at my quote, let a silence happen that I now recognize as standard, and raised one eyebrow. One eyebrow. I would like to tell you he applied pressure, made threats, invoked competitors. He raised an eyebrow, and I said, "Of course, for a partner like you we could look at something closer to..." and gave away forty percent. Unprompted. He had never asked for a discount. He told me later, once we knew each other well, that he had budgeted for my full price and the eyebrow was about his coffee.

Here is what the forty percent actually cost. More than forty percent; that alone would have been survivable. The renewal anchored to the discounted price, for years. The two referrals he sent arrived expecting his pricing, because in a small industry your prices talk to each other at trade fairs. And inside my own company, the discount taught me, and later my first sales hire, that our list price was fiction, which meant every future negotiation started from fear. It took three years and one uncomfortable price increase letter to climb out of a hole I dug in four seconds to make an eyebrow go away.

The rule I carved into the wall afterwards: every discount is a trade. Money moves only when something moves the other way, a longer commitment, payment up front, a case study with their logo on it, a smaller scope. Trading squeezes out more margin, true, but the deeper reason is trust: trading is the only way the buyer can believe your prices. A price that collapses when an eyebrow moves was an opening bid all along, and once you have shown one opening bid, everything you say afterwards is an opening bid.

Discount requests will come regardless. Enterprise procurement sends them on schedule, through people like Priya's Falk, who ask for twenty percent the way other people ask for the time. Take it calmly: it is a ritual, the asker's bonus often depends on the concessions they extract, and your job is to let them win something you priced in advance. What matters is decoding the request, because "too expensive" is five different sentences, and your move depends on which one you heard.

Translating the pricing conversation: what they say, what it usually means, and your move
What they sayWhat it usually meansYour move
"That's more than we expected."An honest report of surprise, not a refusal. You skipped anchoring the number to the cost of their problem.Ask "compared to what?" and re-tie the price to the figures from discovery. If you never got those figures, you proposed too early.
"We don't have budget this year."Either the problem is a low priority, or the money lives in a different pot than your contact controls.Ask what would make it a priority, and who owns the pot. A real deal with a real problem often finds money mid-year; a polite one waits for a January that never comes.
"Competitor X is cheaper."Either they prefer you and need help justifying it, or you are column fodder in a comparison already decided.Ask, warmly, "then what's keeping you talking to us?" The answer tells you which of the two you are, and the buyer says your differentiators out loud.
"Can you do something about the price?" (procurement)Ritual. The asker may be scored on extracted concessions. Treat it as procedure; it is rarely about your value.Trade, never gift: a concession priced in advance, exchanged for term length, prepayment, a reference, or reduced scope. Give a reason with every number that moves.
"Just send us your best price."An invitation to bid against yourself, sometimes to make a cheaper favourite look validated.Decline the auction politely. Your price is attached to a scope; offer to adjust the scope. If they only want a number in an inbox, you have learned where you stand.
"Can we start smaller?"Often genuine: risk reduction from a buyer who wants you to win but cannot justify the full leap.Often yes, and gladly, but shrink the scope with the price, put an expansion path in writing, and beware pilots with no success criteria, which are large delays dressed as small deals.

Two more tools for the twelve seconds, both cheap. The first is options. Where the work allows it, quote three versions: a lean one, the one you recommend, and a fuller one, each with a plain sentence about who it is for. The psychologists will tell you this works as a manipulation trick, and it does, but the honest reasons are better. It changes the question in the buyer's head from "yes or no" to "which." It gives the flincher somewhere to land besides the exit. And it gives procurement a concession path that spares your margin: the discount becomes "take the lean version" instead of "take twenty percent off." The agency quoting a rebrand and the software founder quoting a rollout can both do this. The baker mostly cannot, and the baker's pricing life is simpler for it.

The second tool is payment terms, which founders forget are part of the price. Half up front for project work is a normal ask, and the customers who resent it are running a signal up a flagpole for you. Annual prepayment against a modest consideration turns a software deal into a cashflow event. Deposits on large orders separate the serious from the curious better than any qualifying question. I will not redo the runway arithmetic, chapter six already made you cry about it, but a slightly smaller number that arrives now is often worth more to a young company than a slightly larger one that arrives in ninety days, after a reminder, and a second reminder, and a phone call you dreaded making. Terms are tradeable. Trade them like they are money, because they are.

Pricing conversations happen far from enterprise too. The agency founder quoting a rebrand across a café table, and the baker naming a price for two hundred wedding pastries, face the same twelve seconds, usually with the customer physically present, which is harder. The mechanics hold. Say the number in a sentence with its context, stop talking, and when the customer flinches, resist the urge to rescue them. "I understand, it's a real investment. Shall I walk you through what's in it?" is a complete response. The flinch is part of buying. It was never an emergency.

Keeping Deals Alive Without Becoming a Pest

Between the great conversation and the signature stretches the middle of the deal, and the middle is where founder pipelines go to die quietly. No drama, no rival swooping in, no angry email. The deal just goes still, like a pond. Understand why and you can prevent it: your deal is one of your three most important things, and one of your buyer's forty-seven. The buyer means no malice. You have drifted down their list under the pressure of their actual job, and unless something specific and dated pulls the deal upward, it settles to the bottom like sand.

The single habit that prevents most of this costs nothing: never end any interaction, call, meeting, coffee, corridor chat, without a specific next step, a date, and a named owner. Not "I'll follow up in a couple of weeks," which is sand. Instead: "I'll send the revised proposal Thursday. Can we book thirty minutes Tuesday the 14th to walk through it while it's fresh?" If the buyer will not put anything on a calendar, that is information, and your pipeline should hear about it.

The proposal itself deserves a paragraph, because founders reliably misuse it. A proposal is a confirmation, not an exploration. It should contain, in the customer's own recorded words, the problem, the cost of the problem, what you will do about it, what success looks like, and the price they have already heard. Already heard: that phrase carries the whole rule. No customer should ever meet your price for the first time in a PDF. In a conversation you can watch the number land and handle what it stirs up. In a document the number lands alone, gets forwarded to people who never met you, and gets compared against things you cannot see. Say the price out loud first, always. The proposal exists so that your champion can sell you internally when you are out of the room, which is what champions do with their time. Write it for the people you have not met.

Watch out

If every relationship in a deal runs through one person, you have a hostage situation with pleasant weekly calls. Champions get reorganized, overruled, poached, and sent on parental leave. Priya spent a bad week watching her one gearbox believer polish his LinkedIn profile, with no second contact to call if he vanished. He stayed, she got lucky, and she never ran a deal single-threaded again. The fix is unglamorous: in every meeting, ask "who else should see this?" and collect introductions like the deal depends on them. Two contacts is a minimum. Three or more people who would notice if the deal died is a deal with its own pulse.

For bigger deals, the enterprise motion and the upper end of consultative, the next-step habit graduates into something more formal that earns its overhead: a shared plan. After the verbal yes, or even after a serious proposal meeting, you write one page, jointly owned, listing everything that has to happen between here and the product being live, with dates and owners on both sides. Security review, legal, signature, kickoff, training, the first real milestone. Two things make this document powerful. First, it converts "we'll get back to you" into a schedule both sides can see slipping, which makes slippage a topic instead of a mystery. Second, and better, it moves the conversation past the purchase to the outcome, and buyers who spend a meeting planning the rollout with you have, in every way that matters, already bought. Priya credits the gearbox deal's survival through procurement to one artifact: a shared timeline with the next audit date sitting at the bottom like a lighthouse, making every internal delay visibly expensive to the people causing it.

Then there is ghosting, the proposal that vanishes into silence. Here is the etiquette that preserves both the deal and your dignity. Follow up two or three times, spaced over a couple of weeks, and make each follow-up carry something: a relevant article, an answer to an open question, a customer result. Never the naked "just checking in," which asks the buyer to do your work of having a reason. If silence persists, send the closing email, which some salespeople call the breakup email: "I don't want to keep cluttering your inbox. I'm assuming this isn't a priority right now, so I'll close the file on my side. If things change, you know where I am, and I'd be glad to pick it up again." Two things happen. Often, nothing, and you have your answer and your hours back. But surprisingly often the reply arrives within the day, sometimes with an apology and a signature, because permission to say no, sincerely given, is so rare that buyers reward it. Either outcome beats month four of hopeful silence. The deadliest thing in your pipeline is the deal that neither closes nor dies, eating your attention and propping up your forecast, a zombie with a logo.

Try this

Tonight, with a pen, run the pipeline scrub. List every open deal. Next to each one, write three things: the customer's problem in their words, the agreed next step, and its date. Any deal missing one of the three gets exactly one honest email tomorrow morning to establish it. If the email gets no answer within two weeks, the deal moves to "no decision" with a reason logged. The first scrub typically shortens a founder's pipeline by a third and improves their mood by more, because a short true list beats a long flattering one in every way that pays rent.

Losing Gracefully

You will lose deals. Let me say it more precisely: if you qualify honestly and price with a spine, you should be losing deals, regularly, because a founder who wins everything is either lying to their pipeline or charging half of what the work is worth. So this section is about what losing is for. A lost deal, handled well, produces two assets: information and reputation. Handled badly, it produces a small enemy and a lesson you paid for but never collected.

Start with the moment of the no. Whatever you feel, and you will feel it in your stomach, because it is your product and your name, the reply is short and warm: thank them for the time, congratulate the choice if a competitor won, and leave the door visibly open. Do not argue with the corpse. Rebutting a decision already made has never once reversed one, and it converts a neutral outcome into a story the buyer tells about you at dinner. The vendor they chose this year may stumble next year, and when it does they will remember exactly one losing vendor: the gracious one or the bitter one, whichever you decided to be in a five-line email you wrote in four minutes.

Then, once the sting settles, ask for the debrief. Wait a week or two, outside the rejection thread, and frame it as a favor between professionals rather than a plea: "We're a small company and we learn the hard way. Would you give me fifteen minutes to hear honestly why we didn't win? No selling, I promise." Perhaps half will say yes, and what they tell you is worth more than most consulting you could buy, with one warning: treat the first stated reason as a curtain. "It came down to price" is the polite exit, because price is a no that needs no further conversation. Ask one gentle question behind it, "if the prices had been identical, who would have won?", and watch the real reason step out: they never quite believed a six-person company could support them, the other side knew their industry's jargon, the IT director had a preference all along and the process was theater. Log every reason. Six months of logged loss reasons will tell you more about your product, positioning, and pitch than any strategy offsite, and in the customer's voice.

Remember, too, that your most common loss will have no winner at all. "No decision," the buyer keeping the spreadsheet and the sighing, deserves its own postmortem question, because the polite explanation, "the timing wasn't right," hides a diagnosis you need. A no-decision loss usually means the pain was real but you never made the cost of doing nothing concrete enough to beat the effort of changing. That is a discovery failure, months old by the time it surfaces. Logging it as "timing" teaches you nothing; logging it as "never quantified the do-nothing cost" changes how you run the next first meeting.

And sometimes, be the one who ends it. The graceful loss has a proactive cousin: the graceful withdrawal. When discovery reveals a poor fit, a problem your product only half solves, a fantasy timeline, the strongest move is to say so and step back, ideally pointing them somewhere useful. It costs you a deal you were going to lose anyway, slowly and expensively, and it buys you the rarest asset in any market: the reputation of a seller whose yes means yes. People remember the vendor who talked them out of a purchase. They come back years later, with better problems, and they bring their friends.

Story

The same spring the gearbox deal was crawling through procurement, Priya lost a different deal, a mid-sized automotive supplier, to a competitor four times her size. The buyer, a quality director named Anneke, picked up the phone to tell her, which buyers almost never do, and Priya, exhausted and briefly free of strategic ambition, answered with plain honesty: thanks for calling, good choice given your global footprint, and one piece of unsolicited advice about migrating certificates out of the old system. Then a two-line note the next morning wishing them a smooth rollout. Total investment: one phone call she did not enjoy and an email.

Two winters later, Anneke changed jobs, as ambitious quality directors do. Her new employer had the same document chaos and no vendor. She ran no comparison this time. She called Priya directly, opened with "you were so decent when we didn't pick you," and closed in five weeks at full list price. Priya, who tracks everything now, tells founders that her single highest-converting pipeline source, measured over years, is people who told her no the first time. Buyers move. Their memory of how you lost moves with them.

Which brings us back, finally, to Stuttgart. The gearbox deal closed in month nine, and closing looked nothing like the movies. Three factories instead of fourteen, a pilot scoped around the audit calendar, with expansion criteria written into the contract in plain language. Falk got his discount, four percent, traded against a three-year term and a reference visit, and seemed as satisfied with the ritual as with the result. Priya survived the security questionnaire with a freelance consultant and two long evenings. And the head of quality, her champion, stood up in the final meeting and presented the business case himself, from her proposal, in his own words, which by then were also her words, because she had taken them down in a notebook in the meeting where she finally stopped demoing. Priya called me afterwards, from what I choose to believe was the same parking garage. "They signed," she said, and then, before I could ask anything: "Three factories, signature verified, first invoice sent, and I know exactly why they bought." That is the sentence. The whole chapter in one breath, and she got there in nine months, which beat my own pace by roughly four years.

You Will Not Be the Only Salesperson Forever

Everything in this chapter assumes it is you on the calls, you writing the proposals, you saying the number into the silence. That season ends, and it should. A point will come, usually once selling competes with everything else for your calendar and loses, when the company needs salespeople beyond you, and a machine around them: hiring profiles, ramp plans, territories, commission structures that reward the behavior you actually want. That is chapter fourteen's territory, and I will not poach it. The general craft of hiring anyone at all is chapter ten, which is conveniently next.

But there is one thing you must do now, during the founder-selling season, because no future chapter can do it retroactively: write it down. Every time you notice what works, capture it somewhere unglamorous. The discovery questions that open people up. The exact phrases customers use for their problems, in their dialects, by industry. The objections that recur and the answers that landed. The loss reasons, logged. The stage definitions and their evidence. The pricing lines you rehearsed in your kitchen. None of it needs to be a manual yet; a running document with a terrible title will do. I called mine "sales stuff.doc" for six years. When the day comes to hire your first salesperson, that document is the difference between handing over a craft and handing over a hope. The founders who skip it stand behind their first sales hire six months in, wondering why the magic failed to transfer, never realizing the magic lived nowhere but their own reflexes.

And here is the quiet gift of doing this phase properly, the one nobody mentions at networking events. Founder-led selling is the last time you will be this close to your market with this little in between. No reports, no dashboards summarizing summaries, no account manager's interpretation. Just you, a notebook, and customer after customer telling you, in their own words, what your company is actually for. Some of what they tell you belongs in this chapter's pipeline. Some belongs three chapters back, in what you sell and who you are. Take the notes either way. Out there, closing deals, you are also running the cheapest, most honest market research your company will ever get, at the only moment in its life when the person hearing the answers can act on all of them.

The Short Version

  • You are the sales department, and for now you should be: early selling produces learning first and revenue second, and both die if you outsource the conversations. Scaling a sales team is chapter fourteen's problem.
  • "They loved it" is weather. A deal moves on specifics: a date, a name, a number, a new stakeholder, a question about implementation. Listen for those and discount the rest.
  • Pick the sales motion your deal size can afford, and notice when a deal from a different row walks in. An enterprise deal is a different animal that happens to eat the same food.
  • Discovery before demo, always. Verify misery, money, mandate, and moment, in the customer's own words, and write the words down verbatim. Their words close deals; yours decorate them.
  • Ask the question, then shut up. The real answer arrives around second four of the silence you were about to smother.
  • A pipeline is a list of people with a problem, a budget, and a date, where every stage is earned by customer evidence rather than your activity. Your biggest competitor in it is doing nothing.
  • Say the price in a full sentence, then stop talking. Rehearse it out loud until it sounds like a fact. The first person to speak after the number usually concedes.
  • Discounts are traded, never gifted. A price that collapses at a raised eyebrow was an opening bid all along, and it anchors every renewal, referral, and negotiation that follows.
  • End every interaction with a next step, a date, and an owner, and kill zombie deals with a clean breakup email. A short true pipeline beats a long flattering one.
  • Lose on purpose and lose warmly: log the real reason behind the polite one, and treat every graceful loss as a deposit. Buyers change jobs, and their memory of your no travels with them.

Chapter 10

Hiring People

The day you hire your first employee, you stop being someone who does the work and start being someone other people bet their mortgage on. Nobody tells you these are different jobs.

Marta called me on a Sunday evening, which was unusual, because Marta guards her Sundays the way other people guard their PIN codes.

"Third one," she said, before I had finished saying hello. "Third resignation in five months. Lena handed me her letter on Friday and I have spent the whole weekend pretending I don't know why."

At the time, Marta's design agency was about fourteen people. She had built it from her spare bedroom into one of those studios that wins the kind of awards other studios pretend not to care about. And for five months, her designers had been leaving. Every exit conversation produced the same phrase, personal reasons, delivered with the same careful eye contact, the kind people make when they have rehearsed not saying something.

"So why are they leaving?" I asked.

There was a long pause. I could hear her kitchen tap running, then stopping.

"Viktor," she said.

Viktor was her best designer. I want to be precise about this, because the story falls apart if you round him down: he was uncomfortably good. Marta had hired him two years earlier, when the agency was twelve people and drowning in work, and he had walked in with a portfolio that made her a little dizzy and a salary demand she met without negotiating. Clients asked for him by name. A rebrand he led won the agency its biggest award, the one that sat on the shelf by the entrance so that everyone saw it on their way in.

He was also, and it took Marta two years to say this out loud to anyone including herself, corrosive. He rolled his eyes in critiques. He rewrote juniors' work at two in the morning and shipped it to clients without telling them, so they found out in the meeting, in front of everyone. He took the best projects the way weather takes a coastline, gradually, then obviously. To clients and to Marta he was warm, funny, generous with his time. The charm pointed up and out. The corrosion pointed down and in. That is the classic configuration, by the way.

"He is my best designer," Marta said. "If he leaves, I lose the award work. Two clients would probably follow him out the door."

"What did the three who left cost you?" I asked. "Not emotionally. In euros. Recruiting, onboarding, the projects that slipped, the clients who noticed the new faces. Run the number."

She ran the number. I will tell you what it was, and what she did about Viktor, near the end of this chapter, because the end of the hiring story is where Viktor belongs. But I am telling you the beginning now, up front, for a reason. Every hiring mistake in this chapter, and I have made most of them myself, grows from the same root: deciding what you want after you have already met someone, instead of before. Marta hired a portfolio, and the problem came free with it.

This chapter is about employees: finding them, choosing them, landing them, and, when it comes to that, saying goodbye to them like a decent human being. If your question is about cofounders and equity, that is chapter five, and please keep the two apart, because a cofounder is a marriage. If your question is about what all these people should report into once you have them, that is chapter eleven. And if you have not yet worked out what your company actually values, the raw material every hiring decision is secretly made of, that is chapter one, and it is cheaper to read it before your first job ad than after your fifth exit interview.

The Most Expensive Sentence in Your Company

The most expensive sentence in your company is "we need someone."

It sounds like progress. You usually say it late in the evening, after the third week in a row of doing invoices at midnight, and it arrives with a warm feeling of maturity, the sense that the business has grown up enough to need staff. Everyone around the table nods. Someone opens a job board. And at that moment, with the best intentions in the world, you have started the process most founders do worse than anything else they do.

Here is the uncomfortable arithmetic. A hire in most of Europe will cost you, all in, somewhere between 1.3 and 1.8 times their gross salary once you count employer contributions, insurance, equipment, software seats, and the desk they sit at. A 45,000 euro salary is a 65,000 euro decision, per year, before they have produced anything. A mediocre hire produces some value against that. A wrong hire produces negative value: their salary, plus your time managing them, plus the work you redo, plus the customers they handle averagely, plus, and nobody budgets this part, the effect on the people around them. The research bounces around, but every founder I know who has run their own numbers lands in the same range: a bad hire costs one to two times their annual salary, and a badly handled bad hire costs more, because the handling is where the collateral damage lives.

Now the other side of the ledger, because the arithmetic should frighten you into hiring well rather than scare you off hiring at all. A good hire is the single highest-leverage purchase available to a small business. Not software, not ads, not a rebrand. A person who is right for the job you actually have will return multiples of their cost, year after year, and will make your next three hires better, because good people are the best recruiting asset ever invented. In a ten-person company, the gap between a good hire and a bad one is the difference between a good year and a lawyer.

Which brings us to the strange fact at the center of this chapter: hiring is the highest-stakes skill in your company, and the skill you have practiced least. You have been a customer thousands of times, so sales feels familiar. You have managed your own money your whole life, so the finance chapter at least rhymes with experience. But most first-time founders have been hired a handful of times and have hired nobody, ever. You formed your entire mental model of recruitment on the other side of the table, trying to be liked. It points exactly backwards for the job you are about to do.

So we are going to build the skill properly, in the order the decisions arrive: what to hire for, how to define it, how to select for it, how to land the person, how to make their first months work, and what to do when, despite all of it, you got it wrong.

What to Hire First: Follow the Drain, Not the Dream

Ask a founder what their first hire should be and you will usually hear a title from a company five times their size. A marketing manager. A developer to build the platform. Once, at a founder dinner, a head of people, for a company that consisted of two people, both of them at the dinner.

Titles are the wrong starting point. The right starting point is an audit of your own week, and it works like this. Take everything you did in the last month and sort it into three piles. Pile one: things only you can do, because they need your authority, your relationships, or your particular skill. Pile two: things you are good at and enjoy, but that someone else could learn. Pile three: things that drain you, that you do badly, that get done late at night or not at all, and that the business genuinely needs.

Your first hire almost always lives in pile three, and this is where founders flinch, because pile three is boring. It is the invoices, the scheduling, the customer emails, the production work that has become routine, the quote follow-ups from chapter nine that never happen because you hate doing them. Nobody dreams of hiring for pile three. It feels like spending precious money on the dull part of the business. But look at what pile three is doing to you: it is consuming the hours you should spend on pile one, and pile one is where you build the company's future. Your first hire exists to buy back the founder's best hours, currently the most misallocated resource in the company.

There is a second flinch, which sounds like this: "by the time I explain it, I could have done it myself." True, for the first month. Ruinous afterwards. That sentence, repeated weekly, is how founders end up at year four doing the same pile-three work at midnight, except now with fifteen employees waiting on their bottleneck. If you catch that sentence coming out of your mouth often, the deeper problem is delegation, and delegation gets its own treatment in chapter twelve. Here I will just say: the explaining is the hire. It converts knowledge that lives only in your head into something the company owns, and it pays rent forever.

One more thing about the first hire, and it is the emotional part nobody warns you about. The day their contract starts, the weight changes. Until now, if the business had a terrible quarter, you ate pasta and pushed through. Now a terrible quarter has someone else's rent in it. Every founder I know remembers their first payroll run the way they remember their first customer. It is a wonderful, sobering feeling, and you should let it sober you, because it is also the correct amount of seriousness for every hire after this one. You are making a promise about the future of the company to someone who will build their life partly on your judgement. Check your runway math from chapter six before you make that promise, not after. The kindest thing you can do for a future employee is to hire them only when you can carry them through a year of bad news.

A practical European note before we go further, because the first-hire decision has more settings than on and off. Between "just me" and "an employment contract" sits a whole staircase that founders on this continent underuse in one direction and overuse in the other. A freelancer for two days a week, a payroll company that carries the formal employment so you can postpone the paperwork, a part-time contract, a fixed-term year: all of these let you buy back pile three while the revenue is still wobbly, and several let you and a person try each other out honestly before either of you signs anything long. My brother-in-law Jonas, the baker you met in chapter four, staffed his second bakery almost entirely this way for the first year, weekend students and one semi-retired baker on Tuesdays, and converted the ones who fit. The underuse: founders who think hiring means a permanent full-time contract or nothing, and so hire nothing for two years too long. The overuse is its mirror: founders who keep a person on rolling freelance terms for three years because commitment frightens them, while the person does the job of an employee, waits for a promise, and eventually accepts one from someone else. The staircase is for climbing. Use the lower steps to learn, then commit like you mean it, because the best people can tell a company that is being careful from a company that is keeping its options open at their expense.

And one more fear to name, because it sits under more bad first hires than anyone admits: the fear of hiring someone better than you. It usually disguises itself as budget prudence, "we cannot afford someone that senior," but you can hear the real note underneath, which is "what is my job, if she is better at this than me." Get over it as fast as you can. In a small company, every hire who is merely a diluted copy of the founder lowers the average. The entire game, and I mean this arithmetically, is to hire people who raise it, people you will learn from, people who make you slightly nervous in the interview for the right reasons. At the routing company, things turned the year I hired two people who were plainly better than me at their jobs and, after a wobble I am not proud of, got out of their way. Your job, increasingly, is to assemble people who outclass you at theirs, and if that sentence unsettles you, fold the corner of this page and read chapter twelve when the unsettling gets loud.

Hire for the Company You Are, Not the One in Your Head

Now the mistake I own, in its purest form, so you can recognize its shape.

Story

At the routing company, when we were eight people, I hired a sales director from a large logistics corporate. Let's call him Maarten. Maarten had twenty years of experience, a suit that fit properly, and a way of saying "go-to-market motion" that made me feel like we had already succeeded. In the interviews, I basked in Maarten instead of assessing him. His big-logistics CV walked in ahead of him and did the interviewing for me, a halo so bright I mistook it for evidence. He described the sales organization he would build, with account tiers and a partner channel and quarterly business reviews, and I saw the company I dreamed of becoming, and I hired the dream.

Maarten lasted seven months, and I want to be fair to him: he did nothing wrong except believe me. I had sold him the same imaginary company he had sold me. He arrived expecting a marketing department to feed him leads. We had a shared inbox. He expected an assistant, a travel budget, a CRM with data in it. We had a spreadsheet named FINAL_v3. The job we actually needed done, driving to mid-sized haulage firms and drinking coffee with sceptical planning managers until one of them said yes, was a job he had not done himself in fifteen years and, reasonably enough, did not want to do again. He left politely. The polite ones hurt more. It cost us about a year of sales momentum and, I later worked out, roughly 130,000 euros, and every cent of it was me paying for the difference between the company I ran and the company I described in the interview.

Hire experienced people all you like. Just know that every hire is a fit between a person and a company, and you only get the fit right if you are honest about which company is doing the hiring. Not the one in the pitch deck. Not the one in three years. The one that shows up on Monday, with its shared inbox and its spreadsheet named FINAL_v3.

Being the company you are cuts in two directions, and both matter.

First, it changes who you look for. A ten-person company needs the person who built the function the last time it was this size, or who is hungry to build it for the first time and has the raw material. The person who ran the function at scale solves a different problem than the one you have. Building means deciding with no data, doing the work yourself, and living with the consequences at close range. Running means optimizing a machine someone else built. The skills differ in kind, not degree. When you interview someone from a big company, the most predictive question I know is embarrassingly simple: "tell me, concretely, what you did yourself, with your own hands, in the last month of your current job." Some big-company people have excellent answers. Many discover, live, in front of you, that the honest answer is "attended meetings about work other people did." Better everyone finds out now.

Second, it changes how you sell the job, because make no mistake, you are selling, and everything you learned about honest discovery in chapter nine applies to this pipeline too. The temptation is to compensate for your smallness by borrowing glamour: unlimited growth, huge impact, we're like a family. Resist all of it, especially the family one. Families cannot fire each other and you can, so it is a lie with a delayed detonation. What a small company can honestly offer is specific and, to the right person, valuable: real responsibility from week one, the absence of politics because there is nobody to politick with, direct sight of the customer and the consequences, learning at a speed no corporate can match, and proximity to the founder, which is either a perk or a warning depending on the founder. Say those things, and say the hard parts too. "The salary is decent but not corporate. Some weeks are chaotic. The coffee machine is a kettle." The candidates this loses were going to leave in month four anyway. The candidates it wins arrive with their eyes open, and eyes-open people stay.

Warning

The most dangerous moment in early hiring is when a candidate is impressive in a way that has nothing to do with the job. A famous employer on the CV, a fluent way with strategy words, a portfolio with an award in it. Impressiveness is a feeling in you. Every time you catch yourself feeling flattered that this person would even talk to your little company, treat it as a fire alarm: you have stopped assessing and started courting.

The Scorecard: Decide What Good Looks Like Before You Meet Anyone

Everything in this chapter hangs off one discipline: write down what success in the role looks like before you meet a single candidate. On paper. In sentences. Agreed by everyone who will interview.

The document is called a scorecard. A job description lists activities: "manage customer inquiries, maintain the CRM, support the sales team." A scorecard defines outcomes: "by month twelve, customers get a first response within four hours and our renewal rate is back above ninety percent." Feel the difference? A job description is a list of ways to be busy. A scorecard is a definition of done. People can perform activities beautifully for years without producing outcomes, and an interview process built on the job description selects for people who are good at describing activities. Which is to say: good at interviews.

A scorecard has four parts, and fits on one page.

The mission of the role, in one sentence a smart outsider would understand. "Own the customer success function" fails that test. "Make sure the customers we worked so hard to win actually succeed, notice it, and stay" passes it. If you cannot write this sentence, you need an afternoon of thinking before you need a hire, and it will be the cheapest afternoon of your year.

Three to five outcomes, each measurable or at least observable, each with a rough date. These are the results you will hold the person to, and they are what you build your interview around. You stop asking "is this person impressive" and start asking "will this person produce these five outcomes in this company." Different question, different answers.

Behaviours, drawn from the values you actually hold, the real ones from chapter one rather than the poster ones. Three or four, phrased so concretely that you could point at a moment in a workday and say "that, that is the behaviour." "Team player" points at nothing. "When they finish their own work early, they look for who is drowning" points at something you can watch happen.

Deal-breakers, stated in advance, because deal-breakers decided in advance get enforced, and deal-breakers decided in the moment get negotiated away by charm. Marta had no written deal-breakers when she met Viktor. She has them now. The first one reads: "no one gets hired who is rude to anyone we are not paying them to be nice to."

The one-page scorecard, filled in for a real role: first customer-facing hire at a small software company
SectionWhat you writeExample
MissionOne sentence: why does this role exist?Make sure the customers we win actually succeed with the product, notice that they are succeeding, and renew.
Outcome 1Measurable, datedBy month 3: every inbound customer question gets a first response within 4 working hours, without founder involvement.
Outcome 2Measurable, datedBy month 6: a written onboarding path exists; new customers reach first value within 14 days instead of the current 40.
Outcome 3Measurable, datedBy month 12: renewal rate above 90%, and we hear about at-risk customers from this person before the customer tells us.
Outcome 4ObservableProduct team receives a monthly summary of the ten most painful customer problems, ranked, with evidence.
Behaviours3 to 4, concrete, from your real valuesWrites things down so others can find them. Tells customers the truth even when the truth is "we broke it." When their own queue is empty, looks for who is drowning.
Deal-breakersDecided before you meet anyoneRude to anyone they don't need to impress. Blames the previous employer for everything. Cannot describe a mistake of their own with any specificity.

Two practical notes. First, share the outcomes with the candidate in the final round. It is astonishing how clarifying this is in both directions. Strong candidates lean in and start asking sharp questions about outcome two. Weak candidates get vague, or start renegotiating the outcomes before they have the job. Both reactions are data you cannot buy any other way. Second, keep the scorecard after you hire. It becomes the spine of onboarding, the agenda of your first quarterly review, and, if things go wrong, the honest reference point for the conversation in the last section of this chapter. One page, working that hard, is the best deal in management.

Try this

Take the next hire you are considering, or the last one you made, and write the scorecard for it now, from memory, in twenty minutes: mission, three outcomes with dates, three behaviours, two deal-breakers. If you are currently hiring and you cannot fill it in, pause the vacancy until you can. If you wrote it for an existing employee and realized they are meeting it, tell them so this week. If you realized they are not, the last section of this chapter is waiting for you, but read the onboarding section first, because the gap is sometimes yours.

Interviews That Predict Instead of Charm

Here is the dirty secret of the standard job interview: it measures the ability to be interviewed. A real skill. Just not the one you are paying for, unless you are hiring interviewers.

Researchers have studied the unstructured interview, the friendly hour of "tell me about yourself" and "where do you see yourself in five years," for decades, and the results humiliate everyone: it predicts job performance barely better than chance, while leaving every interviewer certain they are the exception. The mechanics of the failure are worth understanding, because you cannot fix what you cannot see. In an unstructured conversation, you form an impression in the first few minutes, mostly from confidence, fluency, and similarity to yourself. Then you spend the rest of the hour, without noticing, gathering evidence for that impression and letting go of evidence against it. The candidate, meanwhile, answers hypothetical questions with hypothetical answers, describing what they know they should say instead of what they do. Everyone knows the right answer to "are you a team player." Interviews built on hypotheticals select for people who know the right answers. Viktor, Marta will tell you, gave a magnificent interview.

An interview is a prediction you will have to live with, made under charming conditions.

The fix is structure, and structure means three things: every candidate for a role gets the same core questions, the questions are about the past instead of the hypothetical future, and every interviewer scores the answers against the scorecard the same day, before anyone talks and averages their impressions into mush. Structured interviews are less fun. They are also, in study after study and in every honest founder's experience, far better at predicting who will actually do the job. You are running a small business, not a talk show. Optimize for prediction.

Ask about the past

The single biggest upgrade available to you costs nothing: replace every hypothetical question with a behavioural one. "How would you handle an angry customer" becomes "tell me about the last angry customer you dealt with. What did they say? What did you do? What happened?" The past has texture that invention cannot fake. Someone who has really talked a furious customer down remembers the specifics, the ugly first email, the thing they got wrong themselves, the exact sentence that turned it. Someone improvising gives you a tidy story with a moral, and the introduction taught you to distrust tidy stories with morals in business books, so distrust them in interviews too.

Then, and this is where the prediction actually happens, follow up. Once is a story; the follow-up is the truth. "What was the hardest part?" "What did your colleague think you got wrong?" "What would the customer say about it, if I called them?" Three follow-ups deep, prepared answers run out and you meet the actual person. You are listening for specificity, for the presence of other people in the story as humans rather than props, and for ownership, the difference between "the project failed because the client kept changing scope" and "I let the client keep changing scope because I hated the confrontation." The second candidate has a flaw and knows it. The first one has the same flaw and will bring it to work for you, unexamined.

Questions that charm versus questions that predict
What charms (skip it)What predicts (ask this instead)What you are listening for
"What are your strengths and weaknesses?""Tell me about the last serious critical feedback you received. What exactly was it, and what did you change?"Specificity, and whether they changed anything. "I care too much" means they have never really been told anything, or never listened.
"Where do you see yourself in five years?""Walk me through last Tuesday at work, hour by hour."What the person actually does all day, told in a register that is very hard to fake. Also whether they do the work or coordinate it.
"How would you handle a conflict with a colleague?""Tell me about a colleague you found genuinely difficult. What did you try? How did it end?"Whether other people appear in the story as humans. Whether every villain in their career had the same face, which is a pattern about the narrator.
"Why do you want to work here?""What did you do to prepare for this conversation?"Effort under their own steam. The candidate who used your product, read your site, and arrived with two sharp questions just showed you their working style for free.
"Are you comfortable with responsibility?""Tell me about a decision you made that was yours alone, that went wrong. What did it cost, and who did you tell?"Ownership. Whether they can hold a mistake without flinching or forwarding the blame.
"Would you say you're a self-starter?""Tell me about something you built, fixed, or organized that nobody asked you to."Whether initiative is a fact of their history or a word in their vocabulary.

The work sample: watch them do the job, briefly, and pay for it

Talking about work predicts work moderately well. Doing work predicts it far better, which is why the work sample is the strongest tool in your process, and the most abused one, so let me give you both halves.

The strong version: design a small, realistic slice of the actual job, two to four hours, doable at home or in a session with you. For a designer, a rough concept for a real brief you have already shipped, so you can compare. For a customer role: here are five real, anonymized customer emails, answer three. For a developer, a small task in a codebase like yours, followed by a conversation about their choices, and the conversation is the point, because "why did you do it this way" teaches you more than the code itself. For a baker, and I checked this with Jonas: a morning shift, paid, watching how they treat the dough, the floor, and the seventeen-year-old apprentice, roughly in ascending order of importance.

The abused version, which candidates rightly resent and which will poison your reputation in exactly the small communities you recruit from: a vague, sprawling assignment that takes a weekend, on a live problem you actually need solved, unpaid. Do not do this. Keep samples short, keep them separate from real deliverables or pay for the time, a hundred euros and an invoice is nothing against the cost of a wrong hire, and always, always give real feedback afterwards, both directions. The way you run your work sample is the first sample of you that the candidate gets. Strong candidates are assessing you right back, and they talk to each other.

Deciding: score first, talk second

However good your questions are, the decision meeting can still dissolve everything into soup, and it dissolves in a specific way. The interviewers gather, the most senior or most confident person speaks first, "I really liked her," and every impression in the room bends toward that opening verdict. Twenty minutes later the group has manufactured a consensus that nobody individually held, and the scorecard sits unopened on the table like a decorative napkin.

The countermeasure takes ten minutes of discipline. Everyone who interviewed writes down their scores against the scorecard, outcome by outcome, behaviour by behaviour, with one piece of evidence per score, before anyone says a word to anyone. Then you compare. The numbers are rough. The divergences are the treasure: when one interviewer scored "tells customers the truth" a five and another scored it a two, somewhere in those two interviews is a contradiction worth digging into, and that digging is exactly the conversation the decision meeting exists to have. Small companies wave this ritual off as corporate overkill. They have it backwards. A corporate can absorb a mis-hire in the roundings. For you, one wrong yes is two percent of the whole company.

While I am here, let me take one beloved heuristic outside and deal with it: the airport test, "would I want to be stuck in an airport with this person." I understand its appeal, and I want you to notice what it actually measures, which is similarity to you. Same jokes, same references, same background, same schools. Hire by airport test for three years and you will look up from your desk into a room of your own reflections, agreeing with each other, sharing your blind spots in stereo. The team that wins is the one where the detail-obsessed pessimist, the charging optimist, and the person who asks the awkward question in the quiet voice all have a seat, and all get listened to. That team would probably drive each other mad in an airport. What they need to share is the values on the scorecard and the standard of the work. Everything else, and I say this with love, is you recruiting drinking company on the payroll.

References: the phone call founders skip

Reference checks have a terrible reputation because most people do them terribly: a dutiful call to two names the candidate supplied, "would you recommend them," "oh yes," goodbye. Conducted like that, skip them, you will learn nothing. Conducted properly, they are twenty of the highest-value minutes in your whole process, because a former manager on the phone will tell you things no interview can surface.

Three upgrades. First, ask the candidate, in the interview, "when I call your last manager, what will they say was your biggest weakness?" Watch the answer, then compare it with the actual call. The gap between the two measures self-awareness, the trait that predicts whether someone can grow. Second, on the call, never ask yes-or-no questions. Ask "what should I know about how to manage them well?" and "in which situations do they struggle?" and then be quiet and let the silence work, exactly like the discovery calls in chapter nine. Third, listen for temperature. Almost no European referee will say anything damning on the record; employment culture and, in some countries, the law lean against it. But enthusiasm is unmistakable and its absence is deafening. "They were fine. Reliable. Yes, fine," delivered flat, from someone who managed a person for three years, is a red flag wearing a beige coat.

Field note

Know what you may not ask. Across the EU, questions about pregnancy, family plans, health, religion, orientation, and age are off limits in interviews, and rightly so. Beyond legality, every one of those questions is a bad prediction tool anyway: none of them tells you whether this person will hit the outcomes on your scorecard. If a line of questioning would not change a correct hiring decision, it has no business in the room.

The Funnel Is Honest Even When You Are Not

Hiring is a pipeline, exactly like the sales pipeline in chapter nine, and it deserves the same honesty about its leaks. Founders misjudge two things about it: how many candidates the top requires, and how fast the good ones move through the middle. Both misjudgements are expensive, so here is a realistic funnel for a decent role at a small, unknown company, with the leaks labelled the way they actually happen.

Three lessons live in that picture. The first is about the top: one hundred applications sounds like abundance until you watch the funnel eat it, so put real effort into where the vacancy travels. Your own customers, your suppliers, the good people your team used to work with, the small professional communities where your kind of work gets discussed. A personal note from a founder outperforms a job-board posting by an order of magnitude, and referrals from your best people outperform everything, because good people rarely recommend someone who will embarrass them.

A word about the ad itself, because the ad is the first filter in the machine, and most job ads maximize exactly the wrong thing: application volume. An ad optimized for fit does three unfashionable things. It describes the actual week rather than the aspirational function: "you will spend mornings answering customer email, and Thursday is invoice day" costs you the candidates who wanted the title without the Tuesdays. It prints the salary range, which half of small-company ads in Europe still refuse to do, out of some inherited poker instinct, and which pay-transparency rules are settling for everyone anyway. Printing the range deletes the single biggest leak in your funnel before it happens, spares everyone the mutual embarrassment of discovering a 20,000 euro gap in call three, and signals, at zero cost, that you are a company that says true things. And it ends with one small, specific request, "tell us in three sentences about something you fixed that was not your job to fix," which costs a good candidate two minutes and removes the carpet-bombers who send the same application to forty companies before lunch. Marta's ads run two hundred words, contain a sentence about the worst part of each job, and she swears by the effect: fewer applications, and twice the density of real ones.

The second lesson is speed. Look at the leak on the work sample stage. The best candidates, the ones with options, move through the market in two or three weeks, and every silent day between your stages reads to them as a preview of working for you. A small company cannot outbid a corporate, but it can outrun one. Corporates take six weeks and four committees to make an offer. You can meet someone on Tuesday, run the work sample Thursday, take references Friday, and make an offer with a heartfelt phone call inside a week. Speed, decisiveness, and warmth are the small company's recruiting superpowers. Use all three.

The third lesson is the one founders resist: if nobody survives the funnel, run it again. The most expensive words after "we need someone" are "let's just take the best of the three we saw." The best of a weak field is a weak hire with a rosette on it. An empty seat costs you overtime. A wrong hire costs you the seat, the salary, the redo, and a piece of the team's trust in your judgement. Between a vacancy and a doubt, choose the vacancy.

The First Ten Hires, in the Order the Pain Arrives

People ask me for a hiring roadmap the way they ask for a workout plan, hoping the plan will do the lifting. So let me give you one, with the same disclaimer a good trainer gives: this is the typical shape, and your body will disagree with parts of it. The sequence below is what I have seen work across software companies, agencies, and, with the job titles translated, bakeries. Pain makes it a sequence: each hire answers the pain the previous hires created or exposed.

The first ten hires: typical sequence, what each unlocks, and the classic mistake at each step
#The hire, typicallyWhat it buys youThe classic mistake
1An all-rounder in the core work itself: a developer, a designer, a baker, a consultant. Does the thing customers pay for.The founder's best hours back, and proof the work can be done by someone who is not you.Hiring a manager or a strategist before there is anyone to manage or any doers to strategize for.
2Your opposite. If you are product-shaped, someone customer-facing. If you sell all day, someone who builds.Coverage of the half of the business you have been doing badly at midnight.Hiring a second you, because interviews with people like you are so pleasant. Two of you is one blind spot with two salaries.
3 and 4More hands in the core work. Capacity, plainly.The ability to say yes to demand without the quality wobbling. Redundancy, so one flu no longer stops the company.Skipping ahead to exotic specialists while the core work is still understaffed and everyone is quietly burning out.
5Operations and administration: invoicing, scheduling, contracts, the inbox. Often part-time at first.An enormous, embarrassing amount of founder time. Most founders report this is the hire they wish they had made a year earlier.Treating it as a junior catch-all and paying accordingly. A great operations person is a multiplier on everyone else.
6Customer care ownership: support, success, aftercare, whatever your world calls keeping promises after the sale.Retention stops depending on the founder's guilty Sunday evenings. Renewals and repeat business become someone's actual job.Waiting until churn is visible in the annual numbers. By then you have been leaking for a year.
7The first junior, and ideally the first hire selected mostly by someone other than you.Cheap capacity, fresh eyes, and a test of whether your team can teach, which is a test of whether you have a company or a group of freelancers with one payroll.Hiring juniors before anyone has time to train them, which is how you turn a promising 23-year-old into a demoralized one.
8A specialist aimed at your most chronic pain: the tax mess, the marketing you keep not doing, the technical debt.Depth where the generalists have hit their ceiling.Choosing the specialty by fashion rather than by pain. You need the specialist for your bottleneck, not the one your competitor just announced on LinkedIn.
9Often, around now, the first person with coordination in their role, a senior who runs projects or a shift.You stop being the only router of information, which by now costs you entire days.Minting a manager title without changing anything else. What structure that person needs around them is chapter eleven's whole subject.
10The hire that replaces a founder job entirely: the first salesperson who is not you, or the production lead who owns quality.The company begins to exist independently of your daily presence, which is the beginning of everything in Part IV.Making this hire number two instead of number ten, before there is a company for them to run their part of. See Maarten, above.

Notice what is missing from the list before number eight or nine: anyone whose job is mainly to think about work rather than do it. In a company of this size, everyone touches the actual product or the actual customer, including you. Notice also the quiet milestone hiding at number seven, the first hire you did not personally select. That is the moment hiring stops being your craft and starts being your company's craft, and it deserves more ceremony than it gets. Write down how you hire, the scorecard discipline, the structured questions, the work sample, the reference calls, and teach it like you would teach any other process you care about. Otherwise every interviewer in your company reverts to the talk-show format on their first solo flight, because that is the format television taught us all.

One honest caveat about sequence, in the spirit of the introduction: you will not follow it exactly, and you should not. A bakery needs hire number three before hire number two. An agency lives and dies by number six earlier than a software company does. The table maps the typical terrain, and, as with everything in this book, when the map and your terrain disagree, believe the terrain. What I will defend at any dinner table is the underlying rule: hire against pain you can point at today, never against an org chart you drew for the company you might be in three years. Growth-story hiring is how funded startups burn their runway, and how unfunded ones burn their founders.

Onboarding: The Ninety Days You Already Paid For

Here is a number that should bother you more than it does: a large share of new hires decide within their first few months whether they will stay long-term, and the biggest factor in that decision is whether anyone seemed ready for them. Bigger than salary. Bigger than workload. And here is the founder's confession that goes with it: by the time the new person walks in, you have spent weeks on the search, you are exhausted by hiring, and the vacancy pain the hire was meant to fix is screaming louder than ever. So the strongest temptation in this entire chapter is to point the new person at the pile and go back to your own pile. Which is roughly like training for a marathon and then, on race morning, deciding you have already done the hard part.

Story

Marta learned onboarding from a designer named Inge, who quit in week three. Inge was, by every signal in the process, an excellent hire. On her first morning, the studio was in full deadline crisis. Her laptop had not arrived. Nobody had decided which projects were hers. Marta, mortified, waved her toward a spare desk and said the sentence she still quotes at herself, in a bad falsetto: "just look around and settle in, we'll do everything properly next week." Next week was the pitch. The week after was the rework from the pitch. Inge spent three weeks guessing what her job was, asking questions of people visibly too busy to answer them, redesigning a menu nobody had asked for because it was the only work she could find, and concluding, reasonably, that the chaos was the company. Her resignation email was two sentences and one of them was kind.

What Marta built afterwards is almost embarrassingly simple, and she has used it for every hire since. A one-page plan, written before the person's first day, with four lines on it: what you will have done by Friday, by week four, by month three, and the name of the one person whose job it is to answer your stupid questions, with time blocked in that person's calendar for it. Plus one rule she stole from a hotelier client: the workspace is completely ready the night before, login working, tools present, one handwritten line from the team on the desk. "It costs two hours," she says. "It buys you a person who tells the story of their first day for years. Both versions of the story last years, actually. You are choosing which one."

Let me turn Marta's page into the general pattern, because it scales down to a bakery and up to a fifty-person firm without modification.

Day one is for belonging, not paperwork. The contracts can wait until the afternoon. What cannot wait is the tour of how things really work, an actual task completed before going home, however small, and lunch where the new person does not have to choose a chair. Human beings decide fast whether they are welcome somewhere, and they make the decision on signals this cheap.

Week one is for the customer. Whatever the role, the new person should meet the thing the company exists for: sit in on support, visit a client with you, stand at the counter on Saturday morning, read the last twenty won-and-lost deals. Every week of delay makes the company's purpose more abstract, and people who find their work abstract do abstract work.

The first ninety days belong to the scorecard. You wrote the outcomes before you hired, so onboarding is the same document with nearer dates. Sit down at day thirty, sixty, and ninety, thirty minutes each, and ask three questions: what is going better than expected, what is harder than expected, and what do you know now that I should have told you on day one.
