That third question, asked honestly and acted on, will improve your onboarding faster than any template, because every new hire is a consultant on your company's confusions who gets more expensive to interview with every passing month, as the strangeness fades and they stop noticing what is strange.

To show you what the day-thirty conversation sounds like when it works, here is a nearly verbatim one from the routing company, with our first support hire, a quietly excellent woman named Petra. Me: "What do you know now that I should have told you on day one?" Petra, after a long pause: "That when Willem says a customer is 'being difficult,' he means the customer found a bug." Which was, first, very funny, and second, a small flare over a real problem: our unofficial vocabulary was covering for our defect rate, and a thirty-day-old employee could see it where the rest of us had gone noseblind. We fixed the vocabulary, and eventually the defect rate. Every new hire arrives carrying a free audit of your company. The whole trick of onboarding conversations is to collect it before it expires.

And say the quiet part early. If something is off in the first weeks, name it in week two, gently, in private, with specifics. Founders hoard early doubts out of politeness and cash them in month eight as a grievance the employee never got the chance to fix. Kindness with a delay mechanism is cowardice, and terrible management besides. Most early wobbles are fixable precisely because they are early: a misread of priorities, a habit from the old employer, a gap you can train. The probation period, which in most European countries gives both sides one or two months of easy exit, exists exactly so both sides can speak the truth while the stakes are small. Use it as a conversation device, not a trapdoor.

The Brilliant Jerk

And so, back to Viktor, because by now you have the equipment to see exactly what happened to Marta.

She hired without a scorecard, against a portfolio, in an unstructured interview where Viktor was magnificent, which we have established is what unstructured interviews measure. There were no written deal-breakers, so when the first reports of the eye-rolling and the 2 a.m. rewrites drifted up, she adjudicated each incident individually, against his brilliance, and brilliance won every hearing. The math in her head was simple and wrong: best designer, biggest award, key clients, therefore most valuable, therefore protected. What the math left out: value in a company is networked. Viktor's personal output was a large positive number. His effect on the output of everyone within reach of him was a larger negative one, paid in resignations, in juniors who stopped proposing ideas because proposals got rewritten at 2 a.m., in the growing silence in critiques, which in a design agency is the sound of the product dying.

When Marta finally ran the number I asked her for on that Sunday call, three departed designers, recruitment fees, six months of reduced output while replacements ramped, one client who left citing "turbulence," she got to roughly 180,000 euros, and then she stopped counting because the exercise had made its point. Viktor's salary premium over a merely very good designer was about 15,000 a year. She had been paying a 15,000 euro premium for brilliance and financing a six-figure loss from its side effects, annually, while telling herself she could not afford to lose him.

Look at the grid for a moment, because three of its quadrants are easy and cheap. Skilled and generous: keep them, and by the way, your best people watch what you tolerate more closely than they watch what you reward. Unskilled and corrosive: everyone agrees, though everyone still takes six months. Unskilled but generous deserves real patience, because the deficit is often the role or the onboarding rather than the person, and coaching someone generous into competence is one of the most profitable things a small company can do. The remaining quadrant decides the whole character of your company, and it decides it in public, in slow motion, because everybody sees the behaviour and everybody sees your response. Every week the brilliant jerk keeps their seat, the team reprices your stated values, the chapter one ones, at their true market rate: decoration.

The playbook, when you find yourself where Marta was, is short. One conversation, direct and documented: the behaviour, its cost, the change required, the timeline, usually four to six weeks, and the consequence, stated plainly. No hints, no hoping, no general team workshop about communication styles purchased so you can avoid one specific conversation, and yes, that is a thing founders actually do, I have watched the invoices. Some brilliant jerks genuinely change, more than you would think, because nobody impressive ever told them the truth before; their brilliance has been buying silence since school. The ones who do not change have made your decision for you, and the only remaining question is whether you act on it in weeks or in resignations.

Letting People Go Kindly

My editor asked me, while I was writing this book, to flag its hardest paragraph when I reached it. This section is where it lives. I have fired people. I have been part of hiring decisions that put good humans in the wrong jobs and then cost them a year of confidence when it failed. If you build a company of any size, you will do both, and how you do them will say more about you than your mission statement ever will. So let me walk you through it the way I wish someone had walked me.

First, the decision itself, which is where most of the cruelty in business actually originates: in the not-firing, long before any firing. Here is the pattern: you know by month five. You act in month fourteen. The nine months in between, which you experience as patience and kindness, the employee experiences as a slowly dropping temperature nobody will explain, fewer projects, tighter feedback, meetings they are no longer in. Their colleagues, meanwhile, are covering the gaps and privately downgrading their opinion of you, because they knew in month four. When the conversation finally comes, it lands on someone who has spent most of a year being quietly demoted from the truth. Delay buys your comfort with their time, at their expense, in a currency they cannot see being spent.

Before anything else, apply the test I use for every doubted role: knowing everything you now know, would you enthusiastically rehire this person into this job today? Enthusiastically is the load-bearing word, because almost nobody is terrible. If the answer is no three months running, and one honest scorecard conversation with a real chance to change has not moved it, you have your answer, and everything after is execution and decency.

Try this

Tonight, with a pen, list everyone who works for you. Next to each name, answer the rehire test: knowing what you know now, would you enthusiastically rehire them into their current role? For every "no," write one more line: the honest reason, and the date you last told them the substance of that reason to their face. If the second part is blank or old, the next conversation you owe is the truth, with time and help attached; the dismissal question comes later, if it comes at all. Some of my best people, at the routing company, were "no"s who became "yes"es because the conversation finally happened.

Second, the mechanics, and here I have to speak plainly to readers on my side of the water, because Europe runs on different rules than America. In most European countries you cannot simply end an employment contract because you feel like it. Depending on where you operate there are notice periods, mandatory severance or transition payments, required documentation of underperformance, dismissal permits or court routes in some countries, and, once you pass certain headcounts, works councils with a voice in how things are done. Founders discover this landscape in two moods: outrage, or preparation. Choose preparation. The rules are knowable, your accountant or a labour lawyer will explain your country's version in one billable hour, and that hour, spent before you hire rather than before you fire, is some of the best money in this book. The practical consequences come in three parts. Take probation periods seriously, because they are the one window where parting is simple, and they exist precisely so both sides can act on early truth. Document honestly as you go, a record of real conversations that actually happened rather than a trap you assemble later. And build the cost of doing this properly into your plans, because kind and legal both cost money, and being surprised by the cost is how founders end up doing it neither kindly nor legally.

Preparing the kind goodbye: what to have ready before the conversation
What to prepareWhat it looks likeWhy it matters
The decision, actually madeYou are informing, not discussing. If you are still deciding, you owe a performance conversation instead, and it should have happened already.A dismissal conversation that reopens into negotiation is the cruellest format of all: it hands the person hope and then takes it away twice.
The legal and financial pictureNotice period, severance or transition payment, holiday balance, what happens to their equipment, phone number, pension, all checked with your advisor for your country.Getting a detail wrong turns a sad day into a grievance procedure. Precision is a form of respect.
Two or three true sentences"This role needs X. Over the past months, despite the conversations in March and May, we have not gotten there. So we have decided to end your employment, and I want to spend our time on making the landing as good as possible."Long explanations get argued with, softened openings get misunderstood, and people remember the first thirty seconds of this conversation for years. Clarity is kindness.
The landing packageReference letter drafted, honest and warm. Offer of introductions where you genuinely can. Agreement on how their departure is announced, written together.The goal is that they leave with their dignity, their story, and their next chapter intact. Also, your industry is a village, and everyone watches how you do this.
The team plan for the same dayWho covers the work, and what you will say to the team within hours: brief, respectful, no autopsy, no ghosting the topic either.Silence breeds two rumours, "it could be me next" and "they'll trash me too when I go." Both are answered by calm, visible decency.
The right moment and placePrivate room, early in the week, early in the day, never on a birthday, never by surprise ambush at the end of an unrelated meeting.Early in the week means support systems, friends, family, recruiters, are awake and available. Friday firings hand someone a weekend alone with it.

Third, the conversation. Say it in the first minute. Not after the weather, not after a compliment sandwich, which everyone tastes coming and which teaches your whole company to fear your compliments. The kind version is short, true, and takes the responsibility that is genuinely yours, because some of it always is: you hired them, you designed the onboarding, you waited too long. "This is not working, here is why, the decision is made, and here is how I am going to help with what comes next." Then stop talking and let them react however they react. Anger, tears, relief, and it is relief more often than you would guess, because people usually know. They have been carrying the mismatch too, often longer than you have.

Story

Marta let Viktor go on a Tuesday morning, eleven days after that Sunday phone call. She had done it properly: the documented warning conversation had happened a month earlier, with a specific list and a real chance, and he had responded by being charming to her and worse to the juniors, which told her he had received the warning as a negotiation. The conversation itself took eleven minutes. He was, she says, charming to the end, then coldly furious, then gone, and one client did leave with him, which cost real money and was, she wants me to tell you, still cheap.

What she did not expect was the week after. A senior designer she assumed was Viktor's ally came to her office and closed the door, and Marta braced for a resignation. Instead: "we didn't think you'd ever do it." Within a month, critiques got loud again, in the good way. Within a year, one of the three designers who had left came back, and the agency did the best creative work of its life with no award-winner on staff, because, as Marta puts it now, the talent was always in the building, it was just keeping its head down. The award is still on the shelf by the entrance. She keeps it there on purpose. "People think it reminds me of Viktor," she told me. "It reminds me of the three people it cost, and that I knew for two years and called it patience."

One goodbye deserves its own paragraph, because it is the one that will actually break your heart, and no founder believes me until they are in it: the loyal early employee the company outgrew. Employee number two, who did every job, who moved boxes on the weekend the office flooded, who took the small salary when the salary had to be small, and who is now, at thirty people, visibly underwater in a role that has grown three sizes past them. Everyone loves them. Everyone covers for them. And you, the founder, owe them more than anyone in the building, which is exactly why the situation curdles: you read the debt as a reason to leave them where they are, and so you repay years of loyalty by letting them fail slowly in public. The honest move, and it is brutal and I have done it exactly once and still think about it, is to separate the debt from the seat. Sometimes that means reshaping a role around what they genuinely do brilliantly, without the euphemism-title that fools nobody. Sometimes it means the goodbye, done with more generosity than the law requires, more notice, more money, more real help, because the law is a floor and this person built your house. What it can never mean is the seat held as a monument. The seat belongs to the company's future. The gratitude belongs to the person. Founders get into the worst trouble of their careers by handing the first to the second and calling it loyalty.

And fourth, the part nobody writes down: what it does to you.

The first time you let someone go, done properly and kindly and legally, you will still feel like a small war criminal for about a week. You will replay the conversation, you will see them in the supermarket in your imagination, and you will be tempted to conclude that you are not cut out for this. You are. The feeling is the correct emotional price of holding power over someone's livelihood, and the founders who should worry are the ones who stop feeling it. Pay the price, learn what the hire taught you about your own process, upgrade the scorecard, and go make the next promise more carefully. That is the whole loop of this chapter, and every company that lasts runs it hundreds of times.

The Short Version

  • Hiring is the highest-stakes skill in your company and the one you have practiced least. Treat it as a craft, not an errand.
  • Your first hires buy back the founder's best hours. Hire against pain you can point at today, never against the org chart of an imaginary future company.
  • Hire for the company you are, and sell the job honestly, hard parts included. Eyes-open people stay.
  • Write the scorecard, mission, outcomes, behaviours, deal-breakers, before you meet anyone. A decision made after you have met a charming candidate is courtship.
  • Unstructured interviews measure the ability to be interviewed. Ask about the real past, follow up three levels deep, use a short paid work sample, and make reference calls that listen for temperature.
  • Run the funnel with honest numbers, move fast because speed and warmth are your advantages, and never hire the best of a weak field. Between a vacancy and a doubt, choose the vacancy.
  • Onboarding is the cheapest retention tool ever invented: a ready desk, a real task on day one, the customer in week one, and the scorecard at days 30, 60, 90.
  • The brilliant jerk is a net negative with a medal on it. One documented warning, one deadline, then act. Your values are worth exactly what you tolerate.
  • Delay buys your comfort with the employee's time. Apply the rehire test, tell the truth early, learn your country's rules before you need them, and when the end comes, say it in the first minute and land the person as softly as you can.
  • The bad feeling after a kind, well-done goodbye is the correct price of the job. Worry when you stop paying it.

Chapter 11

Building the Skeleton and Nervous System

A growing company needs a structure to hold its shape and an information flow to feel its own pain. You have to build both on purpose, because neither grows on its own.

Marta called me on a Tuesday evening in November, and she opened with a sentence I want you to memorize, because one day, if things go well for you, you will say it too.

"Nobody tells me anything anymore."

You have met Marta before in this book, usually mid-crisis, which is unfair to her, because between the crises she built one of the best design agencies I know. By that November the agency had grown to twenty-five people. Two floors of a canal building, a real management team, a waiting list of clients. From the outside, the good years. From the inside, Marta was discovering something nobody had warned her about, and that I am now warning you about: a company can grow itself deaf.

The trigger was small, almost comic. She had been at the opening of a client's new flagship store, glass of wine in hand, doing the founder thing where you represent the company by standing near its logo. The client's marketing director came over, squeezed her arm, and said, "I just want to say, your team handled the whole rebrand mess so gracefully. Most agencies would have hidden it from us."

Marta smiled, said something warm, and spent the rest of the evening trying to find out, without admitting she was trying to find out, what the rebrand mess was.

It turned out to be substantial. A junior designer had built three weeks of campaign work on the client's old brand guidelines, the ones the client had retired in the spring. A file server folder with a misleading name, an account manager who spotted it late, a heroic weekend of rework, an honest and rather elegant apology call to the client. Her team had handled it well. Better than Marta herself would have handled it at twenty-six, and possibly better than she would handle it now.

What kept her up was the timeline. The team had found the mistake five weeks before the store opening. The rework weekend was four weeks before. The apology call, three and a half. And the founder of the company learned about it from the client, at a party, from a woman holding a tray-sized glass of Grüner Veltliner.

So she did what you do at two in the morning: she inventoried every other thing she might not know. By the time she called me she had found three. Her most senior designer was interviewing at a competitor, which everyone on the design floor knew and no one upstairs did. A retainer client had halved their monthly scope, which finance knew and the account team assumed finance had escalated, and finance assumed the account team had. And the studio had switched project management tools, an actual migration of the actual system the company ran on, and Marta learned about it when her old login stopped working.

"Twenty-five people," she said on the phone. "I hired every single one of them. I know their partners' names. I know who takes oat milk. And I found out about a client crisis from the client. At a party. Wouter, they are hiding things from me."

Nobody was hiding anything, and if you ever stand where she stood, nobody will be hiding anything from you either. Your brain reaches for that diagnosis first because it is the dramatic one, the one with villains in it. Betrayal, cliques, disloyalty. In Marta's case it was wrong on every count. Her people liked her. Several of them, we later found out, had each assumed she already knew the things she did not know. One had drafted an email to her about the rebrand mess and deleted it because "the Monday meeting seemed like the right place, and then the Monday meeting got cancelled."

Marta had a physics problem, not a people problem. Her agency had outgrown its skeleton and its nervous system. Or rather, it had never had them. It had Marta. She had been the skeleton and the nervous system both, and at twenty-five people, one woman's spine and synapses can no longer hold the shape of the thing or feel its pain. The company had grown. The infrastructure was still one person tall.

This chapter is about building that infrastructure on purpose: the structure that holds a growing company's shape, which I will call the skeleton, and the information flow that lets it sense what is happening to itself, which I will call the nervous system. Roles, meetings, documentation, feedback loops, and metrics. The boring words. Behind each one, your company is either standing upright right now or going numb.

The Mathematics of Silence

Let me take the drama out of "nobody tells me anything anymore" with some arithmetic, because the arithmetic is the actual villain, and once you see it you will stop suspecting your people.

Information in a small company travels through pairs. A conversation is a pair. A Slack message, a shared cigarette, a car ride to a client, a raised eyebrow across the studio: all pairs. With four people, you have six possible pairs. Everyone hears everything, usually twice. With eight people you have twenty-eight pairs, and it still mostly works, because you all fit in one room and information behaves like smell. Whatever is cooking, everybody knows.

At twelve people, sixty-six pairs. At twenty-five, three hundred. At forty, where Marta's agency eventually landed, seven hundred and eighty. The number of possible conversations grows with the square of headcount, and your working hours grow not at all. Somewhere between twelve and twenty-five people, the smell model of information stops working, and it fails silently, which is the cruel part. No alarm goes off. The company stops smelling like anything, and everyone assumes that means nothing is burning.

A second mechanism stacks on top of the arithmetic, and this one is about you. In the early years, you are the hub. Every important piece of information passes through you because every important decision passes through you, and people learn the habit: when in doubt, tell the founder. Growth erodes that habit from two directions at once. First, you become busy in a new way, visibly busy, calendar-blocked busy, and every person who might have mentioned something small now runs a quick cost-benefit calculation in your doorway and concludes that their small thing does not justify interrupting your big thing. Multiply that doorway calculation by twenty-five people and every working day, and you have built a company that filters out small things by design. Unfortunately, every large problem you will ever have starts life as a small thing.

Second, you have become the boss in a way you were not before, even if you hate the word, even if you sit in the middle of the room and take out the recycling. Hierarchy has a gradient. Information flows down it easily and up it badly. Telling the founder good news is a pleasure. Telling the founder ambiguous news is a chore. Telling the founder bad news is a risk, and people manage risk by waiting, softening, and delegating the telling to someone else, who is also waiting. Call it what it is: humans behaving the way humans behave around power. You have power now, whether you ordered it or not.

Add a third mechanism: diffusion of responsibility. In a company of six, if you know something important, you know you are probably its only path to the founder. In a company of twenty-five, there is always a plausible someone else. Surely the account director mentioned it. Surely it came up in the management meeting. The rebrand mess reached everyone in Marta's company who could act on it and reached her not at all, because every single person who knew was certain she already did. In a growing company, information fails to arrive while everyone believes it has arrived. That is why the founder is always the last to know, and always astonished.

The silence is structural. That should comfort you, and then it should worry you in a more productive direction, because structural problems shrug off the fixes founders reach for first. Marta's initial plan, sketched in that midnight phone call, was to have more coffees. Walk the floor more, ask more questions, be more approachable. All fine things. None of them scale. She would have been buying back individual pairs of communication at retail price, three hundred pairs and rising, with hours she did not have. What she needed was to stop being the infrastructure and start building some. That is the rest of this chapter.

An Anatomy Lesson

Every growing company has to build two different things at roughly the same time, and most founders build at most one, which is why the metaphor in this chapter's title deserves a few minutes of your attention.

The skeleton is structure. Roles, reporting lines, decision rights. Who owns what, who answers for what, where one person's job ends and another's begins, and at which joints the company bends when it needs to move. The skeleton's job is to hold the company's shape without anyone holding it up. A company without a skeleton keeps its shape the way a tent keeps its shape, with the founder as the pole. Take the founder out for two weeks and the tent sags. You can measure how much skeleton your company has by imagining your own uninterrupted holiday and counting the things that would stop.

The nervous system is information flow. Meetings, documentation, metrics, feedback loops. Its job is carrying signal: when something happens at the fingertip, the brain finds out, at a speed proportional to how much it hurts. A company without a nervous system can look magnificent and be injured at the same time, because nothing connects the injury to anyone who could act on it. Marta's rebrand mess was exactly this, a burn on the hand that the head learned about five weeks later, from a bystander, at a party.

The two systems fail differently, and the failures smell different, which helps diagnosis. A company with nerves but no bones is all signal and no shape: everyone knows everything, everyone discusses everything, and nobody decides anything, because no question has an owner. It feels warm and collaborative and it moves like a jellyfish. A company with bones but no nerves is the opposite: a crisp org chart, tidy job titles, clean reporting lines, and total numbness. People make confident decisions with no idea what is happening three metres away. Big companies usually die the second death. Small companies usually die the first. Companies in between, the twenty-five-person kind, manage both at once, jellyfish in the studio and skeleton in the boardroom, and the two halves stop speaking.

One warning before we start building. The order matters less than founders think. The pairing is everything. Every bone you add needs a nerve attached, and every nerve needs a bone. Give someone ownership of client relationships without a channel through which they report on client relationships, and you have created a silo with a nice title. Create a weekly reporting ritual without anyone owning the things being reported on, and you have created a book club. Bone, then nerve, then check they are connected. That is the whole method, applied five times, and it is what the next sections do: roles, meetings, documentation, feedback loops, metrics.

A boundary note, so you know what this chapter leaves out. How you personally lead the people inside this structure, delegation, feedback, your own bottleneck behaviour: chapter twelve. Whether you adopt a packaged operating system for the rhythms described here, EOS or one of its cousins: chapter thirteen. Finding the people who fill the roles: chapter ten, which you have just read. This chapter is the architecture between those three. The shape of the machine, not the operator, and not the brand of the machine.

Bones: Roles That Carry Weight

Start with the skeleton, because signal without structure has nowhere to land. And start the skeleton with a distinction that sounds pedantic and turns out to run the whole show: the difference between a job title and a role.

A job title goes on a business card and a contract. A role is a bundle of ownership: a set of things one person sees, decides, and answers for. Titles serve the outside world. Roles serve the inside one, and inside a company of eight to forty people they almost never line up one to one. Your studio manager might hold four roles: capacity planning, supplier relationships, the office itself, onboarding logistics. Your senior developer might hold two: the architecture of the product and its security. The title is singular. The ownership is plural, and the ownership is what you have to make explicit, because ownership is where things fall when nobody catches them.

The test for whether a role is real, as opposed to decorative, has three parts, and a role has to pass all three. The owner sees it: information about that domain reaches them by default, without hunting. The owner decides it: within agreed limits, they act without asking. And the owner answers for it: when the domain goes well or badly, everyone, including them, knows whose name is on it. Sees, decides, answers. A role that sees and answers but cannot decide is a scapegoat position. A role that decides but never answers is a hobby with a budget. You will find both in most growing companies, usually created by accident, usually occupied by someone quietly going mad.

Two rules govern the whole exercise, and they do most of the work.

Rule one: every important thing has exactly one owner. Not zero, which is how the rebrand mess happened: the retired brand guidelines were a domain nobody owned, so nobody archived the old folder. And not two, which feels safer and is worse, because shared ownership is a machine for manufacturing assumptions. Marta's halved retainer sat between finance and the account team for six weeks because both owned client revenue a little, which meant neither owned it at all. When I hear "we all own quality here," I translate it in my head to "no one owns quality here, and we have agreed not to mention it." If a thing needs two people, split the thing, not the ownership. One owns the promise to the client, the other owns the process that delivers it. Now it is two things, each with one name on it.

Rule two: the org chart describes the company you are, not the company you are imitating. At twenty-five people you do not need a head of people, a chief revenue officer, and an operations director because a scale-up on LinkedIn has them. You need the actual load-bearing work of your actual company mapped to actual humans. Draw it from the work upwards, not from the template downwards. List the ten domains that would hurt if someone dropped them for a month: client relationships, delivery quality, cash and invoicing, the pipeline, the product or the craft itself, the team's wellbeing, the tools everyone runs on. Then put one name next to each. That page, one column of domains and one column of names, is worth more than any organogram, and it fits on one page for years.

Joints: Where the Decisions Live

Bones alone are rigid. What makes a skeleton useful is the joints, the agreed places where movement happens, and in a company the joints are decision rights: who may decide what, up to what limit, after consulting whom. Most growing companies never write these down, and the result is a strange double failure. Half the decisions queue outside the founder's door, because nobody is sure they may make them. Three different people make the other half, each certain it was theirs. Bottleneck and chaos at the same time, which people read as a contradiction. It is what missing joints look like.

The fix is a short, boring, glorious table. For each recurring decision type, write down who decides, who they must consult before deciding, and who they must tell after. Here is roughly what Marta's looked like once we built it, translated so a software founder or a bakery owner can steal it equally well.

Decision rights: who decides what, up to what limit
DecisionWho decidesConsulted beforeTold after
Spending under €500 on tools or materialsAny role owner, from their domainNobodyFinance, in the monthly review
Spending €500 to €5,000The domain ownerFinanceManagement team
Discount or scope concession to a clientAccount lead, up to 10%Nobody up to 10%, founder aboveFinance, always, same week
Hiring into an approved roleThe hiring managerFounder (final interview only)Whole company, before the start date
Changing a tool the whole company usesOperations ownerEvery team that touches it, founderWhole company, with a migration date
Firing a clientFounderAccount lead, financeWhole company, honestly
Anything touching brand promise or valuesFounderManagement teamWhole company

Notice what the table does. It pre-answers the doorway calculation. The person hovering at your office door, wondering whether their €300 software subscription justifies interrupting you, now has an answer that never involves your door. Every row you add buys back founder hours and, more importantly, buys back speed for everyone else. And notice the last column, "told after," because that column is the nerve attached to this particular bone. A decision right without a reporting duty creates silos. The account lead may give the 8% discount alone, and finance hears about it the same week, every time, no exceptions. Autonomy in the decision, transparency in the aftermath. That trade is the joint working as designed.

Notice also what stays with the founder, and why. Firing a client and guarding the brand promise stay with you because they are identity decisions, the kind that define what sort of company this is. Euros have nothing to do with it; identity is the one domain a founder at this size cannot delegate. If that sentence raises questions about what your company's identity even is, that is chapter one, and it is cheaper to answer there than here.

A caution about the most common bone-setting mistake at this stage: the player-coach. You promote your best designer to lead the design team, and you let her keep a full client load, because you cannot spare her hands. Now she has two roles fighting for the same hours, and the coaching role loses every time, because clients phone and team members do not. Six months later you conclude she "was not management material," when what happened is that you set a bone across a joint and were surprised the limb would not bend. If someone is to own a team's output, take real weight off them first. The skeleton has to obey physics.

Try this

Take a pen and list the last ten meaningful decisions made in your company, anything from a hire to a discount to a tool change. For each one, write who made it, who believed they should have made it, and how long it waited in someone's head. You are looking for two patterns: orphans, decisions that circled for weeks because nobody was sure they owned them, and doubles, decisions made more than once by different people. Every orphan and every double is a missing row in your decision table. Write those rows tonight. The table can be seven lines long and still change your month.

Synapses: Meetings That Move the Company

Now the nerves, starting with the most maligned organ in business: the meeting.

Founders at this stage tend to hold one of two theological positions on meetings. The first camp believes meetings are where work goes to die, cancels as many as possible, and is proud of the empty calendar. The second camp responds to every dropped ball by scheduling a recurring meeting about that category of ball, and after two years of this the calendar looks like a mosaic and nobody can find three consecutive hours to think. Both camps are managing their feelings about meetings rather than the function of them. The function is this: a meeting is a synapse, a place where signal jumps from one part of the company to another. A company with too few synapses is numb. A company with too many is having a seizure. So ask where signal needs to jump, how often, and what the cheapest reliable way is to make it jump there. Whether you like meetings never enters into it.

Cheapest matters, because meetings have a price and almost nobody prices them. A one-hour meeting with six people is six working hours, and at a blended cost of, say, €60 an hour once you include everything an employer pays, that meeting costs €360 each time it runs. Weekly, that is around €17,000 a year. A decent used car, every year, for one recurring slot in the calendar. You would never approve a €17,000 invoice without asking what it buys. Meetings arrive without invoices, which is the only reason they survive unexamined.

The Three Honest Purposes

Every meeting worth having does one of three jobs, and a meeting that cannot say which job it does is already dead, whatever the calendar says.

Synchronize. Move current state between people so they make next week's decisions with the same map. Sync meetings should be short, rhythmic, and ruthless about staying at the level of state: what changed, what is stuck, what is coming. The moment a sync meeting starts solving a problem, it is stealing time from the five people the problem does not need.

Decide. Put a specific question, the options, and the people with the authority and the context in one room, and leave with a decision and an owner. Decision meetings need preparation to exist beforehand, which is why they pair so well with the written material from the next section. A decision meeting without a written question at the top is a debate club.

Create. Do actual joint work: shape a proposal, workshop a design, take apart a failure. Creating meetings are the only kind allowed to be long, and they earn the length by producing an artifact, something that exists afterwards and did not exist before.

Synchronize, decide, create. Status theater is missing from that list on purpose, and status theater is what most recurring meetings decay into: a circle of people reading out loud to a founder things they could have written down, while everyone else rehearses their own paragraph. The tell is that nobody in the room changes their plans based on anything they hear. Signal jumps to no one. The synapse fires into the void, weekly, at €360 a firing.

Story

Two weeks after the Grüner Veltliner incident, Marta and I sat down with her calendar and did the audit you are about to see in table form. We found eleven recurring meetings. She could explain the purpose of six. The other five included a Thursday "alignment hour" born two years earlier, during a crisis with a hotel client, to coordinate daily fixes. The hotel client had left, on good terms, fourteen months before. The meeting had continued, weekly, seven attendees, because it was in the calendar and the calendar is a form of law. Nobody could say what it was for, and nobody felt entitled to kill it, because meetings, unlike expenses, have no owner and no invoice.

Marta did the arithmetic on that one meeting herself, on a napkin, and I watched her face do something complicated. Seven people, one hour, roughly fifty runs. "That meeting cost more than my first year's salary at the agency," she said. Then she went quiet for a moment and said the more important thing: "And the rebrand mess never came up in it. Seven people, an hour a week, and the biggest fire in the company never once made it onto the table." That is the double crime of a dead meeting. It burns hours, and it squats in the place where a live synapse should be, so everyone feels informed while knowing nothing.

The audit that catches this takes an afternoon, and I think every company should run it once a year, the way you service a boiler. List every recurring meeting. For each one, write down its cadence, its yearly cost in hours, the job it claims to do, the job it actually does, and a verdict: keep, fix, or kill. Be as honest in the "actually does" column as you would be about a competitor's meetings. Here is Marta's, abbreviated, with the arithmetic done at that same blended €60 an hour.

Meeting audit: every recurring meeting, priced and sentenced
MeetingCadence & sizeCost / yearClaims to doActually doesVerdict
Monday all-handsWeekly, 25 people, 45 min~€54,000Align the whole companyAnnouncements everyone forgets; frequently cancelledFix: 20 min, fixed agenda: numbers, one client story, one decision made, questions. Never cancelled
Management team meetingWeekly, 5 people, 90 min~€22,500Run the companyActually runs the company, badly documentedKeep: add a written decision log
Thursday alignment hourWeekly, 7 people, 60 min~€21,000Nobody remembersRitual sacrifice of ThursdayKill
Project status roundWeekly, 9 people, 60 min~€27,000Surface project risksReading out loud things already in the toolFix: written updates by Friday noon; 25-min meeting discusses only exceptions
Client debriefsAfter each project, 4 people, 60 min~€4,800Learn from projectsHappens only when the project went wellFix: mandatory within two weeks of every project, especially the bad ones
1:1s, leads with their peopleFortnightly, 30 min each~€15,000Support and early warningFirst thing cancelled every busy weekKeep, protect: may be moved, never dropped
Friday drinks planningWeekly, 3 people, 30 min~€2,700Plan Friday drinksPlans Friday drinks admirablyKill the meeting, keep the drinks: a rota and a group chat

Three patterns in that table generalize to almost every company I have seen inside. First, the fix is very often "write it down first, then meet about the exceptions." A written weekly update takes each person ten minutes to write and two minutes per reader, and it frees the meeting to do the one thing writing cannot: argue well. Second, the meetings most worth protecting, the one-to-ones, are the ones that get cancelled first, because their cost is visible and their value stays invisible until the quarter after you stop. A cancelled one-to-one is exactly how a senior designer ends up interviewing at a competitor with everyone downstairs knowing and nobody upstairs. Third, every meeting needs one named owner: the person who writes the agenda, starts it on time, and holds the standing right to conclude it is no longer needed. A meeting without an owner cannot be killed, and what cannot be killed becomes the Thursday alignment hour.

Set cadences to match the speed of the underlying reality, not the gravity of the topic. Things that change weekly get weekly synapses: delivery, pipeline, cash if it is tight. Things that change quarterly get quarterly ones: strategy, the shape of the team, pricing. The classic error inverts this. You meet weekly about strategy, which does not change week to week, so the meeting invents strategy news to fill the hour, while cash, which changes daily, gets one anxious look a month. And if you want a full prefabricated cadence, an annual, quarterly, weekly rhythm with names and worksheets, that is what operating systems like EOS sell, and they are chapter thirteen. Here it is enough that each meeting knows its job, its price, and its owner.

Long-Term Memory: Documentation People Actually Use

Meetings move signal through space, from person to person. Documentation moves it through time, from the person who knew to the person who will need to know, months later, possibly after the first person has left. A company without documentation has anterograde amnesia: charming, energetic, and condemned to relive its own mistakes with a fresh sense of discovery each time. The junior designer who built three weeks of work on retired brand guidelines did exactly what the company's memory told her to do, because the company's memory was a file server where the old truth and the new truth sat side by side, identically confident.

Founders resist documentation for one respectable reason and one embarrassing one. The respectable reason: they have seen the failure mode. The wiki nobody reads, the process manual obsolete before the ink dried, the quality handbook written for a certification audit and never opened since. The embarrassing reason: while everything lives in the founder's head, the founder is indispensable, and some part of every founder likes being the only one who knows where the bodies are buried. I will deal with the respectable reason here. The embarrassing one is chapter twelve's problem, and chapter twelve deals with it.

The failure mode is real, but it comes from writing the wrong things. Companies that drown in useless documentation almost always documented processes first, in exhaustive imperative prose: how to do everything, in eleven steps, with screenshots that expired the next quarter. Useful company memory has three shelves, and process is only one of them, and not the first.

The Three Shelves

Shelf one: what is true right now. The current price list. The current brand guidelines, with the old ones archived where nobody trips over them. Who owns what, the one-page role list from earlier in this chapter. The current org chart, the current client list, the current standard contract. This shelf is small, a dozen documents, and its whole value is a single guarantee: if it is on this shelf, it is current, and if it is current, it is on this shelf. One person owns the shelf, its contents each have owners, and whoever replaces a document moves the superseded one out the same day. Marta's rebrand mess was a shelf-one failure costing five figures. The shelf costs an afternoon a month.

Shelf two: what we decided, and why. A decision log. One page per meaningful decision: the date, the question, the options considered, what we chose, why, and who owned it. Ten minutes to write, and it appreciates every year, because the "why" is the part of a decision that dies first. Two years from now nobody will ask what tool you chose; the tool is right there being used. They will ask why, usually in a tone suggesting the decision was idiotic, and either the log answers them in thirty seconds or the company re-litigates the whole question from scratch, with the added spice that the people who remember the context have left. I started a decision log at the routing company in year five, after we spent an entire offsite reversing a pricing decision for the exact reasons we had made it in the first place. The log would have cost ten minutes. The offsite cost a weekend and two friendships' worth of goodwill.

Shelf three: how we do things. The runbooks and processes, yes, but under a strict admission rule: write a process down the second time someone asks how to do it, not before, and the person who answered writes it, in twenty lines or fewer, linked from the place where the work happens. Not a manual. A set of recipes, each one earned by a real repeated question. This rule keeps shelf three honest. Documentation written on demand describes work that recurs. Documentation written in a visionary mood describes work the author wishes recurred, and that is the wiki nobody reads.

Where should the shelves live? In the most boring tool you already have, and I mean that as rigorous advice. The gains come from the guarantee and the habit, never from the software, and every hour you spend evaluating knowledge platforms is an hour of shelf-one work you did not do. One place, searchable, linked where people work. If your company can hold the guarantee in a folder tree, hold it in a folder tree.

Field note

Write documentation for readers, not for the writer. Before saving any document, ask the reader's three questions: how will they find this, will they trust it is current when they do, and can they act on it in under five minutes? A document that fails the first question does not exist. One that fails the second is worse than not existing, because a reader burned once by a stale document never trusts the shelf again, and the guarantee, once broken, costs a fortune to rebuild.

One more thing documentation buys you, and at this size it is a big thing: calm onboarding. Every new person who joins a company with a real shelf one and shelf three gets productive weeks earlier and interrupts their colleagues hundreds of times less. The mechanics of onboarding belong to chapter ten, but the raw material of onboarding is this section, and companies that complain new hires take six months to be useful are usually companies where the first three months are an oral history project.

Reflexes: How Fast Does Bad News Travel

Here is the section that would have saved Marta her November, so let me put its central claim in the plainest terms I can manage. Good news travels through a company on its own. Bad news needs infrastructure. Build nothing, and you will still hear about every won pitch, every happy client, every launch, usually within the hour, with photographs. What you will miss: the senior designer interviewing elsewhere, the retainer cut in half without a word, the project three weeks late and concealed by people who intend to fix it before you notice. The gradient we met earlier explains why. Carrying bad news uphill costs the carrier something, and unless you build structures that lower the cost, most people, most days, will do the math and keep quiet.

Think of it as a reflex arc. When you touch a hot stove, your hand pulls back before your conscious brain knows anything happened, because the body does not route pain through committees. A healthy company has the same property: the people closest to the burn act at once, and the signal still travels up, at pain-proportional speed, so the rest of the organism can adjust. Marta's agency had half of this. The hand pulled back; her team fixed the rebrand mess with real skill. The signal never travelled. A company that acts locally but never informs centrally will handle each fire well and learn nothing across fires, because learning lives at the level that never heard.

Silence in a growing company is packet loss.

So build the reflexes on purpose. Four of them cover most of what a company this size needs, and none takes more than an hour a week from anyone.

The written weekly update. Every role owner writes a short weekly note, and the format is the whole trick: what moved, what is stuck, what is coming, and, the load-bearing line, what I am worried about. Four headings, ten minutes, published where the management team and ideally everyone can read it. The worry line is the reflex. It creates a cheap, low-drama, socially normal channel for exactly the information the gradient suppresses. Saying "I am worried the Meridian project is drifting" in week two is easy, because nothing has happened yet. The line costs the writer nothing and buys the company three weeks of options. Without the channel, that same worry has to mature into a confession before anyone voices it, and confessions arrive late by definition.

The post-project debrief, especially for the good ones that were secretly bad. Within two weeks of any project ending, the team spends forty-five minutes on three questions: what happened versus what we planned, what surprised us, what will we do differently. Written down, on shelf two, and the founder does not run the meeting and ideally is not in the room, because the gradient attends every meeting you attend. The discipline that matters is doing them always, not just after disasters. Debriefs held only after failures become tribunals, and people prepare defences instead of observations. Debriefs held always become boring, and boring is the goal. A boring debrief is a company examining itself without flinching.

The skip-level conversation, done honestly. Once a quarter, sit down with people who do not report to you, one at a time, and ask questions they can answer: what is harder than it should be, what would you fix tomorrow if you ran the place, what do you think I am wrong about. Then, and this part decides whether the channel lives or dies, do something visible about at least one thing you hear, and credit the channel: "several of you told me the review process is strangling small projects, so we are changing it." The first time you do that, the channel's bandwidth triples. And a warning from someone who got this wrong at the routing company: never use a skip-level to check up on the manager in between, and never repeat what you heard with a name attached. One traceable quote reaching the wrong ear closes the channel for a year, and everyone in the company will know why, even though nobody will say it in front of you.

The closed loop. The most neglected reflex, and the cheapest. When anyone reports a problem, something visible must happen: it gets fixed, or it gets a named owner and a date, or someone explains honestly why it will stay unfixed. Any of the three keeps the nerve alive, even the no. What kills the nerve is the fourth outcome, silence, the report that vanishes into the founder's inbox. People will forgive one report that goes nowhere. The second one teaches them, and then they train the people around them: "don't bother, nothing happens." When a founder tells me "my people never raise problems," I ask what happened to the last three problems someone raised. There is usually a pause, and inside the pause is the answer.

Try this

Measure your bad-news latency. Take the last three pieces of real bad news that reached you: a slipping project, an unhappy client, a person on the way out. For each, write two dates: when the first person in the company knew, and when you knew. The gap is your latency, and the founders I make do this find weeks where they would have guessed days. Then, for the worst one, trace the route: who knew, who they told, where it stalled, and what would have un-stalled it. Hunt the missing reflex, not the person who stayed silent: the update line, the debrief, the closed loop that was never built. Build that one first.

Sense Organs: Metrics That Carry Signal

Reflexes carry pain. Metrics are the other half of the sensory system, the eyes and ears, the numbers that let a company perceive things too slow or too diffuse for anyone to feel: margins eroding a point a quarter, a pipeline thinning, one client growing until it holds the company hostage. Nobody feels these in their fingertips. You need instruments.

And here I have to make a distinction that took me an embarrassing number of years to learn, so I will give it to you at the price I wish I had paid: the difference between a metric that carries signal and a metric that is decoration. Most companies at this size have plenty of numbers. The dashboards fill up with decorative ones, tracked because they are easy to track, presented because they look rigorous, and connected to no decision at all. Decoration is worse than ignorance, because ignorance at least knows itself. A founder with a dashboard feels informed, and a wall of green numbers is the corporate equivalent of a body that cannot feel pain: it photographs well and walks into fires.

A metric carries signal if it passes four tests, and it has to pass all four, which most dashboard numbers fail.

Someone owns it. One person, the role owner from earlier, whose number it is, who knows it moved before the meeting and arrives with the story of why. A metric without an owner is weather, as the sales chapter would put it: interesting, discussed, acted on by no one. This is the bone-and-nerve pairing again. A sense organ has to wire into a limb that can move.

It can change a decision. Before adopting any metric, name the decision it informs and the threshold that triggers it: if utilization stays over 90% for six weeks, we hire or we refuse work; if one client passes 30% of revenue, we rebalance sales effort. No nameable decision, no threshold, no metric. Track it in a spreadsheet if it comforts you, but keep it off the dashboard, because attention is the scarcest resource in the room and decoration spends it.

It is allowed to look bad. The metric measures reality, not the team's morale or the founder's mood. The instant you punish a number for being red, it stops being a sense organ and becomes a performance, and everyone downstream starts optimizing the number instead of the thing. You have then paid to blind yourself.

It leads where possible. Revenue tells you what happened two quarters ago in your pipeline. Proposals sent, first conversations booked, project margin at the halfway mark: these tell you what revenue will do while there is still time to act. A dashboard of only lagging indicators is a rearview mirror, honest and useless.

Signal versus noise: the same domains, instrumented honestly
DomainDecoration (noise)SignalThe decision it feeds
SalesWebsite visits, social followers, "buzz"Qualified first conversations per month; proposals outstanding in €Where founder selling hours go next month (ch. 9 owns the pipeline itself)
DeliveryHours logged, tickets closed, busynessMargin per project at completion vs. at quote; % of projects late at the halfway checkRepricing, staffing, or scoping the next quarter's work
MoneyRevenue, celebrated aloneCash cover in weeks; % of revenue from the single largest clientWhen to slow spending; when to rebalance sales effort (mechanics in ch. 6)
ClientsAn annual satisfaction survey, averagedDays since each key client heard from a human who was not invoicing them; complaints reaching the owner within one weekWhich relationship gets attention before it wobbles
TeamHeadcount growth, perks list, party photosRegretted departures per year; % of 1:1s that actually happened; time to fill an open roleWhether the skeleton and the load still match

Notice the shape of the signal column: small, uncomfortable numbers, each owned, each wired to a nameable decision. Notice also its size. Five domains, roughly ten numbers. At twenty-five people you need no more, and in a real sense you cannot afford more, because every number on the wall dilutes the attention paid to the others.

Story

At the routing company, somewhere around thirty-five people, we built the dashboard of my dreams. Forty-one metrics, refreshed live, on a television in the office. Sign-ups, uptime, support response times, feature usage, revenue in three cuts. Visitors were impressed. I was impressed, and I had commissioned it. And in the two quarters that television glowed its confident green, the company had its worst stretch in years: our biggest customer was integrating a competitor, our sales cycle had lengthened by six weeks, and two of our best engineers were burning out on a rewrite I kept extending. The television knew none of this. Forty-one numbers, and not one owned by anyone, not one wired to a decision, not one capable of turning red for the things that threatened us. It was a stained-glass window: expensive, beautiful, and there to be admired, not seen through.

We eventually replaced it with eight numbers on a shared page, each with a name next to it, reviewed weekly by the person named. And we added the rule I now give to every founder who will hold still long enough: a dashboard on which nothing is red is broken. Reality always contains at least one problem. If your instruments disagree, the fault sits in the instruments, and the repair is a standing question at the weekly review: "what should be red here that isn't?" The first time someone answers honestly, your dashboard starts working, and it never looks impressive on a television again.

Two traps to step around as you build this. The first is measuring what is easy instead of what is load-bearing, hours logged instead of margin earned, because the tool exports one and not the other. The tool's convenience is a bad argument; get the number you need. The second trap is the metric review that changes nothing, ten minutes of nodding at numbers before the real agenda. The cure is mechanical: every red number gets a sentence in the decision log, either what we are doing about it or why we accept it this quarter. Written acceptance is honourable. Silent nodding is how a company practices ignoring its own instruments, weekly, until it gets good at it. And to keep this chapter in its lane: which numbers deserve to be company-wide goals and how they cascade into quarterly targets is chapter thirteen's territory. Here we only care that the instruments exist, have owners, and are allowed to hurt.

How Much Skeleton, and When

By this point in the chapter, a certain kind of reader is compiling an enthusiastic to-do list: role charters, decision tables, three shelves, four reflexes, a dashboard. Before you build all of it this weekend, we need to talk about dosage. Structure is a medicine, and like all medicine it has a therapeutic range. Too little and the disease proceeds. Too much and you have poisoned the patient with the cure, and a small company poisoned by structure is a sad thing to visit: nine people, a steering committee, a change request form, and a founder who read a book like this one with too much appetite.

The dosing principle: add a bone when the pain recurs, not the first time it twinges. Every structure in this chapter answers a pattern. One orphaned decision is a Tuesday; the same decision orphaned three times is a missing row in the table. One person asking how to invoice a client is a conversation; the second person asking is a shelf-three recipe. One late project is a project; late projects as a genre are a missing halfway-mark metric. Waiting for the second or third occurrence protects you from building structure for problems you do not have, the more common failure among founders who read books. The founders who do not read books fail in the other direction and wait for the ninth occurrence, by which point the pattern has cost five figures and a resignation.

Rough thresholds, which you should treat as rules of thumb rather than physics. Up to about eight or ten people, you need almost nothing from this chapter: one page of who-owns-what, a weekly sync, a shared folder with a current price list, and honesty at lunch. The pairs arithmetic still works at that size, and premature structure adds friction to a company whose whole advantage is having none. From ten to about twenty, build the first full set: real roles with the sees-decides-answers test, the decision table, the weekly written updates, the small dashboard. Somewhere between twenty and thirty comes the wall Marta hit, where a second layer of ownership becomes unavoidable, some people now owning domains through other people. This is exactly where founders stall, because adding that layer feels like admitting the family has become a company. It has. It became one around hire eleven, and pretending otherwise deprives the company of joints while keeping you as the load-bearing pole. Past thirty-five or forty, the machine needs a formal operating rhythm tying all of this together, and that conversation, frameworks included, is chapter thirteen, with the what-breaks-next inventory in chapter fourteen.

How do you know your dose is right? The company tells you, in symptoms, and it pays to learn both dialects. Too little skeleton sounds like: every decision waits for the founder, the same fire twice, "I assumed someone else was handling it," a two-week holiday that requires a month of preparation and a month of repair. Too much sounds like: a meeting to prepare for a meeting, people quoting process at each other instead of talking, a form where a conversation used to be, and the phrase "that's not my job" arriving in a company too small to contain it. When in doubt, under-build and listen. Adding a bone to a company in visible recurring pain is far easier than removing one a department has grown fond of.

Warning

Do not import your skeleton from a company ten times your size, and be careful when you hire senior people from large organizations, because they will, with the best intentions, prescribe the anatomy they know: job families, committees, approval chains, quarterly business reviews with pre-reads for the pre-reads. Big-company structure solves big-company problems, most of them problems of coordination at a scale you have not reached and may never reach. Your problems are speed, clarity, and staying able to hear. Steal individual tools from the big companies by all means, they have excellent tools, but let the recurring pain of your actual company, not someone's former employer, decide which bones you build.

And a final word for the founder who has read this far while privately planning to build none of it, because structure feels like the death of the thing they loved. I have real sympathy for this position. I held it for years. Here is what dissolved it. Skip the structure, and the shape-holding and signal-carrying still happen. You do them, personally, with your calendar and your evenings and your marriage, and every year the company grows, the toll goes up. The pole in the middle of the tent does not experience the tent as free and unstructured. Structure, built on purpose and dosed right, spares one human from being consumed to fake it. That is what it is for.

Marta, Two Years Later

I want to end with what actually happened at the agency, partly because you have earned an ending and partly because the honest version resists a tidy arc, which is itself instructive.

Story

Two years after the November phone call, I visited Marta's agency, thirty-two people by then, on an ordinary Wednesday. At the Monday all-hands two days earlier, twenty minutes, never cancelled, an account lead had stood up and said, in front of everyone including two people who had joined that month, that the agency's biggest retainer client was making unhappy noises about response times, that it had been her worry line three weeks running, and that she and the studio lead had changed the staffing on the account and would know within a month whether it had worked. Total drama: none. Total elapsed time between the first unhappy noise and the founder knowing: two days, and Marta had read it in the weekly update before the all-hands said it out loud.

"That exact situation," Marta told me, "is the rebrand mess. Same size, same client type, same slow leak. In the old company I would have found out at a party." Then, because she is honest, she gave me the other half of the ledger. The first decision table had needed three rewrites, because she kept drafting herself into the "consulted" column of everything, and her management team kept crossing her out. Two of the four reflexes had died on the first attempt and needed relaunching with owners who believed in them. One person, a talented designer who had loved the old formlessness, had looked at the new skeleton and left, without bitterness, and Marta still counts it as a real cost. "The book version of this story ends with the all-hands," she said. "The true version is that we built it wrong twice first, and it cost us someone I liked."

That is the shape of the work: a fit you maintain, not a renovation you complete, because the company keeps growing and the skeleton that fits at twenty-five pinches at forty. What changes for good is the founder's job description. Marta now knows less raw detail about her company than she has ever known, and learns the important things faster than she ever has. Those two facts feel contradictory and are actually the whole point. You build the skeleton and nervous system so the company can know things without you, act on them without you, and tell you what hurts while there is still time to do something about it. The version of the company where you knew everything is gone, and chasing it is how founders become bottlenecks with excellent intentions.

Which leaves one last uncomfortable question sitting in the founder's chair: now that the company has a spine that is not you and senses that are not yours, what exactly is your job, and are you any good at it yet? That is chapter twelve, and I would bring something to write with.

The Short Version

  • Past a dozen people, "nobody tells me anything anymore" is arithmetic, not betrayal. Communication pairs grow with the square of headcount, and the founder-as-hub model fails silently.
  • Build two systems on purpose: a skeleton (roles, reporting lines, decision rights) that holds the company's shape, and a nervous system (meetings, documentation, feedback loops, metrics) that carries its signal. Every bone needs a nerve attached, and every nerve a bone.
  • A real role passes three tests: the owner sees it, decides it, and answers for it. Every important thing has exactly one owner, and "we all own it" means nobody does.
  • Write the decision table: who decides what, up to what limit, consulting whom, telling whom after. Every row buys back founder hours and everyone else's speed.
  • Price your meetings in euros and audit them yearly: keep, fix, or kill. Every meeting gets one owner and one honest job, synchronize, decide, or create. Write status down; meet about exceptions.
  • Company memory has three shelves: what is true now (guaranteed current), what we decided and why, and how we do things (written on the second ask, in twenty lines, linked where the work happens).
  • Good news travels alone; bad news needs infrastructure. Weekly worry lines, always-on debriefs, honest skip-levels, and closed loops. Measure your bad-news latency in days, not vibes.
  • A metric carries signal only if someone owns it, it can change a named decision, it is allowed to look bad, and it leads where possible. Ten numbers beat forty-one. A dashboard on which nothing is red is broken.
  • Dose the structure: add a bone when pain recurs, not on the first twinge, and never import a big company's anatomy into a small company's body.
  • The goal is a company that can know, act, and feel pain without routing everything through you. The version where you knew everything is gone; build for the one you have.

Chapter 12

Evolving Your Own Management and Leadership Skills

The biggest bottleneck in your company shaves your face every morning, and this chapter is about what happens after you finally admit it.

The first real holiday I took from the routing company, three years in, lasted nine days. I had prepared for it like a military operation: briefings, handover documents, a laminated sheet of phone numbers taped inside the server cabinet, and a solemn speech about how I trusted everyone completely. Then I flew to Portugal, checked my email eleven times a day, and came back braced for smoke.

There was no smoke. That was the horrifying part.

Nothing had burned down. Nothing had happened at all. I walked in on Monday morning and found forty-one decisions waiting for me, stacked in neat piles like airport luggage when the belt stops: a discount request from sales, a candidate the team liked but had not called back, a supplier contract printed out with a sticky note that said "when Wouter returns," a developer who had spent four days on the wrong feature because he was unsure and would not risk guessing wrong. My company, the thing I bragged about at birthdays, had paused without me. Like a video. Nine days of my team's working life, spent waiting for one man to come back from the beach.

I remember standing at the whiteboard where someone had actually written a list titled "For W," feeling two things at once. The first was a warm, shameful little glow. They need me. I matter. The second, arriving a few seconds later and staying for years, was the correct reaction: I have built a machine with a single point of failure, and the single point of failure gets sunburned.

I did what I did in those years whenever something confused me more than it should. I drove to Henk's house and sat at his kitchen table, and I complained.

Story

I gave Henk the full performance. My team would not take initiative. They escalated everything. Quality dropped the moment I stopped checking. I had hired adults and somehow ended up running a kindergarten with payroll. Henk drank his coffee, black as always, and let me finish, which should have been my first warning, because Henk never let me finish when I was right.

Then he stood up, walked me into his hallway, and positioned me in front of the mirror by the coat rack, hands on my shoulders like he was lining up a fence post.

"Look. You see him?"

I said I saw him.

"That is the manager of everyone you just complained about. Every complaint you made in my kitchen is a note about this man's work. His people wait? He taught them waiting is safe and guessing is dangerous. His people escalate everything? He grabs the wheel every time the car wobbles, so now nobody else steers. Quality drops when he looks away?" Henk tapped the glass, once, with one thick finger. "Then he built quality out of his own eyeballs instead of building it into the work. That is a design problem, and there is the designer."

I started to defend myself and he talked over me without raising his voice, the way he did everything.

"When one machine makes bad parts, maybe the machine. When every machine makes bad parts, the factory. You are the factory, boy. Come back when you have a complaint about the man in the mirror. That one we can fix."

It took me an embarrassingly long time to forgive that conversation, and slightly longer to understand it. This chapter is everything I learned after I did.

Here is the shape of the thing. Somewhere between roughly ten and forty people, every founder-led company runs into the same wall, and the wall is the founder. The job changed underneath them, quietly, without a memo, and they kept doing the old job with more hours and more heroics. The skills that built the company, doing everything, deciding instantly, being the best at the craft, caring about every detail, stop being the engine and start being the ceiling. Chapter 11 was about building the company's skeleton and nervous system. This chapter is about the remaining piece of infrastructure nobody audits: you.

Fair warning: this is one of the three chapters the introduction flags for emergencies, and if the field note sent you here on a bad night, welcome. You are load-bearing, that is all, and we are going to fix that.

How to Know You Are the Bottleneck

Nobody thinks they are the bottleneck. The bottleneck experience, from the inside, feels like being indispensable, which feels wonderful. You are busy, needed, consulted on everything, cc'd on everything, thanked constantly. Every symptom of the disease arrives disguised as a compliment.

So diagnose it by queue, never by feeling. A bottleneck, in a factory or a founder, is the place where work stacks up and waits. You find it the same way Henk found it on a shop floor: you walk around and look for the piles.

Here are the piles, translated for a company:

  • The decision queue. Count every decision currently waiting on you and only you, down to the 200 euro ones. If the number surprises you, and it will, you have your answer.
  • The latency test. How long does a routine question take to get answered in your company? If the honest answer is "however long until Wouter reads Slack," your calendar is your company's clock speed.
  • The holiday test. The one I failed. Leave for a week, offline for real. If the company breaks, you have a competence problem in the team, which is chapter 10. If the company pauses, you have a you problem, which is this one. The pause is worse than the fire, because a fire at least tells you where it is.
  • The sentence test. Listen for "let me check with" followed by your name. In small doses that is prudence. As a company motto, it is a diagnosis.
  • The meeting test. Do discussions visibly reshape themselves when you enter the room? Do people wait to hear your view before offering theirs? Congratulations, your opinions have stopped being contributions and started being weather.

To see what the queue costs in practice, follow one item through it. A customer asks your account manager for a 15 percent discount on a renewal. She knows the customer, knows the margin, knows the answer is "10 percent against a two-year term," and she is right. But discounts are Wouter territory, so she writes it up and sends it to you. You are in interviews all day, so it waits. The customer emails her again on Thursday; she replies with something warm and empty. You read the request Friday evening, tired, between two other queued items, ask a clarifying question she answered in the original message, and by the time the answer is agreed, the customer has spent eight days learning that this supplier cannot answer a simple question in less than a week. The discount you finally approve is the one she proposed on Monday. Total value you added: zero. Total cost: eight days of latency, one slightly insulted account manager, one customer doing arithmetic about what support response times must look like if pricing takes this long. Now multiply by forty-one.

The cruel arithmetic is that all of this used to be fine. At five people, the founder touching everything is the operating model, and a good one. Every decision passing through you is fast, consistent, and informed by the whole picture, because at five people you genuinely hold the whole picture. At fifteen, you hold most of it, and touching everything costs a little. At thirty, you hold maybe half of it, and touching everything means half your decisions are made with worse information than the person who brought you the question already had. They knew the customer, the code, the oven, the situation. You knew a two-minute summary, and you overruled them with it.

That is the moment the compliment becomes a tax. Past it, every hour of company growth adds to the queue behind you, and the queue does something more expensive than waiting: it teaches. Every time someone brings you a decision they could have made and you make it, brisk and competent, you teach them that bringing decisions is how things work here. Each answer trains the asker. A year of that training produces exactly the team I complained about at Henk's table: capable adults who have rationally concluded that guessing is punished and waiting is free.

And be honest about one more thing, because I was not for years: part of you built the queue on purpose. Being the person everything waits for is the last version of being the person who does everything, and giving it up means finding out who you are when the company can breathe without you. Some founders keep the bottleneck the way other people keep an untidy garage: clearing it would raise questions they would rather not answer. If a small voice just objected to this paragraph, that voice is the one we are here to interview.

And say it plainly: they are behaving correctly. Given the incentives you built, waiting for you is the smart move. Which is why speeches about initiative change nothing. I gave the speech, twice. It works for about a week, until the next time you grab the wheel, and then everyone drifts back to the old rules, a little more cynical than before. The fix is changing what happens when they decide without you, and we will get to that in the delegation section, the longest in this chapter because it deserves to be.
