Your strengths built the company. Applied one company size too late, the same strengths build the ceiling.

What Got You Here Stops Working

There is a well-worn phrase in the coaching world, what got you here won't get you there, and like most well-worn phrases it is worn because it is load-bearing. But I want to make it more uncomfortable than the poster version, because the poster version lets you off easy.

The poster version says you will need new skills. True, and toothless. The uncomfortable version says the exact behaviors that built your company will, past a certain size, damage it. Same founder, same moves, opposite effect.

Take the greatest hits of the early years:

  • Doing it yourself. Year one, this is the whole company. Year six, every task you do yourself is a task someone was not trained on, plus a signal that you do not trust the person paid to do it.
  • Deciding instantly. Year one, speed is your only advantage over the big slow competitors. Year six, your instant decisions land on people who were halfway through deciding it themselves, and each one teaches the lesson from the previous section.
  • Being the best at the craft. Year one, of course you are, there is nobody else. Year six, if you are still the best developer, baker, or designer in the building, that is an indictment of your hiring, and your best people can feel the ceiling an inch above their heads.
  • Caring about every detail. Year one, the details are the product. Year six, a founder who reviews everything is a queue with opinions.
  • Heroics. Year one, the all-nighter saves the customer and becomes a founding legend. Year six, your heroics paper over broken processes that would otherwise get fixed, and they set a standard of self-harm that your best people either imitate, resent, or leave over.

Notice what is not on the list: your judgment, your care for customers, your standards. Those transfer. It is the delivery mechanism that expires. The job stops being "apply my talent to the work" and becomes "build a machine that applies talent to the work," and those are so different that they might as well be different professions. The first is a craft. The second is a craft about crafts, and nobody is born with it, which is good news, because it means the awkwardness you feel is the standard tuition. Everyone pays it.

Why the year of lag? Because the old skills keep paying out small, immediate rewards long after they have stopped paying out large ones. Fix a bug yourself and you get the hit of visible progress in twenty minutes. Coach a developer to fix it and you get nothing today, a slightly slower fix this week, and a person who never brings you that bug again, which pays out forever but feels like nothing. The old job has better dopamine. The new job has better compounding. Every founder I know, me very much included, chased the dopamine for at least a year past the crossing, and most of us needed either a mirror speech or a small disaster to stop.

Delegation: The Skill Everyone Claims and Almost Nobody Has

Ask a room of founders whether they delegate and every hand goes up. Ask their teams and the hands come down. The gap exists because most of what founders call delegation is one of two cheaper things wearing delegation's coat.

The first is dumping: handing over a task with no context, no authority, and no definition of done, then expressing disappointment at the result. "Can you take care of the newsletter" is dumping. The person now owns your anxiety but not your information.

The second is puppeteering: handing over a task while keeping every decision. The person executes your choices with their hands. It looks like delegation on the org chart and feels like data entry from the inside. Puppeteering is worse than doing it yourself, because it costs two salaries to produce one person's judgment, and it slowly teaches a good hire to stop thinking.

Real delegation transfers decisions, not tasks, at an explicitly agreed level of autonomy. The load-bearing phrase there is "explicitly agreed." Almost every delegation disaster I have caused or witnessed came from two people holding different unspoken assumptions about who decides what, discovering the difference in production.

The tool that fixed this for me is old, unglamorous, and works: a delegation ladder. It names the levels of autonomy so that two people can point at a rung instead of guessing. Mine has six rungs, and the exact wording matters less than the fact that both of you can say the number out loud.

The delegation ladder: six rungs of autonomy, to be agreed out loud, per topic, per person
RungWhat you sayWho decidesWhen it fitsWhat it costs you
1. Do exactly this"Follow these steps, exactly, and tell me when it is done."You, completelyNew person, high stakes, or genuine emergenciesEverything. You still own the thinking, forever, and they learn nothing except obedience.
2. Research it for me"Dig into this and bring me the options. I will choose."You, with their homeworkDecisions you must own but lack time to investigateYour evenings. Also a rung people get stuck on for years if you like it too much.
3. Recommend, I approve"Bring me your best answer and your reasoning. Default is yes."Them, with your vetoThe training rung. Most new responsibilities should start here.A short delay per decision, plus the discipline to veto rarely and explain always.
4. Decide, then tell me straight away"Make the call. Tell me the same day so I am never surprised."ThemProven judgment, decisions that are reversible or boundedYour reflexes. You will hear about decisions you would have made differently, and you must say nothing.
5. Decide, tell me routinely"Make the call. I will read about it in the weekly notes."ThemTheir domain, your occasional curiosityDetail. You now learn about their area in summaries, like an adult.
6. Own it"This is yours. Spend, decide, hire within these limits. Bring me the results."Them, within written limitsLeaders of functions. The rung real companies are built from.Identity. Some part of the company is now genuinely not yours anymore, which is the whole point and still stings.

Three rules make the ladder work, and skipping any of them turns it back into decoration.

Rule one: assign rungs per topic, not per person. Your operations lead might be rung 5 on supplier choices, rung 3 on pricing, and rung 1 on anything involving lawyers. That is a map. The failure mode is granting one global trust level per human, which forces you to set it at the level of their weakest area, which makes strong people feel handcuffed everywhere because of one domain.

Rule two: climb one rung at a time, on schedule. The ladder is an escalator, and it should be moving. When you hand something over at rung 3, say in the same breath when you expect it to reach rung 4: "Three months of recommendations, then you decide and tell me." Without a schedule, rung 3 becomes a permanent residence, and you have built an approval bureaucracy with extra steps.

Rule three: when the ladder breaks, fix the rung, not the person. A bad outcome at rung 4 is information. Maybe the rung was right and the decision was one of the acceptable losses of letting humans decide things. Maybe the boundaries were fuzzy. The one thing you must never do is the thing you will most want to do, which is grab the topic back to rung 1 in front of everyone. I know exactly what that costs, because I paid it.

Story

Four years into the routing company I finally delegated pricing to my sales lead, a careful, sharp man who had earned it. Rung 4, though we did not have the language then: decide, tell me straight away. For two months it went fine, which means I found something else to worry about.

Then he closed a three-year deal with a fleet operator at a discount that made my eyes water. Sixty-something thousand euros lighter than my mental price. He had reasons, decent ones, reference customer, strategic segment, their procurement had squeezed hard. I did not hear the reasons, because I was not listening. I was composing.

And in the Monday meeting, in front of everyone, I announced that all pricing above a certain size would now come across my desk again "for a while." I remember feeling decisive. Leaderly, even. A correction, swift and clear.

Here is what I actually bought for my sixty thousand euros. My sales lead never made an unprompted decision again in the time he worked for me, and he left within the year, politely, for a company that let him do his job. The rest of the team, who had watched, updated their rules: autonomy here is real until the first mistake, so keep receipts and get sign-off. My support lead started forwarding me refund requests she had been handling herself for a year, "just to be safe." One public snatch-back, and delegation died in every corner of a thirty-person company, for at least a year. Nobody announced it. It just went quiet, the way trust does.

The deal, for the record, turned out fine. The customer renewed twice and referred us to two others. The only lasting damage from the whole affair was the part I did in the Monday meeting.

Warning

The snatch-back is delegation's cause of death, and it is always available in a flattering disguise: quality control, prudence, "just for now." If a delegated decision goes wrong, correct in private, adjust the rung openly and calmly if you must, and say what would need to be true to climb back. Grab the wheel in public and the lesson lands on the twenty people watching, and their lesson costs more than any single bad decision ever will. If you cannot leave a topic delegated, be honest and take it back formally, once, with an explanation. Even that is survivable. Yo-yo autonomy is not.

The handover conversation, word for word

Because "delegate more" is advice the way "eat better" is advice, here is the actual conversation, using a real example: handing customer refunds under 500 euros to your support lead. It takes fifteen minutes and has five parts, and I now refuse to consider anything delegated until all five have been said out loud.

The what and the why: "I want you to own refund decisions under 500 euros. You handle these conversations all day; you have better information than I do by the time it reaches me, and my queue is adding days of delay to customers who are already unhappy." The rung: "Rung 4. You decide, you tell me the same day in the channel, one line is enough. I am aiming for rung 5 within a quarter, where I just see them in the weekly summary." The boundaries: "Under 500 per case, under 2,000 a month total. Anything involving a legal threat or one of our ten biggest accounts still comes to me. If you are unsure whether something is inside the box, that question is always welcome and never counts against you." The definition of good: "I care that customers feel treated like adults and that we spot patterns. A refund that buys us a loyal customer is money well spent. Ten refunds for the same bug is a bug, and I want to hear about it." The failure clause, which almost everyone skips and which does most of the work: "You will make some calls I would have made differently. That is expected and priced in. If one goes properly wrong, we look at it together, in private, and we fix the boundary, not your authority. The only ways to lose this are hiding a mistake or ignoring the box."

Fifteen minutes. Compare it to what usually happens, which is "you can handle refunds now, right?" tossed over a shoulder, followed six weeks later by shock on one side and whiplash on the other. Every delegation disaster I have audited, mine and other people's, was missing at least two of the five parts, and it was usually the boundaries and the failure clause, which is to say, the two parts that require you to think before you speak.

What to hand over first

Founders always want to start by delegating the thing they hate most. Wrong order. The thing you hate is usually either genuinely yours to keep, which is why it feels heavy, or so tangled that it will fail in the hands of whoever receives it, and the failure will "prove" that delegation does not work here. Start instead where three things overlap: decisions that recur weekly or more, decisions that are reversible or financially bounded, and decisions where someone on the team already has better information than you. Refunds, scheduling, routine supplier orders, first-round interview screens, small discounts inside a written band. None of these are glamorous, and that is the point. Each one is a low-stakes repetition of the trust loop: hand over, watch the dip, hold your nerve, watch them exceed you, climb a rung. Every handover clears your queue and, more useful, drills the exact muscle you will need when the material gets expensive. Theirs too.

One more thing about delegation, because it is the part I resisted longest: the dip is mandatory. Whoever takes over will, for a while, do the thing 70 or 80 percent as well as you, slower, with mistakes you would not have made. That is the middle of delegation, the same way falling off a bike is the middle of learning to ride one. Your choices are a temporary 80 percent that grows into 105 percent, because they will exceed you at anything you let them own outright, or a permanent 100 percent that caps the company at the size of your calendar. Written down, nobody picks the second option. Live, at 17:40, watching someone draft a clumsy customer email you could fix in ninety seconds, everybody does. The whole discipline of delegation is refusing that ninety-second fix, every day, until the dip has passed.

Try this

Run a one-week bottleneck audit. Keep a page with three columns: O for decisions only you could legitimately make (spending above your comfort line, firing, signing), A for decisions where you added real value but were not required, and N for decisions that should never have reached you. Every time someone brings you a decision this week, one tally mark, no exceptions. On Friday, count. Every founder I have talked into this predicted mostly O and found mostly N. Then take the three fattest N clusters and assign each a name and a rung from the ladder, out loud, this month.

Feedback: The Currency You Have to Spend Both Ways

If delegation is the structural half of leading, feedback is the circulatory half, and founders are bad at it in both directions, for opposite reasons. We flinch from giving it because we like being liked, and we stop receiving it because of a physics problem nobody warned us about. Take them in turn. Chapter 11 covered feedback loops as company plumbing, meetings, metrics, retrospectives. This section is about you personally as a sender and receiver, which no amount of plumbing replaces.

Giving it: small, fast, and about the work

The feedback founders avoid is the small daily kind: the report that was late again, the tone in the meeting, the corner that keeps getting cut. We skip it because each single instance is too minor to justify an awkward conversation, and so we save them up, unconsciously, at compound interest. Then, months later, some 4 percent trigger releases 100 percent of the stored account, and the person on the receiving end learns two things: that they had been failing for months, and that nobody thought them adult enough to be told. Both are your fault, not theirs.

The fix is boring and works: shrink the unit. Feedback the size of a sentence, delivered within a day or two, in private, about behavior rather than character. The pattern I finally settled on has three moves and no acronym. Say what you observed, plainly: "The proposal went out with pricing errors twice this month." Say the impact, honestly: "The customer now checks our numbers, which is exactly the doubt we cannot afford." Then hand over the pen: "What is going on, and what would fix it?" That last move matters most, because half the time the answer surprises you. The proposal was late because it waited three days for your review, dear bottleneck, and the person rushed the final hour they actually got. Feedback at this size is maintenance, and like all maintenance it is cheapest on schedule and ruinous deferred.

To make the size of the unit concrete: the whole conversation should fit in the gap between two meetings. "Hey, two minutes. The demo yesterday, you talked through the customer's question twice instead of answering it, and I watched them switch off. You know this material better than anyone, so what happened?" Then you listen, and it turns out he had been told, by you, in passing, three weeks earlier, never to promise dates, and had over-corrected into answering nothing at all. Ninety seconds, one behavior, same week, and you both walked away smarter. The annual-review version of that same feedback, delivered in month eleven as "communication skills: needs development," would have helped nobody and insulted everyone.

Two habits multiply the effect. First, keep the positive-to-corrective ratio honest. If the only feedback you emit is corrective, people learn to flinch when you approach, and your praise budget is the cheapest leadership money you will ever spend, provided the praise is specific. "Good job" is noise. "You told the customer no without making them feel stupid, and I have been trying to learn that for ten years" is currency. Second, never let feedback travel through you sideways. When Anna complains to you about Tomas, walk Anna back to Tomas's door, coach her on the sentence if she needs it, and follow up that it happened. Accept the parcel even once and you become the company's courier of resentments, and the delivery route only gets longer.

Receiving it: you live inside a distortion field now

Here is the physics problem. The moment you sign someone's payslip, the truth they send you passes through a filter of self-preservation. The filter comes standard, has nothing to do with your character, and does not care that you are friendly. You decide raises. You decide who stays. However approachable you feel, and I felt very approachable, complaints about my approachability notwithstanding, people will round their opinions toward what is safe. The scary thing about the distortion field is that it is silent. Nobody tells you that nobody tells you things. The information simply stops arriving, and its absence feels exactly like everything being fine.

I learned to treat signals of dissent as endangered and therefore protected. When someone disagreed with me in a meeting, especially someone junior, especially clumsily, the only acceptable first response was some visible form of "thank you, say more," even when they were wrong, especially when they were wrong. The first punished dissenter is the last dissenter. You do not get to correct the facts until you have rewarded the courage, and if that sounds like coddling, consider what you are otherwise breeding: a company that watches you walk toward a cliff in respectful silence.

Approachability is the passive half. Go extract the truth as well, because vague invitations produce nothing. "Any feedback for me?" is a question with one safe answer and everyone knows it. What works are narrow, specific, pre-committed questions asked in one-on-ones: "What is one thing I should stop doing?" "Where did I slow you down this month?" "What do you all discuss that you would not raise with me in the room?" And then the actual test, because the questions are the cheap part: what your face does during the first answer, and what you do about it within two weeks. Feedback to a founder is a market. If honesty pays, measured in visible change and public credit, supply increases. If honesty costs, measured in your defensiveness or a chill in your tone, the market closes, quietly, and it stays closed for a long time. People will assure you the market is open. On this one topic, trust the traffic and nothing else.

Self-Awareness: Which Kind of Problem Are You?

Every founder is a problem for their company in some specific, patterned way: reliably, along the grain of their personality, under stress, on repeat. Having a failure mode is universal. The damage comes from founders who cannot name theirs, who therefore cannot see themselves doing it, and who therefore explain the wreckage some other way, usually by complaining about their team at a mentor's kitchen table.

Self-awareness sounds like a retreat-and-incense word, so let me make it mechanical: self-awareness is knowing your default move under pressure before you make it, early enough to insert one breath between the trigger and the move. That is all. The move itself may never go away. Mine has not. But a named failure mode with a pause in front of it does a tenth of the damage of an unnamed one running on automatic.

Here are the seven I have seen most often, in myself and across every founder I know. Most of us have one home mode and one travel mode for special occasions. Read the table looking for yourself, not for your cofounder, although I know exactly which row you looked at first.

Founder failure modes: what the team sees, what you feel, and the tell that gives you away
ModeWhat the team experiencesWhat it feels like from insideThe tellFirst fix
The HeroEvery crisis ends with you swooping in. Nobody else ever finishes anything hard.Rescuing. Being needed. Honestly? Being magnificent.You feel a small lift when things go wrong, because now it is your kind of day.Next crisis, coach from the wall. Hands in pockets, questions only. Let them win one ugly.
The SeagullWeeks of absence, then you swoop in, make noise, redirect everything, and vanish again.Staying strategic. Trusting the team. Then one glance at the work and pure alarm.The team announces your visits afterwards, in warnings: "heads up, he has seen the roadmap."Pick a fixed, boring rhythm of involvement (chapter 11 has the machinery) and forbid yourself the drive-by.
The BottleneckEverything waits. Initiative is quietly punished, so nobody offers any.Being indispensable. Busy from dark to dark. Weirdly proud of the queue.Your holiday pauses the company. Forty-one items, in my case.The bottleneck audit and the ladder, this chapter, this month.
The GhostYou have vanished into product, strategy, or a hobby you have relabeled strategy. Decisions starve.Deep work. Finally some real thinking. Mild dread of the office.People start prefacing requests with "when you have time," and they have stopped expecting an answer.Show up on a schedule people can set clocks by, even if shorter. Predictable beats plentiful.
The WeathervanePriorities change with your latest podcast, flight, or impressive dinner companion. Whiplash as culture.Vision. Pattern recognition. Each new direction feels like clarity at last.Your team has learned to wait three weeks before acting on any announcement, and they are right to.New ideas go into a parking document, in writing, and survive two weeks before anyone is allowed to hear them.
The Smartest PersonEvery discussion ends with your answer. Arguments are technically winnable and never worth it.Rigor. High standards. Why does nobody push back anymore?Silence after you speak in meetings. You mistake it for agreement.Speak last. Ask "what am I missing?" and count to ten before rescuing the silence.
The Nice OneNo hard truth arrives until it is enormous. Underperformers linger for years. Everyone knows, including them.Kindness. Loyalty. A stomach ache before every difficult conversation, so, few conversations.You have described the same person as "getting there" for three consecutive years.Book the conversation before you feel ready, because you will never feel ready. Kind and clear, chapter 10 has the words.

Mine, for the record, are Hero home and Bottleneck away, and they travel well together: the Hero rescues, the rescue routes more decisions to the Hero, the queue grows, the Bottleneck settles in and calls it dedication. I know founders who are Weathervane and Ghost, a combination whose company changes direction quarterly, steered by someone who is not there. Any combination is workable. What matters is whether you know yours.

Once you have named your mode, tell your team, and give them a key to the door. Sounds like oversharing; bear with me, because it is mechanics. The failure mode fires fastest exactly when you are least able to observe it, under stress, in the room, mid-sentence, which means the people best positioned to catch it are the ones watching you do it. But "feel free to call me out" is worthless, because calling out the boss mid-move is the exact thing the distortion field forbids. What works is agreeing on a lightweight, pre-authorized signal. At the routing company, after I finally confessed my Hero mode to the leadership team, we agreed that anyone could say "cape check" when they saw me reaching for a rescue, and that my only permitted response was to stop talking and ask what they were seeing. People used it maybe once a month. It embarrassed me every time. It was also, euro for euro, the cheapest management development program I ever ran, and the first time a junior developer used it, grinning, terrified, correct, I knew the distortion field had a hole in it at last.

How do you find out, given the distortion field from the previous section? Three sources, in ascending order of discomfort. First, your history: look at your last three team-related messes and ask what they have in common, and the common element standing in all three photographs is usually you, doing your move. Second, your exes, professionally speaking: people who used to work for you have left the distortion field, and a former employee at a café table will tell you in twenty minutes, if you ask like you mean it, what current ones would not say in twenty months. Third, ask your current team, but pay the toll upfront by guessing first, out loud: "I think my failure mode is grabbing the wheel. How close am I?" Naming a candidate yourself moves the conversation from "criticize the boss," which nobody sane accepts, to "correct the boss's aim," which people enjoy.

Energy: You Are the Instrument, and You Are Playing It Drunk

Founders manage money with spreadsheets, forecasts, and a healthy paranoia we spent all of chapter 6 installing. Then they manage the machine that makes every important decision, their own nervous system, like a rental car. The tank is somebody else's problem, redlining is normal, and maintenance is for people with smaller ambitions.

Here is the argument for taking energy seriously, made in business terms rather than wellness ones, because I would have ignored the wellness ones and did for years. Your company's most expensive product is your judgment. Every significant decision, pricing, hiring, firing, the tone you take in the Monday meeting, is manufactured by a biological machine whose output quality is measurably a function of sleep, recovery, and load. Run that machine depleted and it does not feel like impairment from the inside. That is the trap. Tired judgment feels exactly like judgment. The dashboard has no warning light. The only gauge is the decisions themselves, which quietly get worse, and which you defend with full confidence, because confidence is the last thing to go.

Story

The autumn the routing company was seven years old, I ran a stretch of about four months on fumes: a big customer migration, a hiring push, a newborn at home, and my personal conviction, held since age nineteen, that rest was something I would purchase in bulk later, after the next milestone. I felt sharp the whole time. I want that on the record. I felt clear, fast, decisive, honestly a little heroic.

In those four months I made three decisions that between them cost more than any two full years of my sleep would have. I hired a senior manager against the visible hesitation of everyone who interviewed him, because the search was exhausting me and he could start Monday. Eleven months and one department's morale later, we paid him to leave. I signed a partnership agreement I had skimmed, tired, on a train, with an exclusivity clause that took fourteen months and actual lawyers to escape. And I snapped, in front of the whole team, at our best developer over a delay that turned out to be my fault, an instruction I had given in one meeting and forgotten by the next. She accepted my apology. She also, and I do not blame her, started answering recruiters.

I told Henk about the manager and the contract, framing both, I am ashamed to say, as bad luck. He listened, looked at me for a while over the coffee, and delivered the shortest performance review of my life.

"Tired men sign anything."

Then, because he could see me preparing to argue: "In the warehouse we had rules. A man on a forklift works so many hours, then he stops, because the clock says so, tired or not. Feeling tired comes after the accident. You are driving a bigger forklift, boy, and you have the pallet over everyone's heads."

Notice the mechanism in Henk's rule: by the clock, not by feel. That is the entire trick, because feel is the first sensor fatigue disables. The practical program that came out of that autumn was three policies, none of which requires a retreat or a single scented candle.

First, sort your work by what it does to you, not just what it needs from you. Two identical hours on the calendar can carry very different costs. Some work charges you, and you leave with more capacity than you brought. Some work drains you at a fair price, fine, that is the job. And some work corrodes you, costing double what it produces. The mix is personal, and finding yours takes a week of honest bookkeeping, which is the exercise below. The point of knowing is placement: corrosive work goes in your strongest hours in small doses, or gets delegated up the ladder first, and big decisions never get made in the hours after it.

Second, schedule recovery like an obligation, because it is one. Sleep is the whole foundation, and every founder folklore story about four-hour nights is either a lie, a rare mutant, or a slow-motion invoice. Real holidays, offline ones, are the test of whether the machine runs without you, and we established at the top of this chapter what my test found. Exercise is the cheapest mood stabilizer on the market. None of this is news. What made it operational for me was Henk's framing: by the clock, in the calendar, defended like a customer meeting, because the customer is every decision I will make that week.

Third, install a fatigue interlock on big decisions. Mine is a rule with three clauses. No irreversible decision after a bad night. No signature the same day as the pitch, ever, however good it sounds, especially however good it sounds. And when I notice I am rushing a big call because deciding feels like relief, that feeling is now itself a red flag: wanting a decision over with is the tired brain begging to put the pallet down, and it will drop it anywhere.

Try this

Keep an energy ledger for one week. In your calendar, after every meeting or work block, type a single character: plus if it gave you energy, minus if it took a fair amount, double minus if it corroded you. Do not philosophize, just mark and move on, ten seconds each. On Friday, review the week and answer two questions with a pen. Which double-minus work could move up the delegation ladder within a month, and to whom? And which big decisions did you make within two hours of a double-minus block? That second answer tends to end the argument about whether any of this applies to you.

Field note

If your honest ledger is minus signs wall to wall, week after week, and the plus column is empty even for the parts of the business you used to love, you have moved past what this chapter can do for you. That pattern deserves a conversation with a professional, a real one, the kind with a diploma rather than a podcast, and booking it is company work of the first order. Everything in the company runs downstream of you being functional, which is the least romantic and most practical reason to take it seriously.

Getting Coached Before You Think You Need It

Somewhere in the last few pages, possibly at the mirror, possibly at the ledger, you may have had the thought every founder has at this point in the chapter: fine, but I can work on this myself. I want to spend a section explaining why that thought is the failure modes protecting themselves. The Hero does not want a coach because heroes do the rescuing. The Smartest Person does not want a coach because what would that say. The Bottleneck has no slot in the calendar. Every mode votes against help, and every vote arrives in the voice of prudence.

Here is the plain case. Every serious performer in every serious field has someone whose job is to watch them work and tell them the truth. Athletes, obviously. Surgeons increasingly. Singers always. The theory is identical everywhere: you cannot see yourself perform, the people around you are paid by you and therefore filtered, so improvement requires an outside eye with no stake in flattering you. Founders are the strange exception, the one performer expected to improve alone, in the dark, using only books and the occasional catastrophe. It is a stupid exception, and it persists because of price tags and pride, so let us handle both.

The price tag first, since it is easier. A good executive coach in Europe runs somewhere between 150 and 400 euros a session, call it three to six thousand a year at a sensible rhythm. Founders who spend that on a conference without blinking will stare at the coaching number like it is a yacht. For calibration: the mishired senior manager from my tired autumn cost north of a hundred thousand euros, all in, and a coach who had made me examine why I was rushing would have paid for two decades of herself in that one avoided signature. Coaching is expensive the way smoke detectors are expensive.

The pride is harder, and the fix is a reframe that happens to be true: the best performers get the most coaching, in every field except ours. Hiring a coach announces one thing, that you have noticed the company's ceiling is made of you, and you have decided to raise it on purpose rather than by accident.

Now, the word "coach" gets used for four different kinds of help, and buying the wrong kind for your situation wastes money and sours founders on all of it. Here is the map I wish someone had handed me.

Four kinds of help, and which problem each one actually solves
KindWhat they doBest forTypical costWatch out for
MentorHas been up your road. Pattern-matches your situation against their scars. Gives answers, and occasionally hallway mirrors.Domain-shaped questions: pricing, hiring, when to scale, "is this normal?"Free, or a coffee and your genuine attention. Not on demand.Their map is their road, not yours. A mentor who insists you replay their exact game has become a nostalgia act.
CoachWatches you work, asks questions until you catch yourself in the act. Gives few answers on purpose. Regular and contracted.You-shaped problems: everything in this chapter. Failure modes, delegation flinches, feedback avoidance.150 to 400 euros a session, every two to four weeks.Credential soup and comfortable chemistry. A coach who never makes you uncomfortable is a subscription, not a service.
Peer groupFive to ten founders, met monthly, confidential, no customers or investors in the room. The only people who truly get it.Loneliness, calibration, accountability. Saying the unsayable numbers out loud.Free to a few thousand a year for organized ones.Groups that curdle into mutual admiration. You want the one that asks follow-up questions, not the one that toasts you.
TherapistWorks on the person, not the professional. The patterns that predate the company and came along as stowaways.When the failure mode has roots: the approval-hunting, the rage, the ledger full of minus signs.Varies; partly covered in much of Europe.Nothing, except the founder pride that books everything on this list before this row. Sometimes the row order should be reversed.

A word for the peer group row, because founders consistently underrate it. Running a company is lonely in a specific, unshareable way: your team should not carry your fears, your partner has heard enough, and your friends with salaries think a slow quarter means a smaller bonus. The first time I sat in a room of eight founders and said an ugly true number out loud, the cash number, the real one, and nobody flinched, two of them nodded, and one said "oh, that year, here is what I did," something unclenched in me that I had not known was clenched. You will get tactics from a peer group, but the tactics are the gift wrap. The gift is calibration: discovering that your secret disasters are standard equipment, and that the confident founder across the table is exactly as scared as you are, on a two-month offset.

Most founders eventually want three of the four, in some rotation. Henk, to be clear, was a mentor, not a coach, and the difference matters: he told me what he saw and occasionally what to do, from his own road. The coach I finally hired, two years after the pricing disaster and one year after the tired autumn, did something Henk never did. She said almost nothing, asked me to describe the last three times I had grabbed the wheel, and then asked, "What are you afraid happens in the thirty seconds after you don't?" I had no answer, and finding one took four sessions and did more for my delegation than every book I had read on it combined, this one now included.

Two practical notes on choosing a coach, since the market is unregulated and full of confident people with laminated methodologies. First, interview three, and ask each to coach you for twenty minutes on something real rather than describe their framework. Buy the one who made you think, not the one who made you comfortable. Second, agree upfront on one observable behavior change for the first three months, something your team could notice without being told, and at month three, ask the team if they noticed. A coach should survive the same measurement culture you apply to everything else you buy. If accountability structures for your whole leadership team are the itch, that is chapter 13's territory, and coaching pairs unreasonably well with it.

The New Job Description Nobody Gives You

If you strip this chapter to its skeleton, it says: somewhere past the crossing on that curve, your job changes from producing the work to producing the people and conditions that produce the work. I want to finish the argument by being concrete about what the new job actually consists of, because "work on the business, not in the business" is a bumper sticker, and you cannot schedule a bumper sticker into a Tuesday.

The new job has, as far as I can tell, four duties that only you can do, which is the correct test for what stays on a founder's desk. Deciding direction: the small number of irreversible, company-shaping calls, a handful a year, which deserve your best hours and your fullest tank, and which is why the energy section is in this chapter and not in a wellness pamphlet. Casting: choosing and growing the few people who lead the rest, since every leader you get right delegates a hundred future decisions in one move. Setting standards: through what you visibly celebrate, tolerate, and refuse, rather than by reviewing everything, which is the Bottleneck's counterfeit of standards. Your worst tolerated behavior on your busiest week sets your company's real values, a thought that belongs to chapter 1 but earns its keep here. And keeping the truth flowing: tending the market for honesty from the feedback section, because you are the only person with the power to make truth-telling safe, and the only one whose flinch can shut the market down.

What does a week look like once the shift has actually happened? Mine, in the good years, was roughly this, and I offer it as one sample rather than a template. About a third of the week in one-on-ones and coaching conversations, which felt like too much until I noticed it was the only work that compounded. One long block, defended with violence, for the direction work: thinking, writing, customer visits, the questions with ten-year answers. A visible, predictable rhythm of showing up in the operating meetings, which chapter 11 built, as a participant with one vote, not as the weather. And, embarrassing to admit, empty space, on purpose, because a founder scheduled to 100 percent is a founder who does all their thinking in fatigue debt and answers every hallway question with their worst brain. The old me would have read that paragraph and seen a part-time job. The old me was also the reason forty-one decisions once waited nine days for a man to come back from Portugal.

Notice what the new job does to your old scoreboard. Your day used to end with evidence: code shipped, bread baked, deals signed, a satisfying pile of done. The new job produces almost no daily evidence. You coach, you unblock, you ask questions in other people's meetings and then, heroically, leave without deciding anything. For months this feels like being paid to be vague. The scoreboard that eventually replaced my pile of done was a single evening question: what can the company do without me this month that it could not do without me last month? When that answer keeps having content, you are doing the new job, whatever your visible output says. And the honest endpoint of this chapter, which I promise arrives feeling like a promotion rather than a funeral: the company's dependence on you should be trending toward zero in operations and toward everything in direction. You are trying to become unnecessary on purpose, in every room except the one where the future is decided.

The Mirror, Again

Years after the hallway, a few months after I sold the routing company, I sat at Henk's kitchen table again. He was older, slower on the stairs. The coffee was still black, still poured without asking, and he still read me from the doorway the way he read a room, in one long look that saved him most of the questions. I told him the story he had never heard in full: the forty-one decisions, the pricing meeting I would pay money to unhappen, the tired autumn, the coach, and the strange final years when the company mostly did not need me and was better at almost everything than it had been when it needed me constantly.

He listened the way he listened, like the story had to clear customs. Then he jerked his thumb toward the hallway.

"Go look."

I went and stood in front of the same mirror, feeling like an idiot, which I have come to understand was a load-bearing part of Henk's method. He shuffled up behind me.

"Complaints?"

I thought about it properly, because he would know if I did not. I said: he still grabs the wheel sometimes. He is still slightly too pleased when there is a crisis with his name on it. He books the difficult conversation about two weeks later than he should.

Henk nodded, satisfied, as if a machine had finally passed inspection. "Good. Same man." A pause, the length of a sip. "Better manager." He was already walking back to his coffee when he delivered the last line over his shoulder, and it is the line I would put on the cover of this chapter if covers worked that way.

"The mirror never gets better, boy. Only the looking."

That is the whole chapter, and the whole phase. You do not graduate from your failure modes, your flinches, your love of the wheel. There is no version of you, five books and two coaches from now, that stands in the hallway and files no complaints. What changes, if you work at it, is the speed of the looking: how fast you catch the move, how honestly you name it, how much company grows in the space between who you are and what you do about it. Everyone else in your company gets a manager. This chapter was about making sure you have one too, and that he is not the last person in the building to hear the truth.

The Short Version

  • Diagnose bottlenecks by queue, not by feeling. Count the decisions waiting on you; the holiday test does not lie. A company that pauses without you is worse than one that burns.
  • Every complaint about your team is a note about their manager. Read it in the mirror first.
  • The skills that built the company become the ceiling: doing, deciding instantly, being the best at the craft. The curves cross quietly, and you will notice about a year late because the old job has better dopamine.
  • Delegate decisions, not tasks, at an explicit rung on the ladder, per topic, climbing on a schedule. The 80 percent dip is mandatory and temporary. The permanent 100 percent caps the company at the size of your calendar.
  • One public snatch-back kills delegation company-wide for a year. Correct in private, adjust rungs calmly, never yo-yo.
  • Give feedback the size of a sentence, within days, about behavior. Saved-up feedback compounds into an explosion that is your fault, not theirs.
  • You live in a distortion field: honesty flows to you only if it visibly pays. Ask narrow questions, reward clumsy dissent, and judge the market by traffic, never by reassurance.
  • Know your failure mode, Hero, Seagull, Bottleneck, Ghost, Weathervane, Smartest Person, or Nice One, well enough to insert one breath before the move.
  • Your judgment is manufactured by a biological machine. Tired judgment feels exactly like judgment; manage energy by the clock, not by feel, because tired men sign anything.
  • Get coached before you think you need it. Mentor, coach, peer group, therapist solve different problems; coaching costs like a smoke detector, mishires cost like a fire.

Chapter 13

The Entrepreneurial Operating System

A good operating rhythm can save your company, and a framework can teach you one, as long as you remember which part is the scaffolding and which part is the building.

The best-run management meeting I have ever attended took place in the back room of a bakery, between a rack of cooling tins and a pallet of flour, and the chair was a kitchen timer shaped like a chicken.

This was a Tuesday, two in the afternoon, in the original shop of my brother-in-law Jonas, the one in Deventer where the whole thing started before there were nine of them. I was there to pick up a birthday cake for my sister, which is the kind of errand you volunteer for when you want an excuse to stand in a warm room that smells like a childhood you never had. Jonas waved me toward a stool in the corner and said, "Sit, we start in two minutes, you can have coffee if you don't talk."

Around a scarred worktable sat five of his shop managers on an assortment of folding chairs and upturned crates. The other four were on a tablet propped against a bread tray, calling in from Almelo, Zutphen, wherever. On the wall, next to the oven schedules, hung a laminated A4 sheet covered in numbers. On the whiteboard, in Jonas's furious block capitals, a single word: STUCK. Below it, a numbered list.

At 14:00 exactly, Jonas wound the chicken and the meeting started. Two managers were still connecting. Nobody waited and nobody recapped for them when they arrived, which told me more about the culture than an hour of interviews would have. First, a round of the table, thirty seconds each: one good thing from your shop this week. A retirement cake with a marzipan tractor. A trainee who showed up early three days running. Then the numbers. Fifteen of them, read aloud off the laminated sheet in under five minutes, each one owned by a named person, each one answered only with "on track" or "off track." Off track got a silent tick on the whiteboard and no discussion. Not yet. Then a check on what Jonas calls the big three, the handful of things the company has promised itself this quarter. On track, on track, off track, tick.

And then, for a full hour, they argued. Properly argued, about the three items from the STUCK list that the room had voted most urgent. Voices rose over rye bread. Someone said "that is not the real problem though, is it" and the room went quiet and then went somewhere more honest. Each argument ended the same way: a name, a date, a sentence on the whiteboard. At 15:25 the chicken went off. Everyone rated the meeting out of ten, out loud, no hedging. Two people said seven, and Jonas asked each of them why, and wrote down the answers. At 15:30 the room was empty and the ovens had their people back.

I sat in the corner with a cake box on my knees and a strange feeling in my chest, because I recognized the shape of what I had just watched. I had run that exact meeting, by that exact clock, perhaps four hundred times at the routing company. "You're running EOS," I said, when Jonas came over. "That was a Level 10 meeting. There's a book. It's called Traction."

Jonas looked at me the way he looks at people who use the word "artisanal." "I'm running a bakery," he said. Then, relenting, because there was family cake involved: "A man at a franchise fair gave me the book years ago. I read it in a weekend. Good book. Terrible words." He walked me through his edits. The book says Rocks, for the quarterly priorities. "I bake bread, Wouter. I'm not calling anything a rock. We call them the big three." The book says Vision/Traction Organizer, a two-page document the whole company shares. His hangs by the flour shelf and is called the one-pager. The book wanted him to appoint an Integrator. He refused on the grounds that, and I quote, "we are not the Avengers." The meeting rating he kept exactly as written, because, he said, it was the only place his managers would tell him the truth about his own meeting.

"I kept the machine," Jonas said, handing me the cake, "and I threw away the costume."

That sentence is this entire chapter, and you could skip to the summary now if you trusted me, which you should not yet. The most jargon-allergic man I know runs the most disciplined operating rhythm I have ever seen, and those two facts live together comfortably, because you can separate the discipline from the costume. This chapter is about the machine: what a business operating system is, a tour of EOS and its two most famous cousins, why the cadence matters more than any of the vocabulary, and how to tell the difference between a company running a system and a company performing one. Because the failure mode here is specific and common, and it has a name I will use more than once: theater with better paperwork.

You Already Have an Operating System

Every company has an operating system. Yours included, right now, today. The only open question is whether anyone can describe it.

By operating system I mean something unglamorous: the agreed way your company decides things, sets priorities, keeps score, and kills problems, week after week, whether or not anyone feels like it. The rhythm, in other words, which runs deeper than the org chart and the values on the wall. Who looks at which numbers, and when. Where a problem goes when someone spots one. How the company chooses what matters this quarter, and how it notices, before the quarter's cremation, that the choice was wrong.

In a company of five people around one table, the operating system is osmosis, and osmosis works fine. Everyone hears everything. Whoever is most alarmed sets the priorities, which at that size usually gets the right answer. If nobody has written any of this down, then the true answer to "how does this company run" is: on the founder's attention and mood. I said in chapter twelve that the founder becomes the bottleneck, and this is the bottleneck's plumbing. You are the scorecard, the issues list, and the meeting cadence, all held in one increasingly tired head.

Then the company grows, and somewhere between twelve and thirty people the osmosis stops working, without sending you a notification. You will know the symptoms when I list them, because this list is why this chapter exists:

  • The team relitigates old decisions, because nobody can remember making them, or where, or who was in the room.
  • Whichever customer or crisis shouted most recently kills Monday's priorities by Thursday.
  • The numbers arrive monthly, from the bookkeeper, as archaeology. They surprise everyone, always, in both directions.
  • The same problems come up in every conversation, warm and familiar, like relatives at a funeral. Everyone knows about the problem. The problem has tenure.
  • Everything important waits for you, and you are the least available person in the building.

A word on borders, because this book has been strict about them. Chapter eleven was about the skeleton and the nervous system: roles, structure, information flow, and how to run meetings that are not a hostage situation. If your individual meetings are bad, go there. This chapter assumes your meetings are tolerable one at a time and asks a different question: do they add up to anything? A company can have perfectly decent meetings and still have no operating system, the way a person can own excellent individual clothes and still be badly dressed. And chapters two and three own the mission and vision themselves. I will not re-explain them here, not even a little, because I promised. This chapter cares only about the machinery that keeps those documents connected to what people actually do on a Tuesday.

So why do packaged frameworks exist, and why would a self-respecting founder buy one instead of building their own rhythm? Two honest reasons. The first is that every growing company reinvents the same five or six mechanisms, badly, in the wrong order, while distracted. A framework is somebody else's version with the bugs already found, debugged across a few thousand companies more than you will ever run. There is humility in buying it, the good kind. The second reason is subtler: a framework's real product is permission. It is much easier to tell your team "we are trying this system, it has a book, other companies use it" than to say "I have personally invented some meetings." The book takes the argument out of the room. That is worth actual money, and I say that as someone who resisted it for two full years longer than I should have.

The Six Jobs, in Plain Language

EOS, the Entrepreneurial Operating System, organizes itself around six components, and I am going to use its list even though this chapter will not insist you use its system, because the list is a good census of the jobs any operating rhythm must do. Strip the branding and the six components are six questions. Every framework you will ever meet, and every homemade system that works, answers these same six, just with different furniture.

Vision. Not writing it, you did that in chapters two and three. Circulating it. The job here is that everyone in the company can say where this is going and how, without rehearsal and without you in the room. Alignment decays like everything else, and the operating system's job is scheduled maintenance.

People. Right people, right seats, assessed honestly on a schedule rather than in the annual panic. The hiring and the letting go live in chapter ten, and your own growth as a leader in chapter twelve. The operating system just makes sure someone asks "is everyone in the right seat" out loud at intervals, instead of only during resignations.

Data. A small set of numbers, reviewed weekly, that catches trouble while trouble is still cheap. Chapter eleven made the case for signal over noise in your metrics. Here the emphasis is on the cadence: a good number reviewed monthly is a history lesson, the same number weekly is an early warning.

Issues. A place where problems go to be written down, named honestly, and killed, instead of circulating forever in the corridor. Most companies know their problems by heart. What they lack is a scheduled venue for executing a problem with witnesses.

Process. The core ways of working, documented just enough that you can train from them and improve them. Skip the wiki nobody reads. Write down the twenty percent of activity that produces most of the value, at the altitude of a recipe rather than a legal contract.

Traction. The framework's word for the whole point: a short list of priorities per quarter, and a meeting pulse that checks them weekly. Ambition converted into dated commitments, and commitments checked at a frequency that leaves time to correct.

Here is the whole set at a glance, with the official tooling and, because I find it clarifying, the translations Jonas actually uses across nine bakeries.

The six components of EOS, what each one is actually for, and what a jargon-allergic baker calls them
EOS componentThe job in plain languageThe tool EOS hands youJonas's translation
VisionEveryone can say where the company is going and how, without rehearsalVision/Traction Organizer (V/TO), two pages, reviewed with everyone twice a year"The one-pager by the flour shelf"
PeopleRight people in the right seats, judged honestly and on a scheduleAccountability Chart, People Analyzer"Names on jobs, and one hard conversation per quarter"
DataA handful of weekly numbers that catch trouble while it is still cheapScorecard: 5 to 15 numbers, each with an owner and a goal"The numbers page"
IssuesProblems get written down, named precisely, and killed with witnessesIssues List, worked with IDS (Identify, Discuss, Solve)"The stuck list"
ProcessThe core ways of working, written down enough to train fromDocumented core processes, "followed by all""How we do it here, on paper"
TractionFew priorities per quarter, checked weekly, with names and datesRocks (90-day priorities) and the Level 10 weekly meeting"The big three and the Tuesday meeting"

If you take nothing else from this chapter, take the list. You can reject every framework in the coming pages and still owe your company an honest answer, per row, to the question: what, in our shop, currently does this job? For a lot of founder-led companies the honest answer, four rows out of six, is "the founder, when he remembers." Treat that answer as a to-do list.

Try this

Take a pen and write the six jobs down the left side of a page: vision circulation, people review, weekly numbers, issue killing, documented process, quarterly priorities. Next to each, write what in your company does that job today. Name the actual mechanism, a meeting that exists, a document with a date on it, a number someone owns. The rule: "we talk about it a lot" does not count as a mechanism, and neither do you. The blank rows are the diagnosis, and they are usually blank in the same two or three places for everyone.

EOS Without the Merchandise

Now the tour. EOS comes from Gino Wickman's book Traction, and Wickman built it for companies like the ones in this book: founder-led, roughly ten to two hundred fifty people, past the kitchen-table stage and drowning slightly. Its genius, and I mean this as the highest compliment I can pay a business book, is that there is almost nothing original in it. Wickman assembled mechanisms that already worked, filed off their rough edges, connected them into one machine, and wrote the manual in language a tired founder can absorb on a Sunday. Original thinking is overrated in operating systems. You do not want an avant-garde heartbeat.

What follows is the machine, tool by tool, with commentary. I ran a lightly modified version of this for years at the routing company, so the commentary comes with scars attached.

The two-page vision

The V/TO compresses your entire strategic existence onto two pages: core values, core focus, a ten-year target, your marketing strategy, a three-year picture, a one-year plan, this quarter's priorities, and the long-term issues list. If you did the work in chapters one through three, you already possess every ingredient, and the V/TO is just the storage format. Its value is the compression. You can read a two-page vision aloud to the whole company twice a year, and EOS insists that you actually do this, which is the part everyone skips and the part that matters. Wickman's phrase is "shared by all," and he means shared the way you share bread, not the way you share a network drive.

Seats before people

The Accountability Chart looks like an org chart until you learn the drawing order. You draw the seats the business needs, define each seat by its five core responsibilities, and only then write names in, one name per seat, though one person may hold several seats in a small company. The discipline: you design the structure for the business you are, instead of letting it accrete around whoever you happen to employ, which is how most org charts form, like coral. Chapter eleven covered structure properly, so I will only add the one EOS idea I find load-bearing: every seat has exactly one owner, and every important function in the company appears on exactly one seat. Shared ownership is the polite Northern European way of saying no ownership.

EOS also makes much of the pairing it calls Visionary and Integrator, the founder who generates ideas and weather, and the operator who converts both into order. It is a real pattern, and if you recognized yourself in chapter twelve's description of the founder as bottleneck, the Integrator conversation is worth having. Just know that this corner of EOS comes with its own sub-industry of books and assessments, and you should wander in with your wallet in your front pocket.

Rocks, or whatever you decide to call them

Every ninety days, the leadership team picks three to seven priorities for the company, and each leader picks a few of their own. Each has one owner and a due date, and you define "done" on the day you set it, so nobody renegotiates it in week twelve. That is the whole tool. The power is in the fewness. The routing company's first attempt produced eleven company priorities in one quarter, which is a way of announcing that you have decided not to decide. If everything is a rock, you have gravel.

Ninety days, it turns out, is a magic length. Long enough that something real can get built, short enough that people can feel the deadline from day one, and short enough that a wrong bet costs you one season instead of one year. The quarter is the largest unit of time a company can steer. Years are for accountants and postcards.

The scorecard

Five to fifteen numbers, one row each, reviewed every single week, thirteen weeks visible at a time so trends have nowhere to hide. Every number has an owner and a goal, so the reading of the scorecard is a fast public ritual of on-track and off-track, not a seminar. The craft is in choosing numbers that lead rather than lag, numbers that twitch this week about problems that would otherwise surface in the quarterly accounts. Sales calls made, quotes sent, orders in, complaints opened, cash collected. I will say more about leading numbers when we get to 4DX, which built a whole religion on them, and more about scorecards that lie when we get to the theater section, which is where mine did.

The Level 10 meeting

The weekly pulse, ninety minutes, same day, same time, always held, never long. The agenda is fixed and timed: five minutes of good news to remind everyone the company employs humans, five for the scorecard, five to check the quarterly priorities, five for headlines from customers and staff, five to review last week's to-dos, then sixty full minutes of solving the top issues, then five to conclude, recap the to-dos, and rate the meeting out of ten. The name comes from that closing score, and from the ambition that the meeting should earn a ten from its participants.

Notice the arithmetic, because it is the whole design: sixty of the ninety minutes are for solving. Most companies run this meeting inverted, seventy minutes of reporting things everyone already knew, then ten minutes of a real problem handled in the doorway with coats on. The Level 10 spends a third of its time confirming reality at speed, and two thirds changing it. How to conduct a meeting so people actually speak is chapter eleven's territory. What EOS adds is the ratio.

IDS, the actual engine

Issues go on a list the moment anyone spots one. Weekly, the team picks the three most important, and takes them through Identify, Discuss, Solve. Identify is the hard one and the valuable one: the issue as reported is almost never the issue, and the discipline is to keep asking what the real problem is until the room agrees it has been named. Discuss means everyone says their piece once, and the meeting kills the polite recycling of positions. Solve means the issue leaves the list as either a decision, a to-do with a name and a date, or an honest admission that it belongs on the long-term list. The three outcomes all count. Circulation does not.

I have come to believe that most issues in a small company die at the Identify stage, from nothing more violent than being named precisely, in public, with the right people present. It sounds too simple to be a management technology. So does washing your hands, and it took surgeons decades.

Story

Jonas's Almelo shop kept running out of rye bread by eleven in the morning. Before the system, this problem had enjoyed a rich six-week social life: mentioned at every gathering of managers, diagnosed over coffee by everyone, owned by no one. The baking team blamed the forecast, the forecast blamed the weather, one manager had a theory involving a new gym opening nearby, because there is always a theory involving a gym.

The first Tuesday the stuck list existed, "Almelo rye, out by 11:00" got voted into the top three. Identify took most of the allotted time, and it should have. Under questioning it turned out the shop manager was ordering less rye than her own sales suggested, on purpose, because her waste number was on the numbers page with her name next to it, and unsold rye at closing time made that number worse. She was doing her job. She was optimizing, with precision, for the exact target her leadership had handed her. Two of Jonas's numbers were fighting each other, and the customers were the battlefield.

Solve took four minutes: waste targets adjusted per shop and per product, sold-out-by-noon added to the numbers page as its own tracked failure, one line, one owner. Jonas told me later it was the moment he stopped being embarrassed about running a bakery with a laminated scorecard. "Six weeks of opinions," he said. "Eleven minutes of looking."

So that is EOS, and here is my honest verdict after years inside a version of it. The machine is excellent. The tools are unoriginal in the best way, the manual is clear, and the whole thing is tuned for exactly the companies its critics have never run. What deserves your skepticism is the periphery: an ecosystem of certified implementers, add-on books, and licensed software that would very much like the system to feel un-self-installable. It is self-installable. Jonas installed it between a Saturday and a Monday with a highlighter and a contempt for vocabulary. And watch the scripture tendency, the team member who starts saying "that's not how EOS says to do it" in the tone of a man citing case law. The book is a tool. When people start serving the tool, skip ahead to my theater section, because you are already in it.

The Cousins: OKRs and 4DX

Two cousins share the shelf with EOS, and depending on the shape of your company one of them may fit you better. Both deserve a proper look, partly because they are good, and partly because some new hire from a bigger company will one day propose one of them to you with the confidence of a missionary, and you should be able to have that conversation from knowledge rather than from allergy.

OKRs: ambition with a scoreboard

Andy Grove invented Objectives and Key Results at Intel in the seventies. John Doerr carried them to a very young Google in 1999, and eventually wrote them up in Measure What Matters. The mechanism is small enough to fit in one sentence: each quarter you set a handful of Objectives, which are qualitative and ambitious, and under each you write three to five Key Results, which are numbers, and at the end of the quarter you score yourself in the cold light of day.

The Objective is the direction: memorable, motivating, slightly out of reach. The Key Results are the evidence: measurable, dated, impossible to argue with afterwards. "Become the obvious first choice for mid-size fleets in the Benelux" is an objective. "Win 14 of the 30 open tenders, raise trial-to-paid conversion from 22 to 35 percent, get 10 reference customers on stage or on record" are key results. At quarter's end, each key result scores between zero and one, and here is the culturally radical part: on ambitious objectives, around 0.7 counts as success. You set OKRs beyond reach on purpose, and the system only works when the team greets a 0.7 with respect rather than a performance-improvement plan. Doerr also distinguishes committed OKRs, where 1.0 is simply expected because you promised, from aspirational ones, where 0.7 means you aimed properly.

That stretch culture is the whole trick, and also the whole risk. Done honestly, OKRs separate ambition from sandbagging: people can commit to bold targets because nobody punishes falling short of bold. Done dishonestly, the system collapses in one of two directions. Either everyone sandbags anyway, and you get a wall of 1.0 scores measuring nothing but self-protection, or some well-meaning person couples OKR scores to bonuses, at which point every number in the building starts lying to you at once. I will come back to that with a warning label later, because it deserves one.

Where OKRs shine is in organizations whose output is measurable and whose teams need to align without a daily line of sight to each other: product and software companies, mostly, and anything over about fifty people. Where they curdle is in the cascade. Big companies fell in love with waterfalling OKRs down every layer, each objective spawning children, until middle managers spent the first three weeks of each quarter negotiating spreadsheets, a process with the approximate energy cost of the quarter itself. If you are under thirty people, my advice is blunt: company-level OKRs only, one set, visible to all. The moment individual OKRs appear in a small company, you have built a bureaucracy with extra steps and worse humor.

Notice also what OKRs do not give you. There is no meeting cadence in the box, no issues mechanism, no scorecard beyond the key results themselves, nothing about people or process. OKRs are a goal-setting layer, not a full operating system, and most OKR disappointment I have witnessed traces to companies that installed a goal vocabulary and expected it to run their week.

4DX: one goal, defended against your own business

The 4 Disciplines of Execution, from Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling, is the least famous of the three among software people and the most loved among people who run operations: hotels, retail chains, factories, and, if he ever admitted to reading two business books, bakeries. It begins from the best single insight in the entire genre, which the authors call the whirlwind: the day job eats goals. The urgent work of keeping the shop running is hungry, screaming, and legitimate, and it will consume any goal that requires new behavior unless you defend that goal on purpose. Undefended goals die of natural causes by February.

The four disciplines are the defense. First, focus on a Wildly Important Goal, one, at most two, phrased as "from X to Y by when." Not five goals. The book is fanatical about this and the fanaticism is earned. Second, act on lead measures. A lag measure is the result you want and cannot directly push on, monthly revenue, staff turnover, customer satisfaction. A lead measure is something your team can influence this week that predictably moves the lag: tastings booked for the wedding-cake line, callbacks made within an hour, prep checklists completed before opening. Finding a true lead measure, influenceable and predictive, is hard, valuable work, and the second-best idea in the genre. Third, keep a compelling scoreboard, made by the team, visible to the team, simple enough that anyone can tell in five seconds whether they are winning. Fourth, create a cadence of accountability: a twenty-minute weekly session in which each person reports on last week's commitments, reviews the scoreboard, and makes one or two specific commitments for the coming week. People keep commitments to teammates, the book notes, at rates that commitments to bosses never reach.

4DX covers even less of the whole job than OKRs do. It says nothing about vision, structure, or issues, and it assumes you already run the whirlwind reasonably well. What it gives you is the best available tool for a specific and common situation: a business that must execute one significant change while continuing to run itself at full speed. If EOS is an operating manual and OKRs are an ambition layer, 4DX is a crowbar, and there are quarters when a crowbar is exactly the tool.

Side by side, without the sales brochure

EOS, OKRs and 4DX compared, as honestly as I can manage
EOSOKRs4DX
The bookTraction, Gino WickmanMeasure What Matters, John DoerrThe 4 Disciplines of Execution, McChesney, Covey and Huling
Built forFounder-led companies, roughly 10 to 250 peopleAny size with measurable output; grew up at Intel and GoogleTeams that must execute one change while running daily operations
Unit of focusRocks: 3 to 7 priorities per quarterObjectives with 3 to 5 measurable key results eachOne or two Wildly Important Goals, "from X to Y by when"
HeartbeatWeekly 90-minute meeting, quarterly and annual resetsQuarterly setting and scoring, weekly check-ins if you are disciplinedWeekly 20-minute WIG session, scoreboard visible at all times
Strongest ideaThe issues list: problems get named and killed on a scheduleSeparating ambition from sandbagging: stretch goals scored without punishmentLead measures: act on what you can influence that predicts the result
Watch out forThe vocabulary, and the certified-implementer economy around itCascading spreadsheet hell; coupling scores to bonuses kills honestyEverything becoming Wildly Important; lag measures disguised as leads
Cost to runHighest: a full meeting cadence and shared documents to maintainMedium: mostly discipline at the edges of each quarterLowest: one goal, one scoreboard, one short weekly session
What it really isA complete operating manualA goal-setting layer, not a full operating systemA focus tool bolted onto whatever you already run

There are other cousins, and I will wave at them from the road. Verne Harnish's Scaling Up, descended from his earlier Rockefeller Habits, is EOS's more corporate sibling: a one-page strategic plan, a heavier emphasis on daily huddles, and far more content on cash and finance, which makes it worth a read alongside chapter six, and again when chapter fourteen becomes your life. Holacracy is the one where the company replaces managers with a constitution, and everything I have to say about it fits in one sentence: I have never met a company that adopted it and got quietly better, and I have met two that adopted it and got loudly worse. And then there is the most common framework of all, the homemade one, which is what most healthy companies over about forty people run: a mongrel assembled from two books, one bad experience, and a founder who finally got tired of surprises. That mongrel is usually the destination.

Field note

If you want the sources rather than my summaries, the reading order I suggest is: Traction first, because it is the most complete and the fastest read, then The 4 Disciplines of Execution for the whirlwind and lead measures, then Measure What Matters if you are heading past fifty people or into anything venture-shaped. Read all three in a month and steal shamelessly. Between them they cost less than one hour of any consultant who will later summarize them to you with a straight face.

The Cadence Is the Product

Strip any of these systems for parts and you find the same chassis underneath: a nested set of rhythms, each one winding the next like gears in a watch. Annual, quarterly, weekly, daily. The vocabularies differ, the chassis never does, and I have concluded that the chassis is the product. The tools are just each framework's way of making you keep the rhythm.

Here is the wheel, from the outside in.

Annually, the leadership team leaves the building for two days. Leaves properly, phones down, somewhere with bad reception and good walks. You check the vision against reality; the writing happened in chapter three and should mostly survive contact. You look at the year's numbers without flinching, you decide the one-year plan, and you have the arguments everyone has been postponing for months. Two days feels indulgent to a founder who has not done it. It is the highest-leverage sixteen hours in the calendar.

Quarterly, a day, ideally away from the office, at minimum away from the ovens. You score the quarter that just ended, honestly, including the priorities that failed, because a failed priority examined in daylight is tuition, and a failed priority quietly renamed is theater. Then you pick the next quarter's few. The quarterly is where strategy and reality negotiate, four times a year, with witnesses, and it is the meeting I would keep if I were forced to give up all others.

Weekly, the pulse: the ninety minutes, or the WIG session, or Jonas's Tuesday, whatever your chassis calls it. Numbers first, at speed, then the stuck things, argued to names and dates. The weekly is the flywheel that makes the quarterly real, because a quarterly priority checked thirteen times cannot drift far, and a quarterly priority checked zero times was a wish with a date on it. Same day, same time, held even when it is inconvenient, especially when it is inconvenient, because the weeks when the meeting feels impossible are the weeks containing the information.

Daily, optionally, a huddle: ten minutes, standing up, no chairs because chairs are how ten minutes becomes forty. What is today, what is stuck, who needs whom. Operational businesses, shops, kitchens, support teams, get enormous value from this. A six-person software company may not, and should skip it without guilt. Of all the rings, this is the only optional one.

The compounding is the point. A year is four quarterly bets, each quarterly bet is thirteen weekly corrections, each week is five days of people knowing what matters today. Miss the weekly and the quarterly priorities die of neglect by week six. Miss the quarterly and the annual plan becomes a document you find in December, like a gym membership. The rings only work wound together.

What does the wheel actually buy you? Protection from your own nervous system, mostly. Recency steers a company without a cadence: the loudest customer, the scariest email, the founder's most recent aeroplane idea. Chapter twelve talked about founder weather, and a cadence is climate control. When something alarming happens on a Wednesday, a company with a rhythm has a place to put the alarm, on the list, for Tuesday, where it competes with the other alarms instead of winning by freshness. Half the value of Jonas's stuck list is that it converts panic into an agenda item. Panic does not survive being scheduled.

Story

I once sat in on one of Jonas's quarterlies, upstairs from a café in Deventer, nine managers, a paper flipchart, and enough coffee to float a barge. The morning was scoring: the previous quarter's big three read out, one done, one half-done, one dead, and the dead one got twenty full minutes of autopsy, no blame, all mechanism, until the room could say exactly why it died.
