It died, for the record, because it had secretly been two projects wearing one coat.

The afternoon was the part I stole. Choosing the next big three, the managers generated fourteen candidates, every one of them reasonable, which is exactly the problem with growing companies: nobody proposes stupid priorities, they propose fourteen sensible ones. Jonas handed out three sticky dots per person, votes on the flipchart, no campaigning allowed. Then he drew a line under the third-place item, and said the sentence I have since repeated to every founder who will hold still.

"Everything below this line is officially nobody's fault this quarter."

The room exhaled. You could hear it. The eleven items below the line went to the long-term list, still alive, but nobody would quietly judge the manager who left the Zutphen storage problem unfixed this quarter, because the company had decided, out loud, together, that storage loses to the trainee program. That is what choosing means, and most companies never do it. They rank things and then hold people accountable for the whole list anyway. The relief in that room was the sound of an operating system working.

Choosing One, or Building Your Own

So which one? The honest answer is that the choice matters less than the commitment, the way the choice of gym matters less than the going. But there are real differences in fit, and after watching a few dozen companies wear these systems, here is how I would decide.

Start with size. Below about ten people, do not install a full framework. I want to be emphatic about this, because frameworks are most seductive exactly when you are smallest and most overwhelmed, and that is when they cost the most relative to what they return. A six-person company that adopts full EOS spends a scandalous fraction of its week administering itself, and worse, it learns to enjoy it, because administering a company feels like running one and is much easier. Below ten, you need the minimal kit: one weekly hour with numbers and a stuck list, a quarterly half-day to score and choose, one annual day to look up from the road. That is a complete operating system for a small company. It fits on an index card and costs nothing.

From ten to fifty, the shape of your work decides. If your company is operational, output measured in loaves, tickets, shipments, projects delivered, EOS or a lightly translated version of it is the strong default, with 4DX layered on in any quarter that contains one big scary change. If your company is a product company where the hard question is "are we ambitious and aligned" rather than "are we executing," OKRs start earning their keep, though I would still steal EOS's weekly mechanics underneath them, because OKRs alone will not run your Tuesday. And whatever you pick, pick one. I have watched a company run EOS and OKRs and a homegrown KPI tree simultaneously, and the only thing all three systems agreed on was that the meetings were now full.

Then there is the question nobody asks out loud: what is your culture's tolerance for vocabulary? This is a real constraint, as real as cash. Marta's design agency could never have adopted anything with the word "synergy" adjacent to it; forty people would have laughed the system out of the building by lunch, and the laughter would have been correct, because in that culture jargon signals that thinking has stopped. Jonas solved it by translation. The routing company solved it by translation. I have come to think of translation as a compulsory step, not a stylistic one: renaming the tools in your company's own words is how the system stops being the book's and starts being yours. Rocks become the big three. The V/TO becomes the one-pager. The Level 10 becomes the Tuesday. The words are yours, and then, slowly, so is the machine.

One rule before you customize anything else, though, and I hold this one firmly: run the mechanics by the book for two full quarters before you change them, because you do not yet know which parts are load-bearing. Every framework has pieces that look ornamental and are structural, and the meeting rating is my favorite example. Everyone cuts it first, it feels like kindergarten, and it is quietly the system's only feedback loop on itself, the one place the operating system gets operated on. Cut it and the meetings decay at a rate of about one minute of drift per week, and nobody says anything, because you removed the place where they would have said it. Two quarters by the book, then translate the vocabulary freely and prune the mechanics carefully, one change at a time, like a chef adjusting a recipe rather than a toddler improving a clock.

A minimum viable operating system, by company size
SizeWeeklyQuarterlyAnnuallySkip, for now
Just youThirty minutes on Friday: five numbers, what got stuck, the one thing that matters next weekA half-day alone: score the quarter, choose at most three prioritiesOne day away, and an honest letter to yourself about the yearAll frameworks, all software, all dashboards
2 to 9 peopleOne hour, everyone: numbers at speed, then the stuck list, argued to names and datesA half-day together: autopsy the old priorities, vote the new big threeOne day off-site, plus a dinner that is not a meetingAccountability charts, individual goal sets, paid implementers
10 to 40The full 90-minute pulse with the leadership team; each team keeps its own numbersA full day away: scores, autopsies, next quarter's few, one hard people conversationTwo days away from the building, vision check includedCascading goals below the leadership team, until the leadership rhythm has held for a year
40 and upLeadership pulse, plus each department running its own weekly, synchronized so issues can climbQuarterly with department leads presenting their own scoresTwo days, plus a separate budget cycle (chapter six) so money and ambition stop sharing a chairNothing, but expect chapter fourteen to make you formalize what you have

At the routing company we came to EOS the usual way, which is to say backwards, through failure. Around thirty people I read Traction on a holiday, came home glowing, and installed the entire apparatus in one heroic fortnight: accountability chart, scorecard, rocks, the vocabulary, all of it, announced at an all-hands with slides. It lasted eleven weeks. The team had correctly identified it as weather, another founder enthusiasm to wait out, like the standing desks. The second attempt, a year later, I did everything opposite: leadership team only, no announcement, no vocabulary, just a weekly meeting with a fixed shape and a numbers page, run for two quarters before we so much as named it. That one held for years, and pieces of it are probably still running there now, under whatever the new owners call meetings. The lesson cost me a year: an operating system grows or it dies, and the founder's enthusiasm is the least reliable soil there is.

Theater with Better Paperwork

Now the failure mode, the one from the chapter's subtitle in the table of contents, and I want to describe it carefully because it looks like compliance. From the founder's chair it looks like success.

The meetings happen, on time, rated nine. The scorecard comes back filled in, and green. The rocks get set each quarter and reviewed each week. The V/TO hangs laminated by the door. The company performs every ritual of the operating system and stays exactly as confused, congested and founder-dependent as before, sometimes more so, because now the confusion has a schedule. This is theater with better paperwork, and it is common because it is comfortable. You can perform every ritual without any of the conflict the system exists to force, the way you can go through the motions of a workout without picking up anything heavy.

You learn to spot it by the smell. The scorecard drifts toward numbers that are easy to collect and pleasant to read, activity instead of truth: demos given rather than deals closed, tickets resolved rather than customers kept. Ops people call these watermelon metrics, green on the outside, red inside, and every scorecard trends toward watermelon unless someone resists. The issues list stops being a killing floor and becomes a parking lot, the same issue appearing week after week in fresh words, because naming it precisely would mean naming a person, or a pricing mistake, or the founder. Rocks arrive seven per person, hover at ninety percent done for twelve weeks, and slide into next quarter under new wording, unautopsied. The meeting ratings are all nines, which sounds like health and is actually a politeness index; a team that never rates a meeting below eight has stopped using the rating to say anything. And the vocabulary, this one is subtle, becomes a moat: leadership speaks fluent framework, everyone else needs subtitles, and the operating system becomes a private language in which the people with the actual information cannot raise an issue without feeling like tourists.

An operating system is a machine for scheduling uncomfortable conversations. Remove the discomfort and all you have left is the schedule.

That is the diagnosis underneath every symptom on the list. Vision alignment, scorecards, issue lists, quarterly autopsies, every tool in every framework is a way of forcing a specific uncomfortable conversation to happen on a calendar instead of at a crisis. Which numbers are bad. Which priority failed, and by whose hand. Which seat has the wrong person in it. Companies adopt frameworks, whether they know it or not, to schedule conflict they have been avoiding. And a company that adopts a framework in order to keep avoiding it, running the rituals while omitting the discomfort, has bought a gym membership to carry around. The paperwork improves. Nothing else does.

Warning

The fastest way to turn a working system into theater is to bolt money to it. The week you tie bonuses to the scorecard, or salary reviews to OKR scores, is the week every number in the building acquires a motive to flatter you. Economists call this Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a measure. Pay people well, judge performance broadly, and let the operating system's numbers stay what they must be to be useful, which is safe to be ugly.

Story

Year two of the routing company's operating rhythm, the good version, the one that held. Our scorecard had grown, a number here, a number there, each addition reasonable at the time, until it had twenty-three rows, and one autumn I realized it had been green for six straight weeks. During those same six weeks, two of my best engineers resigned and our cash position dipped enough that I made the mistake of doing runway arithmetic during a wedding, not my own, mercifully. Twenty-three green numbers, and the company was having its worst quarter in three years.

I printed the scorecard and went through it with a pen, and the pattern was so obvious it was embarrassing. Demos given. Tickets closed. Uptime. Releases shipped. Support response time. Every row measured activity, effort, motion, things a hardworking team will keep green through sheer professionalism right up until the day the company dies. Not one row would have twitched when a strategic customer went quiet, when offers stopped converting, when the engineers started interviewing. We had built a dashboard for the engine and nothing for the road.

We cut it to nine numbers, and the rule I imposed then is the one I now give away: every scorecard needs at least one number you would rather not show your mother. Offer-to-close rate, ugly. Regrettable departures, trailing twelve months, uglier. Weeks of runway at current burn, chapter six's favorite, never once flattering. The meeting got tenser and the company got healthier, in that order, within a quarter, and I stopped confusing a green dashboard with a good week.

For calibration, here is the same set of instruments in both states. If you already run a system, read this table as an inspection checklist, and read it in a bad mood, because the theater column is written to be recognized, not admired.

The same tools, alive versus performed
InstrumentAlive looks likeTheater looks like
ScorecardA number goes red and someone winces; at least one row is permanently uncomfortableGreen for months; rows measure activity, not truth; nobody remembers why a number was added
Issues listIssues die weekly; naming is blunt enough to make the room briefly quietThe same issue returns week after week under a new name; the list is a parking lot
Quarterly prioritiesThree or four, some fail, and the failures get autopsied in daylightSeven per person, all "ninety percent done" forever, quietly rephrased into next quarter
Meeting ratingSevens and eights with reasons; the occasional four that changes the next meetingStraight nines; the rating is a goodbye ritual performed while packing laptops
Vision one-pagerQuoted in arguments to kill options, chapter two's bouncer doing its jobLaminated, admired on walls, consulted never
VocabularyTranslated into the company's own words within two quartersLeadership speaks fluent framework; everyone else needs subtitles

If you recognized your company in the right-hand column, resist the reflex to blame the framework and shop for a new one. Founders in theater switch frameworks the way insomniacs switch pillows. Somebody defanged the framework, probably you, and the same hand will defang the next one, because the discomfort the system keeps trying to schedule is usually a conversation the founder wants to avoid. Chapter twelve has more to say about that mirror. The repair is small and specific: pick the single most theatrical instrument, usually the scorecard, put one true, ugly number back on it, and defend that number's right to be ugly in front of everyone. Systems come back to life the same way they die: one honest row at a time.

Installing It Without the Eye-Rolls

Suppose you are convinced, or at least curious. How do you introduce an operating system into a company that has survived this long without one, staffed by adults who have all, at some previous employer, been through a Transformation? Carefully, is the answer, and mostly by not calling it anything.

Start with the leadership team only, and stay there for at least two quarters. The pull to roll it out everywhere at once is strong, because rollouts feel like progress, but an operating rhythm the leadership team has not sweated inside for six months is a rumor, not a system, and the rest of the company will treat it accordingly. When the weekly pulse has held through a holiday period and at least one genuine crisis, when the leadership team would riot if you cancelled it, then it earns the right to spread, one team at a time, carried by people who can say "this works, I use it" rather than "management has announced."

Be honest about what it is: an experiment with a review date. The speech I should have given at the routing company the first time, and did give the second time, is short: we are going to try running our week to a fixed shape for two quarters, here is the shape, here is the date we will decide whether to keep it, and the deciding will include your opinion of it. That framing costs you nothing and buys you the benefit of the doubt, which is the only currency that matters in week three, when the new rhythm is still awkward and the old chaos is still charismatic.

The founder goes first, and goes ugliest. Your priorities on the board with everyone else's, your numbers on the scorecard, including at least one that shames you, your meeting rated to your face. The fastest way to kill an operating system is to stand slightly outside it, reviewing, and the fastest way to bring one to life is to be visibly subject to it. The week my own rock went red at the routing company and got the same public autopsy as everyone else's was worth more than every speech I gave that year. People believe exactly one thing about a system: what happens to the boss inside it.

Expect the first quarter to be bad, and say so in advance. First rocks are always too big, because nobody yet knows what ninety days holds. First scorecards are always wrong, because you chose numbers by plausibility instead of experience. First meetings are stiff, first ratings are dishonest, first issue namings are diplomatic to the point of uselessness. All of it is the system finding out the truth about your company, which is what you paid for. Budget one full quarter for calibration and one for habit, and judge the whole thing only at the end of the second.

And the money question, because this is a book with euros in it: do you pay for help? The EOS world offers certified implementers who will facilitate your sessions. The good ones earn their fee, and the fee is real: serious four figures per session day in most of Europe, and a full guided journey runs well into five figures over two years, which is a junior hire, so treat the decision with that seriousness. My honest rule: below about twenty-five people, self-implement, the book is thirty euros and Jonas is proof of concept. Consider paying when the leadership team is large or political enough that the founder cannot both play and referee, which is a real condition, not a weakness, and chapter twelve already made the general case for buying an outside mirror. What I would not pay for is mystique. Everything the implementer knows is in the book. What you are buying is a neutral human with a timer, and you should price it as exactly that.

Try this

Tonight, with a pen, draft your company's nine-number scorecard. Five numbers you would want read to you weekly if you were sailing somewhere unreachable: cash first, chapter six insists. Three numbers that would twitch a week before trouble surfaced anywhere else, leading numbers, things your team can influence by Friday. And one number you would rather not show your mother. If you cannot think of an ugly one, ask whoever runs your books or your support inbox, they will have suggestions. Then read the list and ask the only question that matters: how much of this do I currently see weekly? The gap between that answer and "all of it" is your operating system project, sized.

Outgrowing the Scaffolding

One more thing, and it is the thing the framework books, for understandable commercial reasons, do not dwell on: operating systems have a shelf life, and a healthy company will outgrow several.

The minimal kit that ran you at eight people strains at twenty. The EOS cadence that saved you at thirty will need renovation at eighty, when departments need their own pulses and issues need a way to climb between layers without losing their teeth; that renovation is a load-bearing part of chapter fourteen, and I will leave it there. The point for this chapter is the habit of inspection. Once a year, at the annual, put one strange item on the agenda: the operating system itself. Two questions. Is the system still smaller than the company, meaning does it consume less attention than it returns? And which parts have quietly become theater since we last looked? Prune what fails. Systems accrete like scorecards do, one reasonable addition at a time, and nobody ever proposes the deletion meeting.

And know that you have permission, eventually, to leave the framework altogether. Keep the rhythm forever. The branding can go the way stabilizer wheels go, once the balance they taught you is yours. Most durable companies I know ended up somewhere post-framework: a cadence with its own names, its own rituals, its own scar tissue, unrecognizable as any book and unmistakably an operating system. The framework was scaffolding. The building stands, the scaffolding comes down, and only tourists miss it.

Last month I was back in the Deventer shop, collecting another cake, my niece is at the age where birthdays are load-bearing. The Tuesday meeting was just breaking up. Nine shops now run on that chicken timer, and the laminated numbers page has a row I noticed was new, and ugly, and I complimented Jonas on it, and he looked pleased in the way he only ever looks about bread. I asked him, because I was already writing this chapter in my head, whether he ever worried the whole apparatus was a bit much for a bakery. The one-pager, the stuck list, the ratings.

He picked up the timer and turned it over in his flour-white hand. "People think the system bakes the bread," he said. "It's a timer. It makes sure somebody looks in the oven before things burn."

Then he wound the chicken for the next batch and went back to work, which is, of course, what the wheel was protecting the whole time.

The Short Version

  • You already have an operating system. If nobody wrote it down, the system is your attention and your mood, and it does not scale past about a dozen people.
  • A framework is a boxed set of debugged mechanisms: rhythm, numbers, priorities, issues. Its real product is defaults and permission. Buy the box, keep what fits.
  • EOS is a complete operating manual for founder-led companies. OKRs are an ambition layer, not a full system. 4DX is a crowbar for executing one big change inside the daily whirlwind.
  • The cadence is the product: annual, quarterly, weekly, daily. Each ring winds the next, and if you drop the weekly, the rest is decoration within six weeks.
  • Few priorities, with names and dates, and a line under which things are officially nobody's fault this quarter. If everything is a rock, you have gravel.
  • Every scorecard needs at least one number you would rather not show your mother. All-green dashboards measure politeness, not health.
  • An operating system is a machine for scheduling uncomfortable conversations. Perform the rituals without the discomfort and you have theater with better paperwork.
  • Never bolt bonuses to the system's numbers. The week you do, the numbers start lying.
  • Run it by the book for two quarters, then translate the vocabulary into your company's own words and prune the mechanics one change at a time. Jargon is optional. Discipline is not.
  • Inspect the system itself once a year, and be willing to outgrow it. The scaffolding comes down. The rhythm stays.

Chapter 14

Scaling Up

Scaling multiplies whatever you already are, which is wonderful news or terrible news, and most founders find out which one after signing the lease.

My brother-in-law Jonas opened his ninth bakery on a Tuesday in March, and by the following January it had very nearly taken the other eight down with it.

You have met Jonas before, in chapter four, and again in the money chapter, and once more in the operating-system chapter, where he runs his weekly leadership meeting at a flour-dusted table with an agenda taped to the wall. By the time of the ninth bakery he was, by any reasonable standard, good at this. Eight shops, all profitable. Head bakers he trusted. A rhythm of numbers and meetings that meant he knew by Thursday lunch how every location's week was going. He had turned one bakery into eight over eleven years, and every one of those openings had gone roughly the way he planned, which is to say over budget by a manageable amount and stressful in ways he recognized.

The ninth was different, and the ways it was different make up a nearly complete catalogue of this chapter's mistakes, which is why I asked his permission to hang the whole thing on it.

The ninth bakery was in the big city, forty minutes from home instead of fifteen. It was on a corner, in a listed building with tall windows, twice the floor space of anything he had. It was going to be his first shop with a full café: thirty seats, table service, lunch. The rent was 4,800 euros a month against a portfolio average of about 2,100. The previous tenant, a restaurant, had gone broke, which is why Jonas got the lease on friendly terms, and which he chose to read as luck rather than as a message.

He financed the fit-out from the operating cash of the other eight shops. No loan. "We are profitable," he told me at a birthday party, holding a beer, sounding like a man reading from a brochure about himself. "Why would I pay a bank interest to lend me my own money?" He budgeted the fit-out at 180,000 euros, including the marble counter he had coveted since his apprentice years. A listed building, it turned out, does not let you just punch an oven flue through a seventeenth-century wall. Permits, a heritage consultant, a custom extraction system, twelve weeks of delay. The fit-out landed at 271,000 euros, the opening moved from March to June, then to September, then it was March again, a full year late, and eleven new hires spent months on payroll deep-cleaning an unopened shop.

Meanwhile the ninth bakery was eating the other eight. Jonas deferred maintenance. He stretched the flour supplier's payment terms, then stretched them again. And because the ninth shop kept stumbling, he did the thing that felt like leadership: he sent his best people to fix it. His two strongest head bakers went to the city. Within a quarter, the quality in three of his older shops dipped in that way customers never mention and never forgive, the reviews sagged, and revenue across the old shops fell four percent while their best people stood in a beautiful unopened café forty minutes away, arguing with a heritage consultant about a flue.

The worst week came in January. Payroll for nine locations, the stretched flour invoices finally due, the fit-out's last instalment, and a VAT payment, all in the same ten days. Jonas sat at his kitchen table at two in the morning with a spreadsheet, moved his personal savings into the company, and made a phone call he had sworn after the events of chapter six he would never make again: he called his flour supplier and asked for time. Eight profitable bakeries. Eleven years of doing everything right. One growth step, and he was back to begging at two in the morning.

The ninth bakery survived, and so did the other eight, and we will get to how, because the rescue teaches as much as the wreck. But hold on to the shape of the thing: a working business, a proven owner, an expansion that looked from every angle like more of the same, and close to two years of living one bad week from the end. That is what scaling is like when it goes only slightly wrong. This chapter is about making it go slightly wrong on purpose, with your eyes open and your hands on the controls, instead of very wrong by surprise.

Growing Is Not Scaling

People use these words interchangeably, and the confusion costs real money, so let me split them the way I wish someone had split them for me.

Growing is getting more output by adding proportionally more input. One more baker, one more oven, so much more bread. Ten more customers, one more support person. The machine stays the same shape and you turn the handle faster. Growth is honest work and most healthy businesses do it most of the time.

Scaling is changing the machine so that output grows faster than input. A production kitchen that bakes for five shops. A sales team that closes deals the founder never touches. A second country. Onboarding that turns a stranger into a competent colleague in three weeks instead of six months of shadowing whoever has time. Scaling means the business gets structurally bigger gears, and the whole point of bigger gears is that they do not spin up gently.

The distinction matters because the two things break differently. When growth goes wrong, you have too much or too little of something, and you adjust. Hire one more, buy one more, wait a quarter. When scaling goes wrong, the machine itself is wrong, and no amount of handle-turning fixes it. Jonas's ninth bakery only looked like one more bakery. It was a different business wearing his logo: a café with table service, a city clientele, a manager-run location. He priced it, staffed it, and financed it like bakery number nine, when it was company number two.

Keep the words apart for a second reason too. Scaling has a property growth lacks, and it matters enough to get the fancy formatting.

Scaling multiplies whatever you already are. If there is a crack in the model, scale is how you turn it into a canyon.

A mediocre product at one location is a mediocre product with rent of 2,100 euros. At nine locations it is a mediocre product with rent of twenty thousand. A sales process that works because you personally are charming does not scale into a charming sales team; it scales into a confused one, because charm was never written down. A culture held together by everyone sitting within earshot of you scales into no culture at all. Whatever is quietly wrong in your business right now is the thing scale will make loud. So the honest first move of any scaling decision is an inspection. The growth plan can wait its turn.

One more piece of vocabulary and then I will stop. In this chapter, a step is one deliberate act of scaling: a new location, a new market, a sales team, a production facility. Steps are lumpy. You cannot open forty percent of a bakery or hire sixty percent of a German subsidiary. The lumpiness is the whole problem, and the whole opportunity, and it is why the picture of healthy scaling looks nothing like the chart in your pitch deck. We will draw the real picture shortly.

When to Scale, and When You Only Want To

Founders decide to scale for two kinds of reasons: because the business is pulling them, or because something inside them is pushing. Only one of these is a good reason, and it is worth being embarrassingly honest about which one is operating on you.

The pull signals

The business pulls when demand is arriving that you cannot serve. You are turning customers away, or making them wait so long that turning them away would be kinder. Your shop has a queue out the door on Saturdays, and the queue has been there for a year. Your software has a waitlist you did not build as a marketing trick. Customers are asking, unprompted, whether you also operate in Antwerp, whether you can handle a fleet of four hundred vans, whether they can buy the bigger version. Your unit economics are boringly repeatable: the last shop, the last cohort, the last segment behaved like the ones before it, and the margins held without you personally standing in the room.

Pull evidence is external, specific, and slightly annoying. It shows up as work you had to decline. If you cannot point at concrete demand you refused in the last quarter, be suspicious of your own enthusiasm.

The push signals

The push comes from inside, and it wears convincing costumes. Boredom, dressed as ambition: the current business runs well, running things well is dull, and a new location or a new country is a legitimate-sounding way to make life exciting again. Envy, dressed as strategy: a competitor opened in Rotterdam, so apparently the race is on. Ego, dressed as vision: nine sounds so much better than eight when someone at a birthday party asks how many you have. And sometimes it is a spreadsheet, dressed as inevitability: a projection, yours or an investor's, in which the growth is already assumed and your job is to go execute the assumption.

None of these feelings are shameful. I have scaled out of boredom, and I got the outcome boredom deserves. Feel the push all you like. The trouble starts when you let the push write cheques that only pull can cash. Scaling driven by push has a signature: the plan works only if everything goes right, and the person proposing it gets irritated when you ask what happens if it does not.

Here is my boredom purchase, itemized. Around year five of the routing company, the business was in a healthy tread: growing, digesting, dull. So I decided we should build a second product, a warehouse management module, on the reasoning that our customers had warehouses, which is the kind of insight that sounds like strategy and is actually a founder looking for something shiny. Nobody had asked for it. Not one customer, not once, not even politely. I took my two best engineers off the routing product for nine months, we launched to the sound of one hand clapping, and I kept it alive for another year out of pride before killing it. Total bill: roughly the cost of a proper market entry, a routing roadmap that slipped two quarters, and a competitor closing a feature gap while my best people built shelving software for an audience of me. The market had never pulled. I had pushed, and dressed the push in a strategy costume, and the costume fooled exactly one person.

The readiness inspection

So here is the inspection I promised. Seven questions, each answerable with evidence rather than mood. Jonas and I filled this in together, retroactively, a year after the ninth bakery's worst January. He scored two out of seven, laughed the laugh of a man who has stopped being defensive about it, and said, and I am quoting him exactly because it deserves it: "I would not have let me open a market stall."

The scale readiness checklist. Six or seven yes: take the step. Five: fix the gaps first, they are cheap now and ruinous later. Four or fewer: you are gambling, with the existing business as the stake.
QuestionWhat yes looks likeWhat no looks like (and founders call yes)
1. Is there demand you are already refusing?Named customers, real queues, real waitlists, requests you declined in the last quarter."The market is huge." A trend report. A competitor's press release.
2. Does the model work without you standing there?At least one location, team, or segment hits target margin with the founder absent for a month.Everything runs fine, as long as you check in daily and personally rescue the tricky cases.
3. Is the recipe written down?A new hire reaches competent-without-supervision in weeks, using documents and training that exist."Training" means shadowing whoever has time. The real process lives in three heads.
4. Can you fund the step, plus the overrun?Committed money covers the plan at 150% of budgeted cost and six months of delay, without touching the old business's working capital.The plan is funded by the old business's cashflow and the assumption that nothing slips.
5. Is there a bench?Someone besides you could run today's business for a quarter, and someone credible is named to run the new thing.The plan for the new thing is that you will manage it. Also everything else.
6. Are the core quality numbers stable?Whatever tells you the product is good (churn, repeat rate, complaints, reviews) has been flat or improving for two or three quarters.Quality wobbles and you plan to fix it during the expansion, with the money the expansion makes.
7. Is the step one change, not three?New location or new product or new market or new sales motion. One.A new format, in a new city, with a new menu, run by a manager, which is also your first manager.

Look at question seven and then look back at the ninth bakery. New city, new format, new size, first café, first manager-run opening, first fit-out in a listed building. Jonas took five steps at once and counted them as one, because eight previous successes had convinced him he knew how to take steps. The successes were real. They were also all the same step, repeated, which is the most dangerous kind of experience there is: it feels like general competence and it is one well-rehearsed move.

A word on the other direction, because it exists. Sometimes not scaling is the risk. If your business has real network effects, if a market window is genuinely closing, if regulation or a platform shift is about to reward whoever is biggest, then sitting still can be the gamble. These situations are real and they are rarer than the people selling urgency want you to believe. In fifteen years I have seen perhaps three businesses punished for scaling too late, and I have lost count of the ones punished for scaling too early. The asymmetry is your friend: the too-late founders lost some upside. Several of the too-early ones lost the company.

Try this

Print the readiness checklist. Score your business, alone, honestly, in pen. Then give a blank copy to the most sceptical sensible person who knows your company, a cofounder, your bookkeeper, your longest-serving employee, and have them score it without seeing yours. Compare. Treat every question where you said yes and they said no as a map pin marking the exact place scale will hurt you, discovered for the price of a coffee.

The Stair-Step, Not the Hockey Stick

Every pitch deck contains the same chart. Revenue along the left, time along the bottom, and a curve that hugs the floor politely for two years and then leaves the top right corner of the slide like it heard good news. The hockey stick. I have drawn it myself, with a straight face, more than once.

Here is what I have never seen: a real business, up close, that grew like that chart. I have seen businesses whose long-run summary, viewed from far enough away, smooths into something curve-shaped. But zoom in on any of them, mine included, and the curve dissolves into stairs. A step up, then a long flat. Another step, another flat. Sometimes a step down, which the summary chart forgets the way memory forgets, as discussed in the introduction.

The stairs are the true shape of healthy scaling, and each part of the stair has a job.

The riser is the step itself: you open the location, enter the market, hire the sales team, build the production kitchen. During the riser, everything gets deliberately worse before it gets better. Costs jump now, revenue follows late. Margins dip. The error rate rises, because new people and new process always produce errors. Your own calendar becomes a casualty. A riser is controlled overload, and the only honest way to enter one is knowing it will feel like a mild emergency for months.

The tread is the flat, and this is the part ambitious founders get wrong, because the flat looks like stagnation and is actually digestion. On the tread you stabilize the new thing: the location finds its regulars, the sales hires reach quota, the errors get engineered out. Margin climbs back to where it belongs. Cash refills. Your bench recovers, and the people stretched by the last step grow into their new size. The tread is where the business becomes, again, the kind of business that passes the readiness checklist, which is what qualifies it to take the next riser.

Notice the little dip after each riser in the drawing. I drew it on purpose. Nearly every new copy of your business, a new site, a new team, a new market, performs worse than the original at first, because the copy is missing ten years of invisible corrections. The dip is normal. The dip becoming the new normal is not, and the difference between those two is whether anyone is watching the quality numbers from question six of the checklist.

Three practical rules fall out of the stair shape.

One step at a time. A riser consumes management attention, cash buffer, and error tolerance, and you have a fixed supply of all three. New market or new product or new sales motion or new format. Pick one, finish digesting it, then pick the next. Founders resist this because sequential feels slow. It is slow the way not crashing is slow.

Size the step to what you can survive, not to what you can imagine. Skip "how big could this be?" and ask instead: "if this step performs at half the plan for twice the time, do the existing stairs still hold?" Jonas's ninth bakery fails this test instantly: the working capital of the other eight funded its overrun, so a stumble in the new thing became a haemorrhage in the old thing.

Respect the tread. After a step, the boring quarters where you fix onboarding and rebuild the cash buffer are the strategy itself, however much they feel like a pause in it. Most self-inflicted scaling disasters I know are really tread-skipping: a founder who took step two while still bleeding from step one, usually because a competitor did something, or a landlord called with a beautiful corner unit, or the flat part got dull. If you want a number, the founders I know who scaled well spent one to two years per stair, and the ones who spent less gave the time back later, with interest, in the currency of crisis.

And a fourth rule, which never makes it onto the poster: stairs also go down, on purpose, and a deliberate step down is a move, not a defeat. Jonas shrinking the ninth bakery's café to a counter and eight seats was a step down, taken in daylight, and it saved the company. The trick is to decide the retreat criteria before you take the step, while you are still calm. Write down, next to the plan, the sentence "if we have not reached X by month Y, we shrink to Z," and give the paper to someone who is not you to hold. Retreats decided in advance cost money. Retreats improvised at two in the morning cost money, plus the credibility of every future plan, plus about a year of the founder insisting the step down was the strategy all along, which everyone can see through and nobody enjoys.

What Breaks, and in What Order

The introduction to this book spoiled the answer: when you scale, what breaks is people, then process, then cash, then you, roughly in that order. Having watched the sequence from inside twice and from the next barstool a dozen times, I stand by the order, with one correction: cash breaks third but it is usually the first thing you notice, because cash is the only one of the four with the courtesy to send a bank statement.

Size changes what a company is. Not gradually, either. There are thresholds. Every business crosses them at slightly different numbers, and the pattern holds anyway, so consistent you can navigate by it. Here is the map I wish I had owned, with headcounts for the software founders and locations for the people who, like Jonas, count in shops.

What breaks at what size. The numbers are typical, not exact; you might hit each wall twenty percent earlier or later. You will not skip one.
Around this sizeWhat breaksWhat it feels likeWhat usually fixes it
~10 people, or the 2nd locationOsmosis. Everyone no longer automatically knows everything."Nobody told me." You learn about problems from customers. Two people solve the same problem differently on the same day.Writing things down, one weekly rhythm, one place where decisions live. Chapter 11 has the details.
~25 people, or 4 to 5 locationsThe founder as everyone's manager.Decisions queue outside your door. Your calendar is other people's blockers. Good people go quiet because getting your attention is a competition.Real managers with real authority, and the founder actually delegating outcomes, not tasks. Chapters 11 and 12.
~50 people, or 6 to 8 locationsCulture by proximity."Who are all these people?" An old guard and a new guard form, and they describe each other with a slight edge. New hires learn the culture from whoever happens to sit nearby.Explicit values taught in onboarding, culture carriers seeded deliberately into every new team or site. This chapter, final section.
~80 to 150 people, or 10+ locationsHeroics, including yours.Firefighting stops working because there are more fires than heroes. Finance produces surprises. The best operators burn out first, because they were the load-bearing walls.A middle layer that manages, a real finance function, processes with teeth, and an operating rhythm you defend like it is revenue. Chapter 13.
Any size, during a stepCash and quality, together.Costs arrive on schedule, revenue arrives fashionably late, and the product wobbles exactly when you can least afford refunds.Buffers sized to overruns, one step at a time, and someone watching the quality numbers who is not also running the expansion.

People break first

People break first because a scaling step changes every job in the company without asking anyone's permission, and it changes some jobs into jobs their current holders never applied for.

The classic case deserves naming because you will meet it: the loyal early person who ran everything at twelve people and is drowning at forty. She was your third hire. She did five jobs at once, back when five jobs fit into one heroic human. Now each of those jobs is a department, and the skill that made her great, gripping every detail herself, is the exact skill that no longer works. Meanwhile she has watched you hire polished strangers above the people who built the place, and she is wondering, quietly, whether loyalty was a mistake.

There are only three honest moves, and all of them start with a conversation most founders delay a year too long. You can grow the person: real support, a coach, an explicit new role description and time, which works more often than cynics claim but only when the person actually wants the bigger job rather than wanting to want it. You can redesign sideways with dignity: the title that fits what they are genuinely great at, named openly, celebrated, not whispered about, and I have seen a "head of operations" become a "founding baker" and gain status rather than lose it. Or you can part kindly, which chapter 10 covers and which is sometimes the truest respect available. The one unforgivable move is the silent one: hiring over someone without the conversation, and letting them discover their demotion in the org chart of a company they helped build.

Because everyone asks what the conversation actually sounds like, here is roughly the shape of the one I finally had, a year late, with the person who had run half the routing company at twelve people. It starts with the truth instead of the compliment sandwich: "The company is changing shape, and it is changing your job whether we talk about it or not, so I would rather we talk about it." Then the specific observation, not the verdict: "You are doing five jobs and being ground down by three of them, and I have watched you stop enjoying this." Then the genuine question, asked with the outcome actually open: "If you could design your next two years here, what would you keep and what would you hand over?" Her answer, for the record, was not the one I had prepared for. She did not want the department-head job I had been dreading offering support for. She wanted the hardest customers and none of the management. She kept that job until the day the company sold, and nobody ever did it better. The conversation I postponed for a year out of fear took forty minutes and ended with both of us annoyed we had not had it sooner. Most of them go like that. The ones that do not were going to go badly anyway, later, worse.

The second people-fracture is directional: whether to hire ahead of the step or behind it. Hire ahead for anything with a long ramp, managers, salespeople, senior engineers, head bakers, because starting the search when you already need them means six months of the gap doing damage. Hire behind for pure capacity, where the work itself trains people fast. Getting this backwards is expensive in both directions: capacity hired ahead is payroll watching you burn cash, and leadership hired behind is a step taken with nobody steering it.

And then there is the moment nobody warns you about, so I will: the first employee you did not interview, did not choose, and could not pick out of a lineup. At the routing company it happened around employee thirty-five, in a kitchen, when a friendly man introduced himself and I realized mid-handshake that I had no idea whether he was a new hire or a customer. It is a small vertigo and it means the machine is working, and it also means the culture is now being transmitted entirely through channels that are not you, which is the subject of this chapter's final section.

Process breaks second

Small companies run on heroics, and heroics are the right technology at small scale: cheap, fast, flexible, and everyone knows who the heroes are. The problem is that heroics scale linearly at best. Every step you take adds surface area faster than it adds heroes, until the same act of improvisation that used to save the week causes the week that needs saving, because three other teams had quietly built on top of the thing the hero just improvised around.

The fix is process, a word that makes founders itch, so let me define it harmlessly: process is the recipe leaving someone's head. Nothing more. Jonas's croissant recipe was, for eleven years, partly a document and partly the hands of the woman who ran his first shop. That was fine, right up until shop nine needed the croissants and the hands were forty minutes away.

My working rule is the rule of the third repetition. The first time you do something, do it however works. The second time, notice you are doing it again. The third time, write it down: one page, numbered steps, verbs first, written by the person who actually does the work rather than by whoever owns the nicest template. A playbook written this way is a floor, not a ceiling; people are free to beat it, and obliged to update it when they do.

What writing it down actually does is more interesting than the document. When Jonas finally sat with his first-shop baker to write the croissant process, two Mondays of dough temperatures, lamination timings, and twenty-seven numbered steps, he expected the effort. The surprise came at steps nine and fourteen, where her own team disagreed about what the process was. The standard had already drifted, at home, in the flagship, among people who saw each other daily. The document went looking for a standard to enforce and discovered that the standard no longer existed, which is the discovery you would much rather make at eight shops than find baked into shop nine. Writing things down is the only reliable way to find out what your company actually does, as opposed to what everyone assumes it does, and the gap between those two grows with every person you hire.

Two failure modes, and you should fear them equally. The first is no process, which at scale produces chaos with your logo on it: nine bakeries making nine slightly different croissants, or a support team giving four customers four contradictory answers, each delivered with confidence. The second is process theater, which chapter 13 warned you about: forms that protect nobody, approvals that exist because of one bad day in 2019, documentation nobody reads maintained by someone everybody avoids. The test for any process is simple: if it disappeared tomorrow, who would notice by Friday? If the answer is nobody, you have found sediment, and you can dredge it without ceremony.

For early warning that process is breaking, watch three numbers: rework (how often the same thing gets done twice), waiting (how long work sits between people), and escalations to the founder per week. That last one is the best process gauge I know, because it counts the exact number of times per week the machine could not answer a question without opening the founder's head to look inside.

Cash breaks third, quietly, then all at once

Chapter six taught the mechanics: cash is fact, profit is opinion, and the two travel on different calendars. If that chapter is fuzzy in your memory, go raid it, because scaling is the exam. Scaling adds one line to the lesson: growth eats cash before it feeds you, always, in every business model I have ever examined, and the meal is bigger and earlier than the spreadsheet says.

Walk through why. A scaling step means spending now for revenue later. You pay the fit-out before the first croissant sells. You pay the salesperson for six to nine months before her deals close. The German entity pays a notary, a lawyer, a payroll provider, and an office deposit before a single German invoice goes out, and when that invoice does go out, a fine upstanding German enterprise will pay it in sixty days. Every euro of the step leaves early and comes home late, and in between, the ordinary business must keep paying its ordinary bills. That in-between is where profitable companies die, and chapter six already showed you the autopsy.

Warning

The most dangerous month of a scaling step is the month things go right. New location busy, new reps closing, big orders landing. Every one of those successes consumes cash the moment it happens, ingredients, stock, payroll, onboarding, and pays you back on someone else's schedule. If you have not pre-funded success, good news will bankrupt you faster than bad news, because bad news at least has the decency to make you spend less.

The protections are unglamorous and they work. Fund the step with committed money, a facility arranged before you need it, an investor already wired, a buffer already saved, never with the hopeful cashflow of the old business, and yes, that pointed sentence is about a bakery. Budget the step at what it costs, then plan your survival at 150 percent of that cost and six months of delay, and if that survival plan does not exist, neither does your readiness. Keep the old business's working capital in a separate pocket the step cannot reach without a deliberate, documented decision. And if the step needs outside money, the instruments and their trade-offs live in chapter six; this chapter only insists that you arrange the umbrella while it is sunny.

One habit upgrade for the duration of any step: whatever cash rhythm you keep in peacetime, tighten it. If you glance at the bank balance monthly, go weekly. If you keep the thirteen-week cashflow from chapter six quarterly, run it every Monday and add a line for the step's spending, separate from everything else, so you can watch the overrun arriving while it is still a trend instead of a crisis. Jonas's version of this is characteristically free of software: during any opening, the week's cash position goes on a whiteboard in his office in his own handwriting, because, as he puts it, "a number you wrote yourself is a number you believe."

Story

The rescue of the ninth bakery, since I promised. In the bad January, Jonas finally did what he later called "the thing I should have done in the leases-and-lawyers phase": he separated the step from the business. He went to his bank, with eleven years of clean numbers, and got a proper loan against the fit-out he had already paid for, refinancing the step and putting the working capital back into the eight shops where it belonged. The interest he had refused to pay out of principle cost him, in the end, about 9,000 euros a year. He worked out on the back of a flour invoice that funding the step from operating cash had cost him roughly 70,000 in deferred maintenance, degraded quality, lost revenue, and stretched-supplier goodwill, plus one January he does not discuss in front of his wife.

Then he shrank the step until it matched his readiness. He cut the café concept, the part that was a new business rather than a ninth copy, back to a counter and eight seats, no table service. His head bakers went home to their shops within a fortnight, and the quality numbers in the old shops recovered in a quarter. The city shop reopened as what he actually knew how to run, a bakery, and only after it had been boringly profitable for a year did he add the café back, one waiter at a time. It is his best location now. "The building was never the problem," he told me. "I tried to climb two stairs and invent a third one, in the dark, carrying the other eight shops." Jonas has never read a business book. It took me four years and a ruined friendship-adjacent sale process to learn what he just said in one sentence.

You break last, and loudest

The fourth thing that breaks is the founder, and it breaks last because founders are load-bearing and stubborn, which means the structure absorbs enormous strain before the crack shows. Chapter 12 is the full treatment, the delegation ladder, the failure modes, the mirror speech Henk gave me that I still flinch at, so here I will only add what scaling specifically does to you.

Every riser on the staircase quietly rewrites your job description without notice. At one location you are a baker. At four you are a coach of bakers. At nine you are the designer of a system that coaches bakers, and the system does not care that you got into this because you love the smell of a proofing room at five in the morning. Scaling replaces the work you chose with work you never chose, a little more with each riser, and the grief about that is real, unnamed, and behind more self-sabotage than any cash crisis. I have watched founders, myself included, dive back into the old hands-on work during the exact weeks the company most needed them on the system, not because it was useful but because it was home.

So during a step, watch yourself like you watch the quality numbers. The reliable early signals: you become the bottleneck and collect praise for how hard you work around it, you stop sleeping through the night, you cancel the same recurring one-on-one three times, and you catch yourself feeling needed by the chaos and a little disappointed by the calm. When two of those are true, the founder is the next thing on the breakage list, and chapter 12 is the raid target.

Scaling the Sales Engine

Chapter nine taught you founder-led selling, the correct technology for finding out what your customers buy and why, whatever stage-obsessed folklore says about growing out of it. This section covers the step beyond: turning the thing only you can do into a thing an engine does, because the founder-led motion has one hard ceiling, and the ceiling is your calendar.

You will know you have hit the ceiling by feel: the pipeline is full, the close rate is fine, and growth has flattened anyway, because every deal still routes through your Tuesdays. The wrong response is the one nearly everyone tries first, which is to work more Tuesdays. The second wrong response is nearly everyone's second attempt, which is to hire a wonderful salesperson and give them your job. I know because I tried both.

Story

Maarten, the sales director I told you about in chapter ten, was that second attempt, and you know how it ended: seven months, almost nothing closed, gone. Chapter ten told you why the hire failed. Here is what the failure taught me about scaling. Maarten had spent his career operating a machine: marketing feeding him warm leads, a solutions engineer for demos, legal for contracts, a brand that opened doors before he knocked. At our place there was no machine. There was me, a shared spreadsheet, and a slide deck with my phone number on the last page. I had hired a train driver and been surprised he could not lay track. The lesson for scaling: build the track first, then hire the driver.

The next attempt worked because we laid track first. Before hiring anyone, I spent six weeks writing down what I actually did in deals: the eleven discovery questions, the three objections that killed us and the answers that saved us, who the real buyer was inside a delivery company (never the person who first emailed us), our walk-away price, the reference customers for each fleet size. Twenty scruffy pages. Then we hired two salespeople at once, a hunter and a farmer by temperament, both from smaller companies where they had sold without a machine. Two, because with one you learn nothing: if she fails, you cannot tell whether you hired wrong or built wrong. With two, if both fail the playbook is broken, if one fails you look at the hire, and if both succeed you have an engine. Both succeeded, at about eighty percent of my close rate. I stayed closer of last resort for another two years, and the day the team asked me to please stop attending their demos was one of the proudest and most insulting days of my career.

The sequence that story encodes has five moves, and the order is the point.

First, write the playbook while you are still the best salesperson. Skip the corporate binder and write the scruffy twenty pages: who we sell to, who we refuse, the discovery questions, the demo that works, the objections and their answers, the pricing floor and who may cross it, the references. If you cannot write it, what you have is a founder who improvises well rather than a sale that repeats, and hiring people to imitate an improvisation is how you fund other companies' training programmes.

Second, hire for your stage, not your aspirations. The person who thrived inside a big machine will suffocate without one. You want people who have sold something unfamous from a company nobody had heard of, who treat the scruffy playbook as a gift rather than an insult. The same logic applies to sales leadership later: you want the person who has taken a team from two reps to ten, not the vice-president who once presided over five hundred, and the latter will interview better every single time.

Third, hire in pairs. One data point is an anecdote with a salary. Two is the beginning of an experiment.

Fourth, feed the engine before it starves. Founder-led selling ran on your network, your reputation, and warm intros, a fuel supply that does not transfer to employees. The week your first reps start, they need a source of leads that is not your address book: whatever fits your motion, outbound lists, partnerships, the marketing engine chapter eight's brand work makes possible. Reps without lead flow chase bad-fit deals and discount hard to win them, which costs you twice, now and at renewal. Sitting idle would be cheaper.

Fifth, change your own job on purpose. You become coach, playbook editor, and closer of last resort, in that order of hours. The transfer takes quarters, not weeks, and there is a table for tracking whether it is actually happening, because founders lie to themselves about this one with special fluency.

A practical word on paying the first reps, because you have no history to set targets with and the internet's advice assumes venture funding. Set the first quotas from your own founder-led numbers, discounted: if you closed a million a year while also running the company, a full-time rep with your playbook and none of your authority is doing well at sixty to eighty percent of that in year one. Pay a higher base and a lower variable than the standard advice suggests, because in an immature pipeline, a starving-artist comp plan breeds discounters and short-timers instead of hunters. Keep the plan simple enough to explain in one breath, no accelerator origami, no seven-condition bonuses, and say out loud, in writing, at the start, that you will recalibrate quotas and rates after two quarters of real data. Reps handle honest recalibration fine. What they do not handle, and should not, is discovering that the target was fiction and the fiction was their problem.

Founder-led selling versus a sales engine. If the middle column still describes you two years after your first sales hires, you hired an audience instead of building an engine.
DimensionFounder-led (chapter 9)Engine (this chapter)
Who sellsYou, evenings includedPeople you hired, coached by you, then coached by someone you hired
What wins the dealFounder conviction, deep product knowledge, the buyer's sense that the top person caresA repeatable process, proof (references, cases), and a story any trained person can tell well
Where the knowledge livesIn your head, updated nightlyIn a playbook anyone can read, updated by whoever beats it
PricingImprovised per deal, defended by youA price list with rules, floors, and named exceptions
The forecastYour gut, which is honestly quite goodPipeline arithmetic that is honest about leak rates, per chapter 9's funnel
Lead flowYour network and reputationA source that works for people who are not you
Cost of a bad quarterA bruised ego and a quiet monthA payroll you must make anyway, which is why the readiness checklist asked about buffers
How it failsYou run out of TuesdaysThe playbook is wrong at scale, and now it is wrong in stereo

One warning shot about discounting, because it is the leak that sinks scaled sales quietly. When you sold, you defended the price with conviction and context. A rep under quota, in the last week of a quarter, defends nothing; she discounts, because the incentive you designed tells her closed is closed. Multiply a casual twelve percent discount culture across an engine and you have scaled a margin problem and attached commissions to it. The fix is structural, not moral: floors in the playbook, exceptions that need a named human's yes, and quota credited at full-price equivalent so a discount costs the rep what it costs you.

Crossing Borders

Sooner or later, a founder in a small country looks at the map, especially those of us from the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, or any other market you can drive across between breakfast and lunch: the home market makes you good, and then it makes you claustrophobic. Internationalization is the scaling step with the best stories and the worst survival statistics, and I say that with affection, as someone who did it badly once and less badly once, in that order.

The core mistake has a name in my head: the neighbor illusion. Germany is next door. They eat bread, they run delivery vans, they use software. Same time zone, similar weather, a language you half-learned in school. How different can it be? The answer, which cost me about 300,000 euros to learn, is: different enough to be a different country, which is what it is, which is what the border was trying to tell you.

Story

The routing company entered Germany the way an optimist enters a revolving door. Our reasoning was airtight: Germany was the Netherlands, but eleven times over, full of delivery fleets, right there. We translated the website and the sales deck ourselves, budgeted six months to first serious revenue, and I started taking the early train to Düsseldorf. Twenty months later we closed our first meaningful German customer. In between, we learned the tuition schedule. Our Dutch reference customers, our pride, the logos that opened every door at home, meant nothing; the first question in every meeting was which German fleets we ran, and the honest answer emptied the room with perfect courtesy. Enterprise procurement wanted a German legal entity, a German data-hosting answer, and German-language phone support during German business hours, none of which were on my six-month plan. One prospect, I promise this is true, asked us to send the draft contract by fax, in 2014, and we had to buy access to a fax service to close him. And our self-translated deck: our first German hire, a formidable saleswoman I will call Ute, read it on her second day and said, "This reads like it was translated by an enthusiastic intern." It had been. The intern was me.

Ute was the turning point, and she matters more to this chapter than the entity, the hosting, or the fax. A senior local person who knew how German logistics buyers think, who rebuilt the deck around their anxieties instead of our features, and who told us to stop discounting for the first lighthouse customer and instead offer a paid pilot with an exit clause, because, in her words, "German buyers do not trust cheap, they trust careful." Two years after Ute arrived, Germany was our biggest market. Later we entered France in eleven months instead of twenty. France is no easier; we simply arrived carrying a checklist written in German scar tissue: local senior hire first, local proof before scale, legal and support plumbing before marketing, and every timeline from the home-market playbook multiplied by two.

Out of that story, and a dozen like it from friends, here is the compact doctrine.

Pick one market, for learnability as much as size. The spreadsheet ranks countries by market size. Rank them instead by how fast you can learn there: language you can operate in, customers who will talk to you, a flight you can take weekly without hating your life. A medium market you can learn beats a huge market you can only guess at. And one at a time; a new country is the most expensive kind of riser there is, and the readiness checklist applies with the volume turned up.

Local proof before local scale. Your home-market reputation does not clear customs. Plan the first two or three customers in the new country as their own project, priced for reference value rather than for margin, structured, per Ute, as something careful rather than something cheap. Until those exist, all you own is a translation, and the market can tell.

A local person beats a local office. The single highest-leverage euro in internationalization is the salary of a senior local hire who has sold to, or worked inside, your target customers. Hire them before the fancy office, before the marketing budget, and listen to them even when, especially when, they tell you your beloved home-market playbook is the intern's deck.

Do the plumbing early, because it is slow. Entity or no entity, VAT registration, employment rules if you hire, where the data lives, what language the contract and the support desk speak. Our German entity took four months and more wet-ink signatures than our mortgage. None of this is strategy and all of it blocks revenue at the exact moment revenue finally shows up, so start the paperwork the week you decide.

Field note

For the Europeans: the single market is a customs arrangement, not a customer arrangement. Your invoice crosses the border freely. Your reputation, your legal assumptions, and your idea of a reasonable payment term do not. Budget for a local accountant and an employment lawyer in every country where you hire, and treat "it is all EU anyway" as the famous last words it usually is.

Ways into a new country, compared honestly. Most durable entries walk down this table over several years; disasters usually start on the last rows without ever visiting the first ones.
ModeCash at riskSpeed to learningWhat it actually teaches youWhen it fits
Sell remotely from homeLow: travel, translation, a lot of your timeFast to start, slow to trustWhether anyone there wants the thing at allFirst toe in the water; products that sell without a handshake
Partner or resellerLow cash, high margin share, real reputation riskMediumWhether the market works, filtered through someone else's incentivesComplex markets you cannot staff yet; be humble about how little you learn
First local hireOne senior salary plus supportFastest genuine learning per euroHow buyers there actually decide, from someone who knowsAlmost always the right second move, and often the right first one
Local entity and teamHigh: entity, payroll, office, management attentionSlow to build, deep once builtHow to be a local company, with local costsAfter local proof exists; when enterprise buyers demand a local counterparty
AcquisitionHighest, plus integration, plus surprisesInstant market, slow truthWhat the sellers did not mention during diligenceRarely, with experienced advisors, and never as a shortcut past the learning

One more thing, because software founders in particular need to hear it: translating the interface is the visible five percent of entering a country. The invisible ninety-five is support hours, payment methods, invoice formats some countries treat as sacred texts, references, pricing norms, and the slow accumulation of being known. Budget and staff for the ninety-five; the translation is the ribbon. Jonas, for the record, finds this entire section hilarious, because his version of internationalization was opening forty minutes away, and every dynamic in it, the worthless home reputation, the local staff who knew the neighborhood, the plumbing, the doubled timeline, applied in full. A different city is a small foreign country. Price the step accordingly.

Keeping the Soul

Every founder scaling up says some version of the same sentence: "I just don't want us to lose what makes us us." It is a good instinct expressed uselessly, because "what makes us us" is doing no work in that sentence. You cannot protect what you have not named. So the first move in keeping the soul is an unromantic one: define it.

Chapter one made the case that values are what you pay for when they are inconvenient, and the same test finds the soul, so skip the poster in the hallway. The soul, practically, is a short list of specific behaviors and promises that would still be recognizable if every current employee were replaced: what you refuse to sell, how you act when you have made a mistake a customer has not noticed yet, what happens to the person who misses a target honestly versus the one who hits it by cutting a corner, whether the boss's bad idea gets challenged out loud. Specific, observable, boring. That list is the cargo, and scaling is the question of how the cargo survives the voyage.

Here is why it will not survive by default, and the arithmetic is so simple it is embarrassing how late I did it. Culture in a small company transmits by proximity: people learn how we behave here by watching you and the first hires behave. Every time headcount doubles, the share of people who learned the culture straight from the source halves. Forget the calendar; the decay runs on your hiring schedule, one doubling at a time, and a company in a scaling phase can double twice in two years.

Deliberate carriage, then. Four mechanisms have earned their keep, and none of them is a poster.

Name the non-negotiables, and separate them from the habits. Write the five things that must never change, in behavior language, not adjective language. Then, and this is the half founders skip, write the list of things that are allowed to die: the Friday beers that worked at nine people and are a logistics problem at ninety, the all-hands where literally everyone spoke, the founder personally tasting every batch or reviewing every deal. Grief for the habits is real and fine. Confusing the habits with the soul is how companies end up defending the beer fridge while the honesty quietly leaves the building.

Make onboarding carry stories, not just forms. New people learn culture from narrative, not from bullet points. The onboarding that works tells the stories with the moral inside: the time we refunded the customer who would never have noticed, the deal we walked away from and why, the promotion that went to the person who reported their own mistake. At the routing company, our onboarding eventually included the Maarten story and the fax story, told by whoever was newest in sales the year before, which kept the stories honest and the tellers humble.

Seed every new team, site, and country with a carrier. Never open a new anything staffed entirely by new people. Jonas learned this in flour: after the ninth bakery stabilized, he made it policy that every new shop opens with a starter jar of the original sourdough culture from bakery number one, which is charming, and with at least one baker who grew up in the old shops, which is the actual mechanism. The dough is the ritual. The person is the culture. Software companies can skip the jar and must not skip the person: the first engineer on the new team, the first rep in the new country, chosen as much for carrying how-we-behave as for the skill on the CV.

Let them see you pay for it. At scale, most employees will never watch you work a customer problem at midnight. What they will see is what you refuse: the revenue you decline because it needs a corner cut, the executive hire you reject for being brilliant and unkind, the discount you will not approve in the last week of the quarter. Every public no is worth a hundred laminated values. This is also, not coincidentally, the cheapest mechanism on the list, except on the days it is the most expensive thing you do all year.

Try this

Write down, in one sitting, the five behaviors that must never change in your company, each as a sentence describing something a stranger could observe. Then hand the list to three people hired in the last six months and ask one question: which of these have you seen happen with your own eyes? Anything they have only read about has already slipped from culture into nostalgia, and now you know exactly what the next onboarding, the next public decision, and the next new-team seeding need to carry.

I will leave the last word on soul, and on this whole chapter, where it started. The ninth bakery is, these days, Jonas's best shop: the café is full, the marble counter earned its keep, and the city customers queue past the tall windows on Saturdays exactly the way the old shops taught him queues are made, one kept promise at a time. On a shelf behind the register there is a plain glass jar of sourdough starter with a strip of masking tape on it, and on the tape, in marker, in Jonas's handwriting, it says "No. 1, since 2009." He put it there for the staff, most of whom have never seen bakery number one; the customers rarely even ask. When to scale, what breaks, how to keep the soul: the jar answers all three, in order. Take the step when the starter is strong. Expect the loaf to slump before it rises. And whatever you open next, carry the culture in with your own hands, because it does not travel on its own.

The Short Version

  • Growing is more of the same with more input. Scaling changes the machine itself, and machines being changed run badly for a while. Budget for the while.
  • Scale multiplies whatever you already are, including the cracks. Inspect before you multiply.
  • Scale on pull (demand you actually refused last quarter), never on push (boredom, envy, or a spreadsheet's assumption). Too early kills more companies than too late.
  • Run the readiness checklist in pen. Six of seven or go fix the gaps. And one change per step: new market or new product or new format, never a bundle.
  • Real growth is a stair-step, not a hockey stick: risers of deliberate overload, treads of digestion. The tread is the strategy; the riser only buys you the right to stand on it.
  • What breaks, in order: people, process, cash, you. Cash just complains first, in writing.
  • Fund every step with committed money, sized at 150 percent of budget and six extra months, kept separate from the old business's working capital. Success eats cash before failure does.
  • To scale sales past yourself: write the playbook while you are still the best rep, hire in pairs, hire for your stage not your aspirations, feed them leads that are not your address book, and put floors under the discounts.
  • A new country is a full-price riser: one at a time, senior local hire early, local proof before local scale, and double every timeline from home. A new city is a small foreign country.
  • The soul dilutes on your hiring schedule, one doubling at a time. Name the non-negotiables, tell the stories in onboarding, seed every new team with a carrier, and let people watch you pay for the values in public.

Chapter 15

Selling the Business

The wire transfer takes four seconds, and everything the books forgot to mention starts right after it lands.

The money arrived on a Tuesday morning at 11:52. I know the exact minute because I have a screenshot of the banking app, taken with unsteady hands at a kitchen table that had, an hour earlier, started belonging to a different man.

The notary had called at 10:40 to say the words she must say a hundred times a year and I will hear once in my life: completion has occurred. Fourteen years of the routing company, forty-one employees, some thousands of delivery vans following our suggestions around Europe every morning, and it all resolved into one sentence from a woman I had met twice, delivered in the tone you use to confirm a dentist appointment. Then she wished me a pleasant day.

I refreshed the banking app somewhere between thirty and forty times. When the number finally appeared, it sat directly on top of the transaction history of an ordinary life: groceries, the gym membership I kept forgetting to cancel, thirty euros to my nephew for his birthday.
