Then this. A number with more digits than the account had ever held, wearing the same font as the groceries, as if it were a normal thing that normal accounts do.

I had imagined that moment many times, I will admit that. In the imagined version there was champagne, or at least other people. In the real version I was alone in the kitchen, because the closing had happened remotely and my wife was at work, since neither of us had understood that this Tuesday would be the Tuesday. I looked at the number until it stopped meaning anything. Then I made a cheese sandwich, standing up, because fourteen years end and nobody hands you a script.

The part I need to tell you about came the next morning. Wednesday, I woke at 6:30 without an alarm, the way I had for years, and reached for my phone to check the overnight support queue. The app was gone. IT had done its job at midnight, clean and correct, exactly as agreed in a schedule I had signed myself. My email said my mailbox no longer existed. The dashboard that had been the first thing my eyes touched every morning for a decade, gone. I sat on the edge of the bed, a wealthy and healthy man of around forty, free in every way a person can be free, and I felt the specific vertigo of a cartoon character who has run off the edge of the canyon and just looked down.

For fourteen years I had woken up as the person the routing company was happening to. That Wednesday I woke up as a man with dead apps on his phone and no reason to get up before nine. It took me a lot longer than I expected to build a new reason, and nobody had warned me, not the lawyers, not the bankers, not one of the eleven advisors who had earned fees on my deal. Their job ends at the wire transfer. The Wednesday after appears on nobody's invoice.

In the introduction I promised that when we reached this cliff, I would bring photographs. This chapter is the photographs. We will walk the whole road: why founders actually sell, what your company is worth and what hearing that number does to you, the kinds of buyers and how to find them, the year-long tunnel of diligence and deal terms, earn-outs and their traps, and then the part that comes after, the cliff itself. I will tell you now what I wish someone had told me: the deal is a project, and the project is the easy part. The hard part is that you are also selling a version of yourself, and that transaction has no notary.

One more thing before we start. Read this chapter even if you never intend to sell. First, because a company built as if it could be sold, with clean books, documented processes, and a founder who is not load-bearing, is a better company to own and to work in. And second, because intentions are lovely and inboxes are patient. One day an email arrives, and you will want to have read this chapter before you answer it, not after.

Why Founders Actually Sell

Ask a founder at the closing dinner why they sold and you will hear the press release: the time was right, the buyer shares our values, this is the best next step for the team and the product. All of which may even be true. But the press release is the third or fourth draft. The first draft, the one written at 2 a.m. somewhere in the preceding years, usually says one of a small number of much plainer things.

I am tired. This is the honest number one, and nobody puts it on a slide. Not tired like a bad month. Tired like year eleven, when the problems started repeating and you noticed you were solving the same three issues you solved in year seven, only with more people in the room. Founder fatigue compounds, and it is a legitimate reason to sell. The trouble is that it is also the worst possible negotiating position, and buyers can smell it the way dogs smell fear. We will come back to that.

Everything I own is in one basket, and the basket has wheels. By the later years of the routing company, my house, my pension, my children's future, and my ego were all riding on one mid-sized software company in one niche of one industry. A single platform shift, one aggressive competitor with venture money, one lost anchor customer, and the family balance sheet would have gone with it. Selling, or selling part, is how a founder finally gets to do what every financial advisor tells everyone else to do on day one: diversify. There is no shame in it. Concentration built the wealth, and concentration is a terrible way to keep it.

The company needs a different owner to become what it should be. Sometimes true, sometimes a flattering translation of reason number one. But it is real: there are moments when the next phase needs a distribution network you do not have, capital you do not want to raise, or an appetite for a fight you have already fought once. If the company needs money to grow while you keep the wheel, be careful: that is raising, not selling, a different decision with a different chapter, chapter six.

The window is open. Industries consolidate in waves. For a few years the buyers are hungry, the multiples are generous, and your phone warms up. Then the wave passes, and the same company fetches a duller price for half a decade. Part of selling well is admitting that the market's calendar and your emotional calendar are unrelated documents. The routing company sold during a consolidation wave in logistics software. If the same buyers had come knocking three years later, I know exactly what the offers would have looked like, because I watched what happened to the founders who waited.

Life happened. Health, divorce, a parent who needs care, a partner who got a job abroad, a shareholder who needs out. These reasons are nobody's business and need no defending. The only advice I have is practical: deals take a year, so if you can feel one of these coming, start earlier than feels necessary.

And then there are the bad reasons, which deserve one honest paragraph. Do not sell to escape a problem that a chapter of this book could fix. Founders regularly try to sell their way out of a broken management team, a cash crunch, or their own burnout, and buyers pay badly for problems, when they pay at all. If the company is struggling, a sale at a distressed price is sometimes right, but check first whether what you are fleeing is fixable, because the fix is almost always worth more than the discount. And do not sell purely because a number turned your head. Numbers do that. It is their job. The real question is what you are buying with the number, and the answer had better be a life you actually want, described in more detail than "not this."

Story

The first serious approach came two years before I sold, an email from the corporate development man of a large logistics group, polite and vague in the way those emails are. I did what I had done with every large decision for twenty years: I drove to Henk's kitchen table.

He was well into his eighties by then, slower on the stairs, a wool cardigan on him even in a warm kitchen, reading glasses parked in his hair as if daring them to be useful. He held my phone at arm's length, read the email twice, and put it down as if it were somebody else's newspaper.

"Do you want to sell?"

"I don't know. The company is doing well, the team is strong, the market is..."

"I did not ask about the company," he said. "The company is fine. Companies are always fine until Tuesday. I asked about you. Do you want to sell?"

I sat there for a while, and then I said the true thing, which surprised me on its way out. "I don't know who I would be without it."

Henk nodded, like a customs officer accepting a declaration. "Now we have found the real problem, and it has nothing to do with price. Wouter. You built this company the way a carpenter builds a table." He tapped the table in question. "You are not the company. Sell it or keep it, I do not care. But do not keep it because you are afraid of meeting the man who is left over. That is fear calling itself loyalty."

Then, because he could never resist the practical footnote: "And if you do sell, sell it while you still love it. Buyers pay for a thing the owner loves. They can smell tired. It smells like discount."

Henk's line, you are not the company, will come back at the end of this chapter, because I did not understand it at his kitchen table. I understood it about eight months after the wire transfer, at the bottom of the cliff. But his practical footnote you can use today: the best time to sell is when you do not need to and do not entirely want to. Everything about a sale gets easier from strength, the price, the terms, the diligence, your own sleep. The paradox of exits is that they reward the founder who could happily keep going, and punish the one who cannot.

Try this

Take a pen and write two letters, one page each, both dated the day after a hypothetical closing. Letter one: to yourself, explaining why you sold, and describing an ordinary Tuesday in your new life, morning to evening, in boring detail. Letter two: explaining why you refused the offer and what the next five years of keeping the company look like. Do not skip the Tuesday detail, it is the whole exercise. One of these letters will be noticeably easier to write. That letter is telling you something the spreadsheet cannot.

The Number: Valuation from the Inside

Here is what every valuation method has in common: it is a way of arguing about the future using arithmetic about the past. Multiples of profit, multiples of revenue, discounted cash flows, comparable transactions. They are all, in the end, negotiation furniture. Useful furniture, you should understand it, but furniture. Your company is worth what a real buyer will actually wire on an actual day. Everything else is astrology with spreadsheets.

That said, the astrology has rules, and you should know them before anyone quotes you a number.

How buyers actually count

For most founder-led companies in Europe, the anchor is a multiple of normalized profit, usually EBITDA, which is roughly your operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization, in other words profit before the accountants get creative. A stable services firm or a distributor might trade at three to five times EBITDA. A well-run niche software company with real recurring revenue might see six to ten, sometimes more in a hot consolidation wave. Businesses with high recurring revenue and low founder dependence sit at the top of their range. Project-based businesses where each January starts at zero sit at the bottom, and sometimes below it.

The word doing the heavy lifting in that paragraph is normalized. Buyers will restate your profit before they multiply it. Out go the one-off windfalls. Out goes the below-market salary you have been paying yourself, replaced by the market cost of a real managing director, which lowers profit and therefore price. Back in come the genuinely private costs you have been running through the company, the car that is nicer than the job requires, the conference in a suspiciously pleasant location. This restatement is called quality of earnings, and it produces the first of many moments in a sale when a stranger tells you what your life's work really earns, per their spreadsheet, and you have to sit still and hear it.

Then come the discounts, and this is where founders get surprised. Customer concentration: if your top three customers are forty percent of revenue, expect the multiple to drop, because the buyer is pricing the morning one of them leaves. Founder dependence: if the biggest deals close because of you, if the product roadmap lives in your head, if key customers have your personal mobile number, the buyer is buying a job with you in it rather than a company, and they will price accordingly. Making yourself replaceable is chapter twelve's subject, and here is where that work pays out in cash. Every hour you spent turning yourself from the hero of the company into its architect converts, at exit, into multiple.

The gap between the headline and your bank account

Whatever number you agree, you will not receive it. This surprises everyone once. The headline is usually an enterprise value, the price of the business as a machine. From it, subtract the company's debt, add surplus cash, adjust for whether working capital is at the agreed normal level. Then subtract the part held back in escrow against future claims, typically for one to three years. Then subtract the earn-out, the slice of the price that exists only as a promise about future performance, which we will treat with appropriate suspicion later in this chapter. Then advisor fees, then tax, which varies wildly by country and structure and is the reason you talk to a tax advisor before the first offer, not after. A founder who sells for a headline of ten million euros and receives something like six on day one has met the normal anatomy of a deal, and you want to understand that anatomy before you start spending the headline in your head.

What the number does to your head

Now the part the corporate finance books skip. The first time someone puts a number on your company, something strange happens: it stops feeling like a price and starts feeling like a grade. A grade on your fourteen years, your marriage's patience, your missed birthdays, the nights you did not sleep in 2016. If the number is lower than you hoped, and it usually is, it lands like an insult from someone you wanted to impress. I have watched calm, rational founders blow up good deals over the last five percent, because the number had become their report card and they wanted the higher grade.

Two defenses. First, get the number early and privately, before any process, by asking an advisor for a cold, unflattering valuation range. Hear it, hate it, metabolize it on your own time. Second, and I say this gently: beware other founders' headlines. Exit numbers travel like fishing stories, and by the time a peer's sale reaches you at a conference dinner, the earn-out that never paid has merged into the headline, the escrow has evaporated, and the taxes have vanished. You are comparing your honest net to their decorated gross. Headline exits are Instagram for founders. You see the number. You do not see the terms.

The Menu of Exits

"Selling the business" sounds like one door. It is a corridor of doors, and they lead to very different rooms. The buyer type determines almost everything downstream: the price logic, the terms, what happens to your people, and what your own life looks like for the two years after closing. So before you think about price, think about which door you are standing in front of.

A strategic buyer, usually a competitor or a larger player in your industry, is buying your customers, your product, your geography, or the removal of you as an annoyance. Strategics tend to pay the best prices because they can count synergies you cannot, but they are also the buyer most likely to dissolve your company into theirs, brand, culture, coffee machine and all. The routing company sold to a strategic, and I will tell you honestly: the price was the best available and the integration still hurt to watch, even though they did it kindly and competently.

A financial buyer, private equity or a family holding, is buying your cash flows and your potential as a platform. They pay with discipline rather than romance, usually a defensible multiple of EBITDA, and they very often want you or your management team to stay and to keep meaningful skin in the game by rolling part of your proceeds into the new structure. This can be a genuine second act with someone else's capital, or it can be five more years of your old job with a new board, and it is worth knowing which one is on offer.

A management buyout sells the company to the people already running it. Prices are fair rather than spectacular, and since managers rarely have millions lying around, you often finance part of your own exit through a vendor loan, which means your money arrives slowly and stays exposed to the company's health. In exchange you get continuity, a protected culture, and the deep satisfaction of handing the keys to people who earned them. For many founders of stable, profitable, unglamorous companies, this is the best door in the corridor, and the least discussed.

Then there are the smaller doors. An individual buyer or search fund, one operator buying one company to run it, which lives or dies on personal fit and financing. Family succession, where the price is often symbolic and the real negotiation is emotional, conducted over years of Sunday dinners. The acqui-hire, mostly a software phenomenon, where the buyer wants your team and the product is a rounding error. And the door nobody photographs: the orderly wind-down, where you conclude the company is worth more as satisfied customers, well-referenced employees, and sold assets than as a going concern. Taken deliberately, early and solvent, it can be the most honest exit on the menu, and the founders who choose it do far better than the ones who arrive at it by exhaustion.

The exit menu: who buys founder-led companies, and what each door really means
Exit typeWhat they are buyingPrice tendencyWhat it means for you and the teamWatch out for
Strategic trade sale (competitor, larger industry player)Customers, product, market position, your removal as a rivalHighest, they can count synergiesIntegration is likely, brand and culture may dissolve, roles may be duplicatedThey learn your secrets in diligence even if the deal dies. Stage your disclosures.
Financial buyer (private equity, family holding)Cash flows, a platform to grow or bolt ontoDisciplined multiple of EBITDA, rarely romanticYou or your managers often stay, frequently with rolled equity and a boardLeverage lands on the company's shoulders. Understand the debt they will load onto it.
Management buyoutThe company they already runFair, not spectacularContinuity, culture preserved, keys go to people who earned themYou often finance it yourself via vendor loan, so your money stays at risk for years.
Individual buyer / search fundA company to personally runModest, financing-constrainedLong handover expected, personal fit decides everythingFinancing falls through late and often. Verify funds before exclusivity.
Family successionContinuity of the family assetSymbolic to modestLegacy preserved, relationships restructuredChristmas becomes a board meeting. Paper the deal as if they were strangers.
Acqui-hire (mostly software)Your teamLow, paid mostly as retention packagesProduct usually sunset, team absorbedMuch of the "price" is salary your people must stay to earn, and it never touches your account.
Orderly wind-downNobody, you sell the partsAsset value onlyDone well: customers placed, team referenced, obligations met, head highPride makes founders wait too long. Deliberate and solvent beats exhausted and forced.

Finding a Buyer Without Hanging a Sign in the Window

You cannot list a company the way you list a house, because the listing itself does damage. If customers hear you are for sale, they delay renewals. If employees hear it, the best ones polish their CVs. If competitors hear it, they tell your customers for you, with embellishments. So the entire buyer-finding process runs on a strange fuel: discretion that is somehow also outreach. Every deal I have watched, including mine, ran under a code name for this reason. The routing company spent eleven months as Project Osprey, and I still feel a small jolt when I see the bird.

The inbound illusion

If your company is any good, you already get emails. Someone from a private equity firm is impressed by your journey and would love a call. A corporate development person at a bigger company happens to be looking at your space. Here is what nobody tells you: most of this is weather, in the chapter nine sense, noise that looks like signal. Junior analysts send hundreds of these to keep pipelines warm, and an eager reply to one of them is how founders end up in the single worst structure that exists, the one-buyer negotiation. With a single buyer at the table, the "market" becomes an appraisal conducted by the person who benefits from a low number. One buyer is a hostage situation with better catering.

Inbound can still be the spark. My own sale started from an inbound email, the one I drove to Henk about. The trick is to let an approach trigger a process rather than a negotiation. The correct response to a serious approach is warm, unhurried, and plural: you take the call, you say the company is not for sale but you are always happy to know your neighbors, and then, if the interest is real and your letters from the exercise above pointed at selling, you go build a market around that one buyer.

Hiring the person who does this for a living

Building that market is what M&A advisors do, and for any company worth more than a couple of million euros, you should probably hire one. Not the global investment banks, they will not return your calls at this size and you would not enjoy their invoices if they did. You want a boutique that closes five to fifteen deals a year in companies your size, ideally in or near your industry. They earn their fee three ways: they know which buyers are hungry right now, they create the plural that gives you leverage, and they absorb the conflict, playing the villain in negotiations so that you can keep being the person the buyer wants to work with afterwards.

The fee structure is a monthly retainer plus a success fee of a few percent of the deal, higher percentages at smaller sizes, often with a ratchet that pays them more above an agreed threshold. That ratchet is worth having, because it points their greed the same direction as yours. When choosing, ignore the league tables and ask three questions: show me the last ten deals you closed at my size, let me call three of those founders, and who exactly, which human being, will work on my deal. The partner charms you at the pitch, then a 29-year-old runs your process. Meet the 29-year-old.

The process itself, run properly, looks like this. The advisor helps you build a longlist of plausible buyers, typically twenty to sixty names, strategics and financials both. Here is a useful exercise even if you never sell: ask yourself who mentions your company in their board meetings, whose expansion plans you sit in the middle of, who loses deals to you and hates it. Those are your buyers.

Then a one-page anonymous teaser goes out, the interested sign NDAs and receive the information memorandum, a document that describes your company the way a good estate agent describes a house, accurate but sunlit. First-round indicative offers arrive, you pick a handful for management meetings, the strange theater where you pitch your life's work across a conference table to people deciding whether to buy it. Second-round offers follow, and then you choose, and here is the part that matters: you choose on price, terms, and believability as a package, never on price alone. A high number from a flaky buyer is worth less than a fair number from a serious one, for reasons the next two sections will make painfully clear.

The Shape of a Deal: A Year of Your Life

Founders consistently expect a sale to take three months. It takes nine to eighteen. Mine took eleven, from the first serious meeting to the notary's phone call, and that was considered brisk. You need to see the whole shape in advance, because the length is a weapon. Buyers know that a tired seller is a cheaper seller, and some of them slow-walk the middle innings on purpose, waiting for deal fatigue to soften you. The founders who get hurt are the ones who mentally sold in month two and then spent seven months negotiating like people who just want it over.

Three things about this shape. First, the early phases overlap, preparation bleeds into marketing bleeds into offers, and that is normal. Second, the LOI in the middle, the letter of intent, is the deal's hinge: before it you have competition and leverage, after it you have granted one buyer exclusivity and your leverage drops by roughly half the moment the ink dries. Negotiate everything important into the LOI while you still have alternatives: price, structure, earn-out mechanics, what happens to the team. Negotiating any of it later means negotiating alone. Third, look at the grey bar at the bottom. The single most expensive mistake in this entire chapter is letting the business sag while you sell it. Your price was built on your trajectory. If the trajectory dips in month seven, the price follows it down, with enthusiasm.

Diligence: Strangers Read Your Diary

After the LOI comes due diligence, and I want to describe it as it happened, because everyone warns you it will be "thorough" and nobody warns you what thorough feels like. For two to four months, teams of accountants, lawyers, tax specialists, and technical experts, none of whom you chose and all of whom bill by the hour, will read everything your company has ever written down. Every contract, every employment agreement, every board minute, every tax filing, every customer renewal, the code, the leases, the insurance policies, the eleven-year-old shareholder agreement with the typo in your own name. They upload questions into a data room portal, hundreds of them, numbered like exhibits, and every question has a deadline and every answer breeds children.

It is not personal, and it feels intensely personal. Somewhere around week six, a 26-year-old you have never met will ask you to explain, in writing, a decision you made under fire nine years ago, and the explanation will sound thin even to you, because decisions made under fire always sound thin once they are written down and read cold. This is the phase where founders get worn down, and remember, the wearing down is partly the point. Deal fatigue is a negotiating tactic that bills by the hour.

Two rules got me through it. Rule one: never lie, and never let an optimistic answer slide into a false one, because the contract you eventually sign contains warranties, your personal promises that the answers were true, and a discovered lie converts your sale proceeds into a lawsuit fund. If there is a skeleton, and every company has a drawer, the unsigned contract with the biggest customer, the VAT question from 2019, the contractor who built half the product with no IP assignment, you disclose it, early and framed, on your terms. Disclosed skeletons cost a little price. Discovered skeletons cost deals, and worse, they cost trust in everything else you said. Rule two: split yourself in two, and give the deal your nights but never your mornings. Mornings belong to the company, because of the grey bar in the diagram. I answered data room questions from nine to midnight for four months and ran the routing company from eight to six, and it nearly broke me, and it was still the right allocation.

The re-trade

Late in diligence, some buyers come back with a lowered price, citing findings that are real but minor. This is called a re-trade, and with some buyers it was the plan all along: get you exclusive, get you tired, get you invested, then clip ten percent when walking away feels unbearable. Your defenses are all built earlier: competitive tension before the LOI, skeletons disclosed before they can be findings, a business that keeps performing, and a number, written down in advance with your advisor, below which you walk. Decide your walk-away price on a calm day in month one. You will not be able to compute it honestly in month nine.

Story

Priya nearly sold her B2B software company. An American strategic buyer arrived with a number that made her laugh out loud alone in her car, an LOI followed in six weeks, and she entered exclusivity in the spring, doing what most first-time sellers do: she started living in the deal. She flew to management meetings, staffed the data room herself, and moved, in her head, into the life on the other side. Sales discovery calls got delegated. The autumn marketing plan quietly died on a whiteboard. Why polish a company that would belong to someone else by Christmas?

In week fifteen of diligence, the buyer's sponsor, the executive whose pet project the acquisition was, left for another company. The deal did not die dramatically. It just got slower and colder, meetings pushed by a week, then two, and then a call in which a man she had never spoken to before cited "evolving strategic priorities" and, noting her softening quarterly pipeline, offered to proceed at seventy percent of the LOI price. The pipeline he cited had softened because she had spent two quarters feeding his data room instead of her funnel. The deal had caused the weakness it was now charging her for.

She walked, which took more nerve than signing would have. It took her company two years to climb back to its old trajectory, and it took her about as long to stop doing the arithmetic of the life she had furnished and lost. She keeps two rules taped inside her laptop lid now, ready for the next serious buyer who calls: the company runs as if the deal does not exist, and the money is fictional until it is in the account. "I sold the company in my head in week three," she told me. "The buyer just never showed up to the version I had already moved into."

Priya's rules deserve to be yours. A signed LOI is not a deal. A handshake is not a deal. A congratulatory dinner where the buyer's CEO toasts your future together is, and I am sorry about this, not a deal. Deals die in exclusivity constantly, at rates that would shock you, for reasons that have nothing to do with you: the buyer's own numbers dip, a champion changes jobs, a bigger target appears, financing wobbles. Until money moves, you are running a company that happens to be in talks, and everyone on your team who knows should be able to recite that sentence from memory.

The good news is that diligence, unlike most ordeals, rewards preparation, and you can start years early. Here is the checklist I wish I had worked through at the routing company in year ten instead of during the deal itself. Companies that do this in peacetime call it vendor readiness. I call it the drawer audit.

The diligence checklist: what buyers will demand, and what to fix in peacetime
AreaWhat they will ask forFix before any process starts
FinancialsThree to five years of statements, monthly P&L, revenue by customer and product, aged debtors, forecasts and how past forecasts performedClean bookkeeping, private costs out of the company, one honest management report you actually use, forecasts with a track record
CustomersConcentration, churn and retention history, signed contracts, renewal dates, willingness of top customers to take a reference callGet every customer contract signed and findable, reduce dependence on the top three, know your true churn number before they compute it for you
Legal & corporateIncorporation documents, shareholder agreements, board minutes, litigation history, licenses and permitsA tidy minute book, resolved shareholder loose ends, no handshake deals with material suppliers or partners
TeamEmployment contracts, org chart, compensation, key person dependencies, notice periods, disputesCurrent signed contracts for everyone, sane notice periods for key people, an org chart that works when you are on holiday
Product & IPWho owns the code, contractor IP assignments, open source licenses, trademarks, or for physical businesses the recipes, leases, and equipment titlesSigned IP assignment from every contractor who ever touched the product, license audit done by you first
TaxCorporate returns, VAT, payroll taxes, any open questions or rulingsClose old disputes even at a cost, get a pre-sale structuring review from a tax advisor, years early if possible
Operations & dataDocumented processes, supplier contracts, insurance, privacy and data protection complianceWrite down what currently lives in your head, and be able to show where personal data lives and why you may have it
The founderThey will not ask for this in writing. They will measure it in every meeting: what breaks if you leaveDelegate until the honest answer is "less than you would think." This is chapter twelve, doing exit work years in advance
Try this

Take the table above and spend one hour, today, with a pen and the honest version of yourself. Grade your company on each row: green, orange, or red, where red means "if a buyer asked tomorrow, I would need to make phone calls and apologies." No fixing today, just grading. Most founders find two reds and are surprised which rows they are in. Then put one red on next quarter's list. Whether or not you ever sell, every row you turn green makes the company calmer to run, easier to delegate, and worth more, in that order.

The Language of the Deal

Somewhere around the LOI, you will notice that everyone in the room is speaking a dialect you do not, and that every term in it quietly moves money from one side of the table to the other. The dialect grew up among people who do ten of these a year, negotiating against people who do one per lifetime, and it favors its native speakers. The single cheapest thing you can do for your exit is to learn the vocabulary before you need it, so that when someone proposes "a standard locked box with a modest escrow and a performance-based deferred component," you hear what was actually said, which is: we fix the price early, keep part of your money hostage, and make another part of it contingent on things you will no longer control.

Here is the glossary I wish someone had handed me, translated out of dialect.

Deal terms, translated for people who will only do this once
TermWhat it meansThe founder translation
LOI / term sheetA mostly non-binding letter setting out price, structure, and process before diligenceYour last moment of real leverage. Anything vague in the LOI will be resolved against you later. Negotiate it like it is binding, because emotionally it is.
Exclusivity / no-shopYour binding promise to negotiate with only this buyer for a period, typically 60 to 120 daysYou are handing over your alternatives. Keep it short, and make extensions something the buyer earns with progress, not something you grant to be nice.
Enterprise value vs equity valuePrice of the business as a machine, versus what shareholders actually receive after debt and cash adjustmentsThe headline is enterprise value. Your bank account gets equity value, minus everything else in this table. Never confuse the two at dinner parties.
Cash-free, debt-freeThe price assumes the company transfers with no cash and no debt, with adjustments either wayFine and normal, but the definitions of "cash" and "debt" are negotiable, and buyers define "debt" creatively. Unpaid bonuses and overdue supplier terms can suddenly become "debt-like items."
Working capital adjustmentPrice adjusts if working capital at closing deviates from an agreed normal levelThe most-fought-over boring clause in every deal. How "normal" gets calculated is worth real money. Let your accountant fight this one, it is what they are for.
Locked box vs completion accountsPrice fixed at a past balance sheet date, versus recalculated after closingLocked box gives certainty and an early effective date. Completion accounts give the buyer a second bite at the price after you have lost all leverage. Sellers generally want the box.
Earn-outPart of the price paid later, contingent on future performanceSee the next section, which exists because this row cannot hold everything I need to tell you.
Escrow / holdbackPart of the price parked with a third party for one to three years against warranty claimsNormal in moderation. Negotiate the size, the duration, and that it earns interest for you. Assume you see it late, and treat it as a bonus, not as budget.
Reps and warrantiesYour contractual statements that the facts disclosed are true, with liability if they are notThese are personal promises with your proceeds as collateral. Disclose everything, cap the liability, and never warrant something you have not personally verified.
W&I insuranceInsurance covering warranty claims, increasingly common in mid-sized dealsCosts a little, can free your escrow and let you sleep. Ask your advisor whether your deal is big enough for it, and let the buyer share the premium.
Vendor loanYou lend the buyer part of the price, repaid over yearsCommon in MBOs and small deals. You are now your buyer's bank, junior to their real bank. Price the risk honestly, and get security if you can.
Non-compete / non-solicitYour promise not to compete or poach staff and customers for a periodReasonable in scope is fine, they are buying the business, not renting it. But read it against your actual plans: three years, your industry, all of Europe, might quietly outlaw your next act. Chapter sixteen has opinions about your next act.
Good leaver / bad leaverClauses deciding what happens to your remaining stake or earn-out if you leave, resign, or are dismissed during the earn-out periodRead twice, then again. In sloppy drafts, the buyer can fire you and thereby cheapen the price. Make dismissal without cause a good-leaver event, always.
Field note

Assemble your own side of the table before the LOI, not after: an M&A lawyer who does deals for a living, not your regular corporate lawyer, however loyal, and a tax advisor who sees the structure before it hardens, because after signing, tax optimization becomes tax archaeology. Together they will cost real money, one to two percent of the deal is normal, and they are the best-paid hours of the entire process. The buyer does this every year. You do it once. Rent the experience gap shut.

Earn-Outs: The Deferred Argument

An earn-out sounds reasonable the first time you hear it, and that is what makes it dangerous. The buyer believes your forecast less than you do, so instead of arguing about the future, you agree to split the difference with it: a chunk of the price is paid over the next one to three years, if the company hits agreed targets. You get your full valuation if you were right, the buyer gets protection if you were wrong. It sounds like fairness. It compresses the entire gap between your optimism and their skepticism into a clause, and everyone signs and goes to dinner.

Here is the flaw, and it is structural, not moral: the earn-out makes your money depend on the performance of a company you no longer control, operated by the people who owe you the money. Buyers rarely cheat. Something quieter happens: the day after closing, your company stops being an organism and becomes an organ. The buyer, within their rights, starts integrating: your prices get aligned to theirs, your star developer gets borrowed for the group platform, your sales team gets a new CRM in the middle of the quarter, head office allocates a share of group overhead onto your P&L, and every one of those sensible integration decisions moves your earn-out, and none of them require your consent. You will sit in meetings watching people optimize the group at the expense of your targets, and the people doing it are ordinary employees doing their jobs inside a system that no longer has your price in its objectives.

Mine was two years, and I collected about sixty percent of it. The forty percent I lost, I lost in a beige meeting room in another city, in a discussion about cost allocation methodology, and the man across the table stayed polite the whole meeting, just applying group policy to a subsidiary. I had negotiated the earn-out on revenue growth assumptions and let the targets be written on profit. Profit is the number integration touches most. That mistake has a price tag I still know to the euro.

So, the rules, earned the expensive way. First, the price is what transfers at closing, full stop. If you would not do the deal for the closing amount alone, do not do the deal. Anything the earn-out later delivers is a windfall, and if it delivers nothing, your life still works. Second, if you must have one, base it on revenue, not profit, because revenue is harder for integration to distort, and define every term with an accountant's paranoia: whose revenue, recognized how, including which products, in which entity. Third, keep it short. One year is an agreement, two is a tolerance, three is a sentence with quarterly reviews. Fourth, negotiate protective covenants: the buyer must run the unit in the ordinary course, must not divert customers or staff, must keep you in the seat with authority over the levers your targets depend on, and if they fire you without cause, the earn-out pays in full. And fifth, know what you are really being paid for during those years, because an earn-out is also a retention device, a way of making sure the founder shows up and hands over the relationships. That part is fair. Just price your servitude honestly: you will be an employee, in your own former building, watching someone repaint it. Some founders sail through that. I did not, entirely, and the next sections are about why.

Telling People

There is a cruel structural fact at the center of every sale: the people the deal affects most are the last to know. You will spend the better part of a year carrying a secret past the desks of people you hired, people who trust you, people who notice, because good people always notice, that you are tired, distracted, and oddly often "at the dentist." You will feel like a spy in your own company. This is normal, it is even correct, and it still corrodes something in you a little every week.

The sequencing that works is concentric circles, widened as late as possible. Your cofounder and shareholders are in from the start, obviously, and chapter five's advice about writing down exit intentions while you still like each other is what makes this circle painless or terrible. Your finance lead comes in early, because the data room cannot be built without them. The rest of the leadership team typically enters around the LOI, when diligence makes secrecy impractical, and each person you tell should hear two sentences from you directly: here is what is happening and why, and here is what I am negotiating on your behalf. Retention bonuses for key people, funded by you from the proceeds, are common, decent, and cheap insurance. Everyone else learns at signing or closing, and the silence protects them as much as the deal: a rumor of a sale with no signed deal behind it is pure poison. Customers pause, competitors circulate the story with improvements, and your best engineer interviews elsewhere as a precaution.

Story

I told the routing company on a Thursday morning, all forty-one of them in the canteen, some on screens from the Lyon office. I had rehearsed for days. I had a speech about journeys and chapters, about how the group's resources would take what we built further than we could alone, and I delivered it adequately, voice cracking only once, at the sentence I had practiced most.

When I finished there was a silence, and then Ilse from support, nineteen years old when I hired her, eleven years ago by then, put up her hand and asked the only question that mattered: "Do we still have jobs?" Yes, I said, all of them, I had it in writing, it had cost me price and I would do it again. She nodded. Then Tomás from the routing team raised his hand and asked whether the good coffee machine would survive the integration, and the room laughed, and I understood something I have never forgotten: the sale was the biggest event of my professional life, and for them it was a Thursday with an announcement in it. Their lives were the mortgage, the commute, the colleagues, the coffee. My epic was their line item. That is health, theirs, and the sooner a selling founder grasps it, the kinder the communication gets.

Afterwards, an older developer named Theo, who had been with me since year two, shook my hand in the corridor and said, "Congratulations. And condolences." He had sold a company once, long before. At the time I thought he was being witty. He was being precise.

You tell customers after closing, together with the buyer, in an order sorted by importance and flight risk, and the message that works is continuity with specifics: same team, same contacts, here is what improves for you. What you say matters less than what happens in the following ninety days, so negotiate the post-closing plan for customers with the same care you gave the escrow. Your reputation rides on how the buyer treats them, for years after your name is off the door, and in your home market, where you will build whatever you build next, that reputation is the only asset from this deal that cannot be wired anywhere.

The Cliff

And now the part of the chapter I actually wrote this chapter for. Everything up to here, other books cover, some of them well. What follows, I have found mainly in late-night conversations with other sold founders, all of us a little embarrassed to be discussing our excellent fortune in the tones people use for a bereavement.

Here is what nobody tells you: closing day is a cliff, and I use the word as a map reference, terrain I have stood on, rather than the usual business-book decoration. There is a before, in which you are a person with a place in the world that requires no explanation, and an after, which begins the moment the wire lands and the phone goes quiet. And the drop between them is severe in exact proportion to how much of yourself you had stored in the company, which, for most founders, after a decade or more, is nearly everything without their noticing.

Think about what the company was doing for you, all those years, beyond the salary. It answered the question "what do you do?" at every party. It structured every day, every week, every year, without you ever once needing to decide what a Tuesday is for. It gave you a tribe with an inside language, a scoreboard that told you whether you were winning, a queue of problems perfectly shaped for your skills, and a reason to get up that renewed itself overnight like bread. Then one Tuesday at 11:52, in exchange for a number, all of it switches off at once. Salary you can replace, the number took care of that. Nobody wires you a reason to get up.

Let me narrate the curve, since I have walked it. The spike at closing lasts somewhere between a day and a month: euphoria, relief, dinners, a holiday that finally deserves the name. Then the pit opens, usually around month two, and it is made of specific things. Grief with no funeral: you have lost something enormous, but nobody sends flowers to a man who just got rich, so the grief goes unwitnessed, which is the loneliest kind. Status vertigo: at parties, "what do you do?" now produces a stammer, and you catch yourself saying "I used to run a company" in the past tense of a person describing someone who died. The strange silence of a phone that rang for fourteen years. The discovery that some friendships were proximity, colleagues you loved who, without the shared building, turn out to have been colleagues. And underneath all of it, if you are on an earn-out, the special limbo of badging into your own former building as an employee, watching the new owners reverse your decisions, needing permission where you used to give it.

The money, and I know how this sounds, is its own strangeness. You will feel guilt at your luck, roughly aimed at the employees who built the value and got salaries. You will be surrounded, within weeks, by well-dressed men from private banks who have your number by means you never quite establish, all offering to help with "the complexity of your new situation." You will notice yourself becoming cagey about the amount with friends, and you will notice a few friends becoming odd about it anyway. I refuse to write the paragraph where a rich man asks for sympathy, so call all of this what it is: disorientation. And disorientation plus idleness plus an unwitnessed grief is the exact recipe for the founders you have heard about who went a bit wrong after their exit, the impulsive yacht, the impulsive divorce, the impulsive new company built out of pure withdrawal. What makes the pit dangerous is how expensive it is to flail in.

The wire transfer takes four seconds. Becoming a person who is not the company takes about a year, and nobody sends flowers, because you are not supposed to be grieving.

What actually helps, from my own year in the pit and from comparing notes since. Keep a structure, immediately: I eventually rebuilt Tuesdays out of exercise, a woodworking course I was reliably bad at, school pickups, and two volunteer advisory roles, and the content mattered far less than the shape. Say yes slowly: I made a rule of twelve months with no major commitments, no new company, no big investments, no board seats collected like stamps, and every good thing in my current life fits through the door that rule kept open, while nearly every exited founder I know who skipped the waiting year bought at least one expensive mistake inside it. Get your grief witnessed: a therapist, or at minimum other sold founders, who are the only people who will not laugh when you describe crying in your car outside your own former office, which I did, in month four, having driven there without any errand, like a dog returning to a house the family moved out of. And protect your marriage or its equivalent through the transition, because the household had also organized itself around the company, and your sudden full-time presence in it is a renovation nobody requested.

And in month eight, at the bottom of the curve, I went back to Henk's kitchen table, because that is what the table was for. He was very old by then, and the stairs took a while, and the coffee was still black and the cigar smell had outlived, as far as I could tell, any actual cigars, possibly by decades.

"So," he said. "You got your money. And now you are nobody, and it is worse than you expected."

I said that was approximately the situation, yes.

"Good," he said, which was not the sympathy I had driven forty minutes for. "It is supposed to be. You put fourteen years of yourself into one thing, and the thing is gone, and it worked. Both are true, and you are the first person you have ever met to whom both happened at once. Give it a year and stop insulting the year by wishing it shorter." He turned his coffee cup a quarter turn, his version of a paragraph break. "I told you before you sold: you are not the company. You did not believe me, because back then the sentence was about the company. Now it is about you. You built one good thing, Wouter. What are the odds you contained exactly one good thing? Men who can build are not emptied by one building."

He was right, as usual, and it took the remaining months of the curve for the sentence to finish arriving. The far side of the cliff, I should tell you, does not return you to the old altitude, and this is the part I misunderstood in advance. You come out lower and wider, if that makes sense: no single thing holds all of you anymore, and once the vertigo passes, that turns out to be the healthiest configuration I have ever lived in. Whether you then take all this hard-won width and immediately roll it into another company, which a suspicious number of us do, is the subject of chapter sixteen, and I will meet you there.

The Short Version

  • Sell while you still love the company. Buyers pay for loved. Tired smells like discount, and the whole process rewards the founder who could happily keep going.
  • Interrogate your reason first: the sale should buy a life you can describe in Tuesday-level detail, not just an escape from a fixable problem.
  • Your company is worth what a real buyer wires on a real day. Normalize your earnings, reduce customer concentration, and make yourself replaceable, because founder dependence is the biggest discount of all.
  • One buyer means an appraisal by an interested party, with catering. Create competition, and rent an advisor who does this for a living to run it.
  • Negotiate everything important into the LOI while you still have alternatives. Your leverage halves the day exclusivity starts.
  • Prepare for diligence years early, disclose every skeleton before it becomes a finding, and write down your walk-away price on a calm day in month one.
  • Run the company as if the deal does not exist, because deals die in exclusivity constantly, and the price rests on the numbers you deliver during the process.
  • Price the deal on what transfers at closing; count the earn-out as a windfall. If the closing amount alone does not justify the deal, do not sign it.
  • The money is fictional until it is in the account. Priya's rule. Tape it somewhere.
  • The cliff after closing is real. Plan the year after the sale as deliberately as the sale itself, say yes slowly for twelve months, and hold on to Henk's line: you built the company, carpenter to table, and builders are not emptied by one building.

Chapter 16

Doing It Again

The second company is a new play, staged by someone who has finally stopped being afraid of the theatre.

Two springs ago, Sam bought me a coffee on a terrace in Utrecht and slid a single sheet of paper across the table, face down, like a man settling an old debt.

The last time Sam slid something across a table at me, we were twenty-two, and it was a pitch deck for a recipe app. Forty slides. A market size with three commas in it. A slide titled "Why Now" that did not survive contact with a single actual cook. You know how that story ends, because chapter five keeps the autopsy on file: eighteen months, no users, no money, and a friendship that needed two years and one very awkward wedding to fully recover.

This time it was one page. On it: a paragraph describing a problem, three numbers, a short list under the heading "Things I believe but have not checked," and at the bottom, in bold, a date and a sentence beginning "If by this date I cannot show..." A kill criterion. Sam, who once defended a recipe app the way a lawyer defends a guilty client, had written the terms of his own execution at the bottom of his own idea.

"Tell me why this fails," he said.

"What do you think" is a request for applause wearing a fake moustache. Sam had asked the other question, the one with teeth. So I spent an hour trying to kill his company. The idea was software for restaurant kitchens, tracking stock and waste, the least romantic corner of the food world he loved. I attacked the pricing, the sales motion, the assumption that chefs would ever touch a screen with wet hands. He wrote down every blow, argued back against about half, and thanked me for the other half. At one point he said, with the quiet satisfaction of a man describing a reliable car, "It is a boring company. That is a feature."

Walking to the station afterwards, it struck me that I had just watched the entire difference between a first company and a second one, performed live, by the same man, at the same kind of table. At twenty-two, Sam and I defended our idea to the death, and it died anyway, partly of our defending. At thirty-eight, Sam prosecuted his idea like a hostile witness, and it lived. That difference, what it is made of, what it costs, and how to get it without paying full price twice, is this whole chapter.

This is also the last chapter, which means it has two extra jobs. It has to talk honestly about the loop at the end of the road, the one the map in the introduction drew with a small arrow and the words "and around again." And it has to say goodbye properly, a thing books are usually as bad at as founders. There is a letter near the end, and after the letter, an epilogue. But first, the loop.

You Will Probably Do It Again

I want to start with the conclusion, because it changes how you should read everything else: if you have built one company, you will probably try to build another, and sooner than you plan to.

I have no clean statistic for this, and I would not trust one if I did, but I can offer you the evidence of every founder dinner I have attended since I sold the routing company. Around those tables sit people who swore, hand on heart, sometimes in writing, that they were done. That they would garden. That they would finally learn to sail, or be present for their children in some vague but emphatic way, or do "a few small angel things." Give them two years. Then watch them lean across the table, lower their voice as if confessing to a crime, and say, "So, I have been looking at something."

Why does this happen? Partly identity. If you spent ten or twenty years being the person who builds the thing, then not building the thing feels like amputation. Chapter fifteen talked about the cliff on the far side of the sale, the strange grief of waking up with money and no mission. That grief has a favourite medicine, and the medicine is a new company. Partly it is that the skill has no other arena. You have spent years getting good at an extremely specific sport, the sport of making promises to customers and keeping them without running out of money, and there is no veterans' league. And partly, honestly, it is that building things with people you chose, for customers who need it, is one of the best games available to an adult human, and you know it, because you have played it.

The itch has a specific texture. You will be on holiday, reading some harmless article about, say, the European market for heat pumps, and you will notice that you have opened a spreadsheet. You will give a friend "just a bit of advice" about her struggling company, and at midnight you will catch yourself rewriting her pricing page in your head, with a level of care and joy you have not felt in months. The itch announces itself as helpfulness, as curiosity, as one small spreadsheet that grows tabs. Ambition never signs its own name.

There is even a schedule to it, reliable enough that friends of exited founders privately bet on it. Year one after the sale, the founder is publicly serene and privately jetlagged in a way no flight explains. Somewhere in year two, the sentences start changing shape. "I would never go back to that life" becomes "I would only do it again if the right thing came along," which becomes "I have been sketching something, purely as an exercise," which becomes a chamber of commerce registration. I sat across from a man at a dinner in Antwerp who delivered the full progression in one evening, between the starter and the cheese, apparently without noticing. Nobody laughed, because everyone at that table had either done the same or was two courses away from starting.

Here is what I need you to hold onto, though, and it is the load-bearing idea of this chapter: the second company is a different play. You are older, richer, better calibrated, more watched, and less hungry. Your starting conditions have changed so much that treating lap two as a rerun of lap one is a category error, and the category error that kills most sequels. Some of what you carry from the first company is treasure. Some of it is expired medicine in an impressive bottle. The work of this chapter is sorting one from the other before you swallow anything.

And there is one more complication, which readers of the introduction will see coming. By the time you consider doing it again, your first company has stopped being an experience and become a story. You have told it at dinners, in interviews if you had them, to yourself in the shower. And stories, as we established on page one, lie about the weather. Your memory has tidied the desk, thrown out the terror and the flukes, and left a narrative in which your decisions caused your outcomes. Before you build on top of that story, you will need to un-tidy it. There is an exercise for that a few sections from now, and it is the least comfortable one in this book.

So this chapter walks the loop in order. What genuinely transfers to a second company. What dangerously does not. The ego trap that is waiting for you, personally, with your name on it. Rest, which turns out to be a phase with its own work rather than a reward with a hammock. The substitutes, angel investing and advising and their cousins, and how to tell whether they will feed you or just take the edge off. Then Sam's second act in full, a decision framework, a letter, and the road home.

What Transfers

Let me give you the good news first, because it is genuinely good and you have paid a great deal for it.

The first thing that transfers is judgment about people. This one is close to priceless. The first time around, you learned to hire by hiring wrong, which is the tuition model described in chapter ten, and the fees were brutal. You hired the brilliant jerk, the charming empty suit, the loyal friend who could not do the job. Each one took months to recognise and longer to resolve. The second time, you can smell trouble in the first twenty minutes of an interview, because you have a library now. The candidate who claims credit in suspiciously round numbers, the client who negotiates hard before the work has even started, the potential cofounder who talks about his last partner the way bitter divorcés talk. You have met them all before. First-time founders have to learn each of these as a surprise. You get them as reruns.

The second is cash instinct. If you did the work of chapter six the hard way, and almost everyone does it the hard way, you now feel runway in your body. You will never again confuse profit with cash, because you have lived inside the gap between the two, in that special month when the P&L smiled and the bank account wheezed. Henk's line, profit is opinion, cash is fact, is engraved somewhere behind your sternum. In the second company this shows up as an almost boring calm about money. You know what a thirteen-week cashflow is for. You know an invoice is not money. You know exactly how long a customer who "just needs sign-off from finance" can take, to the day. This calm is worth more than most of the capital you could raise.

The third is the phase map itself, the thing this whole book has been drawing. You now know that a sales slump can be an identity problem, that a scaling disaster is usually a skipped earlier chapter presenting its bill, that the fire and the fuel are often in different rooms. The first time, every phase ambushed you. The second time, you can hear phases coming down the corridor. You will still have to live them, the map is not the terrain, but you will waste far less time wondering what is happening to you and whether you are the only one. You are never the only one. You now know that in your bones instead of just from a book.

The fourth is calibrated fear, and I want to dwell on this one because nobody talks about it. First-time founders are afraid of everything at the same volume. A one-star review, a resignation, a tax letter, a competitor's press release, all of it arrives at 2 a.m. with the same siren. By the end of company one, your fear has been through calibration. You know which sirens mean fire and which mean a sensitive smoke detector. A big customer going quiet, real siren. A competitor raising a round, smoke detector. This calibration is why experienced founders seem so calm in crises. Their alarm system is better sorted, and it lets them spend their adrenaline where it buys something.

The fifth is craft, plural. You can sell, because founder-led selling forced you to learn discovery and pricing conversations, and that craft moves to any product. You can run a meeting that ends on time with decisions in it. You can fire someone kindly, which is a terrible sentence and a real skill. You can read a contract and know which three clauses matter. None of this needs relearning. It is yours now, like riding a bike, if the bike occasionally invoiced you.

Let me make craft concrete with the least pleasant example, because it is the clearest. The first time I had to let someone go at the routing company, I prepared for a week, slept badly for two nights, and still made every classic mistake: I buried the message in the fourth paragraph of a speech, I negotiated against myself before he had said a word, and I managed to make a kind decision feel cruel through sheer clumsiness. The last time I had to do it, years later, the conversation took eleven minutes, he heard the decision in the first sentence, the terms were generous and clear, and we still exchange messages in December. Same painful act. The difference was a hundred repetitions of adjacent conversations in between. That difference gets on the boat with you to the second company, free of charge, and there are twenty other crafts like it in your luggage.

The sixth is the network, and its shadow twin, reputation. People return your calls now. Talent that would not have gambled on you at twenty-five will listen at forty-five. Banks behave differently. Suppliers extend terms. If you sold well, some customers of the old company will follow you out of pure curiosity. This is real and useful, and it comes with a catch big enough that the next section treats it as contraband.

And the seventh, if you did the mirror work of chapter twelve, is self-knowledge. You know your personal failure modes now. You know whether you are the founder who hides in product when sales get scary, or hires to avoid conflict, or holds on to decisions like a dog with a sock. The second company does not cure these, I am sorry to report. But you see them coming, and seeing them coming is most of the fight.

What transfers to the second company, and the catch bolted to each
What transfersWhy it helpsThe catch
Judgment about peopleYou recognise bad hires, bad clients and bad partners in one meeting instead of one yearPattern-matching can misfire on people who merely resemble old villains, and you will reject a few good ones unfairly
Cash instinctYou feel runway in your body and never confuse profit with cash againCalm about money can slide into casualness when the money is your own exit proceeds
The phase mapYou hear phases coming instead of being ambushed by themKnowing the name of a phase tempts you to skip living it
Calibrated fearYou spend adrenaline only on real firesCalibration was done on the old company; some new sirens are real and unfamiliar
Craft: selling, hiring, firing, running meetingsYears of practice, immediately usableCraft is portable, the playbook it served is not, as the next section explains
Network and reputationCapital, talent and customers return your callsReputation raises the stakes of failing in public, which distorts your choices
Self-knowledgeYou see your own failure modes approachingOnly transfers if you actually did the work, and hindsight loves to award the certificate anyway

Add all this up and you can see why second companies tend to get further, faster, with less drama. The founder is simply operating with better instruments. But the same confidence that carries the treasure also smuggles in the contraband, and the contraband is the subject of the next section, which is the most important one in this chapter.

What Dangerously Does Not Transfer

Now the customs inspection.

The first thing that does not transfer is market knowledge, and this one catches almost everyone, because it feels like the crown jewel. You spent a decade becoming a genuine expert in your old market. You knew the buyers by first name, the price points to the euro, the seasonal rhythms, which trade fair mattered and which was a wine-tasting with lanyards. Here is the uncomfortable truth: that knowledge started expiring the day you stopped using it, and it expires faster than you think. Three years out of a market is a geological age. Your contacts have changed jobs. The channel that built your first company is now saturated, regulated, or dead. The pricing logic has moved. Worse, the knowledge still feels crisp and authoritative, because expertise carries no printed best-before date. You have to stamp one on yourself.

The second thing that does not transfer is the playbook. Your first company's playbook, the sales motion, the hiring sequence, the pricing model, the marketing channel, was a set of answers fitted to one specific body: that product, that market, that decade, that team. The routing company grew up on trade fairs and patient, unglamorous enterprise sales, cycles you measured in seasons, pilots, procurement departments with fax machines. It worked because delivery fleets bought software that way, then. Take that same playbook into a product-led market where buyers want to swipe a credit card before lunch, and you will die politely, in well-run meetings, wondering why your excellent process produces nothing. A tailored suit proves the tailor can cut cloth. The next body still needs its own fitting. Keep the tailoring skill. Burn the suit.

I ran this experiment on myself, involuntarily. Early in my current company, I caught myself budgeting for a stand at an industry fair, because that is what you do, that is how companies find customers, I had a decade of receipts proving it. Then I did the thing I am begging you to do, which is check the fitting before wearing the suit: I asked six people who matched my new customer profile when they had last attended a trade fair for anything. Two laughed. One said 2019, in a tone that suggested bereavement. The channel that built my previous company was, for these buyers, a nostalgia act. The correct channel turned out to be something I would have dismissed as unserious a decade earlier, and finding it required the beginner's work of chapter nine, done again, from zero, by a man who considered himself excused from it. Nobody is excused from it. That is the whole point of the suit metaphor, and I paid a conference deposit to learn it, so please enjoy it at no cost.

The third thing that does not transfer is timing, which is a polite word for luck. Your first company existed in specific weather: an interest rate, a technology wave, a competitor who fumbled, a regulation that landed in your favour, a big customer whose champion happened to like you. You cannot re-book the weather. And here memory, that helpful colleague from the introduction, does its most expensive tidying. The story you now tell about company one has re-filed the lucky breaks as strategy. The customer who found you by accident becomes "our go-to-market." The hire who walked in the door becomes "our talent magnet." Blame being human before you blame vanity. Memory's job is to make you feel coherent. Keeping you honest is someone else's department.

Experience transfers. Luck does not. The second company is how you find out which one you were running on.

The fourth thing that does not transfer, or transfers much less than you hope, is the team. There is a fantasy every exited founder entertains, usually in the bath: getting the old band back together. A few of them may come, and choose those few carefully. Most will stay, and most should, and even the ones who come have changed. They were great in a company that had found its rhythm; a garage is a different instrument. And there is a subtler problem. If you transplant the old company's inner circle wholesale, you transplant its culture, its jokes, its assumptions, into a company that has not yet earned any of them. Chapter one argued that you have to design identity on purpose, and that holds the second time too; a sequel that inherits its identity secondhand starts life in someone else's clothes.

The fifth thing that does not transfer is your own engine. I will be gentle here, but not dishonest. At twenty-four you could sprint on cheap pasta and adrenaline, sleep under a desk, and call it culture. Twenty years later you have a back, possibly a family, certainly a more accurate sense of what a decade of your life is worth. Plan for it. Design the second company for pace rather than sprint: fewer heroics, better delegation from month one, a founder who goes home. Chapter twelve made the case that your energy is a company asset; in the sequel it is a scarcer one, and you are the only person who can budget it.

Which brings us to the least comfortable exercise in this book. Before you trust your experience, audit your luck.

Try this

The luck audit. Write down the ten most important things that went right in your first company. Real, specific things: the anchor customer, the hire that changed everything, the price increase that stuck, the competitor that stumbled. Next to each one, write a single letter: S if it was mostly skill, W if it was mostly weather, B if it was honestly both. Rules: at least three of the ten must be W or the audit is void, and you must then do it again with someone who was there and has no reason to flatter you. Your cofounder. Your first employee. Your accountant, who remembers the weather with terrifying precision. You did plenty; the audit exists so you know, before you bet years of your life on it, which parts of the last miracle were yours to repeat.

The Ego Trap of the Sequel

Everything in the previous section can be handled with humility and a notebook. This section is about the thing that prevents the humility, and it deserves its own heading because it is the single most common way second companies die. Markets kill a few. Motive kills the rest.

Here is the trap in one sentence: the second company gets built to prove something about the first one.

If the first company succeeded, the whisper says: prove it was not luck. Show them the first one was no fluke, that you are a builder of companies, plural, a serial entrepreneur, a phrase that should always be pronounced with one raised eyebrow. If the first company failed, the whisper is crueller and stronger: prove you are not what the failure implied. Either way, you conscript the new company at birth into an argument about the old one, and companies make terrible lawyers. A business built to serve customers makes decisions about customers. A business built to prove a point makes decisions about the audience, and the audience, unlike customers, pays in applause, which your bank does not accept.

The trap has symptoms, easy to spot in others and invisible in the mirror. First: skipping discovery. "I know this market" is the most expensive sentence in second-time entrepreneurship, usually pronounced about a market as it existed several years ago. The humble validation work of chapter four, the interviews, the ugly first offers, the discovery questions of chapter nine, all of it feels beneath you now, like a professor being asked to retake the entrance exam. Do the exam. The market is allowed to have changed while you were away, and it did.

Second: day-one infrastructure. The first-time founder underbuilds; the second-timer overbuilds, magnificently. A brand agency before a customer. A holding structure fit for a group of companies before there is a company. An office with a meeting room named after a philosopher. Three job offers out before the product has survived contact with a single stranger's money. It all feels like professionalism, like the hard-won lesson that you should do things properly this time. But infrastructure is a bet on a specific future, and the only future you know anything about is the previous one.

Third: the announcement. First companies launch quietly because nobody cares. Second companies launch loudly because people do, and the loudness is a debt. Announce big and every later pivot becomes a public confession; chapter seven called pivots a healthy part of a living plan, but they are much harder to make with an audience scoring you against your own press release. The correction is old and simple: sell before you announce, and let the announcement, when it comes, be a report rather than a promise.

A word about the phrase "serial entrepreneur," since the world will start applying it to you around now. Notice what the phrase does: it relocates your identity from the company to the sequence. A founder serves a business; a serial entrepreneur performs a career, and performances need audiences, and audiences need escalation. I have watched this label talk sensible people into raising money they did not need, for companies that did not want to be big, because the sequence demanded a louder next act. You do not have to accept the label. When someone introduces me with it, I say I am between mistakes, which is accurate, gets a laugh, and cancels the expected keynote. Find your own version of that sentence. It is cheaper than the alternative, which is becoming the audience's employee.

Fourth: refusing small revenue. The first invoice of a second company carries strange weight. Some part of you feels that a founder of your standing should not be excited about 400 euros. That part of you is the enemy. Small revenue is the sound of a real customer with a real problem taking you seriously, and it is exactly as informative at forty-five as it was at nineteen.

Story

I will not tell you what my current company does, but I will tell you how it started, because it started badly in precisely the way this section describes, and I wrote the section from the inside.

Within six weeks of deciding to build again, and before I had spoken to one potential customer, I had: instructed a notary to set up a holding structure suitable for a fifty-person group, two notaries actually, because the first one asked questions I found annoying, filed trademarks in three classes, opened conversations with two brand agencies, and drafted a hiring plan with eight roles in it, including, I am ashamed to type this, a Head of Operations. For a company that did not exist. Whose product did not exist. Whose customer I had not met.

What saved me was coffee with the routing company's old CFO, a woman who audits sentences the way she audits ledgers. I talked for ten minutes about the structure and the brand direction and the hiring plan. She let me finish, stirred her coffee, and asked, "Nice. What week are you in?" I asked what she meant. "Of the thirteen-week cashflow. Which week. What came in." There was, of course, no cashflow, because there was no cash coming in, because there were no customers, because the founder had been decorating the theatre instead of writing the play. I went home, cancelled the agencies, parked the trademarks, and spent the next month doing the thing I should have started with: selling something small and ugly to one real person. The first invoice was 400 euros. Roughly the butcher's 350 from when I was nineteen, adjusted for inflation. It taught me more than the holding structure ever has.

Warning

The most dangerous investor in your second company is you. Exit money makes you a lenient backer: you approve your own ideas at board level, you extend your own runway without a milestone, and the company never feels gravity. A business that cannot run out of money learns nothing from spending it. Fund your sequel like a stranger would: a written amount, a written runway, kill criteria with dates on them, and one person with permission to read them back to you in a flat voice. Chapter six's runway math does not stop applying because the investor loves you.

There is one more form of the ego trap, quieter than the others: choosing the market itself to impress someone. The founder who did unglamorous logistics software and now, mysteriously, must do something in space, or AI, or whatever this decade's dinner-party currency is. If you find yourself drawn to a market and cannot explain the pull without mentioning how it will sound at dinner, you have found a mirror, and mirrors make expensive markets.
