The boring test is Sam's, from the terrace: the best second companies are often the ones their founders describe, with satisfaction, as boring. Boring means the founder is done performing. Customers can feel it, the way they could smell improvisation in the introduction's story about our year-four sales mess. Calm is a brand you cannot fake. You earn it, or you inherit it from a previous life.

Rest Is a Phase, Not a Reward

Between the last company and the next one there is a stretch of road with no buildings on it, and almost every founder I know has tried to sprint across it as if rest were something to apologise for. The stretch is a phase, the seventeenth one this book never promised you, and like every phase it has its own work, its own weather, and its own ways of going wrong.

Chapter fifteen owns the cliff itself, the strange grief that follows the wire transfer, so I will not re-teach it here. What I want to describe is what the months after the cliff are actually for, because "rest" suggests a hammock, and what happens is closer to renovation.

The first stretch, call it months one to three, is decompression, and you will be worse at it than you expect. Your body, it turns out, has been keeping books all along, and once the adrenaline stops it presents the invoices: the sleep debt, the molars you have been grinding, the shoulder that has been living somewhere near your ear since the diligence process. You will check your phone with the reflex of a man checking a wound. It will not ring, or worse, it will ring with things that are no longer yours to fix, and you will have to practice, actually practice, the sentence "that is not my problem anymore" until it stops tasting strange. Do the admin of ending things. Sleep like it is a project. Say yes to lunches with no agenda. That is the whole job of this stretch, and it is a real job.

Then, somewhere around month four, boredom arrives in disguise. It knocks, sits down at your desk, and says, "I have an idea." Suddenly everything looks like a company: the bad software at your dentist, the empty shop on the corner, the inefficiency at the marina. Your spreadsheet grows tabs. And here is the distinction that I would tattoo on the inside of every exited founder's eyelids if they would hold still: boredom pushes, curiosity pulls. Boredom is a shove away from an emptiness you have not finished sitting with. Curiosity is a pull toward one specific problem that will not leave you alone. Companies started from the shove are rebound relationships. Companies started from the pull have a chance. The only way to tell them apart is time, which is exactly the thing the shove insists you do not have.

So the rules of the rest phase are mostly rules about reversibility. For six months, make no commitments you cannot walk back over a weekend. No leases. No cofounder promises, which are engagements, and chapter five has shown you what breaking one costs. No term sheets, in either direction. No buying a vineyard, a restaurant, or, and I say this with love for a specific friend, a fishing trawler. Run all the cheap, reversible experiments you like: a landing page, twenty conversations, a weekend prototype, a tab in the spreadsheet. When people push you for decisions, and they will, because the world finds a resting founder unbearable, use the sentence a wise, tired man once gave me: "I will tell you in March." It is astonishing how much nonsense dies quietly between now and March.

You will want a case study, so here is a composite one that several friends will each believe is about the other. A founder I know sold his company in the autumn and by February, month four, note the month, had signed a five-year lease on a building, because the idea that arrived with the boredom needed a home, and the building was a bargain, and doing things properly means committing. By summer the idea had changed shape twice, which healthy ideas do, except each new shape had to fit the building instead of the customer. He describes that lease now as the most expensive way he has ever learned the difference between a decision and an anaesthetic. The company he eventually built, two years later, is doing fine. It operates, he enjoys telling people, from a rented room, month to month, above a physiotherapist.

The rest phase also has deeper work, and you can guess it from chapter twelve: the rebuilding of an identity with more than one leg. Spend the year becoming someone whose whole weight does not stand on the next company. Coach a team. Learn something with your hands, badly, in public. Repair the marriage that survived the company, and say the thank-yous out loud. Call it structural engineering for the next lap, because a founder with one identity leg builds companies that must never wobble, and all companies wobble.

Field note

The timeline I have watched, across many founders: months one to three, sleep and admin. Months three to six, boredom dressed up as ideas. Months six to twelve, real curiosity emerging, usually about something quieter than expected. After twelve, decisions worth trusting. Founders run it faster and slower, but the order almost never changes, and the expensive mistake is always the same one: treating a month-four shove as a month-ten pull.

Angel Investing and Other Ways to Half-Scratch the Itch

Somewhere in the rest phase, an alternative will present itself, in excellent shoes: what if you stayed in the game without playing it? Become an angel investor. Take some board seats. Advise. Mentor. It sounds like the mature synthesis, all of the craft, none of the 2 a.m. It deserves an honest look, so here is one.

Angel investing, first. The pitch to yourself is that you will be the investor you wished you had, and your scar tissue will compound across a dozen companies instead of one. The reality, and I say this as someone with several cheques out in the world, is that you are a passenger. A well-informed, occasionally consulted passenger, but a passenger. You will watch founders drive your favourite road, and some of them will take a bend in a way you would not, and your entire toolkit for the situation is one phone call and the tone of voice you use on it. If your identity is builder, this is a peculiar torture. The money math is also blunter than the dinner-party version: most small cheques die, the winners take years to matter, and the whole activity only works with money you can wave goodbye to, the same honesty chapter six demanded about runway, pointed at your own portfolio.

Since we are being practical: in the European corners I know, a first angel cheque is usually somewhere between ten and fifty thousand euros, you should expect to write ten or fifteen of them before the portfolio tells you anything about your judgment, and you should expect the honest accounting to take most of a decade. Decide the total you are prepared to lose before you meet a single founder, because founders are, professionally, people who are good at moving that number upward in person. And write down, in advance, your rule about follow-on rounds, because the hardest cheque to refuse is the third one into a struggling company, requested by a founder you like, backed by a story you would have told yourself, word for word, fifteen years ago.

There is a real test for whether investing will feed you, and it is this: do you enjoy the companies you cannot control? Enjoy, the way you enjoy a friend's garden, with no urge to weed it? Some founders discover, to their surprise, that they love the pattern across ten companies more than the steering wheel of one, that helping a stranger see her pricing problem gives them the old spark without the old cortisol. Those people convert, genuinely, and become the rare angels worth their cap table space. Others discover that every board meeting is a small bereavement, an hour of watching someone else hold the pen. Those people should build, and the sooner they admit it the cheaper their portfolio will be.

Advising and board work sit one step closer to the action and are cheap to try, which is their great virtue. Done honestly, with preparation and real skin in the conversation, they are useful work and a good way to find out what you actually miss. Done as identity maintenance, a lanyard that says "still relevant," they curdle into theatre within two quarters, and founders can smell it. Buying an existing small business is the underrated middle path, especially in Europe, where a generation of owners is retiring with solid companies and no successors. You skip the chapters this book put first and inherit the ones it put in the middle: real customers, real cashflow, real hiring and structure problems from day one. It is building, with the loneliness moved to different rooms.

Ways to stay in the game, compared honestly
PathWhat it scratchesWhat it does notMoney at riskThe trap
Build againEverything: the making, the promises, the team, the customersYour calendar, your sleep, several yearsAs much as you let yourself invest, see the warning aboveBuilding the sequel to prove a point about the original
Buy a businessOperating, improving, owning outcomesThe blank-page joy of zero to oneSubstantial, often with debt attachedAssuming operating is easier than founding; operating is a different job, and just as hard
Angel investingPattern-matching, staying current, helpingThe steering wheel; you are a passengerOnly money you can wave goodbye toMistaking a portfolio for a purpose
Advising and boardsBeing useful, keeping craft warmOwnership of outcomesMostly time and reputationLanyard theatre: relevance maintenance dressed as work
A serious pursuit outside businessMastery, humility, being a beginner safelyThe specific joy of customersA boat is never finished, ask anyonePretending it is enough when it is not, or that it is not enough when it is

The honest summary is this: the substitutes are real work and real joy for the right people, and methadone for the rest. The question underneath them all is what you actually miss. If you miss being clever about business, investing and advising will feed you. If what you miss is making promises to customers and keeping them with people you chose, nothing but building scratches that, and you might as well know it early, before your portfolio becomes a monument to avoidance.

Sam's Second Act

Now let me tell you the rest of the story from the terrace, because Sam has spent this whole book being the cautionary exhibit, and he has earned the ending.

After the recipe app died, Sam did the thing that looks, on the résumé of a future founder, like giving up: he took a job. Product roles at a food-delivery scale-up, then a supplier platform, ten years, all of it inside the world he had loved from the start, which was food. The app had only ever been his first, clumsiest way of touching it. And in those ten years, mostly in the back of professional kitchens at unsociable hours, he watched. He watched chefs count courgettes on paper at midnight. He watched walk-in fridges eat five percent of a restaurant's margin in quiet, unrecorded waste. He watched a head chef, a woman he admired, do stock counts on a Sunday because the software her owners bought was built by people who had clearly never touched a wet kitchen. The problem picked him, slowly, over a decade. At twenty-two, our idea had arrived in one espresso. This one arrived like a tide.

What he did next reads like a checklist of this book, which is unfair to Sam, who did it years before I wrote any of this down. He kept his job for six months while he interviewed forty kitchens, the discovery work of chapter four done properly at last. The first version of the product was a spreadsheet, an actual spreadsheet, that he charged for, because he wanted the information in the transaction, not the applause. His first customer was a brasserie in Leiden that paid him ninety euros a month and complained every week, which he treated as gold. There was no website for the first year. No press release ever, that I know of. When he brought in a cofounder at month eight, an engineer from the supplier platform, they spent a weekend doing the prenup conversation from chapter five, roles, equity, exits, the works, on paper, like two men who had each been in a crash and could compare scars without flinching. And on one page in his kitchen drawer, updated monthly, lived the plan, with its assumptions and its kill dates, the living document chapter seven begs for.

Story

Two years in, Sam's sync service failed at seven on a Saturday morning, which in his world is the worst possible hour, because breakfast service waits for no database. The head chef of his largest customer called him at 7:04 and swore at him for four minutes without repeating herself, an achievement, Sam noted, that required two languages. He apologised, woke his cofounder, had it fixed by 7:40, and sent the chef a bottle of something serious with a handwritten card.

Then he called me, and I braced for a shaken man. He was delighted. Audibly, indecently delighted. "Wouter," he said, "she swore at me for four minutes. Do you understand? People only swear like that about things they depend on." He let that sit for a second, and then he said the thing I have repeated to every founder who will hold still since: "Nobody ever swore at the recipe app. They just left."

Today the kitchen company is fourteen people and profitable, a phrase Sam pronounces the way other men say the names of their children. It is boring on purpose. The trade press will never write about it, if he can help it. He intends to be running it at sixty, and having watched him across both acts, I believe him. The friendship, for the record, is now structured: once a year, over one long dinner, we prosecute each other's plans, hostile witness rules, notes taken. It is the best board meeting either of us attends.

I once asked Sam what boring actually buys him, because "boring" was clearly a load-bearing word and I wanted to see the engineering. He counted it off on his fingers, and I wrote it down in the car afterwards. Boring means no competitor raises forty million to subsidise his customers into leaving him. Boring means he can charge a fair price without a land-grab discount, so the company was profitable in its second year and every strategic decision since has been made by well-slept people who cannot be forced into anything. Boring means the trade press ignores him, so his roadmap is set by chefs instead of by narrative. And boring means that when he makes a mistake, and he makes them, the mistake happens in private, at a size the company can digest. "The recipe app was exciting," he said, pulling on his coat. "Excitement is what it costs to not know what you are doing."

Here is Sam's two acts side by side, and I want you to notice something before you read it: almost every row is the same founder making the opposite choice. The lesson is what transfers best of all, if you let it. The playbook stays in the grave.

First time versus second time: the same founder, opposite choices
QuestionFirst time: the recipe appSecond time: the kitchen company
Where the idea came fromOne espresso and a shared delusion; we loved it before we tested itTen years of watching one problem refuse to go away; tested before loved
First money inSavings and a family loan, spent on a logo and a launch partyRevenue from month two; the first customer paid before the product deserved it
The planForty slides, never updated, defended like a guilty clientOne page in a kitchen drawer, updated monthly, with kill dates
The cofounder conversationNever had; we assumed friendship was a legal structureA full weekend, on paper, before any code: roles, equity, exits
SpeedSprint: eighteen months of heroics, then collapsePace: kept the day job six months, built for a decade, goes home for dinner
CustomersImagined in a spreadsheet, interviewed neverForty kitchens interviewed before building; the first one complained weekly, which was the product roadmap
What fear felt likeFear of missing the wave, so we skipped every checkFear of wasting a decade, so he ran every check
What ego neededA launch, a logo, a press mention, applauseNothing visible; no website for a year, and "boring" said with a smile
Definition of successVague billions and a keynoteA profitable company he would happily still be running at sixty

One warning about this table, because hindsight loves to frame Sam's second act as caution beating courage. Read it the other way. Starting the kitchen company took more courage than the recipe app ever did, because at thirty-four he knew exactly what failure costs, in years and money and marriages, and he signed up anyway, with his eyes open. The recipe app was fearless the way children are fearless, by not understanding the stove. The kitchen company is brave the way adults occasionally manage to be, which is: informed, and doing it anyway. That is the flavour of courage available to you on lap two, and it is the better vintage.

Deciding with Your Eyes Open

So. You have rested the rest, audited the luck, and looked the ego square in its handsome face. How do you actually decide whether to go again? Here are the tests I trust, in the order I would run them.

First, the pull test, which you already have from the rest section: is this a specific problem that will not leave you alone, or a general restlessness looking for a costume? Interrogate the idea the way Sam interrogates his: can you name the customer, the ache, the moment in their week when they would pay to make it stop? Chapter two taught a question worth re-asking here in its original form: what will people pay you to make go away? If your answer is a market, a trend, or a technology, that is a costume. If it is a person with a problem, on a day of the week, keep going.

Second, the pseudonym test, which is the cheapest ego detector I know. Imagine you had to build this company under a name nobody could connect to you. No announcement, no LinkedIn post, no "excited to share." Every customer won cold, every hire made on the merits of the actual job. Does the idea still glow? If the appeal dims when the audience is removed, you have your diagnosis, and it is section four of this chapter, and the treatment is more rest, not more company.

Third, the kitchen-table conversation, and I mean the one at home. The people who lived through your first company get votes this time, formal ones. Have the conversation before you buy the domain or instruct the notary, and bring real numbers: the years, the money at risk, the version of you that shows up during a bad quarter, because they have met that version and you owe them the courtesy of admitting he exists. I have watched second companies succeed commercially and fail at this table. That trade costs more than it pays, and the founders who made it will tell you so, quietly, at the dinners where everyone else talks about growth.

Fourth, the size permission, which is less a test than a release form. The second company is allowed to be smaller than the first. Read that again, because the whole weight of the phrase "serial entrepreneur" pushes against it. There is no law of sequels that demands escalation. A ten-person company that pays well, serves its customers, funds your life and lets you attend the school play might be the point. Some of the happiest second acts I know are deliberately, luxuriously small, run by founders who finally have nothing to prove and have discovered that nothing-to-prove is a superpower with compounding returns.

If the tests all pass, do one last piece of paperwork before you tell anyone: write the sequel's terms of engagement, one page, dated, signed by you. How many years you are giving it before you evaluate honestly. How much money, the number from the warning earlier, in writing. What you are explicitly not going to do this time, your three vetoes, taken straight from the luck audit and the refuse-to-repeat line on your folded paper. And what "enough" looks like, in revenue, in headcount, in what a Tuesday feels like, so the audience cannot redefine success upward while you are busy. This is chapter seven's living plan applied to your own life, and it takes an evening. The founders I know who wrote it treat it like a keel. The ones who did not tend to discover, three years in, that they are running the exact company they swore they would never build again, and cannot name the meeting where they decided to.

And fifth, the permission that this chapter has been quietly holding until now: you are allowed not to. Some people are one-great-company people, and they are not failed serial entrepreneurs any more than a person with one great marriage is a failed romantic. If the honest answer, after the rest and the audits and the tests, is that you would rather teach, or invest, or sail, or sit on two boards and grow impossible tomatoes, the road still loops for you. It just loops through different country, and it is still the long way, and it still counts.

Try this

Go and get the piece of paper. The one from the introduction, folded inside the back cover, where you wrote the phase your business was loudest in and the phase you were avoiding. If you skipped the exercise back then, this book forgives raiders, write both answers now as you remember that earlier self would have written them. Unfold it. Compare it with what actually happened. Be amused; past you was guessing, and so is present you, just with better instruments. Then turn the paper over and write three lines: "If I ever do it again, the one thing I refuse to repeat is..." with one honest sentence. "The phase I would genuinely enjoy entering again is..." and "The phase that tires me just to imagine is..." If the tired line was easier to write than the enjoy line, you have your answer about timing, and it is: not yet. Fold it up. Put it back inside the cover, for whichever you opens this book next.

A Closing Letter

Dear reader,

Sixteen phases ago I promised you the weather, and I have done my best to report it: what each stretch of this road feels like from inside, while it is raining, before anyone knows the ending. Before you go, three things, briefly, the way you would say them at the door with your coat already on.

First: the phases loop, and you will be a beginner again, repeatedly, forever. The founder of a second company is a beginner at being a second-time founder. The seller of a business is a beginner at being sold. There is no version of this road where you arrive at competence and stay there, and once you stop expecting one, the beginnings become the good part. You now know what almost nobody tells beginners: everyone is doing it sideways, in the rain, making it up. You will be making it up with better instruments, that is all, and that is a great deal.

Second: trust your eyes over this book. I said it in the introduction and it is truer now that you have read the whole map. Where these chapters contradict what you can see in your own business, on your own terrain, with your own customers, the terrain wins. A field guide that outranks the field is a scripture, and I have no interest in writing one of those. Argue with me at any dinner table in Europe. I will bring wine, and Henk's ghostly disapproval of us both.

Third, and this is the one I would fold into your pocket if I could: the road was the point all along. I have been to the exit. It is a Tuesday with a notary and better catering than usual, and then it is chapter fifteen, and then it is this chapter. What lasts is the road itself: the people who became themselves working next to you, the customers whose problem went away for good, the person you had to become to keep all those promises. If you build again, build for that. It is the only return that survives the wire transfer.

Thank you for walking the long way with me. Take care of your people. Tell the truth about the weather when it is your turn to write it down.

Your friend on the road,
Wouter

Epilogue: And Around Again

Story

When I finished the manuscript of this book, I printed it, put it in a bag, and drove to Henk's, to the same kitchen table where a nineteen-year-old once tried to impress him with a famous founder memoir. Henk is old now, slower on the stairs, coffee still black, still faintly cigar-scented, still, in all the years I have known him, never once seen smoking. I put the stack of paper on the table and said nothing, because with Henk you learn to submit evidence and wait.

He read the back page first, which is very Henk. Then he opened it somewhere in the middle, chapter six I think, and read for about ninety seconds, the same sentence he once gave the memoir. Then he closed it and pushed it back across the table.

"Better weather," he said.

We drank the coffee. Then, because he cannot help himself, he asked, "So what are you building now?" I said I was mostly resting, mostly writing, keeping things small on purpose, and he looked at me the way he looked at that memoir all those years ago, like a man being told the truth about decisions and lies about the weather. "Resting," he said. He turned his cup a quarter turn, his version of a long speech. "The road does not care what you call your walking. It goes around anyway."

He is right, of course. He is always right, it remains extremely annoying. Look at the map from the introduction once more, but from higher up this time, the way you can only see a road after you have walked it.

The introduction drew this road as a winding line with a small arrow at the end, doubling back. Sixteen chapters later you can see what the arrow was admitting all along: the line was a loop. The idea leads to the company, the company to the years, the years to the sale, the sale to the rest, the rest to the itch, and the itch, in most of the lives I have watched closely, leads back around to an idea, standing at the top of the map like it never left.

But here is the thing the map cannot show, and it is the last thing I have for you. The road is the same both times. You are not. The bends that terrified you are still bends, but you know them now, you know which ones tighten and which ones only look sharp. The weather is still the weather, but you have stopped expecting it to be fair. And somewhere out on the second lap, or the first, you will pass someone younger, walking the other way around some bend you know by heart, defending their forty slides to anyone who will listen. Buy them a coffee. Tell them the truth about the weather. It is the only toll this road charges.

So: around again, then. The long way. As if there were any other.

The Short Version

  • You will probably do it again. Plan for that on purpose instead of letting it ambush you in year two of your retirement.
  • Judgment, cash instinct, craft, calibrated fear and self-knowledge transfer. Market knowledge, the old playbook, the old team and the old luck do not.
  • Audit your luck before you trust your experience. At least three of your first company's ten best breaks were weather. Find them.
  • The deadliest sequel is the one built to prove something about the original. Companies make terrible lawyers.
  • Do not fund yourself so comfortably that the company never feels gravity. Written runway, kill dates, one person allowed to read them back to you.
  • Rest is a phase with its own work. Months one to three are decompression, month four's brilliant idea is usually boredom in a costume. Boredom pushes, curiosity pulls. Wait for the pull.
  • Angel investing is a passenger seat. Take it only if you honestly enjoy companies you cannot steer.
  • The second company is allowed to be smaller than the first. Nothing-to-prove is a superpower.
  • Not going again is also a valid ending. One great company is a whole career.
  • Same road, new walker. That is the entire trade, and it is a good one.
